1.label: Tier 1
1.summary: Full restoration: Greek names preserve both stress and length; other traditions keep at least one distinctive feature ASCII erases.
rules: Greek: the original contains both stress (acute/circumflex) and at least one long vowel.
All other traditions: the Unicode form preserves ≥1 distinctive feature vs ASCII (any diacritic or a distinctive letter).
Only one historically dominant spelling exists (unlike Dual-Tier).

2.label: Tier 2
2.summary: Greek: one feature preserved (stress or length) or neither. Other traditions: no distinctive feature for ASCII to lose.
rules: Greek original contains only one feature (stress OR long vowel) or neither.
Non-Greek: the restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics.
Still historically defensible and registrable as an IDN.

subtypes.accent-preserving: Keeps the stress mark but not vowel length.
subtypes.macron-preserving: Keeps vowel length but not stress.
subtypes.plain: Neither stress nor length is preserved; still a culturally meaningful name.

dual.label: Dual-Tier
dual.summary: Both stress and length are preserved, and multiple historically valid Unicode spellings exist.
rules: Greek original contains both stress (acute/circumflex) and at least one long vowel.
Multiple historically valid Unicode spellings are attested.
Each variant corresponds to a real, attested alternate restoration.
Both spellings are live as owned domain temples.

variants.note: Stacked acute+macron on omicron: philologically ideal, untypeable on phones
LSJ convention: length only, no stress mark

etymology.derivation: Uncertain; possibly from ἀπόλλυμι "to destroy", or pre-Greek. Associated with Lycian god Apaliunas.

steps: The Greek form Ἀπόλλων is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Apóllōn encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-POL-lone' — stress the second syllable and hold the final 'o' roughly twice as long as English allows.
pronunciation.note: Apóllōn is dual-tier because the Greek Ἀπόλλων carries both stress (acute on the second syllable) and length (omega in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Apóllōn with acute stress and Apollōn with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both are philologically legitimate.

domains.title: The Far-Shooter
domains.subtitle: Light, Music, Prophecy, and Healing
domains.lead: Apóllōn is the most Greek of the gods: not a chthonic power or a primal element, but the embodiment of measured excellence. He is the archer whose arrows strike from unseen distance, the musician whose lyre imposes order on chaos, the prophet who speaks only what Zeus permits, and the healer whose touch can lift plague as surely as his arrows bring it.

cards.name: Solar Radiance
cards.desc: The eye that sees all and the fire that nourishes; Helios is the original solar charioteer, and it is Apóllōn who is increasingly solarized from the 5th century BCE onward.

cards.name: Music and Harmony
cards.desc: His lyre, won from Hermês, orders emotion itself; music, mathematics, and cosmic proportion fall under his patronage.

cards.name: Prophetic Sight
cards.desc: At Delphoí, through the Pythia, he speaks in enigmatic verse; prophecy is not fortune-telling but the disciplined interpretation of divine will.

cards.name: Healer and Purifier
cards.desc: The same bow that sends plague can avert it; his epithets Alexikakos and Paiôn mark him as protector from evil and god of healing.

symbols.name: Laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: Victory, poetic achievement, and the nymph Daphnê transformed to escape him

symbols.name: Lyre
symbols.meaning: Cosmic harmony and the arts; the instrument he received from Hermês

symbols.name: Bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: Far-reaching power: disease, death, and divine justice

symbols.name: Tripod
symbols.meaning: The Delphic seat of prophecy

symbols.name: Raven or swan
symbols.meaning: Solar bird and messenger; the swan circled Delos at his birth

symbols.name: Wolf
symbols.meaning: His archaic epithet Lykeios connects him with wolves and perhaps with light

mythology.lead: Apóllōn's myths are unusually coherent because they consistently dramatize the same theme: the distance between divine perfection and mortal limitation. He is never ridiculous, but he is often terrifying.

myths.title: Born on the Wandering Island
myths.text: Hêra, in jealousy, cursed Lētô so that no land fixed to the earth could give her shelter. All islands refused her — until Dêlos, a floating rock, offered itself. There Lētô clung to a palm tree and bore Apóllōn and his twin sister Artemis. Swans circled the island seven times, and light flooded the Aegean. Dêlos became fixed forever — the weight of divinity anchors what chaos cannot hold.

myths.title: The Slayer of Pythô
myths.text: Apóllōn seized Delphoí by killing the she-dragon Pythôn who guarded the site. From her corpse the oracle took its name: Pythia. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo describes his journey from Delos to Delphi as a triumphal procession; every place he passes becomes Greek through recognition of his power.

lore.culturalLegacy: Apóllōn never stopped shaping Western culture. The Pythian Games at Delphoí were one of the four great Panhellenic festivals; their musical and athletic contests set the model for later competitions. The Delphic maxims — 'Know thyself,' 'Nothing in excess' — were attributed to him. In art, the 'Apollo Belvedere' became the canonical image of male beauty for centuries. The name survives in NASA's Apollo program, in countless operas and symphonies, and in the very idea of the 'Apollonian' as orderly, luminous, rational — set against the 'Dionysian' by Nietzsche. To restore Apóllōn with its full Greek accents is to restore the original sound of this civilizing force.
lore.archaeology: Delphi: temple of Apollo, theatre, stadium, and the Omphalos; the Pythian Games. Delos: sanctuary of Apollo and Artemis, birthplace cult.
lore.syncretism: Apóllōn was one of the most widely exported Greek gods. In Egypt he was identified with Hôros, in Italy with Apollo himself (the Romans adopted him directly without renaming), and in Anatolia with local solar deities. The emperor Augustus made Apóllōn a patron of the Roman state, dedicating a magnificent temple on the Palatine. In Neoplatonism he became the principle of intellect and light; in Renaissance art he embodied the ideal male form. His most durable legacy is linguistic: 'Apollo' still names the brightest, most ordered aspect of civilization, from the space program to the god of poetry.

variants.note: Macron on alpha: length-preserved variant without acute

etymology.derivation: From ἀ- (privative) + εἶδον "to see", lit. "the unseen one".

steps: The Greek form Ἅιδης is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Hádēs encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAH-dace' — the first syllable is pitched high and sharp; the second is long and level, like the floor of the underworld.
pronunciation.note: Hádēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἅιδης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name literally means 'the Unseen,' and the acute on the first syllable gives it the force of a warning.

domains.title: The Unseen King
domains.subtitle: The Dead, Wealth, and the Underworld
domains.lead: Hádēs is not evil; he is the necessary guardian of the dead. His realm is not hell but the place beneath the earth where all souls go — good and bad alike. He is also Plouton, the wealthy one, because the earth holds grain, metals, and the buried dead.

cards.name: The Underworld
cards.desc: Not a place of torment but the common destination of all mortals, ruled with strict impartiality.

cards.name: Wealth of the Earth
cards.desc: As Plouton he owns gold, silver, and the fertility that rises from below.

cards.name: The House of Hádēs
cards.desc: A place of shadow, gates, and the three-headed dog Kerberos who allows entry but not exit.

cards.name: Immovable Justice
cards.desc: Unlike other gods, Hádēs almost never intervenes in human affairs; his realm is governed by law.

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: Wealth and the fertility of the earth

symbols.name: Bident or sceptre
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over the dead

symbols.name: Cerberus
symbols.meaning: The boundary between life and death

symbols.name: Cypress
symbols.meaning: The mourning tree, sacred to the underworld

symbols.name: Narcissus
symbols.meaning: The flower that lured Persephonē

symbols.name: Key
symbols.meaning: He holds the keys to the underworld gates

mythology.lead: Hádēs appears rarely in Greek myth because his realm is separate from the world of the living. His most important myth is the abduction of Persephonē, which explains the seasons and establishes his connection to Demeter.

myths.title: The Rape of Persephonē
myths.text: With Zeús's permission, Hádēs burst from the earth in a golden chariot and seized Persephonē while she gathered flowers in a meadow. Demeter's grief caused famine and winter until Zeús negotiated a compromise: Persephonē spends part of the year above with her mother and part below with her husband. This is the Greek explanation for the seasons — life and death take turns because even gods must share.

myths.title: The Judges of the Dead
myths.text: In the underworld, the dead are judged by Minos, Aiakos, and Rhadamanthys — three former mortals made just. The wicked go to Tartaros, the ordinary dead to the fields of Asphodel, and the heroic few to Elysium. Hádēs presides over this system without passion; his justice is administrative, not punitive.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hádēs remains the archetype of the underworld ruler in Western imagination. Unlike the Christian devil, he is neither tempter nor torturer; he is the strict, fair administrator of death. The Eleusinian Mysteries, which honored Demeter and Persephonē, were among the most important religious institutions of the ancient Mediterranean and influenced later ideas of salvation. In modern fantasy, Hades appears in countless adaptations, usually darker than his Greek original. Restoring Hádēs restores the name of the god who receives everyone in the end.
lore.archaeology: Eleusis preserves the Telesterion and the Ploutonion, the cave from which Hades was said to have emerged to seize Persephone. The Nekromanteion at Ephyra on the Acheron was an oracle of the dead visited by Odysseus in the Nekyia. In Asia Minor, the Ploutonion at Hierapolis (Pamukkale) emitted suffocating gases and was enclosed as a sanctuary of Pluto. Votive reliefs from Locri Epizephyrii and Athens show the god with Cerberus and Persephone.
lore.syncretism: The Romans called him Pluto or Dis Pater, emphasizing his wealth rather than his dread. In mystery cults — especially the Eleusinian Mysteries — he and Persephonē were central figures who promised initiates a better afterlife. Christian writers later used Hades as a name for the underworld itself and, in the New Testament, as a temporary abode of the dead. The name passed into English as the word for the realm of the dead, though the Greek god is morally neutral.

entries.meaning: She who works from afar (from ἑκάς)

variants.note: LSJ convention: length only, no acute

etymology.derivation: Possibly from ἑκάτη "far-shooting", or pre-Greek. Associated with magic and crossroads.

steps: The Greek form Ἑκάτη is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Hekátē encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'he-KAH-tay' — the second syllable rises in pitch, and the final 'ay' is held long like the 'a' in 'say' stretched out.
pronunciation.note: Hekátē is dual-tier because the Greek Ἑκάτη carries both stress (acute on alpha) and length (eta in the final syllable), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Hekátē with acute stress and Hekatē with macron-only length. The form is etymologically debated, but both Unicode forms are orthographically legitimate.

domains.title: The Torch-Bearer at the Crossroads
domains.subtitle: Magic, Crossroads, Ghosts, and the Moon
domains.lead: Hekátē is the most liminal of the Greek gods. She stands at crossroads, doorways, and the boundary between living and dead. Unlike the Olympians who shine in public cult, she belongs to night, household ritual, and secret knowledge.

cards.name: The Three Ways
cards.desc: Crossroads (trioditis) are her sacred places; offerings were left at three-way intersections.

cards.name: Torch and Flame
cards.desc: She carries torches to guide Persephonē from the underworld and to light nocturnal rites.

cards.name: Ghosts and the Dead
cards.desc: She rules phantoms and sends nightmares; her bark brings the dead.

cards.name: Magic and Witchcraft
cards.desc: Patron of pharmakeia and binding spells; Medea and Circe invoke her power.

symbols.name: Twin torches
symbols.meaning: Light in darkness and the guide between worlds

symbols.name: Key
symbols.meaning: She holds the keys to the underworld and to locked mysteries

symbols.name: Dagger
symbols.meaning: Used in magical rites and as protector of doorways

symbols.name: Black dog
symbols.meaning: The Hecatean hound, associated with her nocturnal processions

symbols.name: Pole-star
symbols.meaning: Her celestial guide for sailors and night-travelers

symbols.name: Mandrake and aconite
symbols.meaning: Poisonous plants of witchcraft under her patronage

mythology.lead: Hekátē's mythology is small in scale but vast in implication. She is a Titan who keeps her power after the fall of the Titans, and she becomes Persephonē's companion in the underworld.

myths.title: Daughter of Persês
myths.text: Hesiod (Theogony 409–452) makes Hekátē the daughter of the Titan Persês and the nymph Asteria. Zeús honors her above all other Titans, granting her a share of earth, sea, and sky. This triple portion makes her uniquely able to move between realms — a goddess of boundaries because she owns all boundaries.

myths.title: Torch-Bearer in the Dark
myths.text: When Hádês seized Persephonē, Hekátē heard her cries. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, she meets the grieving Dēmētēr with torches and guides her to Hēlios, who names the abductor. Later, she becomes Persephonē's companion in the underworld — a mediator between the realms.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hekátė's legacy is the persistence of magic itself. Shakespeare's witches in Macbeth invoke her by name; she appears in Goethe's Faust, in the poetry of Baudelaire, and in countless works of fantasy. The word 'hecate' became an adjective for witchcraft. Her triple form — three faces looking down three roads — is one of the most enduring images of the uncanny. Restoring Hekátē in Unicode honors not only a Greek goddess but the long, often persecuted tradition of liminal knowledge that she represents.
lore.archaeology: The great Carian sanctuary of Hekate at Lagina (Stratonicea) produced a sculptured frieze depicting her myth and annual festival (the temple itself is Corinthian); excavations revealed the propylon and sacred way. In Athens and Selinous, inscribed lead curse tablets (defixiones) invoke Hekate for binding enemies. Marble reliefs from the Athenian Agora and Piraeus show the goddess as three-bodied Hekate Epipyrgidia or carrying torches, keys, and daggers beside crossroad pillars.
lore.syncretism: Hekátē absorbed many minor deities of thresholds, ghosts, and night. In Roman religion she was identified with Trivia, the goddess of crossroads, and with the lunar Diana and underworld Proserpina in the famous 'triple Hecate' of later art. In Egypt she was associated with Isis and Nephthys as a goddess of magic. The Hellenistic and Roman world saw her cult spread through household rituals and curse tablets; her name appears in hundreds of magical papyri. In modern Neopaganism she is perhaps the most widely worshipped Greek goddess, embodying feminine magical autonomy.

variants.note: LSJ convention: length only, no acute

etymology.derivation: From νίκη "victory", cognate with Latin vincere, English win.

steps: The Greek form Νίκη is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Níkē encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'NEE-kay' — the first syllable rises in pitch like a shout; the second is long and clear.
pronunciation.note: Níkē is dual-tier because the Greek Νίκη carries both stress (acute on the short ι) and length (long η), and because two historically defensible restorations exist: Níkē with acute stress and Nikē with macron-only length. Both forms are owned and both preserve the goddess's essential meaning: Victory itself.

domains.title: Victory
domains.subtitle: Triumph in War, Athletics, and Contests
domains.lead: Níkē is not merely a personification; she is the divine power of winning. She stands beside Athena, Zeús, and Athletes, crowning the victor with laurel or fillet. In a culture that made competition the organizing principle of politics, athletics, and warfare, Níkē was everywhere.

cards.name: Military Victory
cards.desc: She descends with Zeús to turn the tide of battle; she crowns the conqueror.

cards.name: Athletic Triumph
cards.desc: Every Panhellenic games ended with a victor crowned in her name; she is the glory of competition.

cards.name: Winged Messenger
cards.desc: She is often winged, swift as rumor, bringing news of victory across land and sea.

cards.name: Divine Attendant
cards.desc: She stands with Athena Nike on the Athenian Acropolis, the most famous victory cult in Greece.

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: Speed and the swift arrival of victory

symbols.name: Laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: The crown of the victor

symbols.name: Palm branch
symbols.meaning: Peace and triumph

symbols.name: Filleted trophy
symbols.meaning: The captured arms or athletic prize

symbols.name: Flying drapery
symbols.meaning: Momentum and the moment of triumph

symbols.name: Sandals of swiftness
symbols.meaning: The ability to outrun defeat

mythology.lead: Níkē has few independent myths because she is an attribute of victory rather than a narrative protagonist. But her presence is decisive: she appears at the moment when struggle becomes triumph.

myths.title: Níkē at Zeus's Side
myths.text: In the Theogony (384–385), Styx brings her children Zelos (Rivalry), Nike (Victory), Kratos (Power), and Bia (Force) to Zeús's side at the beginning of the Titanomachy. Níkē is therefore one of the first divine powers to align with the new Olympian order. Her presence guarantees that the war against the Titans will end in triumph.

myths.title: Athena Nike
myths.text: On the Athenian Acropolis, Athena was worshipped as Athena Nike, 'Athena Victory.' A small temple stood at the edge of the citadel, its frieze depicting the victory over the Persians. The cult fused Athens's patron goddess with the abstract power of winning, making military success a religious obligation. The temple's remains still stand, one of the most elegant buildings in Greece.

lore.culturalLegacy: Níkē is perhaps the most widely recognized Greek goddess in the modern world. Her winged image has inspired countless marks of excellence, from athletic victory to artistic achievement. But her ancient importance was far deeper: she embodied the Greek belief that excellence deserves public recognition, that competition produces virtue, and that victory is a divine gift rather than a merely human achievement. The Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis is a monument to this ideal. Every medal, trophy, and laurel wreath descends from her cult. Restoring Níkē restores the name of the goddess who crowns the winner.
lore.archaeology: Athens: Temple of Athena Nike (ca. 427–424 BCE) on the Acropolis; Nike parapet frieze. Olympia: Nike of Paionios (ca. 421 BCE).
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Níkē with Victoria, whose name gives us 'victory' in English. Victoria was a major state cult, and generals built temples to her after triumphs. The winged figure of Victory persisted into Christian art, where she influenced depictions of angels and, in the famous Louvre statue, became a secular emblem of France. The winged figure of Victory became a secular emblem of human achievement and later inspired countless modern marks of excellence. The idea that victory can be personified and worshipped stretches from ancient Greece into the present day.

etymology.derivation: PIE *dyēws > Greek Ζεύς (Doric) > Attic Zeus. The sky god par excellence.

cognates.note: Germanic sky god; survives as English Tuesday

steps: The Greek form Ζεύς is attested from Mycenaean di-we / Diwos and Homeric Greek.
The initial Ζ- in Attic represents the voiced affricate [zd], preserving the PIE cluster *dy- from *dyēws 'sky, god of the sky'.
The diphthong ευ is long for accentual purposes and carries the acute accent, producing the single pitch peak Zeús.
The final -ς is the nominative singular ending of the archaic stem *dyēu-s.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'ZDEWS' — one syllable, beginning with a buzzing 'zd' and ending in a sharp 's', like the sound of distant thunder compressed into a name.
pronunciation.note: Zeús is Tier 1 because the Greek Ζεύς contains both stress (acute on the diphthong ευ) and length (the diphthong itself counts as long for accentual purposes). The acute falls on the only syllable, making the name a single pitched peak — the sonic image of a thunderbolt.

domains.title: The Sky Father
domains.subtitle: Kingship, Thunder, Oath, and Order
domains.lead: Zeús is not merely the king of the gods; he is the principle of cosmic and social order. His domain is the sky, his weapon the thunderbolt, his guarantee the oath. Every legitimate authority on earth — kingship, law, hospitality — traces its sanction to him.

cards.name: Celestial King
cards.desc: Ruler of Olympus and arbiter of divine disputes; his will is fate's executive.

cards.name: Thunderbolt
cards.desc: The weapon forged by the Cyclopes; it strikes oath-breakers, hubristic mortals, and Titans alike.

cards.name: Divine Justice
cards.desc: Protector of suppliants, guests, and kings; Themis and Díkē attend him.

cards.name: Fate and Necessity
cards.desc: Even Zeús cannot fully reverse Moira, but he directs its fulfillment through gods and oracles.

symbols.name: Thunderbolt
symbols.meaning: Sovereign power and the sudden manifestation of divine will

symbols.name: Eagle
symbols.meaning: The bird of Zeús, seen as his messenger and embodiment

symbols.name: Oak
symbols.meaning: Sacred tree at Dodona, where his oracle spoke through the leaves

symbols.name: Sceptre
symbols.meaning: Kingship and legitimate rule

symbols.name: Aegis
symbols.meaning: The goat-skin shield or garment that inspires terror; often shared with Athena

mythology.lead: The mythology of Zeús is dominated by two great struggles: his overthrow of the Titans and his defense of cosmic order against every subsequent threat. He is the last son of Kronos, the only one not swallowed at birth.

myths.title: Hidden in a Cretan Cave
myths.text: Rheia, weary of seeing her children devoured by Kronos, hid the infant Zeús in a cave on Crete — identified by different traditions as Mount Ida or Mount Dikte — and gave Kronos a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes. The Kouretes drowned the baby's cries with their clashing weapons. This substitution of stone for god is the primal image of how order survives by cunning.

myths.title: The War Against the Titans
myths.text: When Zeús grew to strength, he freed his siblings from Kronos's belly and led them in a ten-year war against the Titans. The Cyclopes gave him thunder, the Hundred-Handers turned the tide, and the Titans were cast into Tartaros. Zeús then divided the cosmos with his brothers by lot: sky to Zeús, sea to Poseidôn, underworld to Hádês.

lore.culturalLegacy: Zeús is the archetype of the father-god in Western imagination. The Olympian council, the thunderbolt-bearing king, and the mountain-top temple all derive from him. The Olympic Games were held in his honor at Olympia from 776 BCE onward; his colossal chryselephantine statue by Phidias was one of the Seven Wonders. In law and ethics, his protection of strangers and suppliants underpinned Greek ideas of human solidarity. Modern uses range from planetary names to operatic thunder effects to the phrase 'by Jove.' Restoring Zeús with its acute accent restores the name's original pitch and dignity.
lore.archaeology: Olympia: Temple of Zeus (ca. 470–456 BCE), chryselephantine statue by Phidias, one of the Seven Wonders; Olympic Games from 776 BCE. Dodona: oracle of Zeus in the oak grove.
lore.syncretism: Roman religion identified Zeús directly with Iuppiter, importing his cult wholesale under the name Iuppiter Optimus Maximus. The equation was so natural that Greek and Roman worshippers often treated them as one god with two names. In later antiquity Zeús-Iuppiter was syncretized with Semitic Baal and Egyptian Amun as a supreme sky deity; the Hellenistic ruler cult made him the divine father of kings. Jupiter's planet and Tuesday (*Tīwaz's day) preserve his Germanic cognate. The very word 'deus' in Latin and 'divine' in English descend from the same root.

variants.note: LSJ convention: length only, no acute

etymology.derivation: From Ἄρης, possibly from ἀρά "curse, prayer". Cognate with Avestan aēšma "demon of wrath".

steps: The Greek form Ἄρης is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Árēs encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-rays' — the first syllable is sharp and pitched high, like a command to charge.
pronunciation.note: Árēs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἄρης contains both stress (acute on the first alpha) and length (long η). The name sounds like a wound being named: short, sharp, and final.

domains.title: The Bane of Men
domains.subtitle: War, Battle Fury, and Courage
domains.lead: Árēs is the god of war in its rawest form: battle fury, bloodlust, and the chaos of combat. The Greeks honored him but did not love him; he is necessary, brutal, and often defeated. Athena strategy, Hêphaistos craft, and Apóllōn archery all outshine his sheer violence.

cards.name: Battle Fury
cards.desc: The bloodlust that makes warriors forget fear and reason alike.

cards.name: Courage and Terror
cards.desc: He fills both sides with courage; to fight is to breathe his presence.

cards.name: Defeat and Wounding
cards.desc: Unlike Athena, Árēs is often wounded and driven from the field — war is not always victorious.

cards.name: The Lover of Aphrodítē
cards.desc: His affair with Aphrodítē makes war the counterpart of desire; their union produces Harmonia.

symbols.name: Spear
symbols.meaning: The primary weapon of close combat

symbols.name: Helmet
symbols.meaning: Warrior identity and the anonymity of battle

symbols.name: Shield
symbols.meaning: Defense and the wall of battle

symbols.name: Vulture
symbols.meaning: The bird that feeds on the slain

symbols.name: Burning torch
symbols.meaning: The fire of war and destruction

symbols.name: Dog
symbols.meaning: The animal of war, scavenger of corpses

mythology.lead: Árēs is the only major Olympian whom other gods routinely humiliate. His myths emphasize that war without wisdom is self-defeating.

myths.title: Struck by Diomedes
myths.text: In Iliad 5 (855–863), the Greek hero Diomedes, aided by Athena, wounds Árēs, Athena guiding his spear. The god roars like ten thousand warriors and flees to Olympus to complain. Zeús dismisses him as the most hated of the gods. The scene is comic but serious: raw courage cannot stand against disciplined strategy.

myths.title: Caught with Aphrodítē
myths.text: Hêphaistos, discovering his wife Aphrodítē's affair with Árēs, forged an unbreakable net and trapped the lovers in bed. The other gods gathered to laugh. The myth turns the terrifying war god into a ridiculous adulterer — a reminder that passion and violence, when exposed, lose their dignity.

lore.culturalLegacy: Árēs is the god we prefer not to invoke. Modern culture usually portrays him as a villain or a brute, while Athena gets the credit for strategic warfare. Yet his honesty is valuable: he represents war as it actually is — chaotic, bloody, and often stupid. The Spartans, who worshipped him more than other Greeks, understood that courage is a virtue even when wisdom is absent. In an age of permanent conflict, Árēs reminds us that not all wars are just, and that the god of battle is not the god of victory.
lore.archaeology: The temple of Ares in the Athenian Agora, excavated by the American School, is a Roman-period reassembly of a Classical temple probably moved from Acharnae. Pausanias records sanctuaries of Ares at Geronthrae in Laconia and at Thebes. Thrace yielded weapons and horse-gear dedications to a martial deity identified with Ares. Roman copies such as the Ares Borghese (Louvre) preserve his bearded, helmeted image.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Árēs with Mars, but the equation was imperfect. Mars was an agricultural as well as military god, far more central to Roman state religion than Árēs ever was to Greek civic life. The Roman March (Martius) and Tuesday in Romance languages preserve his name. In later European art, Mars became one of the seven planets and a standard allegory of war. The contrast between Greek contempt for Árēs and Roman reverence for Mars reveals how differently the two cultures understood organized violence.

etymology.derivation: From ἀφρός "foam", born from sea-foam (Hesiod). Possibly Semitic loan via Cyprus.

pronunciation.note: Aphrodítē is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀφροδίτη contains both stress (acute on the short iota) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name's foam etymology makes the long final vowel sound like a wave receding.

domains.title: She Who Was Born of Foam
domains.subtitle: Love, Beauty, Desire, and Fertility
domains.lead: Aphrodítē is the goddess of desire in all its forms: sexual love, beauty, fertility, and the longing that binds mortals and gods. She is not a youthful virgin but a sovereign power who can make Zeús himself fall in love against his will.

cards.name: Sexual Desire
cards.desc: The force that overwhelms reason and unites bodies, whether in marriage or adultery.

cards.name: Beauty
cards.desc: The visible form of desire; her presence makes the ordinary radiant.

cards.name: Fertility and Generation
cards.desc: She guarantees the continuity of life through sexual union and the growth of crops.

cards.name: Divine Power
cards.desc: Even gods and heroes submit to her; no one is immune to desire.

symbols.name: Dove
symbols.meaning: The bird of love and the vehicle of her chariot

symbols.name: Rose
symbols.meaning: Beauty, secrecy, and the blood of Adonis

symbols.name: Scallop shell
symbols.meaning: The sea-foam from which she was born

symbols.name: Mirror
symbols.meaning: Self-knowledge and the power of appearance

symbols.name: Girdle
symbols.meaning: Her magical zone that inspires irresistible desire

symbols.name: Myrtle
symbols.meaning: The plant sacred to her, symbol of love and immortality

mythology.lead: Aphrodítē's myths explore the power and danger of desire. She can raise a mortal to divine love or destroy a city for an insult.

myths.title: Born from the Sea
myths.text: When Kronos castrated Ouranos and threw his genitals into the sea, white foam gathered around them. From this foam Aphrodítē arose, first at Cythera and then at Cyprus. The Theogony calls her 'foam-born' and 'Cypris,' and her birth unites violence and beauty in a single image: love emerges from wounded power.

myths.title: The Apple of Discord
myths.text: Eris threw a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest' among the goddesses. Paris awarded it to Aphrodítē after she promised him Helen, the most beautiful mortal woman. That promise launched the Trojan War. The myth makes desire the engine of history: beauty, when contested, becomes catastrophe.

lore.culturalLegacy: Aphrodítē shaped Greek culture more deeply than any martial god. Marriage, prostitution, homosexual love, and civic festivals all fell under her patronage. The Aphrodisia was celebrated across the Greek world; her temples at Corinth and Cyprus were famous. In philosophy and poetry she became the symbol of erôs, the force that draws all things toward beauty and unity. The modern cosmetics and fashion industries are secular continuations of her cult. Restoring Aphrodítē with its full Greek accents restores the original sound of the goddess who rules desire itself.
lore.archaeology: Sanctuary of Aphrodite at Palaepaphos (Kouklia, Cyprus): a 12th-century BCE shrine with later ashlar temple, altar courts, and the famous Cypriot syllabary dedication 'Aphrodite's sanctuary.' At Cythera, the sanctuary of Aphrodite Ourania overlooked the sea from the sixth century BCE. Corinth's temple of Aphrodite on Acrocorinth is attested by Pausanias and excavation. The Knidia of Praxiteles (Roman copies, e.g., Vatican Museums) was housed in a circular tholos at Cnidus.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Aphrodítē with Venus, originally a goddess of gardens and spring whose cult became one of the most powerful in Rome. Julius Caesar claimed descent from Venus through Aeneas, making her the divine ancestress of the Roman people. In the Renaissance she became the supreme subject of painting — Botticelli's 'Birth of Venus' is perhaps the most famous image of a pagan goddess in Western art. The planet Venus and the concept of 'venereal' preserve her name. Modern culture still uses her as the archetype of beauty and desire.

pronunciation.note: Athénā is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀθηνᾶ contains both stress (acute on the long η) and length (η plus long alpha with iota subscript). domains.title: The Grey-Eyed Strategist
domains.subtitle: Wisdom, Warcraft, Crafts, and Civilization
domains.lead: Athénā is unique among the Olympians: a warrior who fights only for just causes, a virgin goddess who needs no consort to validate her power, and the patron of the practical arts that make city life possible. She is intelligence made divine.

cards.name: Strategic Warfare
cards.desc: She favors counsel, discipline, and defensive battle over the berserk fury of Árēs; heroes like Odysseus and Diomedes fight under her sign.

cards.name: Wisdom and Counsel
cards.desc: The mind that sees all sides; her advice is practical, ethical, and far-sighted.

cards.name: Weaving and Crafts
cards.desc: Patron of weaving, pottery, carpentry, and olive cultivation — the technologies that sustain the polis.

cards.name: Guardian of Cities
cards.desc: Polias and Poliouchos: the goddess who protects the citadel and whose olive tree marks the land.

symbols.name: Owl
symbols.meaning: Wisdom, night-vision, and the bird sacred to Athens

symbols.name: Olive tree
symbols.meaning: Her gift to Athens, defeat of Poseidôn in the contest for the city

symbols.name: Aegis
symbols.meaning: The goat-skin fringed with serpents; worn by Zeús and Athena, it inspires terror

symbols.name: Helmet and spear
symbols.meaning: Warrior identity, but always disciplined and defensive

symbols.name: Gorgoneion
symbols.meaning: The severed head of Medousa on her breastplate, turning enemies to stone

symbols.name: Spindle and loom
symbols.meaning: Weaving as the emblem of ordered, intelligent labor

mythology.lead: Athénā's myths center on intelligence overcoming force. She is born from Zeús's head, defeats Poseidôn by gift rather than combat, and guides the heroes who win by cunning.

myths.title: Born from the Head of Zeús
myths.text: Zeús swallowed his pregnant first wife Mêtis, fearing a son who would overthrow him. Later, Hephaistos split Zeús's skull with an axe, and Athénā sprang forth fully armed with a shout that shook Olympus. She is therefore the only Olympian whose parent is purely paternal — intelligence born directly from sovereignty.

myths.title: Athena and Poseidôn for Athens
myths.text: The two gods competed to become patron of Athens. Poseidôn struck the Acropolis with his trident and produced a salt spring; Athénā planted the first olive tree. The judges — Cecrops and the Athenian people — chose the olive, because it gives food, oil, and wood. Poseidôn flooded the land in anger, but Athénā's city endured. The myth makes civilization superior to maritime power.

lore.culturalLegacy: Athénā is the divine patron of everything the Greeks most valued in civic life: wisdom, craft, disciplined courage, and strategic thought. The Athenian democracy claimed her protection; the Panathenaea was the city's greatest festival. In philosophy she became the emblem of reason; in art the model of dignified female power. Her owl, her olive, and her helmet are still instantly recognizable symbols of classical civilization. Restoring Athénā preserves the name under which the world's first democracy invoked its guiding intelligence.
lore.archaeology: The Athenian Acropolis preserves the Parthenon (447–432 BCE), Erechtheion, and Temple of Athena Nike, whose sculptural program celebrated Athena Polias, Parthenos, and Nikephoros. The colossal gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos by Pheidias stood inside the Parthenon; fragments of its base survive. The Panathenaic frieze and pedimental sculptures show the goddess in birth and triumph. Outside Athens, the temple of Athena Alea at Tegea and the sanctuary at Lindos on Rhodes attest her wide civic cult.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Athénā with Minerva, a goddess already associated with crafts and strategy, so the equation was unusually smooth. In Egypt she was equated with Neith, the warrior-weaver goddess of Sais, and Hellenistic Jews identified her with Sophia, divine Wisdom. During the Renaissance she became the emblem of rational virtue; in modern Athens she remains the namesake and symbol of the city, her helmeted head on coins and official seals. The Parthenon, her temple, is the canonical image of Classical Greece.

etymology.derivation: Δᾶ (Doric for γῆ "earth") + μήτηρ "mother". The earth goddess.

steps: The Greek form Δημήτηρ is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.

pronunciation.approximation: 'deh-MEH-ter' — stress the middle syllable; the final syllable is light and quick.
pronunciation.note: Dēmētēr is Tier 1 because the Greek Δημήτηρ contains both stress (acute on the short ε) and length (long η in the first syllable). The name is transparently a compound: *dʰeh₁- 'grain' + *māter- 'mother.' Her Roman equivalent Ceres gives us 'cereal.'

domains.title: The Grain Mother
domains.subtitle: Agriculture, Fertility, Sacred Law, and the Eleusinian Mysteries
domains.lead: Dēmētēr is the foundation of Greek civilization. Without her, no bread, no wine, no city. She is the goddess of the grain that must die and rise again, and her mysteries at Eleusis promised initiates a better fate after death. Where Athena protects the city wall, Dēmētēr protects the field behind it.

cards.name: Grain and Agriculture
cards.desc: Wheat, barley, and the agricultural cycle; the deity who turns seed into harvest through death and rebirth.

cards.name: Fertility of Earth and Woman
cards.desc: Patron of marriage, childbirth, and the fertility of the land; her power moves through both soil and womb.

cards.name: Sacred Law
cards.desc: Thesmophoros: she establishes the laws and rituals that bind society, especially those governing women.

cards.name: The Eleusinian Mysteries
cards.desc: The most famous mystery cult of the ancient world, promising initiates blessedness after death.

symbols.name: Wheat sheaf
symbols.meaning: The grain that is her body and gift

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: Her search for Persephonē through the darkness

symbols.name: Poppy
symbols.meaning: Sleep, death, and the seed that returns

symbols.name: Pig
symbols.meaning: Sacrificial animal at the Thesmophoria

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: Chthonic power and the guardian of the mysteries

symbols.name: Mystic basket (ciste)
symbols.meaning: The container of secret objects shown to initiates

mythology.lead: Dēmētēr's mythology is dominated by one event: the loss and recovery of her daughter Persephonē. That single story encodes the origin of winter, the foundation of agriculture, and the hope of immortality.

myths.title: The Rape of Persephonē
myths.text: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 1–89), Hādēs bursts from the earth on the Nysian plain and seizes Persephonē while she gathers a narcissus planted by Gaia at Zeús's command. Dēmētēr's search takes her across the world for nine days, until Hekátē and Hēlios reveal the truth. Her grief is the origin of winter: the earth refuses to bear fruit while the grain goddess mourns.

myths.title: Nursing Demophoôn at Eleusis
myths.text: Disguised as an old woman named Doso, Dēmētēr is welcomed into the house of King Celeus at Eleusis. She attempts to make the mortal child Demophoôn immortal by holding him in the fire each night, but his mother Metaneira interrupts the rite. The goddess reveals herself in blazing glory and demands a temple and mysteries. This is the aition — the founding myth — of the Eleusinian sanctuary (Hymn 90–298).

lore.culturalLegacy: Dēmētēr's legacy is the idea that agriculture is sacred. Every harvest festival, every prayer before a meal, every image of a mother and child owes something to her. The Eleusinian Mysteries shaped later mystery religions, including Christianity's emphasis on initiation, sacrament, and afterlife hope. Archaeologically, her sanctuary at Eleusis remains one of the most important religious sites in Greece, and the Homeric Hymn to Demeter is a foundational text for the study of Greek religion. In modern environmental thought, Dēmētēr has become a symbol of the earth's fertility and humanity's dependence upon it. Restoring Dēmētēr restores the name of the goddess who first made bread possible.
lore.archaeology: Eleusis: Telesterion and sanctuary of the Mysteries, in use from Mycenaean to Late Roman times. Thesmophorion sanctuaries across Greek cities.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Dēmētēr with Ceres, an Italic grain goddess whose name gives us 'cereal' and 'breakfast cereal.' The syncretism was so complete that the two names became interchangeable in the Roman world. In Egypt she was equated with Isis, another grieving mother goddess whose mysteries promised salvation; the iconography of Isis holding the infant Horus influenced later images of the Virgin Mary. The Thesmophoria, a women-only festival in Dēmētēr's honor, was one of the most widespread and politically significant religious institutions in the Greek world, giving women a recognized role in civic religion.

domains.title: The Queen of Olympus
domains.subtitle: Marriage, Sovereignty, Women, and the Ritual Year
domains.lead: Hēra is the queen of the gods by marriage, not birth. Her power is inseparable from her status as Zeús's wife, and her mythology is dominated by the defense of legitimate marriage and royal order against every challenge — especially her husband's infidelities.

cards.name: Marriage and Fidelity
cards.desc: Patron of the wedded state; the gamos, or sacred marriage, is her rite.

cards.name: Royal Sovereignty
cards.desc: Queen of gods and men; kingship legitimized through her partnership with Zeús.

cards.name: Childbirth
cards.desc: Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, acts at her command; she protects women in labor.

cards.name: The Peacock
cards.desc: The hundred-eyed Argos, her faithful watcher, set in the tail of her sacred bird.

symbols.name: Pomegranate

symbols.name: Sceptre
symbols.meaning: Queenship and authority

mythology.lead: Hēra's myths are almost all variations on one theme: the wronged wife defending her throne. She cannot overthrow Zeús, but she can punish his lovers and their children with relentless ingenuity.

myths.title: The Sacred Wedding of Zeús and Hēra
myths.text: Zeús and Hēra were married in a sacred ceremony on the island of Samos, one of her great cult centers. Their wedding night lasted three hundred years, according to one tradition, establishing the pattern of divine marriage. The hieros gamos, or sacred marriage, was reenacted in ritual across the Greek world to ensure fertility and cosmic order.

myths.title: The Persecution of Hēraklēs
myths.text: Hēra hated Hēraklēs because he was the son of Zeús and the mortal Alcmene — living proof of her husband's infidelity. She sent serpents to kill him in his cradle, drove him to madness, and imposed the Twelve Labors. Yet her persecution made him immortal: without Hēra's hatred, there is no Hēraklēs. The myth turns a queen's vengeance into the engine of heroism.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hēra is the archetype of the queen consort — powerful because of her position, dangerous because of her pride. Her peacock remains a symbol of beauty and watchfulness; her jealousy has been a literary theme from Euripides to opera. The Argive Heraion, her massive sanctuary near Argos, dominated the plain and testified to her political importance; Argos claimed to be her favorite city. In modern feminist readings, Hēra has been reinterpreted as a figure of constrained power, a goddess whose authority is real but always mediated through marriage. Restoring Hēra restores the name of the goddess who made marriage a cosmic institution.
lore.archaeology: Argive Heraion: major sanctuary near Argos from the 8th century BCE. Samos: Heraion of Samos, one of the richest Ionian sanctuaries.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hēra with Iuno, the queen of the Roman gods and protector of marriage. Iuno was central to the Roman state cult; every woman had a personal Iuno, just as every man had a personal Genius. In the Hellenistic east, Hēra was syncretized with Egyptian Isis and Phoenician Astarte as a supreme queen goddess. Her great sanctuaries at Argos and Samos were among the richest in Greece, and the Heraia festival at Olympia included athletic competitions for women. The very word 'hero' is probably unrelated to her name, but the association has shaped her reception for centuries.

domains.title: The Messenger
domains.subtitle: Travel, Commerce, Thievery, and Boundaries
domains.lead: Hermês is the fastest, cleverest, and most adaptable of the gods. He moves between Olympus, earth, and the underworld; he protects travelers, merchants, thieves, and heralds. Where there is a boundary, there is Hermês.

cards.name: Messenger of the Gods
cards.desc: He carries Zeús's commands and guides souls to the underworld.

cards.name: Boundaries and Thresholds
cards.desc: Herms marked property lines, roads, and doorways; he protects those who cross from one place to another.

cards.name: Commerce and Exchange
cards.desc: Patron of merchants, markets, and honest — or clever — dealing.

cards.name: Trickster and Thief
cards.desc: On his first day he stole Apóllōn's cattle; his cunning is as divine as his duty.

symbols.name: Caduceus
symbols.meaning: The herald's staff entwined with serpents, symbol of peace and negotiation

symbols.name: Winged sandals
symbols.meaning: Speed and the ability to cross all boundaries

symbols.name: Traveler's hat
symbols.meaning: Protection on the road

symbols.meaning: The instrument he invented and traded to Apóllōn

symbols.meaning: From whose shell he made the first lyre

mythology.lead: Hermês's myths are almost always about crossing boundaries and getting away with it. He is the divine child who outwits his older brother on the day of his birth.

myths.title: Born in a Cave on Mount Cyllene
myths.text: Hermês was born to Zeús and the nymph Maia in a remote Arcadian cave. By midday of his first day he had invented the lyre from a tortoise shell and slipped out to steal Apóllōn's cattle. He made them walk backward to confuse the tracks. When Apóllōn accused him, the infant denied everything with such charm that even the accusation became comic.

myths.title: The Lyre for the Herd
myths.text: Zeús ordered Hermês to return the cattle. Hermês played the lyre he had invented, and Apóllōn was so enchanted that he traded his whole herd for the instrument. Thus Hermês became the god of music (after Apóllōn), commerce, and negotiation. The myth makes theft the origin of trade: what is taken is returned as exchange.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hermês is the god of everything that moves: messages, money, travelers, thieves, and souls. The herm was one of the most common religious objects in Athens; every doorway and road was under his protection. In philosophy, Hermes Trismegistus became a founder of alchemy and Hermeticism. Modern concepts of communication, commerce, and even the internet — a network of boundaries crossed at speed — would have seemed to the Greeks like the domain of Hermês. Restoring Hermês restores the name of the god who first made exchange possible.
lore.archaeology: Thousands of herms—four-sided pillars topped with Hermes' head and genitals—stood at doorways, crossroads, and gymnasia across Athens; the mutilation of the herms in 415 BCE is recorded by Thucydides and left numerous surviving examples. The Hermes of Praxiteles (Archaeological Museum of Olympia) is a fourth-century BCE marble of the god carrying the infant Dionysos. The herm of Andros and the Archanes herms illustrate his role as boundary guardian.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hermês with Mercurius, the god of commerce and travel, whose name gives us 'merchant' and 'mercury.' The planet Mercury, swift in its orbit, bears his name. In Egypt he was fused with Thoth, the ibis-headed god of writing and wisdom, producing the figure of Hermes Trismegistus, central to Hellenistic and Renaissance occultism. The caduceus, though often confused with the rod of Asclepius, remains a global symbol of diplomacy and medicine.

domains.title: The Divine Smith
domains.subtitle: Fire, Craft, Metalwork, and Volcanoes
domains.lead: Hēphaistos is the only ugly Olympian, the only crippled one, and the only one who works for a living. His craft gives the gods their weapons and armor, and his forges lie beneath the volcanoes of the Aegean. He is the god who proves that making is a form of divinity.

cards.name: Fire and Forge
cards.desc: The elemental fire that shapes metal; his workshops lie under Lemnos, Etna, and Hiera.

cards.name: Metalwork and Craft
cards.desc: Armorer to the gods; maker of Achilles' shield, Athena's aegis, and countless automata.

cards.name: Volcanoes
cards.desc: His lame gait matches the earth's limp; every eruption is his forge at work.

cards.name: Automata and Invention
cards.desc: He builds self-moving tripods, golden maidens, and unbreakable chains — the first robots in Western literature.

symbols.name: Lame leg
symbols.meaning: His disability, source of both mockery and pity

symbols.name: Donkey
symbols.meaning: The animal that carries him; symbol of patient labor

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: The transformative element he commands

mythology.lead: Hēphaistos's myths turn disability into mastery. Rejected at birth, he returns to Olympus as the indispensable artisan.

myths.title: Thrown from Olympus
myths.text: Hēra bore Hēphaistos without male aid, and when she saw he was lame, she cast him from Olympus. He fell for a full day and landed in the sea, where the nymphs Thetis and Eurynome raised him in a cave. There he learned his craft, forging jewelry so fine that Thetis wore it to Olympus. The myth makes rejection the origin of skill.

myths.title: The Golden Throne
myths.text: Hēphaistos sent Hēra a golden throne as a gift. When she sat in it, invisible bonds held her fast. No god could release her until Dionysos made Hēphaistos drunk and led him back to Olympus. The smith exacted recognition from the queen who had thrown him away, and was restored to divine society.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hēphaistos is the patron of everyone who makes things with fire and skill: blacksmiths, metalworkers, engineers, and today, roboticists and materials scientists. His forge beneath the volcano is the ancestor of every industrial revolution. The Shield of Achilles remains a foundational text for understanding how the Greeks imagined the world as a crafted artifact. In disability studies, Hēphaistos has become an important figure: rejected for his body, he becomes essential through his skill. Restoring Hēphaistos restores the name of the god who proved that the maker is as divine as the warrior.
lore.archaeology: Athens: Hephaesteion (Temple of Hephaestus) in the Agora, best preserved Doric temple in Greece. Lemnos: volcanic island and early cult center.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hēphaistos with Vulcanus, a god of destructive fire and volcanoes whose festival, the Vulcanalia, was celebrated in August. The equation emphasized his volcanic aspect more than his craftsmanship. In the early modern period, Vulcan gave his name to the hypothetical planet between Mercury and the Sun. Hephaestus's automata — self-moving tripods and golden servants — made him a patron figure for engineering and robotics in science fiction. The volcano as divine forge is one of the most enduring images in Western culture.

etymology.derivation: From Ἑστία "hearth", cognate with Latin Vesta. The hearth goddess.

steps: The Greek form Ἑστία is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Hestía encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'hess-TEE-ah' — the middle syllable carries the pitch, and the final 'ah' is short and open.
pronunciation.note: Hestía is Tier 2 because the original Ἑστία bears the acute stress only; the final alpha is short, so a single feature is preserved. The name is built on the PIE root *h₂wes-, 'to dwell,' making her literally the goddess of the dwelling-place.

domains.title: The Hearth
domains.subtitle: Home, Hearth, Family, and Civic Fire
domains.lead: Hestía is the quietest Olympian. She never leaves Olympus, never quarrels, never takes lovers. She is the hearth-fire itself — the fixed point around which the family, the city, and the world are organized. Every sacrifice begins and ends with her.

cards.name: The Domestic Hearth
cards.desc: The fire at the center of every home; the place where family gathers and offerings are made.

cards.name: Civic Fire
cards.desc: The prytaneion in every Greek city housed her eternal flame; colonists carried her fire to new lands.

cards.name: First and Last
cards.desc: The first libation and the final prayer of every sacrifice belong to Hestía.

cards.name: Refusal of Strife
cards.desc: She rejected Apollo and Poseidôn's suits and swore eternal virginity; Zeús granted her the first share of every sacrifice.

symbols.name: Hearth fire
symbols.meaning: The center of home, city, and cosmos

symbols.name: Kettle or cauldron
symbols.meaning: The vessel that holds the sacred flame

symbols.name: Pig
symbols.meaning: Sacrificial animal offered at the hearth

symbols.name: Circle
symbols.meaning: The shape of the hearth and the gathering around it

symbols.name: Modest veil
symbols.meaning: Her chaste, domestic nature

mythology.lead: Hestía has almost no myths of her own because she is not a narrative goddess. She is a presence — the fire that must never go out. Her two significant stories both concern her refusal to leave the center.

myths.title: Virginity and Precedence
myths.text: Apóllōn and Poseidôn both sought to marry Hestía, but she asked Zeús to let her remain a virgin. Zeús agreed and granted her instead the first portion of every sacrifice and the honor of the hearth's center. In the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (21–32), Hestía is one of three goddesses — with Athena and Artemis — whom Aphrodítē cannot sway. Her virginity is not absence but sovereignty over her own domain.

myths.title: Hestía in Cosmology
myths.text: For the Greeks, Hestía was not only the hearth but the fixed center of the house, the city, and the cosmos. Philosophers from Plato to the Stoics used her as an image of stability and centrality. The Pythagoreans identified Hestía with the central fire around which the earth and planets moved. She is therefore one of the few Olympians whose theological importance exceeds her mythological activity.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hestía's legacy is the sanctity of home. The English word 'hearth' still carries emotional weight far beyond its practical function. The concepts of hospitality, asylum, and household gods all descend from her cult. The Roman Vestal Virgins were among the most powerful women in the ancient world; their oath bound the state itself. In modern usage, 'Vestal' and 'hearth' evoke purity, warmth, and centeredness. Restoring Hestía restores the name of the goddess who made the home a temple.
lore.archaeology: Every Greek city maintained a Prytaneion with an eternal hearth fire sacred to Hestia; remains have been excavated at Athens, Olympia, Delphi, and Priene. In Magnesia on the Maeander, the agora contained a circular Hestia temple mentioned in inscriptions. Public inscriptions from Samos and Cos record civic oaths taken 'by Hestia and the other gods'.
lore.syncretism: The Roman identification with Vesta was exact: same goddess, same function, same eternal flame. The Vestal Virgins gave the cult an institutional form unmatched in Greece. In Christianity, the hearth's sacredness was transferred to the household and, in the Byzantine East, to the church's sanctuary lamp. Hestía's archaic importance is visible in the fact that every Greek prayer and sacrifice began with her name. She is the most conservative deity in the pantheon, the one whose worship changed least across millennia.

entries.meaning: Lord of the Earth (from πόσις + δᾶ)

variants.note: LSJ convention: length only, no circumflex

etymology.derivation: From πόσις "lord, husband" + δᾶ (Doric for γῆ "earth"), later reinterpreted as "sea".

steps: The Greek form Ποσειδῶν is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Poseidôn encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'poh-SAY-done' — the second syllable is light, the third is long, pitched, and powerful.
pronunciation.note: Poseidôn is Tier 1 because the Greek Ποσειδῶν contains both stress (circumflex on the long ω) and length (ει diphthong and long ω). The circumflex form Poseidôn is the ideal; Poseidōn is the macron-only LSJ convention.

domains.title: The Earth-Shaker
domains.subtitle: Sea, Earthquakes, Horses, and Storms
domains.lead: Poseidôn is the lord of the waters that surround and threaten every Greek city. He is not a gentle sea; he is the earth-shaker, the tamer of horses, the sudden storm that overturns ships and cracks land. His power is older than Zeús in some traditions, and his rivalry with Athena for Athens defines the tension between maritime force and civic wisdom.

cards.name: The Open Sea
cards.desc: Poseidôn commands the Mediterranean itself — calm or wrathful, generous or deadly.

cards.name: Earthquake
cards.desc: His trident strikes rock and splits the earth; every tremor is his chariot passing beneath.

cards.name: Horses
cards.desc: He created the horse, either as a gift to Athens or as a creature of the breaking wave.

cards.name: Storms and Winds
cards.desc: The sudden gale, the waterspout, and the drowning wave all answer to him.

symbols.name: Trident
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over sea and earthquake; weapon and scepter combined

symbols.name: Horse
symbols.meaning: His gift to humanity and the breaker of waves made flesh

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: Sacrificial animal; the bull from the sea in myths of Minos

symbols.name: Dolphin
symbols.meaning: Messenger and rescuer; guides sailors and heroes

symbols.name: Pine tree
symbols.meaning: Sacred to him; wood for ship masts

symbols.name: Breaking wave
symbols.meaning: The sudden, irresistible force of his domain

mythology.lead: Poseidôn's myths dramatize the rage of the excluded. He is a great Olympian, yet he is repeatedly thwarted — by Athena at Athens, by Odysseus after the blinding of Polyphemus, by the very mortals whose sacrifices he demands.

myths.title: Lord of the Sea
myths.text: After the defeat of the Titans, Zeús, Poseidôn, and Hádês divided the cosmos by lot. Zeús took the sky, Hádês the underworld, and Poseidôn the sea. The earth remained common to all three. This tripartition makes Poseidôn equal in dignity to his brothers, yet his watery realm is restless and uncontainable — a fitting symbol of his temperament.

myths.title: Defeated by Athena
myths.text: Poseidôn and Athénā competed for the patronage of Athens. He struck the Acropolis with his trident and produced a salt spring; she planted the olive tree. The city chose her gift. Poseidôn flooded Attica in revenge, and the Athenians placated him by giving the first fruits of the harvest and by honoring Erechtheus, whom he had destroyed. The myth encodes the Greek insight that sea power must yield to civic wisdom.

lore.culturalLegacy: Poseidôn's legacy is the recognition that the sea is never truly conquered. Every Greek colony, every fisherman, every sailor lived under his power. The Isthmian Games at Corinth honored him; sailors prayed to him before departure. His trident remains a symbol of maritime sovereignty, appearing on coins, naval insignia, and the flag of Barbados. In an age of climate change and rising seas, Poseidôn's ancient title 'Earth-Shaker' has taken on new literal force. Restoring Poseidôn restores the name by which the Greeks named the water that surrounds civilization.
lore.archaeology: Sounion: Temple of Poseidon (ca. 444 BCE) on the Attic promontory. Isthmia: sanctuary and games of Poseidon from 582 BCE.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Poseidôn with Neptunus, an Italic water god associated with fresh water before Greek influence made him the sea. In later antiquity Poseidon-Neptune became one of the most recognizable gods of the Roman pantheon, his chariot drawn by hippocamps. In art he carries the trident that is still his universal attribute. The planet Neptune, discovered in 1846, bears his name. Modern culture uses him as the archetype of the stormy, vengeful sea god, from Renaissance frescoes to blockbuster films.

etymology.derivation: Possibly from πέρθω "to destroy" + φόνος "murder", or pre-Greek. Queen of the Underworld.

steps: The Greek form Περσεφόνη is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Persephonē encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'per-seh-FOH-nay' — the third syllable carries the pitch, and the final 'nay' is long and solemn.
pronunciation.note: Persephonē is Tier 1 because the Greek Περσεφόνη contains both stress (acute on the short ό) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name's etymology is uncertain, which suits a goddess who moves between the known and hidden worlds.

domains.title: The Maiden Queen
domains.subtitle: Spring, the Underworld, Vegetation, and Initiation
domains.lead: Persephonē is the only Greek deity who is fully at home in two worlds. For half the year she is the maiden Kore, daughter of Dēmētēr and goddess of spring; for the other half she is the dread queen of the dead, Hādēs's wife. Her double life is the Greek explanation for everything that dies and returns.

cards.name: Spring and Return
cards.desc: Her ascent from the underworld brings the grain and flowers of spring; her return is the return of life.

cards.name: Queen of the Dead
cards.desc: In the underworld she sits beside Hādēs and rules the shades with a power no other Olympian has below.

cards.name: Vegetation Mysteries
cards.desc: The sprouting seed is her; the buried grain is her; the mystery of Eleusis centers on her journey.

cards.name: Initiation and Rebirth
cards.desc: Initiates at Eleusis reenact her descent and return, hoping for the same promise in death.

symbols.name: Pomegranate
symbols.meaning: The seed that bound her to the underworld

symbols.name: Narcissus
symbols.meaning: The flower whose beauty lured her to the abduction

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: Her mother's search and her own queenly authority

symbols.name: Crown or diadem
symbols.meaning: Queen of the dead

symbols.name: Sheaf of wheat
symbols.meaning: The grain that dies and rises

symbols.name: Black ram
symbols.meaning: Sacrificial animal offered to her and Hādēs

mythology.lead: Persephonē's mythology is the Homeric Hymn to Demeter. Every later retelling is a variation on that poem's architecture of loss, grief, negotiation, and return.

myths.title: The Narcissus and the Void
myths.text: In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter (lines 1–89), Persephonē gathers flowers in a meadow on the Nysian plain when the earth opens and Hādēs carries her away in a golden chariot. Only the helmsman of the sun, Hēlios, sees the abduction. The narcissus she reaches for was planted by Gaia at Zeús's command — a divine trap that makes the earth itself complicit in her descent.

myths.title: Demeter's Wanderings
myths.text: Dēmētēr searches for her daughter for nine days, bearing torches. Hekátē hears the cry and joins the search; Hēlios finally reveals Hādēs's guilt. Dēmētēr's grief withdraws fertility from the earth, threatening all life. The gods are forced to negotiate because even immortals depend on the grain she withholds.

lore.culturalLegacy: Persephonē is the archetype of the dying-and-rising goddess, the divine figure whose descent makes spring possible. Her myth influenced the mystery religions of the Roman Empire and, through them, Christian iconography of resurrection. In literature, she appears from Milton's Paradise Lost to modern novels and films as the queen of the underworld. Psychologically, she has become a symbol of feminine individuation: the daughter who must separate from her mother, enter darkness, and return transformed. Restoring Persephonē restores the name of the goddess who makes death temporary.
lore.archaeology: Eleusis houses the Telesterion and the Mirthless Rock where Persephone was seated in Demeter's sorrow. The sanctuary of Persephone at Locri Epizephyrii has yielded thousands of pinakes (clay plaques) showing the goddess with worshippers, wedding, and abduction scenes. Sicily's Lake Pergusa and the sanctuary at Enna were identified with the rape of Persephone; the goddess's image appears on Syracusan coinage and in terracotta votives.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Persephonē with Proserpina, a goddess whose name may derive from the Latin proserpere, 'to emerge.' The Proserpina myth preserved the same seasonal structure. In later antiquity she was syncretized with Egyptian Isis as a savior goddess and with the moon, whose monthly disappearance and return mirrored her own. The Eleusinian cult spread across the Roman Empire, and emperors including Hadrian were initiated. Christian writers from Clement of Alexandria to Augustine attacked the mysteries, but they also borrowed their themes of death and rebirth.

etymology.derivation: From πρό "before" + μῆτις "mind, counsel". The Titan who gave fire to mankind.

steps: The Greek form Προμηθεύς is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Promētheus encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'pro-meh-THEFS' — the middle syllable is long, and the final diphthong, which carries the accent, glides like the foresight the name denotes.
pronunciation.note: Promētheus is Tier 1 because the Greek Προμηθεύς contains both stress (acute on the long η, realized as acute in our restoration) and length (η and the ευ diphthong). His name means 'Forethought,' the opposite of his brother Epimetheus ('Afterthought').

domains.title: The Forethinker
domains.subtitle: Fire, Craft, Foresight, and Human Civilization
domains.lead: Promētheus is the Titan who sided with mortals. He gave humanity fire, taught the arts of civilization, and accepted eternal punishment for his mercy. He is the patron of every outcast intelligence that chooses compassion over obedience.

cards.name: Fire-Bringer
cards.desc: He stole fire from Olympus in a fennel stalk and gave it to humanity — the origin of technology.

cards.name: Craft and Deception
cards.desc: He tricked Zeús at Mekone, dividing the sacrificial ox so gods got bones and mortals got meat.

cards.name: Teacher of Humanity
cards.desc: He taught writing, mathematics, astronomy, medicine, and the arts that make cities possible.

cards.name: Suffering Savior
cards.desc: Bound to a Caucasian rock, his liver eaten daily by an eagle — the price of his gift to mortals.

symbols.name: Fennel stalk
symbols.meaning: The vessel in which fire was smuggled from heaven

symbols.name: Liver
symbols.meaning: The organ that regenerates, making his punishment eternal

symbols.name: Eagle
symbols.meaning: Zeús's instrument of torture

symbols.name: Chains and rock
symbols.meaning: The bondage of the rebel against cosmic order

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: Knowledge, technology, and divine power transferred to mortals

symbols.name: Ring with stone
symbols.meaning: The ring Zeús made him wear as a reminder of his bond

mythology.lead: Promētheus's myths are the foundation of the Greek reflection on the cost of progress. Every human achievement is a theft from the gods; every theft demands punishment.

myths.title: The Division at Mekone
myths.text: In Hesiod's Theogony (535–557), Promētheus tricks Zeús at Mekone by dividing a sacrificial ox into two piles: one of bones wrapped in glistening fat, the other of meat hidden in the ox's stomach. Zeús chose the bones, and from that day mortals kept the edible meat for themselves. The trick established the ritual pattern of sacrifice and provoked Zeüs's anger, setting in motion the theft of fire.

myths.title: Stealing Fire for Mortals
myths.text: After Zeüs withheld fire from humanity, Promētheus stole it from the forge of Hephaistos or from the sun-chariot and carried it to earth in a hollow fennel stalk. Fire made mortals like gods: they could cook, forge metal, and warm themselves. In Hesiod's darker telling, this gift led to Pandora and the diseases she released; in Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound, it is the foundation of all civilization.

lore.culturalLegacy: Promētheus is the patron saint of human technology and its discontents. Every fire, every forge, every scientific breakthrough reenacts his theft. The Promethean myth underlies debates about artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, and climate change: do our powers exceed our wisdom? Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound remains one of the most influential Greek tragedies, and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein subtitled her novel 'The Modern Prometheus.' Restoring Promētheus restores the name of the being who gave us fire and asked only that we use it.
lore.archaeology: Panathenaic amphorae and red-figure vases depicting Prometheus bound; no major sanctuary, but Prometheus was honored at Athens with torch races.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Promētheus with the Latin Prometheus directly, as the name was borrowed rather than translated. In early Christian thought he was sometimes seen as a type of Christ — a divine being who suffers for humanity — though more often as a warning against hubris. The Renaissance rediscovered him through the recovery of Aeschylus's Prometheus Bound; he became a symbol of human creativity, rebellion, and scientific progress. Goethe, Shelley, and Marx all claimed him. The prefix 'pro-' in 'promethean' still denotes bold, possibly reckless, creative energy.

etymology.derivation: Earth (from γαῖα)

steps: The Greek form Γαῖα is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Gaîa encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'GUY-ah' — the diphthong glides like the earth yielding; the final vowel is simple and vast.
pronunciation.note: Gaia is Tier 1 because the Greek Γαῖα bears a circumflex on the αι diphthong, which marks both stress and vowel length in a single sign. She is primordial: older than the Olympians, older than the Titans, the first power to arise after Chaos.

domains.title: The Earth Itself
domains.subtitle: Land, Fertility, Prophecy, and the Mother of All
domains.lead: Gaia is not a goddess of the earth; she is the earth. In Hesiod's cosmogony she is the first thing to emerge from Chaos, the ever-stable foundation from which sky, sea, mountains, and gods are born. She is the original mother, the ground of being.

cards.name: The Living Earth
cards.desc: Mountains, plains, seas, and caves are her body; earthquakes are her movements.

cards.name: Mother of Gods
cards.desc: She bore Ouranos, Pontos, the Titans, the Cyclopes, and the Hundred-Handers.

cards.name: Oracle and Prophet
cards.desc: Her oracle at Delphi was the first; she is the voice of the earth before Apollo's arrival.

cards.name: Revenge and Justice
cards.desc: When Ouranos imprisoned her children, she forged the sickle and set Kronos against him.

symbols.name: The globe or earth
symbols.meaning: The planet as living body

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: The endless fertility of the soil

symbols.name: Sickle
symbols.meaning: The weapon used to castrate Ouranos

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: The earth's chthonic, regenerative power

symbols.name: Oak tree
symbols.meaning: The deep-rooted tree sacred to her oracle at Dodona

symbols.name: Breast
symbols.meaning: Maternal nourishment; the earth feeds all creatures

mythology.lead: Gaia's myths are cosmogonic. She is the stage on which everything else happens, but she is also an actor who intervenes when cosmic order threatens her children.

myths.title: First After Chaos
myths.text: Hesiod's Theogony (116–122) begins with Chaos, then Gaia 'broad-bosomed,' then Tartaros and Eros. Gaia immediately gives birth to Ouranos (Sky), the Ourea (Mountains), and Pontos (Sea) without mating. She is the self-generating foundation. The repetition of 'Gaia' at the opening of the cosmos makes her the first identifiable reality.

myths.title: The Castration of Ouranos
myths.text: Ouranos hated the children Gaia bore him and pushed them back into her womb. In pain and anger, Gaia fashioned a great sickle of adamant and persuaded her youngest son Kronos to ambush his father. Kronos castrated Ouranos; from the falling blood sprang the Erinyes, the Giants, and the Meliai. The act establishes the pattern of Greek cosmogony: each generation overthrows the one before, and Gaia is always on the side of the next power.

lore.culturalLegacy: Gaia is the oldest and most persistent name for the earth as a living whole. Geology, geography, and geometry all derive from her root gē. The Gaia hypothesis gave her name to modern ecological thought; 'Mother Earth' in many languages translates the same image. In feminist spirituality, Gaia represents the primordial feminine principle and the sanctity of nature. Restoring Gaia restores the first name the Greeks gave to the ground beneath their feet. Scholarly controversy: The Mycenaean evidence for Gaia remains disputed, and modern ecology debates whether the Gaia hypothesis is science or metaphor.
lore.archaeology: At Delphi the stone Omphalos marked the 'navel' of Ge before Apollo's arrival; the goddess's sanctuary lies beneath the later Apollo precinct. Pausanias describes altars of Ge at Olympia, including the oracle of Ge, and at Athens the Boule honored Ge Kourotrophos and Demeter Chloe. Votive reliefs from the Athenian Agora and Eleusinion show worshippers approaching a seated Mother Earth with cornucopia and phiale.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Gaia with Terra Mater, the earth mother, though Terra never achieved the philosophical and cosmological prominence of her Greek counterpart. In later antiquity Gaia was syncretized with Cybele, the Phrygian mountain mother, and with various Near Eastern earth goddesses. In the Scientific Revolution, her name was revived for the Gaia hypothesis — James Lovelock's theory that the earth functions as a self-regulating living system. Modern environmental movements have made Gaia the personification of the planet itself, though this is a philosophical rather than strictly ancient usage.

variants.note: Transliterated form (kh for χ); the temple uses the Latinized Cháos.

etymology.derivation: Gap, yawning void (from χάος)

steps: The Greek form Χάος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Cháos encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: "KHAH-oss" — first syllable like "cat" with a breathy k, second like "oss" in "moss".
