pronunciation.note: Cháos is Tier 2 because the Greek Χάος preserves only stress (acute on the first alpha), not length. There is no long vowel or diphthong. The accent marks the pitch peak of the primordial "gap" — a single prosodic feature, exactly what Tier 2 is designed to record.

domains.title: The First Void
domains.lead: Cháos is not disorder. It is not noise, mess, or confusion. In Hesiod's Greek, Cháos is the yawning gap — the first thing to exist, the empty interval in which everything else could appear. Before Earth, before Sky, before the gods themselves, there was the opening.

cards.name: The Yawning Gap
cards.desc: The original meaning: a gape, a chasm, the interval before form.

cards.name: Undifferentiated Potential
cards.desc: Not empty, but unformed — the reservoir from which all distinctions arise.

cards.name: Cosmic Layer
cards.desc: The first stratum of being, preceding Gaia, Tartarus, and Eros.

cards.name: The Threshold
cards.desc: The boundary between non-being and being; without Cháos, no cosmos.

symbols.name: Open mouth
symbols.meaning: The etymological image of the yawning gap

symbols.name: Abyss
symbols.meaning: The depth before depth existed

symbols.name: Unshaped mass
symbols.meaning: Later Roman reinterpretation as raw matter

symbols.name: First breath
symbols.meaning: The opening from which the world is exhaled

mythology.lead: Cháos has no myths in the usual sense — no loves, no wars, no disguises. It is the stage before the drama. Yet its single appearance in the Theogony is the most important stage direction in Greek literature.

myths.title: First of All, Cháos
myths.text: Hesiod opens the Theogony (116) with the famous line: "Verily at the first Cháos came to be, but next wide-bosomed Gaia." The word "came to be" (genet') is crucial: Cháos is not eternal in the theological sense, but the first event — the first thing to arise from whatever preceded things. Aristotle later read Cháos as space itself, the precondition for place (Physics 208b29).

myths.title: Erebus and Nyx
myths.text: From Cháos come Erebus (deep Darkness) and Nyx (Night). They are not created by an act of will; they differentiate from the gap. Their subsequent union produces Aithḗr (bright upper air) and Hemera (Day) — a symmetrical procession from gap to dark to light.

lore.culturalLegacy: The modern word "chaos" is, ironically, a corruption of Cháos. Because of Ovid, it came to mean disorder, confusion, randomness — the opposite of Hesiod's ordered emptiness. In the twentieth century, "chaos theory" gave the word a new technical meaning: deterministic systems so sensitive to initial conditions that they appear unpredictable. This is closer to the Greek sense than everyday usage: a system with hidden structure, not mere noise. Artists, musicians, and writers still invoke Cháos as the fertile void, the blank page, the silence before the symphony — the necessary absence from which form is born.
lore.archaeology: Although Chaos leaves no direct cult archaeology, its mythic geography is mapped onto real landscapes. The Avernus lake near Cumae and the volcanic Phlegraean Fields were identified with the entrance to the underworld. Roman sarcophagi and floor mosaics depict the bound Titans and the wintry realm beyond order, translating the cosmogonic abyss into visual art.
lore.syncretism: The Romans kept the Greek name but changed its nature. Ovid made Cháos the raw material of creation, a Stoic-inspired mixture awaiting the divine craftsman. In Christian exegesis, Cháos was sometimes identified with the "without form and void" (tohu wabohu) of Genesis 1:2, creating a bridge between Greek cosmogony and biblical creation. Gnostic texts reversed the valuation: Cháos became the fallen realm from which the soul must escape. Through all these reinterpretations, the original Greek sense — a yawning gap, not a turbulent mess — was gradually buried.

etymology.derivation: Deep place (from τάρταρος)

steps: The Greek form Τάρταρος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Tártaros encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: "TAR-ta-ross" — three syllables, the first pitched high like a stone dropping.
pronunciation.note: Tártaros is Tier 2 because the Greek Τάρταρος preserves only stress (acute on the first alpha), not length. The first syllable carries the pitch peak, appropriate for a name that denotes the deepest point of the cosmos. The absence of long vowels makes the name sound hard and abrupt — the acoustic opposite of the bright, sustained Aithḗr.

domains.title: The Primordial Abyss
domains.lead: Tártaros is the deepest place. It lies beneath Hades as far as Hades lies beneath the earth, and the earth beneath the sky. It is not merely a dungeon; it is a cosmic depth, the inverted dome that balances the celestial dome above.

cards.name: The Pit
cards.desc: The bottomless chasm beneath the foundations of the world.

cards.name: The Bronze Gates
cards.desc: Hesiod describes walls and gates of bronze, built by Poseidon, guarded by the Hecatoncheires.

cards.name: Storm and Darkness
cards.desc: The "stormy pit" — winds, gloom, and the roar of imprisoned powers.

cards.name: Divine Punishment
cards.desc: The place where the worst offenders — Titans and mortal sinners — receive eternal justice.

symbols.name: Bronze anvil
symbols.meaning: Hesiod's measure of its depth: nine days' fall from earth

symbols.name: Iron gates
symbols.meaning: The impassable boundary

symbols.name: Triple night
symbols.meaning: The darkness that wraps the abyss

symbols.name: Storm winds
symbols.meaning: The imprisoned forces that issue from its depths

symbols.name: Fettered Titan
symbols.meaning: The defeated gods chained below

mythology.lead: Tártaros appears almost as soon as the world begins. It is the third primordial in Hesiod's list — gap, earth, abyss — and it remains the final destination for every cosmic rebel.

myths.title: The Third Primordial
myths.text: After Cháos and Gaia, Hesiod names Tártaros: "dim Tartarus, in the depths of the broad-pathed earth" (Theogony 119). It is both a place and a power, the body of the pit itself. Homer adds the famous measurement: Tártaros is as far beneath Hades as heaven is above earth (Iliad 8.13–16).

myths.title: The Titans Cast Down
myths.text: After the Titanomachy, Zeus imprisoned the defeated Titans in Tártaros. Poseidon built bronze gates; the Hecatoncheires stood guard. The Iliad describes them seated at the threshold, "a dreadful thing to hear" for any who would approach (Iliad 8.481).

lore.culturalLegacy: Tártaros survives as the archetype of the inescapable prison. Video games, fantasy novels, and comic books use "Tartarus" for the deepest dungeon, the final level, the place where ancient evils are chained. In astronomy, the exoplanet HD 80606 b was nicknamed "Tartarus" for its extreme, hellish orbit. The abyss also shaped psychology and literature: the "Tartarus" within is the unconscious depth where repressed forces rage. The name still carries its original weight: not merely death, but the bottom of everything.
lore.archaeology: Tartaros has no independent cult, but its cosmography appears in texts and images. The Derveni Papyrus (ca. 340 BCE) discusses the underworld prison of the Titans. The Gigantomachy on the Pergamon Altar and the Siphnian Treasury at Delphi depict Zeus hurling enemies into Tartaros. Volcanic regions, especially Mount Etna, were later identified as mouths of Tartaros.
lore.syncretism: The Romans transliterated the name directly as Tartarus and made it the lowest region of the underworld, a place of torment distinct from the neutral infernum. In Virgil's Aeneid, the wicked are judged and cast into Tartarus, while the blessed ascend to Elysium. Christian writers — above all Milton in Paradise Lost — adopted Tartarus as a name for Hell or its precinct, completing a transformation from cosmic depth to moral prison. The word remains in theological vocabulary as a synonym for the deepest place of punishment.

etymology.derivation: From πόντος "sea", cognate with Latin pons "bridge, path". The primordial sea.

steps: The Greek form Πόντος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Póntos encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'PON-toss' — the first syllable is pitched and short, like the peak of a swell.
pronunciation.note: Póntos is Tier 2 because the Greek Πόντος preserves stress (acute on the short ό) but no long vowel. The name means 'sea' but originally 'path' or 'crossing' — the sea as the route one takes, not merely the water itself.

domains.title: The Sea Itself
domains.subtitle: Open Water, Sea Creatures, and the Dangerous Deep
domains.lead: Póntos is the sea as primordial body, older than Poseidôn's rule. He is Gaia's son, the father of sea-gods and sea-monsters, the surface across which Greek life depended and beneath which Greek sailors feared to go. Where Poseidôn is the storm, Póntos is the water.

cards.name: The Open Sea
cards.desc: The surface of the deep, the path between cities, the barrier and highway of the Greek world.

cards.name: Father of Sea Powers
cards.desc: His children include Nereus the Old Man of the Sea, Phorcys and Ceto the parents of monsters, and Thaumas father of the Harpies.

cards.name: The Dangerous Deep
cards.desc: Beneath his surface lie monsters, chasms, and the unknown; sailors propitiated him before voyages.

cards.name: The Black Sea
cards.desc: The Euxine Pontos — the 'Hospitable Sea' — was named after him; Greek colonization spread across his waters.

symbols.name: Waves
symbols.meaning: The surface and motion of the sea

symbols.name: Fish and sea creatures
symbols.meaning: The life teeming beneath the surface

symbols.name: Ship
symbols.meaning: The human path across his body

symbols.name: Shell
symbols.meaning: The boundary between sea and land

symbols.name: Trident
symbols.meaning: Later symbol shared with Poseidôn

symbols.name: Bull from the sea
symbols.meaning: The monstrous or sacrificial bull emerging from the deep

mythology.lead: Póntos has few myths because he is a personification rather than a character. His importance is genealogical: he is the source of the sea's divine population.

myths.title: Son of Gaia
myths.text: In Hesiod's Theogony (131–132), Gaia bears Pontos 'without delightful love' — that is, parthenogenetically. He is therefore as old as the mountains and as fundamental as the sea itself. His birth from Gaia makes him the wet, mobile counterpart to the Ourea, the mountains born from her at the same time.

myths.title: The Sea Gods and Monsters
myths.text: With Gaia, Pontos fathered Nereus (the Old Man of the Sea, father of the Nereids), Thaumas (father of Iris and the Harpies), Phorcys and Ceto (parents of the Gorgons and Graeae), and Eurybia (goddess of the mastery of the sea). This genealogy makes Pontos the ancestor of everything monstrous and marvelous in the Mediterranean.

lore.culturalLegacy: Póntos represents the sea as environment rather than deity. The Greeks lived on islands and coasts; the sea was their road, their food source, their enemy, and their horizon. The Euxine Pontos shaped Greek colonization and the history of the Black Sea region. The word 'Pontic' still names the Greek communities of the northern Anatolian coast and their distinctive culture. Restoring Póntos restores the name of the primordial sea that made Greek civilization a maritime civilization. Scholarly controversy: The etymology of Pontos is debated; the Black Sea name shifted from Axeinos (Inhospitable) to Euxeinos (Hospitable), a case study in colonial rhetoric.
lore.archaeology: Greek colonies around the Pontos Euxeinos preserve sanctuaries and harborworks at Olbia, Sinope, Trapezous, and Pantikapaion. The Milesian colony of Olbia produced bone plaques and coinage honoring Theos Pontos or local river gods. Shipwrecks such as those at Tektaş Burnu and the Black Sea survey by Ballard document trade routes that made the Pontic world a maritime economic zone rather than a theistic cult center.
lore.syncretism: The Romans had no distinct equivalent of Póntos; they used the borrowed name Pontus for the sea and the region. In later Greek, πόντος simply meant 'sea.' The personification was largely absorbed into Poseidon-Neptune. The kingdom of Pontus in northern Anatolia, famous for Mithridates VI, took its name from the Black Sea. Modern Greek still calls the sea πέλαγος or θάλασσα; 'Pontos' survives mainly in historical and geographical names.

etymology.derivation: Grandmother (from τήθη)

variants.note: Owned domain form — the Greek accent of Ὑπερίων itself (acute on í plus macron on ō)

pronunciation.approximation: 'hü-peh-REE-ohn' — round the lips for Hy- (the ü of German 'über'), strike the accent hard on -rí-, and let the final -ōn ring long.
pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the Greek original Ὑπερίων carries both a stress mark (the acute on the iota) and a long vowel (ω), and the restoration Hyperíōn preserves both — the í keeps the accent where Hesiod's auditors heard it, and the ō keeps the quantity of the omega. Both features survive in the Unicode form; the ASCII 'Hyperion' loses them.

domains.title: The Father of Lights
domains.subtitle: Light, Heavenly Watch
domains.lead: Hyperíōn is the High One — the Titan whose very name, from ὑπέρ, means 'he who goes above'. Hesiod makes him the bridge between the raw sky and its fires: son of Ouranos and Gaia, husband of Theía, and father of every light that crosses the heavens — Hēlios the Sun, Selḗnē the Moon, and Ēṓs the Dawn (Theogony 371–374). He has almost no story of his own; he is the genealogy of light itself, and in Homer his name is already spoken as a name of the sun.

cards.name: Celestial Light
cards.desc: Hesiod names him father of the three lights that cross the sky — Hēlios the Sun, Selḗnē the Moon, Ēṓs the Dawn (Theogony 371–374).

cards.name: The Heavenly Watch
cards.desc: His name runs from ὑπέρ, 'he who goes above', and Homer already speaks Hyperíōn as a name of the sun itself (Iliad 8.480).

cards.name: Progenitor of the Luminaries
cards.desc: With Theía he begets every luminary; later poets fold his name into his son’s until Titan and Sun are spoken as one.

symbols.name: The Vault of Heaven
symbols.meaning: His name declares it: from ὑπέρ, 'above', he is 'he who goes above' — the upper sky made personal, the height from which all light descends.

symbols.name: The Sun's Rays
symbols.meaning: In Iliad 8 (479–481) the rays are 'of Hyperion the Sun' (Ὑπερίονος Ἠελίοιο) — Homer speaks the name as a solar title, whether patronymic or epithet.

symbols.name: The Chariot of Day
symbols.meaning: Through his son Hēlios, who drives the four-horse chariot across the sky each day; later poets collapse father and son, and 'Hyperion' rides as the sun itself.

symbols.name: The Three Luminaries
symbols.meaning: Sun, Moon, and Dawn — his children by Theía (Theogony 371–374); his true emblem is genealogical, the whole family of sky-lights.

symbols.name: The Watchman's Station
symbols.meaning: As the one above, he holds the high lookout of heaven — the Titan whose vantage is the zenith itself, from which nothing on earth is hidden.

symbols.name: The Chains of Tartarus
symbols.meaning: After the Titanomachy he shares the Titans' prison 'as far beneath the earth as heaven is above the earth' (Theogony 717–720) — the High One brought low.

mythology.lead: Hyperíōn is a Titan of lineage rather than adventure: Hesiod gives him a birth, a marriage, three luminous children, and a fall — and almost nothing else. His myths are the myths of what his name means and of what his name became.

myths.title: A Son of Heaven and Earth
myths.text: In Theogony (132–136), Hesiod catalogues the children Gaia bore to Ouranos: the deep-swirling Ocean, then Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, and Iapetus, and with them the Titanesses — Theía, Rheía, Thémis, Mnēmosýnē, Phoíbē, and Tēthýs — and finally Krónos, 'crooked-counselled, the most terrible of her children'. Hyperíōn enters the poem with no deed attached, only a station: his name already declares it, from ὑπέρ, 'above'. He is born of the union of Sky and Earth and belongs to the sky's own house. Hesiod's silence about his character is itself telling — this Titan is a fixture of the high order of things, not a personality.

myths.title: Father of Sun, Moon, and Dawn
myths.text: In Theogony (371–374), Hyperíōn takes his sister Theía — 'the divine one' — to wife, and she bears him Hēlios the Sun, Selḗnē the Moon, and Ēṓs the Dawn, 'who shines on all that dwell on the earth and on the deathless gods who hold broad heaven'. The marriage is a small cosmology in itself: the High One wed to the Divine produces every light that crosses the sky. Pindar opens Isthmian 5 by addressing Theía as 'mother of the Sun, of many names', the hymn-like acknowledgement of this same union. Through his children, Hyperíōn is present at every sunrise, moonrise, and daybreak — he never leaves the sky he fathered onto it.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hyperíōn's deepest modern life is linguistic: the English prefix 'hyper-' (hyperactive, hyperlink, hyperspace) descends from ὑπέρ, the very root of his name — every 'hyper-' word unknowingly repeats 'he who goes above'. The Titan himself was given fresh stature by Keats's unfinished epic Hyperion (1820), which made his fall after the Titanomachy a meditation on the succession of gods. Astronomers named Saturn's moon Hyperion at its discovery in 1848, and the tallest known living tree on Earth, a coast redwood in California, was named Hyperion in 2006 — the High One still lends his name to things that out-top everything around them.
lore.archaeology: No temple, sanctuary, or civic cult of Hyperíōn is securely attested anywhere in the Greek world; Pausanias, who records altars of such Titans as Kronos and Iapetus, offers him no shrine. He was honoured, if at all, within the cult of his son Hēlios — above all at Rhodes, where the Sun received a major state cult and the great bronze Colossus — so his archaeological trace survives only folded into his children's worship. His monument is textual rather than stone: the name that Homer and Hesiod carved into the language of light.
lore.syncretism: Rome produced no native Hyperion; the Titan travelled into Latin letters chiefly as a learned name for the sun itself, the Hesiodic father and the Homeric epithet collapsing into one solar word in the poets. Hyginus still lists him soberly among the Titans born of Earth and Sky (Fabulae, praefatio), but in later epic usage 'Hyperion' rides the sky in place of Sol. What survived of him in the West was thus not a cult but a word — the most elevated name Latin poetry knew for the sun.

pronunciation.approximation: 'LAY-toh' — hold the first vowel long like 'lay' without the off-glide, and let the final 'oh' carry a gentle rise-and-fall pitch.
pronunciation.note: Lētō is Tier 1: the Greek original contains both length (ē and ō) and the circumflex pitch contour. The English 'Leto' preserves neither.

domains.title: Mother of the Divine Twins
domains.subtitle: Night, Refuge, and the Letoön
domains.lead: Lētō is the mother of Apollo and Artemis, pursued across land and sea by Hera's jealousy, and at last given refuge by the floating island of Delos. She is the goddess of the hidden journey, the patience of motherhood, and the sanctuary that becomes holy because it sheltered the gods.

cards.name: Mother of Twins
cards.desc: She bore Apollo and Artemis, the archer gods of light and wilderness.

cards.name: Refugee Goddess
cards.desc: Hera denied her a fixed birthplace; Delos alone offered sanctuary.

cards.name: Letoön
cards.desc: Her great sanctuary near Xanthos in Lycia, shared with her children.

cards.name: Chthonic Mother
cards.desc: Her links to night and Lycian cults give her a darker, older dimension.

symbols.name: Date palm
symbols.meaning: The tree to which Lētō clung while giving birth on Delos.

symbols.name: Wolf
symbols.meaning: The animal associated with Apollo and the wilderness of Lētō's wanderings.

symbols.name: Island
symbols.meaning: Delos, the unstable rock that became fixed because it received the gods.

symbols.name: Bow and lyre
symbols.meaning: The attributes of her children, Apollo and Artemis.

mythology.lead: Lētō's mythology is dominated by one of the most famous birth narratives in Greek religion: the persecution of a pregnant goddess and the founding of a holy island.

myths.title: The Wanderings of Lētō
myths.text: Hera, furious that Zeus had fathered children by Lētō, sent the serpent Pýthōn to pursue her and forbade any land under the sun to receive her. Lētō wandered through many lands until she reached Delos, a barren, floating island. The island trembled at first, fearing Apollo's wrath, but Lētō swore that her son would make it famous and rich. There, clinging to a palm tree, she gave birth first to Artemis and then, with Artemis's help, to Apollo.

myths.title: Latona and the Lycian Peasants
myths.text: In Ovid's version, the thirsty Latona stopped at a Lycian pool to drink. Local peasants stirred the mud to prevent her. In anger she transformed them into frogs, condemning them to croak forever in the mire. The story explains the croaking of frogs and warns against insulting a goddess in need.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lētō's most enduring legacy is Delos itself, one of the most important archaeological sites in Greece and a UNESCO World Heritage centre. Her story of persecution and sanctuary also resonates in later narratives of divine mothers and exiled queens. The name Leto appears in literature and astronomy, while her Roman form Latona adorns fountains and gardens across Europe.
lore.syncretism: The Romans knew Lētō as Latona, and her cult spread through Italy with that of Apollo. In Lycia she was identified with a local mother goddess, Lada, and the Letoon became a centre of syncretic worship. Later European art remembered her chiefly through the story of Latona and the Lycian peasants, a favourite subject of Baroque painters exploring divine wrath and metamorphosis.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Λητώ. The first vowel is eta (ē), long [eː]; the final omega (ō) is long [ɔː] with a circumflex accent indicating a falling pitch on a long vowel. The Roman form Latona loses both the vowel length and the pitch contour. PUNICODEX restores Lētō with the macron on ē and the circumflex on ō, since the full Greek breathing marks are not registrable.

steps: The Greek form Ἡρακλῆς is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Hēraklēs encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: "hay-RAH-KLAYS" — first syllable deeper and longer than English 'hay'; the final syllable is held and falls in pitch, like 'klays' sung on a descending note.
pronunciation.note: Hēraklēs is Tier 1 because Classical Attic Ἡρακλῆς contains both length (long η in the first and final syllables) and stress (circumflex on the final -klēs). The registrable form Hēraklēs preserves length with macrons; the acute/circumflex is omitted because fully accented Greek letters are often untypeable and are not reliably registrable as IDN labels. Reconstruction follows Allen, Vox Graeca: The Pronunciation of Classical Greek, 3rd ed. (Cambridge, 1987); LSJ; and Beekes, Etymological Dictionary of Greek (Brill, 2010).

domains.title: Glory Through Suffering
domains.subtitle: Strength, Labours, and Apotheosis
domains.lead: Hēraklēs is the greatest of Greek heroes and the only one to become a full Olympian god. His very name means "Glory of Hera," yet Hera persecuted him from the cradle, driving him to madness and murder. His life is a sequence of impossible tasks performed under duress: the Twelve Labours, the conquest of monsters, the rescue of captives, and finally a death by fire that turned into immortality.

cards.name: The Twelve Labours
cards.desc: Imposed by Eurystheus at Hera's prompting: the Nemean lion, Lernaean hydra, Ceryneian hind, Erymanthian boar, Augean stables, Stymphalian birds, Cretan bull, mares of Diomedes, girdle of Hippolyta, cattle of Geryon, apples of the Hesperides, and Kerberos from Hades.

cards.name: Divine Strength
cards.desc: Son of Zeús by Alkmēnē, he possesses strength beyond mortality from infancy; as a baby he strangled the serpents Hera sent against him.

cards.name: Madness and Atonement
cards.desc: Hera's frenzy made him kill his wife Megara and their children; the Delphic oracle sentenced him to serve Eurystheus, transforming violence into labour.

cards.name: Apotheosis
cards.desc: Poisoned by the blood of the centaur Nessus, he mounted a funeral pyre on Mount Oeta; from the flames he ascended to Olympus and married Hebe.

symbols.name: Club
symbols.meaning: His primary weapon, cut from wild olive on Mount Helicon

symbols.name: Lion skin
symbols.meaning: The impenetrable pelt of the Nemean lion, his first labour

symbols.name: Bow
symbols.meaning: The gift of Apollo, used against the Stymphalian birds and Geryon

symbols.name: The Pillars
symbols.meaning: The western boundary of the world, sometimes said to bear the inscription 'Non plus ultra'

symbols.name: Golden apples
symbols.meaning: The fruit of the Hesperides, retrieved in his eleventh labour

mythology.lead: Hēraklēs's mythology is enormous and contradictory, preserved in epic, lyric, tragedy, and handbook. What holds it together is the figure of a mortal strong enough to challenge gods and monsters, yet vulnerable enough to weep, rage, and die.

myths.title: A Hero Foretold
myths.text: Hesiod already knows Hēraklēs as the hero who will settle the conflict between gods and Giants. In the Theogony (950–955), he appears as the son of Zeús and Alkmēnē, destined to bring order to a world still threatened by chthonic powers. His name, "Glory of Hera," is an irony: the queen of the gods is his enemy long before she is reconciled.

myths.title: The Lion, the Hydra, and the Boar
myths.text: The first labour required Hēraklēs to strangle the Nemean lion, whose hide no weapon could pierce; he wore its pelt ever after. The second pitted him against the Lernaean hydra, a many-headed water-serpent whose severed heads multiplied; Iolaos cauterized the stumps while Hēraklēs struck off the immortal head. The fourth labour brought the Erymanthian boar alive to Eurystheus, a comic image of the terrified king hiding in a storage jar.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hēraklēs never left Western culture. The Roman Hercules gave us the word herculean; his Twelve Labours remain the archetype of the heroic quest, reused from medieval romance to modern video games. The constellation Hercules still dominates the northern summer sky. Renaissance and Baroque artists painted his choice between Virtue and Vice; Disney and Marvel recast him as a family-friendly strongman. Bodybuilding culture, military units, and even NASA have claimed his name. More deeply, Hēraklēs is the type of the suffering hero whose glory is earned through pain — a figure who answers the ancient question of how a mortal can matter in a world ruled by gods.
lore.archaeology: Thebes claimed Hēraklēs's birth and held games in his honor. Mycenaean Tiryns and Thebes have yielded palace remains that later Greeks associated with his legends. Nemea preserves the cave of the Nemean lion and the stadium of the Nemean Games. Olympia's Temple of Zeus displayed the Twelve Labours in its metopes. Athens maintained a prominent Herakleion and depicted him with Theseus on vase paintings. Mount Oeta in Thessaly was the traditional site of his funeral pyre and apotheosis.
lore.syncretism: The Greeks themselves identified Hēraklēs with foreign heroes and gods. Herodotus (2.42–45) argues that the Greek Heracles is the youngest of three figures bearing the name: an Egyptian god, a Phoenician hero identified with Melqart, and the Greek son of Alcmene. The Phoenician Melqart of Tyre, worshipped from Spain to the Levant, was the closest parallel: a god of civic protection, colonization, and annual death-and-rebirth rituals. The Romans made him Hercules and emphasized his civilizing labors; his cult was among the earliest Greek imports to Italy. In Egypt he was sometimes identified with Khonsu or Heryshaf. Through Stoic and Cynic philosophy he became the model of virtuous endurance — the hero who chooses the difficult path of excellence.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Greek as Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklēs), composed of Ἥρᾱ (Hḗrā, 'Hera') and κλέος (kléos, 'glory'). The registrable form Hēraklēs marks both long eta vowels with macrons and omits the final circumflex for DNS compatibility. The result preserves the two length features that make the name Tier 1 while remaining typeable as an internationalized domain label.

etymology.derivation: From Greek ἔρως, derived from the verb ἔραμαι / ἐράω 'to love, desire'; the further Indo-European etymology is uncertain.

steps: The Greek form Ἔρως is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Érōs encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: "EH-ross" — the accent falls on the first syllable; the o of the second is held longer than English allows, deep and sustained.
pronunciation.note: Érōs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἔρως contains both stress (acute on the initial epsilon) and length (the long omega). The acute on the initial É preserves the stress, while the macron on the final ō preserves the long vowel. The name is the full scholarly form of the force that moves the cosmos.

domains.title: Desire
domains.subtitle: Attraction, Union, Cosmic Motion
domains.lead: Érōs is not merely romance. He is the attraction that makes things move toward each other: fire upward, water downward, god toward mortal, atom toward atom. In the earliest Greek cosmogonies, Érōs is a primordial power; only later does he become the mischievous child of Aphrodite.

cards.name: The Bow
cards.desc: His weapon makes the limbs go slack and the mind unmade; no god or mortal is immune.

cards.name: Wings
cards.desc: Desire is swift and sudden; it arrives before reason can arrange a defense.

cards.name: The Heart Aflame
cards.desc: The fire of longing — physical, spiritual, cosmic.

cards.name: The Rose
cards.desc: Flower of Aphrodite and Érōs; beauty that wounds as it invites.

symbols.name: Bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: The sudden wound of desire

symbols.name: Wings
symbols.meaning: The speed and inconstancy of longing

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: Illumination and the burning of the heart

symbols.name: Rose
symbols.meaning: Beauty and the thorn of love

symbols.name: Heart
symbols.meaning: The seat of emotion and the target of the god

mythology.lead: Érōs stands at the beginning in Hesiod and at the margins in Homer. He is one of the oldest gods, yet his stories are few — because his power is everywhere.

myths.title: Fourth of the Primordials
myths.text: Hesiod places Érōs fourth in the procession of being: after Cháos, Gaia, and Tartarus, but before the children of Night. "He is the most beautiful among the immortal gods," Hesiod writes, "he makes the limbs go limp and overcomes the intelligence and prudent counsel in the breasts of all gods and men" (Theogony 120–122).

myths.title: First of All
myths.text: The pre-Socratic philosopher Parmenides made Érōs the first of all gods to come into being — not a child of Aphrodite but the primal force of attraction that organizes reality. In this philosophical reading, love is not an emotion; it is a cosmological principle.

lore.culturalLegacy: Érōs is one of the most productive words in European languages: "erotic," "erogenous." He appears on Valentine's cards, in pop songs, in perfume advertisements, and in psychoanalytic theory. The image of the winged child with a bow — Cupid — is one of the most recognizable figures in Western art. Yet the archaic Érōs was more formidable: a beautiful young man who could unmake kings and gods. To restore the name Érōs with its long omega is to remember that desire is not trivial; it is one of the forces that turns the world.
lore.archaeology: Numerous red-figure and black-figure vases depict Eros as a winged youth or child; the so-called Erotes appear on wedding vessels and funerary reliefs. No major sanctuary, but the Erotes were honored in gymnasia and private devotion.
lore.syncretism: The Roman Cupido inherited Érōs's arrows and wings but gradually shrank from a handsome youth into a plump, blindfolded infant — the Renaissance putto. In Plato's Symposium, Érōs is redefined as the longing for beauty and the ladder from physical desire to the Form of the Good. For the Stoics, Érōs was a natural affinity (oikeiōsis) that binds the cosmos. Freud divided the psyche into Eros and Thanatos, life-drive and death-drive, making the Greek god the name of everything in us that seeks connection, pleasure, and life.

etymology.derivation: From Ἥλιος "sun", cognate with Latin sol, English sun. The solar charioteer.

steps: The Greek form Ἥλιος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Hēlios encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'HAY-lee-oss' — the first syllable rises like the sun; the rest is bright and clear.
pronunciation.note: Hēlios is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἥλιος carries both stress (the acute on the first syllable) and a long vowel (the initial η). The name is built on the same root as English 'sun' and Latin 'sol,' one of the most ancient theonyms in the Indo-European family.

domains.title: The Sun
domains.subtitle: Light, Sight, Oaths, and the Chariot of Day
domains.lead: Hēlios is the sun itself: a god who sees everything and drives his blazing chariot across the sky each day. Nothing hidden escapes him, and mortals and gods alike swear oaths by his light.

cards.name: The Chariot of the Sun
cards.desc: He rises from Oceanus in the east, crosses the sky, and descends into the western sea.

cards.name: All-Seeing Witness
cards.desc: He sees everything on earth; oaths sworn in his name are binding because he cannot be deceived.

cards.name: Revealer of Secrets
cards.desc: He exposed Aphrodítē's affair with Árēs to Hēphaistos; he told Demeter of Persephone's abduction.

cards.name: Healer and Life-Giver
cards.desc: His warmth makes crops grow and bodies live; his withdrawal is winter and death.

symbols.name: Chariot
symbols.meaning: The vehicle that carries the sun across the sky

symbols.name: Winged sun disk
symbols.meaning: The sun as a flying radiant power

symbols.name: Crown of rays
symbols.meaning: The projecting beams of light

symbols.name: Horse
symbols.meaning: The horses of his chariot, often named Pyrois, Eous, Aethon, and Phlegon

symbols.name: Whip
symbols.meaning: His control over the solar horses

symbols.name: Globe or disk
symbols.meaning: The sun itself

mythology.lead: Hēlios's myths all depend on his unique vantage point: he sees everything. This makes him a witness, a revealer, and occasionally a victim of his own children's ambition.

myths.title: Across the Sky and Through Oceanus
myths.text: Each dawn Hēlios rises from Oceanus in the east, drawn by four horses in a chariot of fire. At midday he sees the entire world spread below him. In the evening he sinks into the western Ocean, where he is received in a golden cup and conveyed back to the east. The Homeric Hymn to Helios (1–14) describes this journey as the source of all life and growth.

myths.title: The Exposure of Ares and Aphrodite
myths.text: In Odyssey 8.266–366, Hēlios sees Árēs and Aphrodítē committing adultery in Hēphaistos's house and reports it to the cuckolded smith. Hēphaistos then traps the lovers in a net. The episode shows that Hēlios is not merely a celestial body but a moral witness; nothing done in daylight is hidden from him.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hēlios is the namesake of heliocentrism, helium, and countless words for sunlight. The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, was a giant statue of Hēlios. His crown of rays influenced depictions of Christ as 'Sol Invictus' and the halo in Christian art. In modern culture, the sun god remains a symbol of clarity, revelation, and dangerous power. Restoring Hēlios restores the original Greek name of the star that makes life possible.
lore.archaeology: Rhodes: the Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue of the Sun some seventy cubits high, sculpted by Chares of Lindos (Pliny, NH 34.41); one of the Seven Wonders until an earthquake brought it down in 226 BCE.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Hēlios with Sol, though Apollo increasingly absorbed solar attributes in both Greek and Roman religion. The emperor Aurelian made Sol Invictus the official patron of the Roman Empire in 274 CE, and the cult influenced the dating of Christmas. In Hellenistic Egypt, Hēlios was syncretized with Osiris and with the Egyptian sun god Ra as a universal deity. Neoplatonists saw Hēlios as the visible image of the One. The heliocentric model of Copernicus gave Hēlios's name a scientific afterlife: the sun, not the earth, is the center.

etymology.derivation: From σελήνη "moon", from σέλας "light, brightness". The moon goddess.

steps: The Greek form Σελήνη is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Selēnē encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'seh-LAY-nay' — the second syllable carries the pitch, and the final vowel is long and pale.
pronunciation.note: Selḗnē is Tier 1 because the Greek Σελήνη contains both stress (acute on the short έ) and length (long η in the final syllable). The name shares a root with 'shine' across Indo-European languages.

domains.title: The Moon
domains.subtitle: Night, Cycles, Magic, and Sleep
domains.lead: Selḗnē is the moon personified: a goddess who drives her silver chariot through the night, governs the menstrual cycle, and presides over dreams and magic. Where Hēlios reveals, Selḗnē conceals and transforms.

cards.name: The Silver Chariot
cards.desc: She crosses the night sky in a chariot drawn by oxen or horses, the counterpart to Hēlios's golden car.

cards.name: Cycles and Time
cards.desc: The month is hers; she governs menstruation, tides, planting, and ritual calendars.

cards.name: Dreams and Magic
cards.desc: Hecate's ally; witches draw down the moon to work spells and send dreams.

cards.name: The Lover
cards.desc: She fell in love with the shepherd Endymion and put him to eternal sleep so he would not age.

symbols.name: Crescent moon
symbols.meaning: Her boat or bow; the waxing and waning phases

symbols.name: Silver chariot
symbols.meaning: The lunar vehicle

symbols.name: Oxen
symbols.meaning: The animals that draw her chariot

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: The pale light she carries through darkness

symbols.name: Veil
symbols.meaning: The clouds that obscure and reveal her

symbols.name: Sleeping Endymion
symbols.meaning: Eternal youth preserved by moonlight

mythology.lead: Selḗnē's myths are fewer than Hēlios's because the night was less personified in Greek poetry. Her most famous story is a love affair with a mortal.

myths.title: Endymion on Mount Latmus
myths.text: Selḗnē fell in love with Endymion, a beautiful shepherd or king, and asked Zeús to grant him eternal youth. Zeüs put him into eternal sleep in a cave on Mount Latmus in Caria. Each night Selḗnē visits him; some say their union produced fifty daughters. The myth turns the moon's monthly return into a romantic rendezvous and makes sleep the price of immortality.

myths.title: The Moon's Journey
myths.text: Like Hēlios, Selḗnē drives a chariot across the sky. The Homeric Hymn to Selene (1–7) describes her as 'winged' and 'golden-crowned,' driving her chariot through the night while Hēlios rests. The moon's pale light is her garment; her crown marks her as a queen of heaven.

lore.culturalLegacy: Selḗnē is the archetype of the moon as feminine, cyclical, and magical. She governs not only the night sky but the rhythms of women's bodies and the agricultural calendar. The crescent moon remains one of humanity's most universal symbols, appearing on flags, coins, and religious iconography across cultures. In modern witchcraft and Neopaganism, the moon goddess — whether called Selene, Diana, or Hecate — is central. Restoring Selḗnē restores the Greek name of the moon as a conscious, luminous presence.
lore.archaeology: Reliefs and gems from the Hellenistic and Roman periods show Selene as a winged or chariot-borne goddess with a crescent moon at her brow; the Great Altar of Pergamon includes a Luna/Selene figure. In Elis, Pausanias records a sanctuary of Selene/Sosipolis. Roman marble statues such as the 'Selene and Endymion' group (British Museum) and crescent-moon crowns on imperial coins and Isiac reliefs attest her later astral cult.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Selḗnē with Luna, though as with Hēlios/Sol, the Greek goddess was increasingly absorbed by Artemis-Diana in later periods. In Hellenistic and Roman Egypt, Selḗnē was syncretized with Isis, who wears a lunar disk on her head. Neoplatonists saw the moon as the boundary between the material and immaterial realms, and Selḗnē as the mediator between Hēlios and the earth. The English words 'selenography' (study of the moon's surface) and the chemical element selenium derive from her name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AY-ohss' — two long syllables, the first level, the second pitched and sustained like the rising sun.
pronunciation.note: Ēōs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἠώς contains two long syllables, the second carrying the acute/circumflex. The name is one of the most securely reconstructed Indo-European divine names.

domains.title: The Rose-Fingered Goddess
domains.subtitle: Dawn, Morning Light, New Beginnings
domains.lead: Ēōs is the goddess of dawn, daughter of Hyperion and Theía, sister of Hēlios and Selēnē. Each morning she rises from the sea in a saffron robe and opens the gates of day, scattering light across the world.

cards.name: Bringer of Day
cards.desc: She opens the gates of heaven so Hēlios can ride his chariot across the sky.

cards.name: Rose-Fingered
cards.desc: The Homeric epithet rhododáktylos describes the red light of early morning touching the world.

cards.name: Lover of Mortals
cards.desc: She abducted Tithonos, Kephalos, and Orion, loving mortals whose fates ended in grief.

cards.name: Saffron Robe
cards.desc: She wears the golden-red robe of morning light across sea and mountain.

symbols.name: Saffron or rosy light
symbols.meaning: The color of the dawn sky and her garments

symbols.name: Wings or winged chariot
symbols.meaning: Her swift passage across the horizon

symbols.name: The morning star
symbols.meaning: The last star visible as she rises

symbols.name: Tithonos turning into a cicada
symbols.meaning: The emblem of her failed request for his immortality without youth

mythology.lead: Ēōs is beautiful and inconsolable. Her myths turn on love for mortals and the tragedy of asking the gods for the wrong gift.

myths.title: Tithonos and the Cicada
myths.text: Ēōs loved the Trojan prince Tithonos and asked Zeus to grant him immortality. She forgot to ask for eternal youth. Tithonos aged endlessly, shrinking until he became a cicada, whose chirping is the sound of immortal old age. The myth is a meditation on the limits of divine gifts.

myths.title: The Abduction of Kephalos
myths.text: Ēōs abducted the handsome hunter Kephalos and bore him a son, Phaethon. In some versions she later restores him to his wife Prokris, but the damage is done: suspicion and a tragic hunting accident destroy the marriage.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ēōs lives in every image of dawn breaking, every 'rosy-fingered' sunrise in literature, and the scientific name Eos for certain bright birds. She is the goddess of fresh starts — and of the grief that fresh starts cannot undo. Her failed gift to Tithonos remains one of mythology's sharpest warnings: be careful what you ask for, even from the gods.
lore.archaeology: Ēōs was represented in Greek vase painting and sculpture as a winged woman driving a chariot or rising from the sea. She appears on red-figure vases departing from the bed of Tithonos and abducting Kephalos. Roman sarcophagi and mosaics continued the imagery under the name Aurora. No major Panhellenic sanctuary was dedicated solely to her.
lore.syncretism: The Romans called her Aurora and kept most of her Greek iconography. The Greek-Roman Eos-Aurora influenced later personifications of dawn in European poetry and art. Her Indo-European cognates include Sanskrit Uṣás and Lithuanian Aušrinė, suggesting an ancient shared dawn-goddess. Christian tradition transformed her into the herald of the resurrection morning.

etymology.derivation: Greek Θησεύς, popularly derived from τίθημι 'to set, to place'; the Athenian hero who slew the Minotaur and unified Attica.

pronunciation.approximation: 'THESEUS' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
pronunciation.note: Thēseus is Tier 1 because the Greek form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

domains.title: Heroism
domains.subtitle: Heroism, Athens, Labours
domains.lead: Thēseus belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is associated with heroism, athens, labours.

cards.name: Heroism
cards.desc: The central domain of Thēseus in the greek tradition.

cards.name: The Gatherer (from τίθημι)
cards.desc: The name signifies "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)".

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The restoration Thēseus recovers what plain ASCII theseus flattens.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Attested in the sources as Θησεύς.

symbols.name: Restored Name
symbols.meaning: The Unicode form Thēseus carries the original marks of the Greek tradition.

symbols.name: Source Script
symbols.meaning: Attested in the original script as Θησεύς.

symbols.name: Domain
symbols.meaning: Heroism, Athens, Labours

symbols.name: Etymology
symbols.meaning: The Gatherer (from τίθημι)

mythology.lead: The stories of Thēseus circulate within the Greek corpus, where the figure embodies heroism, athens, labours.

myths.title: Primary Attestation
myths.text: Thēseus is attested in the canonical Greek sources as a figure associated with heroism, athens, labours.

myths.title: Name and Meaning
myths.text: The name means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition.

lore.culturalLegacy: Thēseus continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Greek tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.
lore.archaeology: Thēseus is attested in the textual and iconographic record of the Greek tradition.
lore.syncretism: Thēseus appears within the Greek tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.

etymology.derivation: Memory (from μνήμη)

pronunciation.approximation: 'mneh-MOH-see-nee' — the first syllable is like 'mneh', the stress falls on the third syllable, and both long vowels are held.
pronunciation.note: Mnēmosýnē is Tier 1: the Greek original contains both length (ē) and acute stress (ý), making it the fullest scholarly restoration. The English 'Mnemosyne' flattens the vowels.

domains.title: Mother of Memory
domains.subtitle: Memory, the Muses, and the Waters of Remembrance
domains.lead: Mnēmosýnē is the personification of memory and the mother of the nine Muses. Without her, there is no poetry, no history, no law, no song. She is the deep reservoir from which all the arts draw, and the spring from which the initiates of the mysteries drink so that they may remember their divine origin after death.

cards.name: Mother of Muses
cards.desc: She and Zeus produced the nine Muses, each presiding over an art or science.

cards.name: Memory Divine
cards.desc: Memory is not merely human recollection but the cosmic retention of all that is.

cards.name: Mystery Spring
cards.desc: Initiates drank from her spring to remember the soul's divine past.

cards.name: Fountain of Song
cards.desc: Poets invoked her so that language would not fail at the moment of making.

symbols.name: Spring or fountain
symbols.meaning: The waters of memory from which the dead must drink.

symbols.name: Book or tablet
symbols.meaning: The written record that preserves what time would erase.

symbols.name: Lamp
symbols.meaning: The light that keeps memory visible in darkness.

symbols.name: Laurel
symbols.meaning: The crown of the poet whose work depends on her gift.

mythology.lead: Mnēmosýnē's myths are few because her function is everywhere. She is the ground of narrative itself.

myths.title: Nine Nights with Zeus
myths.text: Hesiod tells how Zeus lay with Mnēmosýnē for nine consecutive nights in Pieria. From this union came the nine Muses, each bearing a province of the arts. The very number of nights corresponds to the months of gestation, as if memory itself must be incubated before it can give birth to song.

myths.title: The Waters of Memory
myths.text: In Orphic gold tablets buried with the dead, the soul is instructed to avoid the spring of Lēthē (Forgetfulness) and to drink instead from the spring of Mnēmosýnē. By remembering its divine nature, the soul is freed from the cycle of rebirth. Memory, in this tradition, is the key to salvation.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mnēmosýnē lives in every museum (from mouseion, 'place of the Muses') and every act of remembrance. She is invoked at funerals, in national memorials, and in the simple act of telling a story. The word 'mnemonic' derives from her name. In a culture of accelerating forgetting, Mnēmosýnē is the guardian of continuity: she asks us not to let the past dissolve.
lore.syncretism: Roman poets identified Mnēmosýnē with Moneta, a title of Juno associated with memory and warning. In the Renaissance she merged with the art of memory, the mnemonic technique by which orators stored speeches in imagined buildings. Modern psychology and neuroscience have taken over the empirical study of memory, but Mnēmosýnē remains the ancient name for the mystery that makes identity possible: the fact that we can recall who we are.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Greek is Μνημοσύνη, from μνήμη ('memory'). The initial Mn- cluster is characteristic of Greek words for memory and remembrance. The first and final vowels are long eta (ē), and the stress falls on the antepenult with the acute on -sý-. PUNICODEX writes Mnēmosýnē with macrons on the long vowels and the acute accent, since the full Greek alphabet is not registrable.

etymology.derivation: Possibly from ἄρκτος "bear" + suffix, or pre-Greek. Mistress of animals (potnia theron).

steps: The Greek form Ἄρτεμις is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Ártemis encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'AR-te-miss' — the first syllable is sharp and high; the name is quick, like the arrow she looses.
pronunciation.note: Ártemis is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄρτεμις preserves stress (acute on the first alpha) but no long vowel. She is the most important single-tier Tier-2 deity in the Greek pantheon: her acute alone carries the entire prosodic signature of the huntress's cry.

domains.title: The Mistress of Animals
domains.subtitle: Hunt, Wilderness, the Moon, and Childbirth
domains.lead: Ártemis is Apóllōn's twin but his opposite. Where he imposes order, she preserves wildness. She is the huntress who protects the animals she kills, the virgin who oversees childbirth, the goddess of the liminal space between city and forest, child and adult, human and beast.

cards.name: The Hunt
cards.desc: She ranges mountains and forests with her nymphs, bringing sudden death to prey and hunters alike.

cards.name: Wilderness and Liminal Space
cards.desc: Marshes, groves, and mountain passes are hers; she guards the boundary between the tamed and the untamed.

cards.name: Childbirth
cards.desc: As Lochia and Kourotrophos, she eases birth and protects the young — despite her own eternal virginity.

cards.name: The Moon
cards.desc: Later tradition identifies her with Selene; her silver bow becomes the crescent moon.

symbols.name: Bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: The hunt and sudden, unpitying death

symbols.name: Deer
symbols.meaning: Her sacred animal and the prey she protects

symbols.name: Cypress
symbols.meaning: The tree of mourning and the wild grove

symbols.name: Crescent moon
symbols.meaning: Later symbol of her lunar aspect

symbols.name: Hunting dogs
symbols.meaning: Her companions in the chase

symbols.name: Bear
symbols.meaning: The arktoi — young girls who served her at Brauron as bears

mythology.lead: Ártemis's myths are almost all about the protection of boundaries — between virgin and sexual, wild and civilized, mortal and divine. Those who cross them pay terribly.

myths.title: Born on Ortygia
myths.text: Ártemis was born to Lētô after the goddess wandered the earth under Hêra's curse. The Homeric Hymn to Apollo places her birth on Ortygia — Delos bore Apóllōn, and Ortygia Ártemis — and the tradition recorded by Apollodorus (1.4.1) makes her the elder twin, born first and then helping to deliver her brother: the virgin goddess of childbirth from her first hour. The island that sheltered Apóllōn became one of the most sacred places in the Aegean.

myths.title: Actaeon Torn Apart
myths.text: The hunter Actaeon stumbled upon Ártemis bathing with her nymphs. In punishment, she transformed him into a stag, and his own hounds tore him apart. The myth is a stark boundary marker: the wild goddess cannot be seen by the male gaze. Some later writers blame Actaeon's hubris, others his bad luck; all agree the penalty is absolute.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ártemis is the archetype of the independent, untamable feminine power. Her sanctuary at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World; its many-breasted statue became an icon of nature's abundance. The Brauronia festival, in which young Athenian girls served as 'bears' in her sanctuary before marriage, was a central rite of female initiation. In modern environmentalism, Ártemis is a patron of wilderness preservation and animal rights. Her bow remains a symbol of focused, lethal skill. Restoring Ártemis restores the name of the goddess who refuses to be domesticated.
lore.archaeology: Ephesus: Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders. Brauron: sanctuary of Artemis Brauronia and the arktoi rite. Delos: shared birthplace sanctuary.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Ártemis with Diana, a goddess of the hunt and the moon who was also patron of the Latin crossroads and the underworld. Diana's cult at Aricia, with its sacred grove and priest-king the Rex Nemorensis, became one of the most famous in Italy. In Hellenistic and Roman Egypt, Ártemis was syncretized with Bastet and other lunar goddesses. The crescent crown of the Virgin Mary in Byzantine and Renaissance art may owe something to the iconography of Ártemis-Diana. Modern Wicca and Neopaganism have made her one of the most widely invoked goddesses of feminine autonomy and wild nature.

etymology.derivation: Enduring, suffering (from τλάω)

steps: The Greek form Ἄτλας is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Átlas encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'AT-lass' — the first syllable is pitched high, as if lifting; the second is level and heavy.
pronunciation.note: Átlas is Tier 2 because the Greek Ἄτλας preserves stress (acute on the first alpha) but no long vowel. The name's short, heavy sound mimics the burden it describes: a single pitched syllable followed by the weight of the final syllable.

domains.title: The Bearer of Heaven
domains.subtitle: Strength, Endurance, Astronomy, and the Western Edge
domains.lead: Átlas is the Titan who holds up the sky. He is not a villain but a defeated rebel, condemned to bear the celestial sphere on his shoulders for eternity. His endurance becomes a kind of heroism: he does not triumph, but he does not collapse.

cards.name: The Celestial Sphere
cards.desc: He holds the sky aloft, keeping heaven and earth apart so that the cosmos can exist.

cards.name: Endurance
cards.desc: His punishment is eternal labor; his virtue is that he endures it without complaint.

cards.name: Astronomy
cards.desc: He knows the stars; his daughters the Hesperides tend the garden of the western sky.

cards.name: The Western Boundary
cards.desc: He stands at the edge of the known world, where the sun sets and the ocean begins.

symbols.name: Celestial sphere
symbols.meaning: The heavens he supports

symbols.name: Pillars
symbols.meaning: The Pillars of Herakles, once called the Pillars of Atlas

symbols.name: Globe
symbols.meaning: Later iconographic fusion of the sky and earth

symbols.name: Book or scroll
symbols.meaning: His astronomical knowledge

symbols.name: Apples of the Hesperides
symbols.meaning: The golden apples guarded by his daughters

symbols.name: Bent posture
symbols.meaning: The weight of the cosmos on his shoulders

mythology.lead: Átlas belongs to the older generation of gods. His myths are few because he is fixed in place, but his presence shapes the geography and cosmology of the Greek world.

myths.title: Leader of the Titans
myths.text: Átlas was one of the leading Titans in the war against Zeús and the Olympians. When the Titans were defeated, Zeús singled him out for the heaviest punishment: he must hold up the sky for all time. Other Titans were imprisoned in Tartaros; Átlas was given a task that required constant, conscious effort. His punishment is a form of forced usefulness.

myths.title: The Hesperides
myths.text: Átlas's daughters, the Hesperides, guarded a garden at the western edge of the world where a tree bore golden apples. One of Heraklēs' labors was to fetch these apples. In some versions Heraklēs took the burden temporarily from Átlas's shoulders while the Titan fetched the apples; in others Heraklēs tricked him into resuming the burden. The garden is the furthest place, where day ends and the marvelous begins.

lore.culturalLegacy: Átlas is the archetype of the burden-bearer. The image of a giant holding up the world is one of the most enduring in Western art and literature. Ayn Rand used his name for her novel Atlas Shrugged, giving him a modern political meaning. In astronomy, the Titan's association with the celestial sphere made him a patron of stargazers and mapmakers. The word 'atlas' is now universal. Restoring Átlas restores the name of the being whose endurance holds the sky in place.
lore.archaeology: The Farnese Atlas in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples (inv. 6374), is a Roman copy of a Hellenistic statue holding a celestial globe; it preserves the oldest complete representation of Greek constellations. The Temple of Zeus at Olympia (ca. 470–456 BCE) displayed a metope of Heracles receiving the apples from Atlas. Numismatic and sculptural images from Roman North Africa identified the Atlas Mountains with the Titan's petrified body.
lore.syncretism: Átlas had no Roman counterpart; the Romans simply kept his Greek name. In Renaissance and Baroque art he became a symbol of fortitude and cosmological knowledge. The Farnese Atlas, a second-century CE marble statue in Naples, is the oldest surviving representation of the celestial sphere and preserves ancient Greek astronomical data. Cartographers from Mercator onward used Átlas as the frontispiece for atlases, making his name synonymous with geographic knowledge. In modern astronomy, the Atlas Mountains and the lunar crater Atlas (adjacent to the crater Hercules) bear his name, and he appears in science fiction as the archetype of the being who holds up worlds.

etymology.derivation: Anciently analyzed as Διός (genitive of Ζεύς) + Νῦσα, a mythical mountain of ecstasy; the second element is of unknown, probably non-Greek origin.

steps: The Greek form Διόνυσος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Diónysos encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: "dee-OH-nee-soss" — but the "y" is like French "u," and the second syllable carries the ancient pitch rise.
pronunciation.note: Diónysos is Tier 2 because the Greek Διόνυσος preserves only stress (acute on the first omicron), not length. The upsilon remains short, and no macron appears in the standard restoration. The acute on ó marks the pitch peak of a name whose second element may come from beyond Greek itself.

domains.title: The Ecstasy
domains.subtitle: Wine, Theatre, Rebirth
domains.lead: Diónysos is the god who arrives from outside. He comes with wine, with music, with the loss of the self that becomes discovery. He is the foreigner who is already inside you, the madness that heals, the drink that loosens tongues and boundaries alike. Where Apóllōn gives form, Diónysos dissolves it.

cards.name: Wine
cards.desc: The gift of the vine — intoxication, liberation, and the blood of the god in the cup.

cards.name: Theatre
cards.desc: Tragedy and comedy were born in his festivals; the mask is his gift to civilization.

cards.name: The Thyrsus
cards.desc: Fennel-rod tipped with pine cone — the wand of ecstatic procession and vegetative power.

cards.name: The Bull and the Leopard
cards.desc: His animal forms — the bull's strength and the leopard's untamed grace.

symbols.name: Thyrsus
symbols.meaning: Ecstasy, vegetation, and the piercing of ordinary consciousness

symbols.name: Kantharos
symbols.meaning: The deep wine-cup of the mysteries

symbols.name: Leopard
symbols.meaning: The god's triumphal chariot and untamed nature

symbols.name: Ivy and vine
symbols.meaning: Persistence, intoxication, and the green world that reclaims ruins

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: Sacrificial power and the animal vessel of the god

symbols.name: Phallus
symbols.meaning: Fertility, comedy, and generative joy

mythology.lead: Diónysos is born twice, dies once, and comes back everywhere. His myths are stories of arrival — from the east, from the underworld, from the thigh of Zeus — and of the resistance he meets from those who fear losing control.

myths.title: Fire and the Thigh of Zeus
myths.text: Semele, daughter of Cadmus, asked Zeus to reveal himself in his full divine glory. The sight killed her. Zeus snatched the unborn child from her womb and sewed it into his own thigh. Months later, Diónysos was born from Zeus's body — the "twice-born" god. (Homeric Hymn 1, Apollodorus 3.4.3.)

myths.title: Pentheus and Thebes
myths.text: King Pentheus of Thebes refused to recognize the new god. He spied on the maenads and was torn limb from limb by his own mother and aunts, driven mad by Diónysos. Euripides' Bacchae makes the lesson explicit: the god punishes not disbelief, but hubris — the arrogance of thinking oneself separate from the divine.

lore.culturalLegacy: Diónysos gave the West theatre: the Athenian City Dionysia was the festival at which tragedy and comedy were performed. From his maenads come images of ecstatic female power; from his wine, the sacramental cup; from his dismemberment and return, the archetype of the dying-and-rising god. Nietzsche made the "Dionysian" one half of his dialectic with the "Apollonian," naming the irrational, creative, self-dissolving force in art. Modern festivals, carnival, rock concerts, and rave culture all trace some lineage to the god who arrives with drums and torches and changes the city overnight.
lore.archaeology: Thebes was Dionysos's mythic birthplace; German excavations revealed the sanctuary of Dionysos Kadmeios and Kadmeia palace deposits. In Athens, the Theatre of Dionysus Eleuthereus on the south slope of the Acropolis hosted the City Dionysia; nearby stood the temple and choregic monuments such as the Monument of Lysicrates. Delphi's sanctuary included the temple of Apollo but also a precinct of Dionysos, where the god was said to rest in winter.
lore.syncretism: The Romans knew Diónysos as Bacchus or the old Italic Liber, a god of fertility, wine, and the dissolution of social constraints. Egyptian priests identified him with Osiris as a dying-and-rising vegetation deity, though Osiris lacked the ecstatic, theatrical dimension. In Orphism, Diónysos was identified with Zagreus, the dismembered son of Zeus and Persephone, whose body was reassembled to become the god of rebirth. Later Neoplatonists read Diónysos as the principle of procession and return — the soul's descent into multiplicity and its ascent back to unity.

etymology.derivation: Guardian, ruler (from μέδω)

steps: The Greek form Μέδουσα is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Médousa encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: 'MEH-doh-sah' — stress the first syllable, as the Greek acute marks; the middle ου is a long closed 'o' [oː] (a spurious diphthong), not 'oo'.
pronunciation.note: Médousa is Tier 1 because the Greek Μέδουσα carries both stress (the acute on the first syllable) and a long vowel (the diphthong ου). The name means 'Guardian' or 'Queen,' an ironic title for a figure whose gaze turns men to stone.

domains.title: The Gorgon
domains.subtitle: Petrification, Monsters, Death, and the Averted Gaze
domains.lead: Médousa is the most famous monster in Greek myth. Once a beautiful maiden, she was transformed by Athena into a creature whose gaze turns the living to stone. She is the horror of the seen that cannot be looked away from — and the power that heroes must confront indirectly.

cards.name: The Petrifying Gaze
cards.desc: To look directly at her is to become stone — the literal freezing of fear.

cards.name: Snake-Haired Horror
cards.desc: Her hair is a writhing mass of serpents, the uncanny made visible.

cards.name: The Decapitated Head
cards.desc: Perseus cut off her head; Athena placed it on her aegis as an apotropaic weapon.

cards.name: Birth from Blood
cards.desc: From her severed neck sprang Pegasus and Chrysaor — death producing wonder.

symbols.name: Snakes
symbols.meaning: Fear, death, and the chthonic power of the gaze

symbols.name: Gorgoneion
symbols.meaning: The severed head used as an apotropaic emblem

symbols.name: Pegasus
symbols.meaning: The winged horse born from her blood

symbols.name: Stone
symbols.meaning: The transformation her gaze inflicts

symbols.name: Mirror or shield
symbols.meaning: The indirect gaze that defeats her

symbols.name: Athena's aegis
symbols.meaning: The divine armor that incorporates her power

mythology.lead: Médousa's myth is unusual because it has a before and after. She was not always a monster. The story of her transformation makes her both victim and threat.

myths.title: From Maiden to Monster
myths.text: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (4.790–803), Médousa was a maiden famed for her beauty and above all for her hair. Poseidôn raped her in Athena's temple, and Athena, enraged at the desecration of her temple, transformed Médousa's beautiful hair into serpents. The earlier Greek sources (Hesiod, Theogony 270–283) present her as simply one of the Gorgons, daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, without the rape narrative. The Roman version makes her a tragic victim; the Greek version makes her an inherent horror.

myths.title: Perseus and the Head
myths.text: Perseus, sent by Polydectes to fetch the Gorgon's head, used Athena's polished shield as a mirror to approach Médousa without looking directly at her. While she slept, he struck off her head with a sickle given by Hermês. From her neck sprang Pegasus and the warrior Chrysaor. The beheading required divine tools and indirect vision: Médousa can only be defeated by not being seen.

lore.culturalLegacy: Médousa is the most visually recognizable monster in Western art. From Archaic gorgoneia to Caravaggio's Medusa to Versace's logo, her face sells protection, danger, and luxury. Psychologically, she represents the moment when desire turns to stone — the paralysis of fear. In feminist theory, she has become an emblem of the violence done to women and the rage that follows. Restoring Médousa restores the name of the figure who turns the gaze back on itself.
lore.archaeology: The earliest monumental Gorgon, the West Pediment of the Temple of Artemis at Corcyra (Corfu, ca. 580 BCE), shows Medousa in running-kneeling pose between panthers. Temples at Selinunte and Athens used gorgoneia as antefixes and akroteria. The Rondanini Medusa (Munich Glyptothek) and the Medusa Rondanini type preserve a late Classical severed head. Archaic coins from Paros, Neapolis, and Sicily spread the apotropaic Gorgoneion across the Greek world.
lore.syncretism: The Romans adopted Médousa directly, and her image proliferated on shields, mosaics, and architectural elements. In Neoplatonism she became a symbol of the material world that must be transcended — the petrifying gaze of illusion. Freud famously interpreted the Medusa head as a castration symbol, while feminist readings from Hélène Cixous onward have reclaimed her as a figure of female rage and the male fear of the female gaze. Her image persists in fashion, film, and psychology as the archetype of the dangerous woman.

entries.meaning: Youngest Titan, personification of time, who castrated and deposed his father Uranus before being overthrown by his son Zeus

etymology.derivation: Traditionally linked to χρόνος (time), but the etymology is disputed; some connect the Titan’s name to a root meaning "to cut" (referring to the castration of Uranus)

steps: The Greek form Κρόνος is written in the Classical Greek alphabet.
Letters with acute, grave, or circumflex accents preserve the pitch accent of Ancient Greek.
Macrons and omegas (η, ω) mark long vowels, a feature lost in the plain ASCII form.
The Unicode restoration Krónos encodes the scholarly spelling as a registrable domain name.

provenanceSources.title: Chantraine, Dictionnaire étymologique de la langue grecque

pronunciation.approximation: "KROH-nohs" — first syllable like "crow" without the w, second like "nose".
pronunciation.note: Krónos is Tier 2 because the Greek Κρόνος preserves only stress (acute on the first omicron), not length. The name's etymology is disputed; the acute marks the pitch peak, while the short vowels keep the name compact and hard, fitting a god whose story is one of cutting and devouring.

domains.title: The Youngest Titan
domains.subtitle: Harvest, Time, Sovereignty
domains.lead: Krónos is the youngest of the first-generation Titans, but he is the one who acts. He takes the sickle his mother gives him and cuts the sky. He swallows his children to stop time from replacing him. He rules a Golden Age that ends the moment his last son is born.

cards.name: The Sickle
cards.desc: The curved blade with which he castrated Ouranos and took power.

cards.name: The Harvest
cards.desc: The Kronia festival linked him to grain, abundance, and the cycles of the year.

cards.name: The Throne
cards.desc: Kingship over gods and men during the mythic Golden Age.

cards.name: The Devourer
cards.desc: He swallowed his children to prevent the prophecy of his overthrow.

symbols.name: Sickle/Harpe
symbols.meaning: The instrument of usurpation and harvest

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: His association with the old chthonic powers

symbols.name: Golden grain
symbols.meaning: The abundance of the Kronia and the lost Golden Age

symbols.name: Swallowed stone
symbols.meaning: The substitute Rhea gave him for Zeus

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: The searchlight of time that consumes all things

mythology.lead: Krónos is the hinge between the primordial gods and the Olympian order. His myth is the myth of generational succession — the son who overthrows the father and is in turn overthrown.

myths.title: The Castration of Ouranos
myths.text: Ouranos hated the children Gaia bore him and hid them inside her. Gaia fashioned a great stone sickle and persuaded her sons to avenge her. Only Krónos was willing. He ambushed his father and castrated him; from the blood sprang the Erinyes, the Giants, and the Meliae, while the severed genitals, cast into the sea, produced Aphrodítē. (Hesiod, Theogony 154–210.)

myths.title: The Swallowed Children
myths.text: Warned that one of his children would overthrow him, Krónos devoured each infant Rhea bore him: Hestía, Deméter, Hera, Hádes, and Poseidôn. Rhea, grieving, hid Zeus in a Cretan cave and gave Krónos a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes. He swallowed it without looking. (Hesiod, Theogony 453–491; Apollodorus 1.1.5–7.)

lore.culturalLegacy: Krónos haunts Western imagination as Father Time. Goya's Saturn Devouring His Son turned the myth into an image of mortality and madness. The planet Saturn bears his Roman name; Saturday (Saturni dies) is his day. In fantasy and science fiction, "Cronus" and "Kronos" name doomsday weapons, time-travel devices, and tyrant-gods. The sickle became the scythe of Death. Yet the original Krónos was also the lord of a lost age of plenty — a reminder that every devourer was once a generous king.
lore.archaeology: At Olympia the Kronion hill and adjacent precinct were the setting for the Kronia festival; votive deposits from the area include terracotta figurines and dedications to Kronos and Rhea. Pausanias mentions a sanctuary of Kronos at Olympia and an oracle of Ge. In Attica, the Kronia celebrated a temporary social inversion. Roman temples of Saturn on the Capitoline and in the Forum preserve the god's Italic successor.
lore.syncretism: The Romans identified Krónos with Saturnus (Saturn), an old Italic agricultural deity. The confusion with Chronos ("Time") began in Hellenistic and Orphic speculation and became fixed in the Renaissance: Saturn appeared with scythe and hourglass, devouring his children as Time devours the years. The Roman Saturnalia — a December festival of gift-giving, feasting, and social inversion — preserves the Golden Age memory of Krónos. In Near Eastern comparative mythology, the succession myth echoes Hittite and Hurrian tales of Anu, Kumarbi, and the storm-god.

pronunciation.approximation: 'RHAY-ah' — begin with a breathy 'r', stress the middle syllable, and draw out the final 'ah'.
pronunciation.note: Rhéa is Tier 2 because the Greek Ῥέα preserves the acute stress on the second syllable, and nothing more — the final alpha is short, so no single feature-rich restoration exists. She is the great mother of the Olympian generation.

domains.title: Mother of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Mountain, Maternal Cunning
domains.lead: Rhéa is the Titaness who gave birth to the Olympian gods and saved the youngest, Zeus, from being swallowed by his father Kronos. She is the mountain mother, the fertile earth, and the cunning protector of divine succession.

cards.name: Mother of Olympians
cards.desc: By Kronos she bore Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

cards.name: Protector of Zeus
cards.desc: She hid the infant Zeus in a Cretan cave and gave Kronos a stone in swaddling clothes.

cards.name: Mountain Goddess
cards.desc: Worshipped on Crete and in Phrygia as a mother of wild things and mountains.

cards.name: Fertility and Flow
cards.desc: Her name's possible link to 'flow' connects her to springs, milk, and abundance.

symbols.name: Swaddled stone (Omphalos)
symbols.meaning: The substitute she gave Kronos to save Zeus

symbols.name: Cretan cave
symbols.meaning: The hiding place of the infant Zeus on Mount Ida or Dikte

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Her attendant beast in later Cybele-like iconography

symbols.name: Tympanon drum
symbols.meaning: The percussion instrument of ecstatic mountain cults associated with the Great Mother

mythology.lead: Rhéa's myth is the hinge between Titanic and Olympian rule. She endures Kronos's violence, then engineers the survival of the son who will overthrow him.

myths.title: The Swallowed Children
myths.text: Kronos, warned that one of his children would overthrow him, swallowed each infant as Rhea bore them. Rhea wept but was powerless until the birth of Zeus. Then she turned from grieving mother to strategist.

myths.title: The Ruse of the Stone
myths.text: Rhea asked her parents Gē and Ouranos for advice. They sent her to Crete, where she gave birth to Zeus in a hidden cave. She wrapped a great stone in swaddling clothes and presented it to Kronos, who swallowed it unaware. The stone was later set up at Delphi as the omphalos.

lore.culturalLegacy: Rhéa is the mother without whom there is no Olympus. Her courage in saving Zeus made the Olympian order possible. In modern usage her name labels one of Saturn's moons and appears in fantasy and science fiction as a figure of primordial motherhood.
