The goddess of the golden hair needs no rescued glyph; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Earth, Harvest
domains.subtitle: The Golden-Haired Wife of Thor
domains.lead: Sif, the golden-haired wife of [[thor|Þórr]], is one of the quietest figures in the Edda and one of the most consequential. When [[loki|Loki]] sheared off her hair in mischief, Þórr's rage forced the trickster down to the dwarfs — and the forges that answered made not only her new hair of living gold but Gungnir, Skíðblaðnir, Draupnir, Gullinbursti, and Mjölnir itself. Her name is the Old Norse word for kinship-by-marriage, sif, and the corpus keeps her exactly there: the bond at the centre of the thunder-god's house, mother of [[ullr|Ullr]], counted mother of Þrúðr, the one voice in Lokasenna that pours Loki mead and speaks him fair.

cards.name: The Golden Hair
cards.desc: The hair of wrought gold the sons of Ívaldi made for Sif, which grew to her head like living hair — Loki's shearing undone by dwarfish craft, and the seed of every treasure that followed.

cards.name: The Crystal Cup
cards.desc: The cup of ancient mead Sif herself poured for Loki in Ægir's hall, hailing him in the one courteous speech of Lokasenna — answered, as courtesy was there, with slander.

cards.name: Mjölnir from the Wager
cards.desc: The hammer of Þórr, forged by Brokkr and Sindri in the contest Loki set running when he cut Sif's hair — the greatest weapon of the Æsir, born of a theft undone.

cards.name: Ullr, Her Son
cards.desc: The archer on skis, god of the yew-bow, whom Gylfaginning names as Sif's son and Þórr's stepson — proof of a union before the thunder-god, of which the sources say nothing more.

symbols.name: The golden hair
symbols.meaning: Sif's defining attribute — shorn by Loki, remade in living gold by the sons of Ívaldi; read since Grimm as the ripe corn of the harvest field

symbols.name: The crystal cup of mead
symbols.meaning: Her single speech in Lokasenna — hospitality offered to the one guest no one else would serve

symbols.name: Mjölnir
symbols.meaning: The hammer that exists because her hair was cut — the wager's greatest prize

symbols.name: Gungnir and Skíðblaðnir
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's spear and Freyr's ship, made in the same commission that remade her hair — her restoration underwriting the gods' whole arsenal

symbols.name: Þrúðheimr
symbols.meaning: The 'world of strength' where her household stands — the fields of Thrúdheimr, Þórr's realm, her home

mythology.lead: Sif's mythology is short in line-count and enormous in consequence: one act of malice against her sets the forges of the dwarfs to work, and the gods' six greatest treasures come out of the fire. Snorri tells the hair-myth whole; the Poetic Edda gives her two smaller scenes — a cup of mead poured for Loki, and a taunt flung at Þórr across the water — and Gylfaginning names her son. Beyond that the corpus is silent, and the silence is data: the tradition kept her at the centre of Þórr's household and gave her no wars of her own.

myths.title: The Shearing of the Golden Hair
myths.text:
Loki Laufeyjarson, Snorri begins, did this for mischief: he cut off all Sif's hair. When Þórr came home and learned it, he seized Loki and would have broken every bone in him, had Loki not sworn to go to the svartálfar and have them make for Sif a head of hair from gold — hair that would grow like other hair. So Loki went to the dwarfs called the sons of Ívaldi, and they made the hair, and it grew to her head the moment it was set there, as if it were her own.

The episode is told in a handful of sentences, but its logic is exact: the injury is domestic, the redress is craft, and the restitution exceeds the loss. Sif does not speak in her own myth — the shearing, the oath, and the making all happen around her — and the tradition leaves her golden hair standing where nature left the first.

myths.title: The Wager That Forged Mjölnir
myths.text:
The sons of Ívaldi did not stop at the hair: in the same commission they made Gungnir, the spear that never misses, for [[odinn|Óðinn]], and Skíðblaðnir, the best of ships, for [[freyr|Freyr]]. Then Loki wagered his own head with the dwarf Brokkr that Brokkr's brother Sindri could not make three treasures as good. In the forge Sindri laid gold, a boar's hide, and iron in the fire in turn, while Loki, in fly-shape, stung the bellows-worker — and out came Draupnir the dripping ring, Gullinbursti the golden-bristled boar, and Mjölnir, the hammer whose handle came short only because the fly stung Brokkr's eyelid at the last draw.

The Æsir judged Mjölnir the best of all the treasures, because with it the gods have their surest defence against the rime-giants. Loki saved his head on a quibble — his neck was not in the wager — and had his lips sewn up for the pleasure of it. Count the consequence of one shorn head of hair: the spear of Óðinn, the ship of Freyr, the ring, the boar, and the hammer of [[thor|Þórr]] all exist because Sif lost her hair.

lore.culturalLegacy: Sif's afterlife runs on two tracks, one scholarly and one popular. In the scholarly line she is the type-case of the Edda's reticence about goddesses: a figure with no cult record and one great myth, whose golden hair made her, from Grimm onward, the default Germanic corn-goddess of the comparative handbooks, and whose name — plain sif, 'affinity' — became the standing example of a theonym that is simply an abstract noun. In the popular line her golden hair carried her into every Victorian retelling of the gods, and modern popular culture has borrowed her outright — most visibly as the Marvel comics and film character — usually trading the wife of the sources for a swordswoman. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities keep the older reading, hailing her at harvest rites as the golden-haired one, patroness of grain, marriage, and household bonds. And her quietest legacy is lexical: the root of her name lives on in English, unbeknownst to its speakers, in sib, sibling, and gossip — kinship worn down into ordinary speech, which is exactly what her name always meant.
lore.archaeology: Sif is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be securely identified with her — a silence she shares with most of the ásynjur, who appear in verse and prose but rarely, if ever, in dedications. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the two Eddas: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Lokasenna and Hárbarðsljóð, and the Codex Regius and related codices of Snorri's Edda for the Skáldskaparmál hair-myth and the Gylfaginning genealogy that names Ullr her son. No certain place-name contains her name, though the root sif- is bound up with ordinary words for kinship across the Germanic languages; and while the Younger Futhark rendering ᛋᛁᚠ is unambiguous, no Viking-Age carving of the theonym has ever been read. The material afterlife of her myth is real but indirect: the treasures her shearing produced — Mjölnir above all — are among the most depicted objects of the Viking Age, worn as amulets in thousands of graves, so that the consequence of her one great scene is archaeologically everywhere while she herself is nowhere.
lore.syncretism: Sif has attracted exactly one great comparative reading, and it begins with her hair. Jacob Grimm, in the Deutsche Mythologie, took the shearing and the golden regrowth as a nature myth: Sif's hair is the ripe corn, Loki's shearing the harvest or the blight, and the dwarfs' gold the field that grows back golden — a reading that made her a Germanic harvest-goddess beside Demeter and the corn-mothers of folklore, and that matches the way the corpus ties her to Þórr, the farmer's weather-god. Twentieth-century scholarship cooled on the certainty without abandoning the observation: Simek and Turville-Petre note that the sources never call her an earth or harvest goddess, that her name means only 'kinship by marriage', and that the corn-gold reading is interpretation laid over a myth that explains itself well enough as the aetiology of the gods' treasures. The clean statement is the lexicon's own: her sphere in the tradition is the household and its bonds; the harvest is what modern readers, following Grimm, have grown in her golden hair.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Sif — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Lokasenna, Hárbarðsljóð) and the codices of Snorri's Edda — beside the common noun sif (plural sifjar), 'affinity, relation by marriage'. The Viking-Age runic rendering in the Younger Futhark is ᛋᛁᚠ (s-i-f): ᛋ (sól) writes /s/, ᛁ (ís) writes /i/, and ᚠ (fé) writes both /f/ and the voiced fricative the manuscripts spell f — the short-twig row underspecifying nothing that matters here, though no runic attestation of the theonym itself survives. The normalized form is plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — which fixes the name in Tier 2. Because it is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: sif.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.note: Old Norse Fulla is a transparent formation on fullr, 'full' — the same word as English 'full' and German 'voll' — so the name means 'Fullness, Plenty', an abstract noun worn as a personal name, like her sister ásynjur Sjǫfn and Lofn. domains.title: The Keeper of the Casket
domains.subtitle: Abundance, Secrets — the Trusted One of Frigg's Hall
domains.lead: Fulla is Frigg's handmaid and confidante — the virgin goddess who goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head, who carries the queen's little box, looks after her shoes, and shares her secret counsels. Her name is Fullness itself: plenty made a person, trusted with everything a queen cannot carry alone.

cards.name: The Eski
cards.desc: Frigg's little casket, which Fulla carries — the portable treasury of the queen of the gods, and the clearest badge of her office.

cards.name: The Golden Band
cards.desc: The gold snood Fulla wears about her loose hair — Snorri's one detail of dress, and the mark of wealth her name promises.

cards.name: The Queen's Shoes
cards.desc: Fulla looks after Frigg's footwear — the humblest duty in the catalogue, and the surest sign of a servant admitted to every chamber.

cards.name: The Shared Counsels
cards.desc: She shares Frigg's leyniráðagørðir — the queen's secret deliberations: the duty that outranks every object she carries.

symbols.name: The eski (little casket)
symbols.meaning: Frigg's portable treasure-box, entrusted to the hand that never lets it go — custody as a form of intimacy

symbols.name: The golden hair-band
symbols.meaning: The virgin's loose hair bound with gold — unmarried freedom dressed in plenty

symbols.name: Frigg's shoes
symbols.meaning: The queen's footwear in her keeping — the lowest duty held by the highest confidence

symbols.name: The finger-ring from Hel
symbols.meaning: Nanna's gift carried back by Hermóðr — a token from the dead addressed, of all the ásynjur, to her

mythology.lead: Fulla has no saga of her own: her dossier is four precise notices, and every one of them places her at Frigg's side. What the tradition lost in narrative it kept in definition — no goddess in the Edda is more exactly described in a single sentence.

myths.title: The Keeper of the Casket
myths.text: Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur gives Fulla her entire portrait in one sentence, and the tradition never varies it: 'Fulla is a virgin and goes with her hair loose and a golden band about her head; she carries Frigg's eski, looks after her footwear, and shares her secret counsels with her.' The three duties descend in rank and rise in intimacy — the box is treasure, the shoes are service, the counsels are trust itself. She is named immediately after Gná, Frigg's errand-rider, and the pairing has stuck: where Gná carries the queen's words out through the worlds, Fulla keeps the queen's words that never leave the hall. Scholars since Grimm have read both as hypostases of Frigg — aspects of the queen walking about as attendants — but the Edda keeps them as persons, and Fulla's golden band and loose hair make her the most visually fixed of all the minor ásynjur.

myths.title: The Warning to Geirröðr
myths.text: Fulla's one errand in the Poetic Edda is given in prose, at the head of Grímnismál. Óðinn and Frigg had quarrelled over their foster-sons: Frigg accused King Geirröðr, Óðinn's favourite, of being so stingy he tortured his guests for lack of food, and Óðinn laid a wager on his man and set off disguised to test him. Frigg, knowing the road, sent her handmaid Fulla to Geirröðr ahead of him, to warn the king to beware of a certain sorcerer coming to his land to bewitch him — and gave her the token by which he could be known: no dog, however fierce, would leap at him. The warning is the trap: Geirröðr seized the blue-cloaked stranger, named Grímnir, and tortured him between two fires — and out of that fire the god spoke the whole catalogue of the worlds. Fulla appears only to deliver the message and vanish, but the wager, the torture, and the poem's entire revelation turn on her errand.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fulla's afterlife is scholarly and liturgical rather than popular. Grimm devoted a chapter of Teutonic Mythology to her and Volla, and every handbook since — Simek, Orchard, Lindow — keeps her as the standing example of the abstract-noun ásynja, the goddess whose name tells you exactly what she is. Her image — loose hair, golden band, the queen's casket on her arm — became the fixed Victorian and modern picture of the trusted northern handmaid, and she appears in nearly every retelling of the Baldr cycle by virtue of one finger-ring. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice keeps her at Frigg's side as a goddess of plenty, household trust, and well-kept secrets, invoked where abundance must be held in confidence. She never became a Marvel character or a video-game boss; she remained what the Edda made her — the most trusted person in the queen's hall, and the proof that in the northern pantheon even abundance has a keeper.
lore.archaeology: Fulla is an entirely textual goddess: no cult site, toponym, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the runic corpus is silent — unsurprising for a figure the sources place inside the queen's household rather than in the public cult. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The Grímnismál prose, which preserves her one errand, survives in the Codex Regius (c. 1270); her portrait in Gylfaginning 35 and her ring in Gylfaginning 49 come with the Prose Edda codices of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and her name recurs in the þulur, the metrical name-lists appended to Skáldskaparmál. The one continental witness is the Second Merseburg Charm, copied into a theological manuscript at Fulda in the tenth century and now in the Merseburg cathedral library: its Volla, sister of Friia, is the only attestation of the figure outside Iceland and, if the identification holds, the oldest by centuries.
lore.syncretism: Fulla's cross-border life runs through one word and one relationship. The word is fullr: Proto-Germanic *fullaz gives English 'full', German 'voll', Gothic fulls, and Old Norse Fulla — a goddess whose name is the ordinary adjective turned abstract noun, 'Fullness'. The relationship is the one the Merseburg Charm preserves: Volla beside Friia, as Fulla beside Frigg — and since Grimm, the identification of the two has been the standing reading, with Simek registering both the fit and the doubt. The deeper syncretic question is what kind of being she is. Gylfaginning's ásynjur catalogue is full of abstract-noun goddesses — Sjǫfn ('affection'), Lofn ('praise, permission'), Vár ('vows') — and scholars have long suspected that Fulla, Gná, and their sisters are facets of Frigg herself, the queen's plenitude and far-ranging given names and errands of their own. Whether she began as an independent goddess of plenty or as an aspect that walked off on its own, the sources keep her a person: she receives a ring, runs an errand, and wears her own gold.

domains.title: Refusal, Defense
domains.subtitle: The Doorkeeper Who Says No
domains.lead: Syn is the eleventh goddess in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur — and the smallest fully grammatical power in the northern pantheon. She guards the door of the hall and shuts it against those who should not enter; at the þing she is appointed to defend the suits she wishes to refute. Her name is the noun itself: syn, 'denial, refusal', and Snorri seals the identity with the proverb the North kept in its mouth — a denial is set up when a man says no. She has no journey, no marriage, no death: her whole mythology is the closed door and the answered accusation, the divine right of refusal.

cards.name: The Hall Door
cards.desc: The door of the hall she keeps and shuts against those who should not enter — the threshold of the divine household made personal, a boundary with a guardian.

cards.name: The Denial
cards.desc: Syn, the noun itself — the word that says no. Snorri's proverb records it: a denial is set up when a man says no, and the goddess is the saying made divine.

cards.name: The Defense at the Þing
cards.desc: At the assembly she is set as defender against the suits she wishes to refute — the lawful no, the answer that stands between an accused person and a false claim.

cards.name: The Eleventh Seat
cards.desc: Her place in Snorri's catalogue of the ásynjur, counted between Vör and Hlín and declared of no lesser rank than Frigg's company — rank among the goddesses for a single, indispensable function.

symbols.name: The hall door
symbols.meaning: The threshold she holds against those who should not enter — the boundary made personal

symbols.name: The denial (syn)
symbols.meaning: The noun itself, the word that says no — refusal elevated to a divine power

symbols.name: The proverb
symbols.meaning: 'A denial is set up when a man says no' — the goddess remembered in everyday speech, her mythology carried in a saying

symbols.name: The seat among the ásynjur
symbols.meaning: Eleventh in Snorri's catalogue, of no lesser rank — standing among the goddesses for one attested function

symbols.name: The defense at the þing
symbols.meaning: The legal shield — the right to answer an accusation with a truthful no

mythology.lead: Syn's dossier is the shortest in the Edda: one sentence in Gylfaginning, one name in the ásynja þulur, one rule in Skáldskaparmál's grammar of kennings. No poem stages her; no saga gives her a second life; no adventure attaches. And yet the tradition never forgot her, because what she guards is not a story but a word — the small, indispensable word 'no' — and Snorri preserves the proverb that proves the North kept both the word and its goddess in daily use.

myths.title: The Eleventh Ásynja
myths.text:
Snorri's catalogue of the goddesses moves from [[frigg|Frigg]] through [[saga|Sága]], [[eir|Eir]], [[gefjon|Gefjon]], [[fulla|Fulla]], [[freyja|Freyja]] and the rest, and arrives at the eleventh: Syn. 'She guards the door of the hall and shuts it against those who should not enter, and she is appointed to defend, at assemblies, the suits she wishes to refute.' Then the sentence that fixes her identity forever: 'hence the proverb that a denial is set up when a man says no.' The catalogue closes with Snotra and Gná, and Snorri adds that these ásynjur are of no lesser rank than the rest.

The whole of her mythology is in that one entry. Two functions are given, and they are one function twice: the doorkeeper who excludes, and the defender who refutes. At the threshold and at the law-court, Syn is the power that keeps the wrong thing out.

myths.title: The Word Made Goddess
myths.text:
Syn's name is not a theonym with a hidden etymology; it is the ordinary noun itself. Old Norse syn means 'denial, refusal'; the verb synja means 'to deny, to refuse', and it saturates the legal prose of the sagas wherever a claim is answered with a no. The lexica connect the word with the family of sannr, 'true' — the denial began as a law term, the truth-speaking by which a false accusation is refused. The goddess of saying no is, at root, the goddess of the truthful answer.

Snorri knows exactly what he is doing when he appends the proverb: he is recording a figure the language itself had already made. Whether Syn was an old goddess whose function shrank to a saying, or an abstraction Snorri's tradition personified on the model of Vör, Hlín and Snotra, the handbooks will not decide; Simek and Lindow class her among the personified functions, and the evidence is too thin to overrule them.

lore.culturalLegacy: Syn's afterlife is the quietest in the pantheon and the most grammatical. The proverb Snorri recorded — a denial is set up when a man says no — remained in circulation as a saying about plain refusal, and the verb synja never died: it lives on in modern Icelandic and Faroese as the ordinary word for denying and refusing, so that the goddess's name is still spoken daily by people who have never heard of her. The handbooks of Norse mythology keep her one-sentence entry with bureaucratic fidelity: Simek, Orchard and Lindow all give her a short article, always the same two functions, always the same scholarly shrug about personification. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities, working through the ásynjur name by name, have found in her a goddess worth invoking for the age of obligations: the patron of boundaries, of the lawful refusal, of the strength to say no at the door and at the judgment-seat — a modern devotion built honestly on the only two functions the sources ever gave her.
lore.archaeology: Syn is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no place-name preserves her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be identified with her — a silence she shares with most of the minor ásynjur of Snorri's catalogue and one that underwrites the scholarly reading of her as a personified function rather than an independently culted deity. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of Snorri's Edda: the Codex Regius and Codex Wormianus for Gylfaginning 35, and the manuscripts of Skáldskaparmál — including the Codex Regius and AM 748 — for the kenning rule and the ásynja þulur that keep her name in the register of the goddesses. The nearest material context is the word itself: the legal prose of the medieval Icelandic laws and sagas, where synja does its ordinary work of refusing claims, is the closest thing the record offers to a cult site — the door and the þing, preserved on vellum.
lore.syncretism: Syn's nearest kin are inside her own catalogue: the company of ásynjur whom Snorri lists around her — Vör, 'awareness', who is wise and searching so that nothing can be hidden from her; Hlín, set to guard those whom Frigg wishes to save from danger; Snotra, wise and courteous; Gná, whom Frigg sends on errands through the worlds. Simek and Lindow treat this whole band, Syn among them, as personified functions and abstractions — the grammatically feminine nouns of Old Norse promoted to goddesses, or faded minor deities surviving only as entries in the list. The comparison most often drawn is structural, not borrowed: the doorkeeper type recurs across the North, and the corpus's own great threshold-guardian is Heimdallr at Bifröst — but where Heimdallr watches for what comes, Syn simply refuses it entry. Cross-culturally, nineteenth-century scholars reached for the door-keeping figures of other traditions, even Janus with his gates, but the modern handbooks are cooler: Orchard and Simek note that nothing beyond the single sentence supports reconstruction, and her attestation will not bear the weight. What can be said cleanly is that no other northern goddess is so entirely a speech-act — a goddess whose whole cult, if she ever had one, fits in the space of the word 'no'.

domains.title: Joy, Wife of Baldr
domains.subtitle: The Wife Who Followed into the Fire
domains.lead: Nanna, daughter of Nepr, is the wife of Baldr the Good and the mother of Forseti — and the only figure in the Norse corpus who dies of a broken heart. When she saw her husband laid on his pyre aboard Hringhorni, her heart burst with grief, and the Æsir laid her on the fire beside him. In Hel she keeps her place at his side, and when Hermóðr comes to ransom the dead god, it is Nanna who sends gifts back up the road: a linen robe for Frigg, a gold ring for Fulla — love's tokens out of the land of the dead.

cards.name: The Linen for Frigg
cards.desc: The robe of linen Nanna sent from Hel to her mother-in-law — a household gift carried up the nine-night road by Hermóðr, proof the dead still keep their obligations of love.

cards.name: The Ring for Fulla
cards.desc: The gold finger-ring for Frigg's maid Fulla, Baldr's sister-in-law by the goddess's own household — the small exact kindness of a woman who remembers her friendships even in death.

cards.name: The Burst Heart
cards.desc: The one death in the Edda that needs no weapon: seeing Baldr on the pyre, Nanna's heart burst with grief, and she was laid on the fire beside him.

cards.name: Glitnir
cards.desc: The hall of gold and silver in heaven where her son Forseti dwells, stilling all strife — the living continuation of the house Nanna and Baldr began.

symbols.name: The linen robe
symbols.meaning: The gift sent from Hel to Frigg — domestic love that death does not cancel

symbols.name: The gold finger-ring
symbols.meaning: Fulla's keepsake from the dead — friendship remembered across the boundary

symbols.name: The pyre of Hringhorni
symbols.meaning: The fire she entered unslain and unbidden — grief as its own cause of death

symbols.name: Glitnir
symbols.meaning: The gold-and-silver hall of her son Forseti — the household's survival in the world above

symbols.name: The high seat in Hel
symbols.meaning: Her place beside Baldr in the hall of the dead — marriage persisting past the grave

mythology.lead: Nanna's dossier is among the shortest in the Edda and among the most devastating: she is named, married, widowed, dead of grief, and found again in Hel — in scarcely more lines than that. Snorri gives her the two moments the tradition never forgot, and Saxo gives her a second life as a wooed princess; between them stands a figure made almost entirely of devotion.

myths.title: The Wife of Baldr
myths.text:
Snorri names her in the catalogue of the Æsir's houses with genealogical economy: Baldr's wife is Nanna, daughter of Nepr, and their son is Forseti. Of Nepr nothing else is told — the father exists only to place the daughter. The son, by contrast, inherits a hall and an office: Forseti dwells in Glitnir, the hall whose pillars are red gold and whose roof is silver, and there he stills all strife, the great reconciler of gods and men. Grímnismál keeps the same hall in its numbered survey of heaven's dwellings.

The ásynja þulur preserved with Skáldskaparmál hold Nanna in the catalogue of the goddesses by name, beside Hlín and Sól. Beyond these notations the corpus gives her no adventure, no quarrel, no single act in life: the tradition saves everything for her death, and for what she does after it.

myths.title: The Heart That Burst
myths.text:
When Baldr fell to the mistletoe and the Æsir could neither weep nor take vengeance in the sanctuary, they bore him to the sea and brought out Hringhorni, his ship, the greatest of all ships. The giantess Hyrrokkin launched it with one shove, and the gods built the pyre on board. Then comes the sentence that defines Nanna for all time: when she saw her husband's body carried to the ship, her heart burst with grief, and she died. She was laid on the pyre beside him, and the fire was kindled. Óðinn laid the ring Draupnir on the flames; Þórr hallowed the pyre with Mjölnir; Baldr's horse was led to the fire with all its gear.

No weapon touches her; no enemy wills her death. In a corpus full of spear-thrusts and poisoned cups, hers is the one death by love alone — the Norse tradition's starkest statement that grief itself can kill, and that the gods are not exempt.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nanna's afterlife runs quietly through the Baldr story's long reception: every retelling of the death of the shining god, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, keeps her two scenes — the burst heart on the shore and the gifts entrusted to Hermóðr. Nineteenth-century romanticism made much of the wife on the pyre; twentieth-century scholarship made her the test case for how little the Edda needs to say. Her sturdiest legacy is the name itself: Nanna never died out in the North and remains a living given name in Denmark and Iceland, borne today by women who inherit the most grief-stricken and most faithful name in the Edda. Modern Heathenry remembers her in Baldr rites as the goddess of devotion measured past death's door.
lore.archaeology: Nanna is a wholly textual goddess: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be securely identified with her. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the Baldr cycle — the Codex Regius and related codices of Snorri's Edda for Gylfaginning 32 and 49, and the medieval Danish tradition of Saxo's Gesta Danorum for her second life as Gevarus's daughter. The nearest material context is indirect: Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (c. 983), quoted in Skáldskaparmál, proves that Baldr's funeral was carved on the panels of Óláfr pái's hall at Hjarðarholt a generation before Iceland's conversion — the procession of gods and the launch of Hringhorni were pictures as well as verses — though the surviving stanzas do not name Nanna herself. The eddic poems that touch her household survive in the Codex Regius (Grímnismál, Völuspá).
lore.syncretism: Nanna's closest kin are inside the corpus itself: she is the divine pattern of which Brynhildr is the heroic echo — the woman who mounts her dead beloved's pyre, as Brynhildr has herself burned beside Sigurðr in the Völsung cycle. Lindow notes the motif as the Norse 'faithful unto the pyre' type, and the parallel is structural, not borrowed. Cross-culturally, nineteenth-century scholars reached for the widows of Greek and Sanskrit tradition — Alcestis dying in her husband's place, the debated Indo-European comparisons around the suttee — but current handbooks are cooler: Simek and Orchard treat Nanna as a figure of the Baldr complex whose attestation is too thin for cult reconstruction, and her etymology too disputed for safe comparison. What can be said cleanly is that no other northern goddess is defined so entirely by a single act of grief, and none answers from the grave with so domestic a grace as a robe and a ring.

domains.title: Valkyrie, Shieldmaiden
domains.subtitle: The Sleep-Thorn, the Wall of Flame, and the Pyre of the Dragonslayer
domains.lead: Brynhildr is the valkyrie of the Vǫlsung cycle: the battle-maid Óðinn pricked with the sleep-thorn for defying his judgment, the shieldmaiden Sigurðr woke behind a wall of flame, the sworn beloved whom a draught of forgetfulness and a changed shape betrayed — and the woman who would not outlive the deceit, burning herself on the dragonslayer's pyre with a drawn sword between them.

cards.name: The Sleep-Thorn
cards.desc: Svefnþorn — the thorn Óðinn struck her with for giving victory against his word: sleep as sentence, and the beginning of the whole tragedy.

cards.name: The Vafrlogi
cards.desc: The flickering wall of flame around her hall on Hindarfjall — crossable only by Grani, only by Sigurðr, and later only by a borrowed shape.

cards.name: The Drawn Sword
cards.desc: Gramr laid naked between the lovers three nights — and laid between them again on the pyre, the sign of the bed that was never shared.

cards.name: Andvaranautr
cards.desc: The ring from the dwarf's hoard, taken in the exchanged shapes and produced at the quarrel — the small gold proof that undid a kingdom.

symbols.name: The sleep-thorn (svefnþorn)
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's sentence on disobedience — sleep as the price of an independent judgment

symbols.name: The wall of flame (vafrlogi)
symbols.meaning: The test that admits only the fearless — the fire no coward's horse will cross

symbols.name: The byrnie grown fast to her flesh
symbols.meaning: War-gear become skin: the valkyrie so long asleep that armor and woman had to be cut apart

symbols.name: The drawn sword between the lovers
symbols.meaning: The chaste bed of the deception — and the same sword laid between them in death

symbols.name: The ring Andvaranautr
symbols.meaning: The token that proves what memory was made to forget — gold as witness

mythology.lead: Brynhildr's story is the tragic core of the Vǫlsung cycle — told across Sigrdrífumál, the Guðrún poems, Sigurðarkviða hin skamma, Helreið Brynhildar, and Vǫlsunga saga with a consistency the corpus rarely achieves: the sentence, the waking, the oath, the deceit, the quarrel, the pyre.

myths.title: The Valkyrie's Sentence
myths.text: The prose frame of Sigrdrífumál gives her the name Sigrdrífa, 'victory-urger', and tells how she fell: two kings fought, Hjálmgunnarr the old and Agnar the young, and Óðinn had promised the victory to Hjálmgunnarr. The valkyrie judged otherwise and gave the day to Agnar. Óðinn pricked her with the sleep-thorn in revenge and declared she should never again fight in victory and should be given in marriage — and she answered that she had bound herself with an oath to wed no man who knew fear. The whole tragedy is already here: a woman whose only crime was an independent verdict, sentenced to sleep until a fearless man should come.

myths.title: The Waking on Hindarfjall
myths.text: Sigurðr, fresh from Fáfnir's hoard, saw a light on Hindarfjall as though a fire burned to the sky, and rode Grani through the vafrlogi — the horse would take no other rider through that flame. Within the wall stood a hall, and in the hall a figure in full armor. He cut the byrnie from her with Gramr, from the neck down, for it had grown fast to her flesh, and she woke and asked what had strength to break her sleep. 'Sigmundr's son,' he answered, 'with the sword that has lately slain Fáfnir.' She taught him then the runes of victory and the counsels of Sigrdrífumál — how to carve, how to trust, how to beware — and they plighted their troth, the valkyrie and the dragonslayer, before fate had its word.

lore.culturalLegacy: Brynhildr's modern afterlife is Wagner's: the Ring cycle made Brünnhilde the most famous valkyrie in the world, and her immolation — riding Grane into Siegfried's pyre with the ring returned to the Rhine — is opera's great closing image of a world redeemed by a woman's refusal to accept its lies. Behind Wagner stand the Victorian rediscoveries: Morris's Sigurd the Volsung gave English readers the whole arc, sleep-thorn to pyre. The archetype she fixed — the warrior woman asleep behind fire, won only by the fearless — runs through the fairy tale of Sleeping Beauty and every later shieldmaiden of fiction. In Iceland the name never left: Brynhildur remains a living given name, and Old Norse Brynhildr stays the standard citation form in every handbook of heroic legend.
lore.archaeology: Brynhildr herself has no cult site, votive deposit, or named image — she is a figure of heroic legend, not of cult. The material record attests the legend around her. The Sigurðr carvings of Södermanland — the Ramsund carving (Sö 101) and the Gök stone (Sö 327), both eleventh century — depict the slaying of Fáfnir, the roasting heart, the talking birds, and the slain Reginn, proving the Vǫlsung cycle's visual currency in the late Viking Age. The carved portal of Hylestad stave church in Norway (c. 1200) retells the saga's scenes in wood, and the Kirk Andreas cross on the Isle of Man shows Sigurðr roasting the dragon's heart. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) shows a woman offering a drinking horn to a rider, sometimes interpreted as Sigrdrífa or Brynhildr, though the identification is debated. The textual witnesses hang on thin threads: the heroic lays survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) — with the famous lacuna of a lost gathering that Brot af Sigurðarkviðu breaks across — and Vǫlsunga saga is preserved in a vellum fragment (NGU 182 4to) and paper copies.
lore.syncretism: Brynhildr lives two lives in the medieval record. The Norse tradition — Sigrdrífumál, the heroic lays, Vǫlsunga saga — makes her a valkyrie, sentenced by Óðinn and woken by Sigurðr. The continental tradition makes her human: the Nibelungenlied's Brünhilt is the proud queen of Iceland whose strength no suitor could master until Siegfried, invisible in his cloak of power, won her for Gunther; Þiðreks saga stands between the two, keeping a martial Brunhild in the far north. Since the Grimms, scholars have linked the legendary name to the historical Brunhilda of Austrasia, the Merovingian queen executed in 613 — a connection plausible for the continental strand and unnecessary for the Norse. Wagner refused the choice: his Brünnhilde is built from the Norse sources, Wotan's daughter and Siegfried's doom, and the Grimm brothers had already heard the svefnþorn echoing in the thorn-hedged sleep of Dornröschen — the fairy tale keeping the valkyrie's sentence alive in the nursery.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GOON-ur' — a hard g as in 'go', a short full 'u' as in 'put', the n held long and doubled, and the final r sounded as a light syllabic trill, as in modern Icelandic Gunnur.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Gunnr is not a theonym built from elements but the common noun itself: gunnr, feminine, 'war, battle' — the valkyrie's name is the thing she governs, personified. The restoration Gunnr keeps the double n and the nominative -r exactly as the manuscripts write them; the name is already plain ASCII, so there is nothing for the restoration to rescue. Tier-2 by rule: no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose.

domains.title: Valkyrie of War
domains.subtitle: Battle Made Divine — the Rider Who Chooses the Slain
domains.lead: Gunnr is the valkyrie whose name is the whole battlefield: Old Norse gunnr is simply the word for war, and the þulur and the Völuspá seeress set her riding among Óðinn's choosers of the slain. Snorri gives her the purest job-description in the corpus: Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and decide battles.

cards.name: The Chosen Slain
cards.desc: The einherjar — the warriors she marks on the field and carries to Valhǫll, the harvest a valkyrie exists to gather.

cards.name: Skuld's Shield
cards.desc: Völuspá's image: Skuld held a shield and Skögul rode with her, and Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul rode behind — the armed company of the god-folk.

cards.name: The War-Spear
cards.desc: The valkyrie's weapon and the battle's own emblem: Snorri says Gunnr, Rota and Skuld ride to every fight to award the victory.

cards.name: The Val-Knot of Choice
cards.desc: The act her office names: val-kjósa, to choose the slain — the divine prerogative of saying who falls and who is taken.

symbols.name: The spear
symbols.meaning: The weapon of the chooser — the stroke that both kills and elects

symbols.name: The shield of the company
symbols.meaning: Völuspá's riding detail: the valkyries go armed and ranked, not as omens but as soldiers

symbols.name: The choice of the slain (valr)
symbols.meaning: The office itself — war's harvest selected by name, the power the name gunnr carries into personhood

symbols.name: The name that is a noun
symbols.meaning: Gunnr the valkyrie and gunnr the battle are one word — war personified walking its own field

mythology.lead: Gunnr has no adventure of her own; her mythology is her office, told in lists that are anything but dry. Three witnesses fix her in the corpus: the Völuspá seeress sees her ride, Snorri states her function in a single sentence, and the þulur keep her name in the valkyrie roll — the tradition's way of saying that battle, in the North, had a chooser, and the chooser had a name.

myths.title: The Riders the Seeress Saw
myths.text: Deep in the völva's vision, between the creation of the world and its burning, the seeress watches the valkyries come: 'She saw valkyries come from far and wide, ready to ride to the gods' people; Skuld held a shield, and Skögul was with her; Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul — now are counted Herjan's ladies, valkyries ready to ride the earth.' Herjan is Óðinn, and the company is his. Gunnr rides fourth-named in the most famous catalogue of the Poetic Edda — not as a character in a story but as a fixture of the cosmos, as certain as the norms and the doom they enforce.

myths.title: The Choosers of the Slain
myths.text: Snorri, explaining Óðinn's household, gives the valkyries their definition and Gunnr her one great sentence: Óðinn sends the valkyries to every battle; they allot death to men and award victory. 'Gunnr and Rota and the youngest norn, who is called Skuld, always ride to choose the slain and to decide the fighting.' The grouping is precise and chilling — two valkyries and a norn riding together, because in Norse thought the choice of the slain and the doom of the slain are the same act seen from two sides. Gunnr's myth is this: war is never random. Someone rides above it. Someone chooses.

lore.culturalLegacy: Gunnr's afterlife flows through two channels. The first is the word itself: gunnr lived on as the battle-element of Scandinavian naming — Gunnarr ('warrior of battle'), Gunnhildr ('battle-fight'), and the living Icelandic and Faroese women's name Gunnur — so that the valkyrie's name is still spoken daily in the North, worn by ordinary people. The second is the image she helped fix: the armed maiden riding to the field to choose the dead, the seed from which the whole later figure of the valkyrie grew — the Valkyries of Wagner's Walküre, the shieldmaidens of modern fiction and games, and the revived valkyrie devotion of contemporary Heathenry. In scholarship she stands as the standing example of the Norse habit of personifying abstractions: not an allegory imposed on war, but war itself, named and riding.
lore.archaeology: Gunnr is a wholly textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no cult site is hers — she shares this silence with nearly all the valkyries, who were functions of Óðinn's household rather than objects of cult. The material record knows the office if not the name. Gotlandic picture stones repeatedly show a mounted warrior received by a female figure bearing a drinking horn — the so-called valkyrie-welcome motif — and small female armed figurines, above all the gilt-silver valkyrie with sword and shield found at Hårby on Funen (Denmark), prove the image's currency in the Viking Age. The textual witnesses are the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270) for Völuspá and the principal manuscripts of the Prose Edda for Gylfaginning and the þulur; the noun gunnr itself is carved on runestones within personal names, where the battle-element lives on in the anthroponymy.
lore.syncretism: Gunnr's nearest kin are not borrowings but reflections. Within the Norse corpus she belongs to the tight triad Snorri names — herself, Rota, and the norn Skuld — where the valkyrie's battlefield choice and the norn's weaving of fate are one operation; [[skuld|Skuld]] carries the same office into the world of time itself. Across the sea, the Old English cognate gūþ never grew a person: Beowulf sings of gūþ as plain war, and the personification stayed Norse. Scholars comparing traditions point to the Irish Morrígan and Badb — battle-goddesses who also decide fights and choose their dead — as the closest functional parallel in the neighbouring mythology, though no historical link is provable and none need be claimed. Gunnr needs no foreign template: she is what happens when a warrior culture declines its own word for war in the feminine and gives it a horse.

domains.title: Valkyrie / Norn of Future
domains.subtitle: The Debt That Comes Due
domains.lead: Skuld is the third of the three norns who dwell at the well of Urðr beneath the root of Yggdrasill, laying laws and choosing lives for the children of men — and she is the only figure in the Norse corpus counted twice. Völuspá names her among the three maidens beneath the tree, and names her again in the tally of valkyries riding to the gods' host, bearing a shield beside Skögul, Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul. Snorri fuses the two offices in a single clause: with Gunnr and Rota always rides 'the youngest norn, who is called Skuld', to choose the slain and decide the battle. Her name is the noun for 'debt' — the future as what is still owed.

cards.name: The Well of Urðr
cards.desc: The holy well beneath Yggdrasill's heavenward root where the three maidens dwell — Urðr, Verðandi, Skuld — and where the gods hold their council; Völuspá sees it in the first vision of the world's frame.

cards.name: The Carved Slips
cards.desc: The wood-slips the norns carve as they lay laws and choose lives for the children of men — fate as inscription, each life written before it is lived.

cards.name: The Shield
cards.desc: The shield Skuld bears in Völuspá's tally of valkyries riding over the earth — the one norn who also rides to the field, death's allotment delivered in person.

cards.name: The Youngest Norn
cards.desc: Snorri's phrase: 'the youngest norn, who is called Skuld', who always rides with Gunnr and Rota to decide the battle — the youngest sister carrying the last and least avoidable portion of every life.

symbols.name: Urðarbrunnr
symbols.meaning: The well beneath the tree where the three norns dwell — fate's spring at the world's root

symbols.name: The carved wood-slips
symbols.meaning: The lots the maidens cut as they lay laws and choose lives — destiny written before it is lived

symbols.name: The shield
symbols.meaning: Skuld's valkyrie gear in Völuspá — the norn who rides, allotment armed and mounted

symbols.name: The white clay of the well
symbols.meaning: The mud with which the norns coat the ash's bark so its limbs do not rot — fate also as the world's maintenance

symbols.name: The laws and the lots
symbols.meaning: What the three maidens lay and cast for the children of men — ordinance and chance, both in their hands

mythology.lead: Skuld's dossier is short and of the highest rank: she appears where the world's frame is described, never in anecdote. The Poetic Edda names her twice — once beneath the tree, once in the air above the battlefield — and Snorri stitches the two sightings into one figure: the youngest norn who rides with the valkyries. What follows is the whole of the primary record.

myths.title: The Three Beneath the Tree
myths.text:
The seeress surveys the world's frame: the ash Yggdrasill, tall, drenched with white loam, whence come the dews that fall in the valleys, ever green, standing over Urðarbrunnr. Thence come maidens, deep in wisdom, three from the lake that stands beneath the tree: one was called Urðr, the second Verðandi — they carved on slips of wood — Skuld the third. They laid laws, they chose lives for the children of men, the fates of men.

The stanza is the foundation text of northern fate-doctrine, and it fixes Skuld's place in the triad without explaining it: the poem gives her no act, no speech, no attribute but her position — the third, the last named, the one whose name is a debt.

myths.title: The Shield in the Tally
myths.text:
Late in the same poem the seeress looks up from the roots to the sky: she saw valkyries come from far away, ready to ride to the gods' host — Skuld bore a shield, and Skögul followed her, Gunnr, Hildr, Göndul and Geirskögul; now the tally of Herjan's maidens is told, valkyries ready to ride over the earth. The list is a roll-call, and Skuld heads it, shield in hand.

No other norn appears in a valkyrie list. The double office is the interpretive crux of the whole figure: the maiden who allots life at the root is the same maiden who collects death in the field — the two ends of one ledger.

lore.culturalLegacy: Skuld's most pervasive legacy is grammatical: her name's root is the English modal shall — and its past, should — so that every English sentence about obligation or the future conjugates, unknowingly, the youngest norn's name; German Schuld keeps the same root in its sense of debt and guilt. In mythography the three norns became the fixed northern counterpart of the Parcae in every retelling of the Eddas, and Skuld's double office — fate at the well, shield in the field — made her the standing emblem of fate that acts rather than merely decrees. Modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice honours the norns at birth-rites and at the year's turning, with Skuld invoked as the portion not yet owed; her name also survives as a rare Scandinavian given name, carrying its ominous register intact.
lore.archaeology: Skuld is a wholly textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no image can be securely identified with her — a silence she shares with her sisters, since the norns belong to the corpus's theological frame rather than to any named cult. Her attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the fate-doctrine: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Völuspá 19–20 and 30, and the Codex Regius, Codex Wormianus and Codex Upsaliensis of Snorri's Edda for Gylfaginning 15–16 and 36 and the þulur lists preserved with Skáldskaparmál. The nearest material context is indirect: the valkyrie figures on Gotland picture-stones and on small Viking-Age brooches and pendants give the visual world her rider-form belongs to, though none names her. No runic carving of the theonym is known; the manuscript spelling of the Eddas remains the primary witness.
lore.syncretism: The comparison that shaped Skuld's modern reading is with the Roman Parcae and the Greek Moirai — three spinners or allotters of fate matched to past, present and future. The mapping was a favourite of nineteenth-century mythography, and it is only half right: the names do not divide time so neatly. Urðr is 'what has become', Verðandi 'what is becoming', but Skuld is not 'what will be' in the same tense-logic — she is 'what is owed', a category of obligation rather than of tense; de Vries and Simek both warn that the clean past-present-future scheme is likely a learned schematization laid over older material. Within the corpus her truest kin are her own sisters [[urdr|Urðr]] and [[verdandi|Verðandi]] and the valkyrie sisterhood she alone joins — [[brynhildr|Brynhildr]] among the named riders — and, at one remove, the English fate-word [[wyrd|wyrd]], cognate with Urðr, through which the whole northern doctrine of allotted debt and doom entered English speech.

domains.title: Giant, Owner of Cauldron
domains.subtitle: The Host at Heaven's End, the Ox-Head Bait, and the Cup Broken on a Giant's Skull
domains.lead: Hymir is the sea-giant of Hymiskviða: the fierce host at the eastern edge of heaven whose herd feeds his hall, whose fishing-ground is the cold reach of the Élivágar, and whose treasure is the one thing the gods lack — the mile-deep cauldron in which Ægir could brew ale for all the Æsir at once.

cards.name: The Mile-Deep Cauldron
cards.desc: The roomy, hard-forged kettle Týr says his fierce father owns — a mile deep, the only vessel large enough to brew for all the gods.

cards.name: The Ox-Head Bait
cards.desc: The head of the black bull Himinbrjótr, torn off by Þórr for bait — the offering that drew the Miðgarðsormr up from the sea-floor.

cards.name: The Crystal Cup
cards.desc: Hymir's unbreakable drinking-cup, which no pillar could crack — smashed at last on the one thing harder: the giant's own skull.

cards.name: The Hall of Cattle
cards.desc: The giant's byre at heaven's end, where Þórr devoured two of the three oxen at supper and beheaded the finest for the fishing.

symbols.name: The mile-deep cauldron
symbols.meaning: The vessel of plenty the giants keep and the gods must win — hospitality's measure in the Eddic world

symbols.name: The ox-head bait
symbols.meaning: The price of the catch: the herd's finest head traded for the serpent that girdles the world

symbols.name: The cup broken on the skull
symbols.meaning: The giant's own hardness turned against his treasure — strength answering strength

symbols.name: The nine-hundred-headed grandmother
symbols.meaning: The monstrous ancestry of the giant-house, set against the golden-browed mother who hides the guests

mythology.lead: Hymir lives in one great poem and its prose retelling: Hymiskviða, the comic and terrible lay of the cauldron-quest, and Gylfaginning 48, where Snorri tells the fishing-trip for the Miðgarðsormr with all its sea-cold detail. It is Þórr's most famous adventure, and the giant is its immovable setting.

myths.title: The Demand for the Cauldron
myths.text: The Æsir had hunted and taken auguries from the blood, and saw that Ægir — called also Gymir — had brew-stuff in plenty. Þórr ordered the sea-giant to brew ale for the gods, and Ægir, to be rid of the demand, set an impossible price: first let them bring a cauldron a mile wide. Týr knew where one stood: east of the Élivágar lives the shrewd Hymir at heaven's end, and "my fierce father owns the roomy kettle, a mile deep." So Þórr and Týr drove to the giant's hall. There they met Týr's grandmother, loathsome, with nine hundred heads — and another woman, golden-browed, Týr's mother, who hid the guests under the great cauldron, for her husband was often cruel to visitors.

myths.title: The Host Comes Home
myths.text: Hymir came in from the hunting with the ice rattling in his beard. The pillar he looked toward burst apart; eight cauldrons crashed from the broken beam, and one hard-forged kettle came down whole. The guests came out, and the hall fed them: three oxen were slaughtered, and Þórr alone ate two before he slept. In the morning the giant eyed his thinned herd and told his guest they must fish for the next day's meal — Þórr might row out with him, if the little fellow dared the cold and the long pull to his fishing-ground.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hymir's afterlife is carried almost entirely by the fishing-trip, which became the most retold of all Þórr's adventures: Victorian mythographies made it a set-piece, modern handbooks open their Þórr chapters with it, and every popular retelling keeps the ox-head, the glaring serpent, and the giant rowing home in silence. In scholarship the poem holds a double distinction — it is both the fullest portrait of a giant household in the Edda and the standing exhibit in the debate over the cauldron-quest's Celtic kin. The name itself stayed where the þulur put it: a giant-name, rarely borrowed, carried into modern fantasy and games chiefly as the surly host of the world's most famous fishing story.
lore.archaeology: Hymir is a textual figure: his attestations are the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), which alone preserves Hymiskviða, and the manuscripts of Snorri's Edda; the þulur keep his name among the giant-heiti. The myth's antiquity is proven by skaldic verse: Bragi Boddason's Ragnarsdrápa (9th c.) describes the fishing-scene on a painted shield — the ox-head bait, the hooked serpent, the hammer raised — with the giant aboard conventionally identified as Hymir. The picture-record follows: the Altuna runestone (U 1161, Uppland) shows Þórr with his foot braced through the boat's bottom and the serpent on the line, and the Gosforth Cross fishing-panel shows two figures in the boat — the angler and his giant companion. No cult site, toponym, or inscription names Hymir himself.
lore.syncretism: Hymir's poem has drawn comparatists for a century because the cauldron-quest is one of the old travelling stories of the North Atlantic: a vessel of plenty, kept by a grudging power beyond the sea, won for the feast of the gods. Scholars since Dumézil have set Hymiskviða beside the Celtic cauldron-quests — the Welsh Preiddeu Annwfn, where Arthur sails for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and the Irish cauldrons that no company leaves unsatisfied — and beside Vedic parallels for the winning of the gods' drink. The fishing scene has its own comparative trail: the thunder-god's combat with the sea-serpent belongs with the wide Indo-European dragon-fight. Inside the Norse corpus the neater tension is genealogical: Hymiskviða makes the giant Týr's father, while Snorri elsewhere counts Týr among Óðinn's sons — two filiations the tradition never reconciled.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Hymir — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᚢᛘᛁᛦ (h-u-m-i-R, the ᚢ rune covering the rounded y and ᛦ writing the final nominative -r). pronunciation.note: Baugi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The tier reports the name's orthography, not the figure's standing; the corpus names him in one story and one list, and both are written in unbroken Latin letters.

domains.title: Giant, Brother of Suttungr
domains.subtitle: The Keeper of the Door at Hnitbjǫrg
domains.lead: Baugi is the giant who holds the one door that matters in the story of the mead of poetry: brother to Suttungr, who hoards the mead inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and master of the nine thralls whose deaths open the way to Óðinn's bargain. He is the hinge of the whole theft — the labour-contractor, the reluctant accomplice, and the would-be cheat whose auger-stroke misses a snake by an inch.

cards.name: Hnitbjǫrg
cards.desc: The mountain — its name plausibly 'the clashing rocks' — inside which Suttungr shut the mead of poetry, with his daughter Gunnlǫð set to guard it. Baugi's auger makes the only door it ever had.

cards.name: Rati
cards.desc: The auger Óðinn puts in Baugi's hands — 'the traveller', from the verb rata. Baugi bores the tunnel with it, and nearly ends the story with one stroke of it.

cards.name: The Whetstone
cards.desc: The sharpening stone Óðinn tosses among Baugi's nine mowing thralls; in scrambling to claim it they cut each other's throats, and Baugi is left with a harvest and no hands.

cards.name: The Mead of Poetry
cards.desc: Kvasir's blood brewed with honey, held in Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són — the drink that makes a poet or a sage of whoever tastes it, and the prize the whole bargain is for.

symbols.name: Hnitbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: The mountain of the mead — hoard and fortress in one, opened by craft rather than force

symbols.name: Rati
symbols.meaning: The auger that gnaws through stone — the tool that makes the door, and nearly the weapon that closes the story

symbols.name: The whetstone
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's thrown bait — the small object whose coveting empties Baugi's fields of nine workers at a stroke

symbols.name: The nine thralls' scythes
symbols.meaning: The harvest-tools honed too well — honest labour's edge turned into mutual death by one act of sharpening

symbols.name: Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són
symbols.meaning: The three vessels of the mead — 'heart-stirrer', 'vessel', and 'reconciliation' — emptied in three draughts

mythology.lead: Baugi's entire mythology is one episode, and it is the most consequential single episode in the mythology of poetry: the mead heist of Skáldskaparmál. He appears only there and in the þulur of giant-names — a figure the tradition needed once, at the one door, and never again. But that once is the door through which all skaldic poetry claims to have come.

myths.title: The Mead Comes to Hnitbjǫrg
myths.text:
The story begins before Baugi enters it. From the peace-making of Æsir and Vanir is made Kvasir, wisest of beings; the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar kill him and brew his blood with honey into a mead that makes a poet or a scholar of whoever drinks it, keeping it in three vessels — Óðrœrir, Boðn, and Són. The dwarfs then drown the giant Gilling at sea and kill his wife with a millstone, and Gilling's son Suttungr takes revenge: he sets the dwarfs on a tide-washed skerry, and they buy their lives with the mead. Suttungr carries it home, shuts it inside the mountain Hnitbjǫrg, and sets his daughter Gunnlǫð to guard it.

Only now does Snorri bring Baugi on stage, in a single sentence of genealogy: Suttungr had a brother, and his name was Baugi. The hoard is sealed, the guard is set, and the god who wants the mead does not go to its owner — he goes to the owner's brother.

myths.title: The Whetstone and the Nine Thralls
myths.text:
Óðinn comes walking to Baugi's land calling himself Bǫlverkr, 'Evil-doer' — a name that is not a disguise so much as an announcement. Nine of Baugi's thralls are mowing hay. Bǫlverkr offers to sharpen their scythes, and the whetstone he pulls from his cloak hones so well that all nine want to buy it. He says it will be sold dearly, and throws it up among them; in the scramble to catch it, each thrall swings his scythe at another's neck, and all nine lie dead in the field.

That evening Bǫlverkr lodges with Baugi, and Baugi pours out his troubles: his nine thralls are dead and the hay harvest stands uncut. The god has engineered the vacancy he is about to fill — the labour shortage is the lock, and he made it himself.

lore.culturalLegacy: Baugi's afterlife is mostly the afterlife of the drink he failed to keep. Skaldic poetry — the entire court-poetry tradition of the Viking and medieval North — called itself by kennings drawn from this myth: Kvasir's blood, the dwarfs' drink, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's theft, Óðrœrir's wave. Every one of those names is a character in the heist except its doorkeeper; the corpus never minted a 'Baugi's mead'. He survives instead as the specialists' hinge-figure: every scholarly treatment of the mead myth, from Finnur Jónsson to Lindow, must reckon with his two functions — the labour-broker who makes the theft logistically possible, and the wavering accomplice whose bore-hole and auger-stroke are the story's closest brush with failure. In modern retellings of the myth he appears under his name in the better handbooks and in the illustrated Eddas of the Norse revival, always in the same posture: halfway through the mountain, one hand on the auger. The mead myth itself has become the North's great parable of inspiration as something stolen, hoarded, and re-stolen — and the god of poetry, [[bragi|Bragi]], pours out what Baugi could not guard.
lore.archaeology: Baugi is an entirely textual figure: no runestone invokes him, no picture stone has been convincingly read as the drilling of Hnitbjǫrg, and no place-name or votive deposit carries his name. His attestation is exactly as wide as his story — Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, preserved principally in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), with the Codex Wormianus and Codex Upsaliensis as the other main witnesses, plus his entry in the þulur of giant-names. The mead myth he serves is materially older than its manuscripts: kennings presupposing it — Kvasir's blood, Suttungr's mead, Óðinn's booty — are already at work in ninth- and tenth-century skaldic verse, which proves the story's currency centuries before Snorri wrote it down. Hávamál's telling survives in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (c. 1270), the same small codex that carries nearly all the mythological poems. The runic record is silent on the theonym, as on nearly all the jǫtnar.
lore.syncretism: Baugi himself has no cross-border reflex — no Old English or continental cognate figure, no cult, no charm; he is a person the Icelandic tradition made for one narrative. The myth he serves, however, sits in one of the oldest comparative dossiers in Indo-European study: the theft of the divine intoxicant. The standard parallel is Vedic — the śyena, the eagle or falcon who snatches the soma and brings it to the gods (Rigveda 4.26–27) — set beside Óðinn in eagle-shape carrying off the mead in his body. The comparison was drawn in the nineteenth century and is still registered, with due caution, in the modern handbooks: Lindow treats the mead myth as the northern member of a genuine inheritance while warning against flattening its specifically Norse machinery — the labour contract, the auger, the broken oath. Baugi's own role belongs to that northern machinery: the intermediary who can be bought, the door that opens from the inside. His closest structural kin in the corpus are the other giants whose households Óðinn penetrates by guile, above all the world of [[suttungr|Suttungr]] itself and the deep giant-lore of [[ymir|Ymir]]'s kin.

Because the name is pure ASCII, its .com address was registered in the ordinary way and is held outside the PuniCodex collection: no form of the name is currently owned, the plain-ASCII domain is watched for release, and this temple claims none.

domains.title: Dwarf, Guardian of Gold
domains.subtitle: The Careful One of the Waterfall
domains.lead: Andvari is the dwarf who lived in the waterfall Andvarafors in a pike's shape, sweeping his gold about him with his fins — the most careful hoarder in the northern corpus, and the owner of the ring Andvaranaut. When Loki caught him in Rán's net and stripped him of everything to pay the otter's ransom, Andvari spoke the curse that made his gold a death sentence for every hand that held it after him: Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, and the whole line of the Gjúkungar.

cards.name: Andvarafors
cards.desc: The waterfall that was his hall — the stream where he swam in a pike's shape and kept his gold, named for him in Reginsmál's prose.

cards.name: Andvaranaut
cards.desc: 'Andvari's jewel' — the last ring of the hoard, hidden in his hand, taken by force, and answered with the curse that every owner would find death in it.

cards.name: Rán's Net
cards.desc: The sea-queen's net that Loki borrowed to drag the waterfall — the tool that turned a fishing into an extortion.

cards.name: The Pike-Shape
cards.desc: The fish-form in which he swept his hoard through the water — the careful one's disguise, netted all the same.

symbols.name: Andvaranaut
symbols.meaning: The ring taken last and cursed first — a treasure that kills every hand it passes through

symbols.name: Andvarafors
symbols.meaning: The waterfall named for its keeper — a hoard-hall that flows and cannot be locked

symbols.name: Rán's net
symbols.meaning: Borrowed catching-power — the gods paying a blood-debt with a fisherman's trick

symbols.name: The pike-shape
symbols.meaning: The disguise of the careful — a form made for guarding, not for fighting

symbols.name: The otter's ransom
symbols.meaning: The wergild that had to cover a dead otter's skin from the inside — gold counted out hair by hair

mythology.lead: Andvari's dossier is a single episode and its long echo: one afternoon's extortion at a waterfall, and a curse that runs through the rest of the Völsung cycle like poison through water. Reginsmál's prose, Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, and Völsunga saga all tell the catching; everything after — Fáfnir's dragon, Sigurðr's sword, the gold sunk in the Rhine — is the curse working itself out.

myths.title: The Otter's Ransom
myths.text:
Óðinn, Loki, and Hœnir were traveling when they came to a waterfall, and there they saw an otter eating a salmon on the bank, its eyes shut. Loki killed it with a stone and boasted of a double catch — otter and fish at one cast. But the otter was Ótr, son of the farmer Hreiðmarr, a shape-shifter who took a pike's or otter's form to fish the falls. That night the gods sought lodging at Hreiðmarr's house and showed their catch; Hreiðmarr called his sons Fáfnir and Reginn, and the three seized the gods and bound them. The wergild was set by the skin itself: the otter's hide was to be filled with red gold, and then covered with gold from the outside until not a hair showed. Óðinn sent Loki to get the gold, and Loki went down to the world of the black-elves to find it where it lay — in the keeping of a dwarf at a waterfall.

Snorri tells the same in Skáldskaparmál as the explanation of gold's kennings: this is why poets call gold the otter's ransom, the forced payment of the Æsir. The episode exists in the tradition to gloss poetry — a myth doing the work of a dictionary.

myths.title: The Net of Rán
myths.text:
Völsunga saga gives the fullest account of the catching. Loki went to Rán, the sea-queen who drowns sailors, and borrowed her net, then came to the waterfall called Andvarafors. There lived the dwarf Andvari, who kept a pike's shape in the water and swept his gold about him, guarding everything. Loki cast the net and caught him, and demanded the ransom: all the gold in the waterfall, or Andvari's head.

The dwarf paid over the hoard — but he kept one ring back, a small thing, hidden in his hand. Loki saw it and took that too, despite Andvari's plea that with the ring kept he could breed gold again and would not beggar himself entirely. Loki answered that one coin would be too many to leave him, and went up out of the water with the whole of it. Reginsmál's prose tells the same catching more briefly: Loki got Rán's net, cast it before the pike, and the dwarf paid the otter's ransom from his own keeping.

lore.culturalLegacy: Andvari's afterlife is one of the largest in all mythology, under another name. Wagner's Alberich in Das Rheingold — the dwarf of the water's depth who is robbed of his gold, lays a curse on the ring forged from it, and watches it destroy owner after owner through four operas — is built substantially on the Andvari of Reginsmál and Völsunga saga, crossed with the Nibelungenlied's hoard; the curse-motif that drives the entire Ring cycle is the sentence spoken at Andvarafors. William Morris's Sigurd the Volsung (1876) kept the original name before English readers, and the Nibelungenlied's Rhine-gold carried the same hoard into German memory. In Iceland the name itself was revived with no curse attached: Andvari is the title of the learned journal of the Icelandic Literary Society, founded in 1874 — the careful one finally keeping something that multiplies without killing. Modern fantasy's treasury of cursed gold, from dragons' hoards onward, runs downhill from his waterfall.
lore.archaeology: Andvari himself is a purely literary figure: no runestone, votive deposit, or named image records him. But the cycle his gold sets in motion is the best-attested narrative in Viking-Age art. The Ramsund carving in Södermanland (Sö 101, c. 1030) cuts the whole Fáfnir episode into a rock face — Sigurðr thrusting up through the serpent's body, the slain Reginn with his smith's tools, Grani loaded with the treasure, and the birds whose speech the dragon-heart taught — and the Gök stone (Sö 327) weaves the same scenes through a runic inscription. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) shows Sigurðr stabbing the serpent, and related scenes appear on the Isle of Man and in English stone sculpture as far west as the Halton cross in Lancashire, tracking the cycle along the Norse sea-roads. The manuscript witnesses are thin in the usual way: Reginsmál and its narrative prose stand in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda, Snorri's account in the codices of the Prose Edda, and Völsunga saga in the paper manuscript NKS 1824 b 4to (c. 1400), the saga's only complete medieval copy.
lore.syncretism: Andvari needs no foreign counterpart to be understood — the cursed-hoard complex is native Germanic and runs through the whole North: treasure extorted is treasure poisoned. The corpus itself supplies the sharpest contrast in another dwarf-ring: Draupnir, forged freely by [[brokkr|Brokkr]] and [[sindri|Sindri]] for the gods, which drips eight new rings every ninth night — the given ring multiplies, the taken ring kills. Continental heroic tradition keeps the same stratum: the hoard of the Nibelungenlied, sunk in the Rhine and deadly to its holders, is the southern telling of the Andvaranaut complex, and scholars from Lindow onward treat the Norse and German versions as one inheritance rather than borrowings. The dwarf caught in fish-shape also has a family resemblance to the water-spirits of later folklore, but the Eddic Andvari is a smith and hoarder first; his pike-form is camouflage, not nature.

Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: andvari.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.
