The temple is served at /sites/rhiannon/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'pruh-DEH-ree' — the y is a soft 'uh', the stress falls on 'der' (the Welsh penult), and the final i is a short 'ee'.
pronunciation.note: Pryderi is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The name's etymology is the tale's own: the First Branch names him from Rhiannon's word pryder, 'care, anxiety', spoken when the lost child was restored — an aetiological naming the medieval author builds into the story itself, and the lexicon's gloss 'Care, anxiety' follows the text.

domains.title: The Lord Who Spans the Four Branches
domains.subtitle: Son of Pwyll, King
domains.lead: Pryderi is the hinge of the whole Mabinogi: the only figure who walks through all Four Branches — stolen on the night of his birth and found outside a stable door, named from his mother's lifted anxiety, emptied out of Dyfed by an enchanter's mist, and killed at last in single combat by Gwydion's craft. Son of Pwyll and Rhiannon, lord of Dyfed, he is the king the tales keep taking things from — and the name he carries is the Welsh word for care.

cards.name: The Stable Door
cards.desc: Outside Teyrnon's stable, where a great clawed hand had come for the newborn foal, lay an infant wrapped in silk brocade — the stolen heir of Dyfed.

cards.name: The Naming
cards.desc: Rhiannon looks at the boy and says her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her; from that word the child is named Pryderi.

cards.name: The Golden Bowl
cards.desc: Hanging by chains above a marble fountain in a fortress that was never there before: when Pryderi grasps it, his hands stick, his feet root to the slab, and his voice dies.

cards.name: The First Swine
cards.desc: The hobeu, first pigs ever brought to Wales — Arawn of Annwn's gift to the house of Pwyll — which Gwydion wins with illusory gold and pays for with Pryderi's life.

symbols.name: The silk brocade wrapping
symbols.meaning: Royal blood declaring itself at a stable door — the foundling child whose swaddling says what no witness can

symbols.name: The clawed hand
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld reaching through the window on May-eve — the unseen power that takes foals and princes alike

symbols.name: The golden bowl on its chains
symbols.meaning: Bait that looks like treasure — the trap at the heart of the enchanted fortress, and the cost of touching what is not yours

symbols.name: The gate-hammer about his neck
symbols.meaning: What he wore out of the enchantment — the humiliation of the Third Branch, borne home and buried in silence

symbols.name: The swine of Annwn
symbols.meaning: Otherworld wealth with a geis upon it — not to be sold or given until the herd had doubled — and the war a broken promise bought

symbols.name: The grave at Maen Tywynog
symbols.meaning: The mound above Y Felenrhyd where the slain lord was buried — the one fixed point of a life lived under enchantment

mythology.lead: Pryderi's mythology is unique in Welsh prose: he is the only character who appears in all Four Branches of the Mabinogi, and his life is the thread the whole cycle is strung on. The First Branch gives his birth, theft, and naming; the Second carries him through the Irish war as one of the seven survivors; the Third empties his kingdom and takes him captive; the Fourth kills him. Every word of it is medieval Welsh prose, preserved in two great manuscripts.

myths.title: The May-Eve Vanishing
myths.text: Pryderi is born to Pwyll and Rhiannon after the nobles of Dyfed have pressed for an heir, and on the night of his birth the six women set to watch all fall asleep — and the child is gone. Terrified of the blame, the women kill the pups of a hound, smear the blood on Rhiannon's face, lay the bones beside her, and swear she has destroyed her own son; her penance at the horse-block begins, and it will last until the boy comes home. The child, meanwhile, has fallen into the strangest rescue in Welsh prose. Teyrnon Twrf Liant, a lord of Gwent Is Coed by the sea, loses a foal every May-eve; keeping watch over his mare, he sees a great clawed hand reach through the window to seize the newborn foal, and strikes it off with his sword. Outside the door he finds a baby boy wrapped in silk brocade. He and his wife rear the child as their own and call him Gwri Wallt Euryn — Gwri of the Golden Hair.

myths.title: The Naming at Arberth
myths.text: Gwri grows with uncanny speed — at the end of his first year sturdier than a child of three, at two like a boy of six — and year by year he bears the very likeness of Pwyll. When Teyrnon hears of Rhiannon's penance, he knows what he must do, and he and his wife bring the boy to Arberth. The court sees the likeness at once, and Rhiannon says that if this is true, her pryder — her care, her anxiety — is lifted from her. Pwyll declares that the boy should take his name from the word his mother spoke when the news was brought to her, and so the child is named Pryderi. The penance ends; Teyrnon will take no reward beyond the boy's friendship; and Pryderi is fostered with Pendaran Dyfed until he is of age, when Pwyll gives him the realm.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Pryderi out of the Welsh manuscripts and into English, and the Victorian Celtic revival made the vanished child of the First Branch one of its set-pieces. Twentieth-century scholarship gave him his modern standing: Ifor Williams's edition fixed the standard Welsh text, W. J. Gruffydd's Rhiannon (1953) built its whole argument about the First and Third Branches around the Pryderi complex, and Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi made the boy who spans all four branches the structural key to the cycle. Evangeline Walton's Mabinogion tetralogy retold his theft and naming for modern readers, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain — five novels built openly on the Mabinogi's world — carried the matter of Pryderi's branches to a vast young readership, though the boy himself never appears under his own name. In modern Druid and pagan practice he is honoured as the lost-and-found divine son and the lord who endured the emptied land, and the name survives in scholarship as the standing example of the Mabinogi's own method: a person named, deliberately and explicitly, out of a single spoken word of grief relieved.
lore.archaeology: Pryderi is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names him, and the early inscribed stones of Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — record personal names in funerary formulae, not the heroes of story. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of his story is real and walkable: Arberth, the chief court of Dyfed, stands by modern Narberth in Pembrokeshire; Y Felenrhyd, where the fatal combat was fought, lies in the country toward the border of Gwynedd and Dyfed; and the Fourth Branch points to his grave at Maen Tywynog above it. The nearest epigraphic horizon is comparative, not his: the Gaulish Maponos of the Chamalières tablet and the northern British dedications to Apollo Maponus — the divine son whose figure-type the handbooks read him against.
lore.syncretism: Pryderi's great comparative frame is the Celtic divine son. The handbooks set him beside Mabon ap Modron — 'Son son of Mother' — the youth of Culhwch ac Olwen who was taken from his mother Modron when he was three nights old and found again after a search that outlasts every living memory, and behind Mabon the Gaulish Maponos, the 'Divine Son' whom Romano-Celtic dedications pair with Apollo. A child of an Otherworld mother, stolen at birth and restored, whose name carries his story: the figure-type is one, and Mac Cana and Koch both register the comparison — but the names are not cognate, and no scholar claims identity. The second frame is sovereignty-by-loss: like the stricken kings of Irish tradition, Pryderi holds a kingdom that enchantment can empty in a night, and his rescue comes not by his own strength but by Manawydan's patience — the Third Branch's quiet thesis about where a king's real safety lies. Within the corpus his closest kin are his parents [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]] and Pwyll Pen Annwn, his stepfather and rescuer [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his benefactor [[arawn|Arawn]] of [[annwn|Annwn]], and his slayer [[gwydion|Gwydion]] — the enchanter whose conjured wealth bought the pigs and, with them, the war.

Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. The temple is served at /sites/pryderi/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'keh-RID-wen' — every c is hard, the r is rolled, and the stress falls on the middle syllable, the Welsh penult.
pronunciation.note: Ceridwen is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The etymology is a genuine scholarly debate: Ifor Williams derived the name from an original Cyridfen, 'crooked woman', while the traditional analysis reads cerdd 'poetry' + gwen 'fair, blessed'; the handbooks register both rather than settle the question.

domains.title: Inspiration, Transformation
domains.subtitle: The Cauldron of Awen, the Three Drops, the Flight of Shapes
domains.lead: Ceridwen is the keeper of the cauldron of awen — the poetic inspiration of Welsh tradition. From her house by Llyn Tegid she brews a year and a day for the three drops of inspired knowledge, hunts the servant-boy who steals them through every shape in creation, swallows him as a grain of wheat, and gives him back to the world as Taliesin, the greatest poet Wales remembers. The early Welsh sources concur on the essential fact: she is the owner of the cauldron that is the source of poetic inspiration.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Awen
cards.desc: Boiled a year and a day from the books of the feryllt, the alchemist's art, until three drops of inspired knowledge should rise from it.

cards.name: The Three Drops
cards.desc: All the virtue of the brew gathered in three drops — meant for her ugly son, splashed instead on the finger of Gwion Bach, who put it to his lips.

cards.name: The Flight of Shapes
cards.desc: Hare and greyhound, fish and otter, bird and hawk — the pursuit through every form until the grain of wheat meets the high-crested black hen.

cards.name: Llyn Tegid
cards.desc: The lake of Tegid Foel — modern Bala Lake, the largest natural lake in Wales — beside which her household stood and which still keeps her husband's name.

symbols.name: The cauldron
symbols.meaning: Inspiration brewed by art and patience — knowledge as something cooked, not granted

symbols.name: The three drops
symbols.meaning: The whole of awen compressed into an accident — inspiration that chooses its own vessel

symbols.name: The high-crested black hen
symbols.meaning: The final shape of the hunt: the swallowing that is not death but the first cell of a poet

symbols.name: The hide bag
symbols.meaning: The coracle-skin sewn round the unwanted child and given to the sea — rejection that becomes deliverance

symbols.name: The weir on the Dyfi
symbols.meaning: Gwyddno's salmon-weir where the bag comes to rest — the threshold between the hunted boy and the radiant brow

symbols.name: Llyn Tegid
symbols.meaning: The lake that still bears her husband's name — the story's anchor in real Welsh geography

mythology.lead: Ceridwen's whole dossier is a single tale — Hanes Taliesin, the Tale of Taliesin — preserved in sixteenth-century Welsh manuscripts and customarily printed with the Mabinogion, though it is none of the Four Branches. Within that tale she owns its great engine: the cauldron, the hunt, and the rebirth.

myths.title: The Household by Llyn Tegid
myths.text: In the beginning, the tale says, Ceridwen lived beside Llyn Tegid in the land of Penllyn, the wife of Tegid Foel — Tegid the Bald — whose name the lake still carries. They had two children whose fortunes were weighed in opposite scales: a daughter, Creirwy, the fairest maiden in the world, and a son, Morfran, so dark and ill-favoured that he was called Afagddu, Utter Darkness. No god could have made the boy handsome; but Ceridwen was skilled in the arts, and she resolved to give him what nature had refused — knowledge and the gift of poetry, so that his birth might yet be honoured among men of culture.

myths.title: The Cauldron of a Year and a Day
myths.text: From the books of the feryllt — the Welsh name for the alchemist's art — Ceridwen compounded a cauldron of Inspiration and Science. It must boil a year and a day, ceaselessly, until three drops of the spirit of inspiration should be won from it. To keep the vigil she set a blind man, Morda, to kindle the fire beneath, and a servant-boy, Gwion Bach, son of Gwreang of Llanfair in Powys, to stir the pot. The design was exact and the patience enormous: everything in the tale that follows is the unmaking of this design by a single splash.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest carried the Tale of Taliesin into English in the nineteenth century, appended to her Mabinogion, and the witch of Llyn Tegid entered the English-speaking imagination beside the Four Branches she never belonged to. Patrick K. Ford's edition and translation fixed the tale's modern scholarly form. Robert Graves made her a figure of international consequence: The White Goddess (1948) read Ceridwen's cauldron and her hunt as the grammar of all true poetry, and though Celticists have never accepted Graves's method, his book set her at the centre of twentieth-century writing about the muse. In Wales the awen she brewed never left the tradition — the word still names poetic inspiration at the National Eisteddfod, and modern Druid orders invoke it in her name — while modern paganism worldwide honours her as keeper of the cauldron of transformation. The name itself, rare in the medieval record, has come back into use as a Welsh given name, carried by the only myth in the language in which a goddess's failure becomes a nation's poetry.
lore.archaeology: Ceridwen is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and pre-Christian Wales left no theonymic epigraphy of the continental kind. Her witnesses are manuscripts. The fullest early text of Hanes Taliesin is embedded in the great world-chronicle of Elis Gruffydd, a Welsh soldier and chronicler, compiled c. 1530–1552 (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, MS 5276D); a second version was copied by the recusant scribe John Jones of Gellilyfdy around 1607. The name itself is older than its tale: medieval Welsh poetry preserves it in spellings such as Kerritwen and Kyrridven, and the triads' editors record that the early sources agree on her one fixed attribute — the cauldron of awen. The geography of the story is real and still legible: Llyn Tegid, her lake, is Bala Lake in Gwynedd, the largest natural lake in Wales, which keeps her husband Tegid Foel's name; and Gwyddno's weir, where the bag comes ashore, stands in the tradition at the Dyfi estuary below his drowned realm. No sanctuary of hers is known, and none is claimed: her monument is the tale itself, and the lake that still carries the name.
lore.syncretism: The strongest cross-border parallels are Irish. The accidental acquisition of a wisdom brewed for another is the plot of the Irish boyhood deeds of Finn mac Cumaill: cooking the salmon of knowledge for his master Finnéces, the boy Finn burns his thumb, puts it in his mouth, and the knowledge intended for the teacher passes to the servant — the same economy of the three drops and the burning finger. The swallowing that becomes rebirth has its Irish twin in Tochmarc Étaíne, where Étaín, transformed into a fly, falls into a cup of wine, is swallowed by the wife of Étar, and is born again into the mortal world. And the cauldron itself is pan-Celtic furniture: [[dagda|the Dagda]]'s cauldron from Murias feeds every company that comes to it, while the Old Irish text The Cauldron of Poesy locates a cauldron of poetry inside every human being. Folklorists — Juliette Wood chief among them — have shown that Hanes Taliesin braids these native strands with international folktale types, above all the magic flight with its transformation chase. The last syncretism is modern: Iolo Morganwg's Barddas set Ceridwen and the awen at the centre of revival Druidry, and modern Druids and pagans honour her as goddess of the cauldron — a reception Ronald Hutton's histories of the revival document and dissect.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Ceridwen — the tale that contains her, Hanes Taliesin, survives in sixteenth-century manuscripts, above all the chronicle of Elis Gruffydd (NLW MS 5276D, c. 1550) and the copy of John Jones of Gellilyfdy (c. 1607), while earlier Welsh poetry attests the name in spellings such as Kerritwen and Kyrridven. Middle and Modern Welsh write the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: ceridwen.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/ceridwen/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AN-oon' — two syllables, stress on the first; the w is sounded as a short 'oo', so the name rhymes with 'cannon' said with Welsh vowels.
pronunciation.note: Annwn is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the realm's fame in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Otherworld, Underworld
domains.subtitle: The Deep, the Abyss — realm of the feast and the hunt
domains.lead: Annwn is the Welsh Otherworld of the Mabinogi and the oldest Welsh poetry — a realm of plenty where the feast never fails, ruled in the First Branch by [[arawn|Arawn]], and hunted across by Gwyn ap Nudd, whom God set over the demons of Annwn lest they destroy this world. Its cauldron, borne home from its fortresses at terrible cost, is the oldest quest of Arthurian tradition.

cards.name: The Cauldron of the Head of Annwn
cards.desc: Kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, it will not boil a coward's food — the prize of Arthur's voyage in Preiddeu Annwfn.

cards.name: The Hounds of Annwn
cards.desc: Arawn's pack — gleaming white with red ears, the colours the Welsh tradition gives every creature from the Otherworld.

cards.name: Prydwen
cards.desc: Arthur's ship on the voyage to the fortresses of Annwn — three full loads went in; except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.

cards.name: The Hunt of Gwyn ap Nudd
cards.desc: The son of Nudd rides with the hunt of Annwn; in Culhwch ac Olwen, God set him over its demons lest they destroy this world.

symbols.name: The cauldron of Pen Annwn
symbols.meaning: Plenty that will not serve the coward — abundance that answers only to courage

symbols.name: White hounds with red ears
symbols.meaning: The colours of the Otherworld made flesh — beauty that marks the boundary crossed

symbols.name: Caer Sidi and the fortresses
symbols.meaning: The revolving castle and its sister fortresses — the Otherworld as architecture that must be won, not visited

symbols.name: Prydwen
symbols.meaning: Arthur's ship — the voyage into the deep from which only seven returned

symbols.name: The year's exchange
symbols.meaning: Arawn and Pwyll trading shapes and kingdoms — the Otherworld close enough to wear a man's face

mythology.lead: Annwn is named in the very first pages of the Mabinogi and in the most difficult poem of early Welsh tradition. Its dossier is small and immense: a king who trades his shape, a cauldron that will not boil a coward's food, a hunt that keeps the world's demons leashed — and, behind all three, the deep itself.

myths.title: The Year in Annwn
myths.text:
Pwyll, prince of Dyfed, is hunting in Glyn Cuch when he drives a strange pack off a stag — hounds gleaming white, with red ears, the colours of the Otherworld — and feeds his own dogs on the kill. Their master rides up: [[arawn|Arawn]], a king of Annwn, and the offense is real. To make amends Pwyll accepts Arawn's bargain: for a year and a day they will exchange shapes and kingdoms, and at the year's end Pwyll must face Arawn's rival Hafgan — a king who can be killed by a single blow only; strike him twice and by the next day he fights as strongly as before.

Pwyll rules Annwn for the year in Arawn's likeness, in a court of unsurpassed plenty — and each night lies beside Arawn's queen without once touching her. At the appointed ford he strikes Hafgan once, refuses the second blow the wounded king begs for, and Annwn is united under Arawn. When the two kings meet again at Glyn Cuch and resume their own shapes, Arawn learns of the year's chastity and the friendship is sealed with gifts of horses, greyhounds, hawks, and gold. From that day Pwyll was called not Pwyll Prince of Dyfed but Pwyll Pen Annwn — Pwyll, Head of Annwn.

myths.title: The Spoils of Annwn
myths.text:
The poem Preiddeu Annwfn, 'The Spoils of Annwfn', preserved in the fourteenth-century Book of Taliesin and spoken in the poet's own voice, is the oldest surviving account of an Arthurian Otherworld raid. Arthur sails in his ship Prydwen against the fortresses of the deep — Caer Sidi, Caer Pedryfan, Caer Wydyr, and the rest — and the refrain tolls after each: 'except seven, none returned from Caer Sidi.' Three full loads of Prydwen went into Annwn; seven men came back.

The prize is the cauldron of the Head of Annwfn — kindled by the breath of nine maidens, its rim set about with pearls, and marked by the rule the Welsh tradition fixes on Otherworld vessels: it will not boil the food of a coward. The poem is elliptical, proud, and mournful at once — the poet stands apart from the swordsmen who went in and never came out — but its facts became permanent: the Otherworld has a cauldron, Arthur went to get it, and almost no one returned.

lore.culturalLegacy: Preiddeu Annwfn stands at the head of the Arthurian tradition: the raid on the Otherworld fortresses is older than every romance of the Grail, and scholars from Loomis onward have read the quest for the Head of Annwn's cauldron — a vessel of plenty that tests the worthy — as the Grail story's deepest Welsh root. The name kept working in Welsh: Annwn remains the living word for the Otherworld, and the white red-eared hounds became the Cŵn Annwn of later Welsh folklore, the pack whose crying in the night sky foretells a death. Gwyn ap Nudd rode out of the texts into modern Druidry and pagan practice as the great huntsman and psychopomp of the Welsh tradition, and Glastonbury Tor — crowned now by the stump of St Michael's tower — still carries his court in the popular imagination. Restoring Annwn in Unicode costs nothing and fixes something: the canonical spelling of the deep, held against the drift of anglicized spellings like Annwvyn and Annwyn.
lore.archaeology: Annwn is a wholly textual realm: no inscription invokes it, and the Romano-British epigraphy of Wales is silent on the Otherworld by name. Its manuscript witnesses, however, are exact. The Mabinogi survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two great codices of medieval Welsh prose; Preiddeu Annwfn is preserved uniquely in the Book of Taliesin (National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century); and Culhwch ac Olwen comes down in a White Book fragment and the full Red Book text. The one site the tradition ties to Annwn is Glastonbury Tor, Gwyn ap Nudd's seat in Buchedd Collen: excavations on the Tor in the 1960s found sub-Roman and early medieval occupation beneath the ruins of St Michael's church — real archaeology on the hill, though none of it speaks to the Otherworld, whose only true location is the text.
lore.syncretism: Annwn's clearest kin are Irish: the síd of the Túatha Dé Danann, where the feast likewise never fails — the Dagda's cauldron of Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standing comparison for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn, and Mac Cana sets the two vessels side by side as one Celtic figure-type. The Irish Otherworld of the immrama and echtrai — Mag Mell, Emain Ablach, lands 'without grief, without sorrow, without death' — matches Annwn's profile point for point: plenty, beauty, and the suspension of age and sickness. Yet the Brythonic tradition is not a copy of the Gaelic one: no Irish text knows the name Annwn, and the Welsh corpus built its Otherworld on its own geography — the ford at Glyn Cuch, the revolving fortresses of the Taliesin poem, the Tor at Glastonbury. The Christian redactors left the structure intact while re-labelling its inhabitants: by Buchedd Collen, Gwyn ap Nudd's splendid court could be dismissed as a demonic glamour without surrendering one detail of the feast.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh has been written in the Latin alphabet throughout its manuscript history, and the normalized form Annwn is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. The manuscripts spell the name Annwfn (Middle Welsh f writes the voiced [v]); the modern normalized spelling is Annwn. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: annwn.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: EKH-ooshkya — stress the first syllable, let the ch rasp as in 'loch', and run the second word tight: the whole compound is one breath, horse and water together.
pronunciation.note: Eachuisge is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Gaelic compound is written in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive character for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone marks the temple form; the creature's standing in the folklore record is beside the point. The hyphens of the dictionaries (each-uisge) are a grammatical courtesy, not a registrable form.

domains.title: The Water Horse of the Lochs
domains.subtitle: The Perfect Stallion, the Adhesive Back, and the Liver That Floated Ashore
domains.lead: Eachuisge — the each-uisge, the water horse — is the most dangerous being in the Highland Otherworld: a shape-shifter that haunts the lochs and sea-lochs of Gaelic Scotland, wearing the shape of a flawless stallion at the water's edge. Mount him and your hands stick fast to his hide; the loch does the rest. The Lowland kelpie haunts rivers and is content to drown you — the each-uisge devours.

cards.name: The Loch
cards.desc: His true country: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the Highlands, where he waits beneath the surface.

cards.name: The Perfect Stallion
cards.desc: His chosen lure: a beautiful horse standing tame by the shore, offered to any traveler in a hurry.

cards.name: The Adhesive Back
cards.desc: Once mounted, the rider cannot dismount: the hide holds the hand like pitch, and the horse runs for the water.

cards.name: The Handsome Stranger
cards.desc: His other shape: a fine young man by the shore — betrayed, the tales say, by the water-weed in his hair.

symbols.name: The flawless stallion
symbols.meaning: The too-perfect gift at the water's edge — beauty as bait, offered where the ground runs out

symbols.name: The adhesive hide
symbols.meaning: The choice that cannot be unmade: once mounted, the mount decides

symbols.name: The liver on the shore
symbols.meaning: The one thing the loch gives back — the Highland record's grimmest detail, and its proof that this horse devours

symbols.name: The weed in the stranger's hair
symbols.meaning: The tell the shape cannot shed: water keeps its mark on whatever walks out of it

mythology.lead: The each-uisge has no medieval manuscript behind him: his mythology is oral, and its primary witnesses are the great nineteenth-century field collections of the Highlands — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. The tales agree on the essentials with the consistency of a warning passed from shore to shore.

myths.title: The Rider Taken
myths.text: The core of every telling is the same. A traveler on the shore of a loch finds a beautiful horse standing idle — fine beyond any horse in the parish, saddled by luck, or so it seems. He mounts; the horse is smooth and willing; and then the rider finds his hands fast to the hide, stuck as if with bird-lime, and the horse's head already turned toward the water. The loch takes them both. In the grimmest tellings the loch gives the rider back in pieces — the tradition is exact about this: the each-uisge devours the whole body, and what floats ashore is the liver alone. That detail is the Highland folklore's way of drawing the line between its own water horse and the Lowland kelpie, which drowns but does not eat.

myths.title: The Boy Who Cut Off His Finger
myths.text: The best-known of the warning-tales gives the creature a longer game. A fine horse appears to children playing by a loch, and one by one they climb its back — and the back lengthens to take them, seat after seat, until all are mounted save one wary boy, who will only touch the hide with a finger. The horse springs for the water with its load of children, and the boy, stuck by that single finger, does the one thing left: he cuts the finger off and escapes. The loch gives back the others the next day, piecemeal. The collectors recorded the tale across the Highlands, and Briggs notes it among the each-uisge's defining episodes: the compound's lesson compressed into a single image — touch with everything and you lose everything; touch with a finger and a finger pays for the lesson.

lore.culturalLegacy: The each-uisge entered print through the great Victorian field collections — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62) and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900) — and it never left. Katharine Briggs's Encyclopedia of Fairies fixed its modern profile as the fiercest of the British water-horses, and MacKillop's Dictionary of Celtic Mythology carried it into the standard Celtic reference shelf. Burns had already put the Lowland cousin into verse — the 'water-kelpie' of the Address to the Deil — and the whole water-horse tradition stands behind the Highlands' most famous modern legend: commentators have long read the loch-monster lore of the twentieth century against this older record of horses in the water. Andy Scott's Kelpies at Falkirk (2013), the thirty-meter horse-head sculptures on the Forth and Clyde Canal, are the tradition's monumental afterlife — kelpies by name, but the image they make permanent is the each-uisge's own: the horse rising out of Scottish water. In Gaelic itself the compound never went anywhere: each-uisge still means the water horse, and the warning it carries is older than any collection that preserves it.
lore.archaeology: The each-uisge has no material witness, and the record must be exact about what that means: no inscription names him, no manuscript illuminates him, and no medieval codex preserves his tales, because he belongs to oral tradition rather than to the literary cycles. His primary evidence is the nineteenth-century field collection — Campbell of Islay's Popular Tales of the West Highlands (1860–62), gathered from Gaelic-speaking informants across the western Highlands and Islands, and John Gregorson Campbell's Superstitions of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland (1900), the fullest single dossier of the water horse's habits. Carmichael's Carmina Gadelica records the same Highland world in its charms and invocations. The landscape itself is the rest of the evidence: the deep freshwater lochs and sea-lochs of the west are the named settings of the tales, and the water-horse complex they belong to is one of the most widely attested figure-types in northern European folklore — a fact the comparatists established from the collections, not from the ground.
lore.syncretism: The each-uisge is the Highland head of a family that runs the length of the Celtic coasts and beyond. His closest cousin is the Lowland Scots kelpie, which haunts rivers rather than lochs and is generally the milder power — drowning without devouring; the two are kindred, not cognate, for the words are unrelated. The Northern Isles keep their own: Shetland's nuggle or njogel, and Orkney's nuckelavee, a far worse thing — a skinless fusion of man and horse that must be distinguished from the shape-shifting water horse proper. The Isle of Man has the cabbyl-ushtey, Wales the ceffyl dŵr, and Ireland the each-uisce and the shape-shifting [[pooka|Púca]], which takes horse-shape among its many forms. The tradition is older than the collections: [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]]'s horse Aonbharr, which runs over land and sea alike, shows the medieval Irish imagination already at work on the horse that owns both elements. Beyond the Celtic world the type recurs — the Scandinavian bäckahäst and the nøkk among them — and the handbooks treat the whole complex as one of the most widespread figure-types of northern European water-lore: the horse as the beautiful face of drowning.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is the ordinary Gaelic common-noun compound each-uisge, 'water horse', written in the Latin alphabet Gaelic has used since the early medieval period — normalized here as Eachuisge for the temple form. There is no older monumental attestation: the figure belongs to oral tradition, and its primary record is the nineteenth-century field collection, not the manuscript codex. The compound is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the restoration changes nothing but the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: eachuisge.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

steps: The name is written with two kanji: 風 'wind' + 神 'god'.
Hepburn romanization Fūjin uses a macron to mark the long vowel /ɯː/.
The compound appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki as one of the kami born from Izanagi's purification.
The Unicode restoration Fūjin preserves vowel length; the kanji form is not used as a domain because CJK scripts are not supported in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FOO-jin' — the first syllable is long and breezy, with lips almost touching for the 'f'; the final 'jin' is quick with a soft 'j'.
pronunciation.note: Fūjin is Tier 1 because the initial ū is long. The name is a straightforward Sino-Japanese compound: 風 (fū, 'wind') + 神 (jin, 'god/spirit'). He is typically paired with Raijin, the thunder god, in Japanese temple and popular art.

domains.title: God of the Wind
domains.subtitle: Storms, Breath, Destruction, and Renewal
domains.lead:
Fūjin is the wind made wild. In Japanese art he appears as a fierce demon, hair streaming, clad in a leopard-skin loincloth, carrying a vast bag of winds on his shoulders. When he opens it, gales tear through forests, scatter roofs, and flatten fields; when he closes it, the air grows still. He is one of the oldest kami in the Japanese pantheon, a destructive force that is also necessary for pollination, dispersal of seeds, and the cleansing of stale air.

He is the brother or counterpart of Raijin, the thunder god, and the two are often depicted together at temple gates, where their terrifying presence keeps danger away from sacred ground.

cards.name: Bag of Winds
cards.desc: He carries a great sack (fūtaku) slung over his shoulders; opening it releases the winds of the world.

cards.name: Demon Guardian
cards.desc: His fierce face and muscular body mark him as one of the powerful oni-like kami who protect temples.

cards.name: Companion of Raijin
cards.desc: He is paired with the thunder god at temple gates and in screen paintings, storm and wind as twin forces.

cards.name: Cosmic Breath
cards.desc: Beyond destruction, wind is the breath that moves pollen, carries clouds, and clears the air for new growth.

symbols.name: Wind bag (fūtaku)
symbols.meaning: The sack from which all winds are released, his most distinctive attribute

symbols.name: Leopard skin
symbols.meaning: His wild garment, marking him as a powerful, untamed kami

symbols.name: Green or red skin
symbols.meaning: His demonic complexion, shared with other fierce protective deities

symbols.name: Streaming hair
symbols.meaning: The visual sign of wind in motion, often rendered with exaggerated dynamism

symbols.name: Temple gate pairing with Raijin
symbols.meaning: The fūjin-raijin-zu motif that protects Buddhist temples from harmful influences

mythology.lead: Fūjin's mythology is grounded in the creation narratives of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, in popular Buddhist iconography, and in the visual tradition of Japanese screen painting. He is both a primordial force and a temple guardian.

myths.title: The Birth of Fūjin
myths.text: The wind kami are older than the name Fūjin. In the Kojiki's birth-of-the-kami sequence, Shinatsuhiko-no-mikoto, the wind deity, is born to Izanagi and Izanami among the elemental gods that follow the making of the islands. The Nihon Shoki adds its own etiology: Izanagi blows away the morning mist that wraps the new-made land, and from that breath the wind kami is born. The thunder kami, by contrast, are born from Izanami's corpse after her death in the birth of the fire god — neither wind nor thunder kami are products of Izanagi's later purification at the misogi. The demonic figure called Fūjin — leopard skin, wind-bag, streaming hair — is the later, Buddhist-inflected portrait of these older wind kami.

myths.title: Wind in the Age of the Gods
myths.text: The wind kami appear in several episodes of the divine age. When the sun goddess Amaterasu withdrew into the cave, the winds stilled and the world grew dark. When she was lured out, life — including the movement of air — returned. Fūjin thus belongs to the same cosmic order governed by the sun and storm; his winds are part of the vitality that returns when divine harmony is restored.

lore.culturalLegacy: Fūjin remains one of Japan's most recognizable kami. The folding screens (byōbu) depicting Fūjin and Raijin by Tawaraya Sōtatsu are national treasures and icons of Japanese art. Temples still display the pair at gates and in festival processions, and Fūjin appears in manga, anime, video games, and advertising as a symbol of overwhelming natural force. His name is invoked in discussions of typhoons and seasonal winds, and the visual motif of a figure with a wind bag has become a global shorthand for the wind itself. The Unicode restoration Fūjin preserves the long vowel that distinguishes this divine name from ordinary fujin (婦人 'women'; 夫人 'wife').
lore.archaeology: Fūjin is best known from Japanese painting and sculpture rather than from archaeological contexts alone. The oldest surviving depictions appear in Heian- and Kamakura-period Buddhist iconography, where he serves as a guardian deity. The most famous visual testimony is the pair of folding screens by Tawaraya Sōtatsu (early 17th century), now at the Kyoto National Museum and Kenninji temple, which depict Fūjin and Raijin in gold-leaf clouds. Temple sculptures and ema (votive plaques) across Japan preserve popular representations of the wind god, while the textual record in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki anchors his mythological origins in the creation age.
lore.syncretism: Fūjin descends from the Chinese wind deity Fengshen, transmitted to Japan along with Buddhism and continental iconography. He also resembles wind gods across Eurasia, from the Greek Boreas and the Vedic Vāta to the Central Asian wind demons depicted on Silk Road textiles. In Japan, however, he became thoroughly domesticated as a kami, paired with Raijin and rendered in a distinctive visual style by artists such as Tawaraya Sōtatsu and Ogata Kōrin. The Japanese fascination with storms — wind, rain, thunder, lightning — produced one of the most dynamic bodies of religious painting in East Asia, with Fūjin and Raijin at its center.

steps: Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha ('Earth Treasury' or 'Earth Womb') was translated into Chinese as 地藏 (Dìzàng).
Japanese borrowed the compound as 地蔵, read in Sino-Japanese as Jizō.
Hepburn romanisation writes the long vowel with a macron: Jizō.
The ASCII form jizo loses the length mark, collapsing the distinction between short and long ō.
The Unicode restoration Jizō is registrable in .com; the kanji form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

Nelson, The Original Modern Reader's Japanese-English Character Dictionary

pronunciation.approximation: 'JEE-zoh' — the first syllable is like 'jee', the second is a long, drawn 'zoh'.
pronunciation.note: Jizō is Tier 1: the macron on ō marks the long vowel of the Japanese reading. The full Sanskrit name would require retroflex and aspirated consonants not registrable in the DNS root zone.

domains.title: Earth Treasury Bodhisattva
domains.subtitle: Guardian of Children, Travelers, and the Dead
domains.lead: Jizō is the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha as known and loved in Japan: a gentle monk-like figure who refuses buddhahood until all beings, especially those in hell and the spirits of dead children, are saved. His statues stand by roadsides, cemeteries, and temples, clothed in red bibs and caps offered by grieving parents.

cards.name: Guardian of Children
cards.desc: He protects children, including mizuko, the spirits of miscarried and aborted foetuses.

cards.name: Savior of Hell-beings
cards.desc: He descends into the hell realms to rescue those tormented by their karma.

cards.name: Patron of Travelers
cards.desc: Roadside Jizō guide and protect those on journeys, both living and dead.

cards.name: Bodhisattva Vow
cards.desc: He postpones his own enlightenment until every hell is emptied.

symbols.name: Staff (khakkhara)
symbols.meaning: The ringing staff that warns small creatures and opens the gates of hell.

symbols.name: Wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)
symbols.meaning: The gem that grants all needs and dispels darkness.

symbols.name: Red bib or cap
symbols.meaning: Offerings by parents for the protection of their children in the afterlife.

symbols.name: Lotus seat
symbols.meaning: Purity within the muddy world of suffering.

mythology.lead: Jizō's mythology blends Indian scripture, Chinese translation, and Japanese folk belief. He is one of the most actively worshipped Buddhist figures in Japan.

myths.title: The Original Vow
myths.text: The Kṣitigarbha Sutra recounts that in a previous life the Bodhisattva was a Brahmin maiden whose mother had slandered the Dharma. After her mother's death, the daughter made offerings at a temple and was transported to hell, where she met a demon guardian. Moved by the suffering there, she vowed to save all beings in the hell realms, life after life, until not a single one remained.

myths.title: Sai no Kawara
myths.text: On the banks of Sai no Kawara, the riverbed between life and rebirth, the souls of dead children are forced to pile stones as penance. Demons scatter their work, but Jizō appears in the guise of a monk to hide the children in his robes and comfort them. The red bibs and caps placed on his statues are gifts intended to warm these child-spirits.

lore.culturalLegacy: Jizō is everywhere in Japan: thousands of stone statues line mountain paths, village boundaries, and temple precincts. The practice of mizuko kuyō—memorial rites for foetal and infant deaths—centres on him, making him a focus of modern debates about abortion, grief, and maternal responsibility. Contemporary artists and writers return to Jizō as an emblem of patient, non-judgmental compassion.
lore.syncretism: Kṣitigarbha entered China from India and absorbed functions of local earth gods and tomb guardians. In Japan he merged with the kami of roads and boundaries (Sae no Kami / Dōsojin) and with popular protectors of children. He is also syncretised with the Christian St. Christopher in some hidden-Christian communities. The result is a uniquely Japanese figure: a Buddhist Bodhisattva who feels, to many worshippers, like a local spirit.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Japanese name 地蔵 is read Jizō, from Middle Chinese 地藏 Dìzàng, which translates the Sanskrit Kṣitigarbha. 地 (ji) means 'earth' and 藏 (zō) means 'storehouse' or 'womb'. The macron on ō marks the long vowel of the Japanese reading. The full Sanskrit would require retroflex ṣ, aspirated bh, and other characters not registrable in the DNS root zone, so PUNICODEX uses the Japanese form.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OH-koo-nee-NOO-shee' — five even morae; the long Ō is a doubled plain O, never an English diphthong; 'shi' is the soft Japanese shibilant.
pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the restoration Ōkuninushi preserves the long vowel (macron Ō) that the ASCII Okuninushi erases — the very feature that marks Ō- 'great' as distinct from a plain o-. One preserved feature, mechanically verifiable: a single-tier Tier-1 name.

domains.title: The Lord of the Reed-Plain
domains.subtitle: Nation-Building & Marriage
domains.lead: Ōkuninushi — the Great Land-Master — is the earthly sovereign of Japanese myth: the heir of Susanoo who subdued wild Izumo, built it into a nation with the dwarf-god Sukunabikona, and codified medicine, agriculture and the rites of marriage. His was the visible world — Ashihara no Nakatsukuni, the Central Land of Reed-Plains — until he ceded it to the heavenly line of Amaterasu in the act of statecraft the chronicles call kuni-yuzuri, the transfer of the land.

cards.name: Land-Building
cards.desc: With the dwarf god Sukunabikona he “made the land”, binding the borders of the Reed-Plain in the Kojiki’s land-building cycle.

cards.name: Marriage & Alliance
cards.desc: He survives Susanoo’s underworld trials to win Suseri-hime and takes the Yakami bride, sealing rule through union (Kojiki).

cards.name: Medicine & Spellcraft
cards.desc: Remembered as a healer: with Sukunabikona he teaches the medicines and incantations that cure both men and beasts.

symbols.name: White hare of Inaba
symbols.meaning: His first patient and his prophet: the flayed hare of Cape Keta whose healing proved Ōkuninushi's medicine and foretold his marriage to Yakami-hime; emblem of the province of Inaba.

symbols.name: The great shimenawa
symbols.meaning: The colossal sacred rope hung across the halls of Izumo-taisha — among the largest in Japan — marking the boundary of his enshrined presence.

symbols.name: Susanoo's sword, bow and lute
symbols.meaning: The regalia of lordship he carried out of Ne-no-Kuni with Susanoo's blessing — the storm-god's own charter for his rule over the land.

symbols.name: The tiny boat of Sukunabikona
symbols.meaning: The skiff of Metaplexis pod-husks (ama-no-kagami-no-fune) and the moth-skin cloak of the dwarf-god, emblem of the small partner in nation-building.

symbols.name: Herbs and the mortar
symbols.meaning: The pharmacology he and Sukunabikona devised for gods and men — beginning with the remedy of fresh water and katami (cattail) pollen prescribed for the hare.

symbols.name: The high pillars of Izumo
symbols.meaning: The towering hall promised at the kuni-yuzuri, to be raised with pillars 'high as the heaven of the gods' — his eternal seat after the surrender of the land.

mythology.lead: Ōkuninushi's cycle, preserved in the Kojiki (712) and the Nihon Shoki (720), is the longest and most novelistic narrative in Japanese myth — a story of escape, ordeal, sovereignty and renunciation at the meeting-point of earth and heaven.

myths.title: The White Hare of Inaba
myths.text: In the Kojiki (Book I), a hare from the isle of Oki tricks the wani sea-beasts into forming a bridge, is flayed for the deception, and meets the eighty cruel brothers of Ōnamuji, who mockingly prescribe a bath in salt sea-water — agony for its wounds. The youngest brother, Ōnamuji (later Ōkuninushi), advises instead a rinse in fresh river water and a roll in the pollen of katami, the cattail rush; the hare is healed. Grateful, the hare prophesies that Ōnamuji — not his eighty brothers — will win the hand of the princess Yakami-hime of Inaba. It is the first medical prescription in Japanese myth, and the deed that marks the future land-master out from his rivals.

myths.title: The Trials of Ne-no-Kuni
myths.text: Fleeing his brothers' repeated attempts to kill him, Ōnamuji descends to Ne-no-Kuni, the root-land of Susanoo, as the Kojiki (Book I) relates. There he loves Susanoo's daughter Suseribime, and the storm-god tests him: a night in a hall of snakes, a night in a hall of centipedes and wasps — each survived through Suseribime's protective scarves — and a burning meadow where a mouse leads him to safety underground and retrieves the arrow Susanoo had fired. When Ōnamuji at last washes the great god's hair and steals away with Suseribime, Susanoo's sword, bow and heavenly lute, the pursuing god yields and proclaims him Ōkuninushi-no-kami, Great Land-Master, bidding him drive out his brothers and rule the land.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ōkuninushi still anchors the Izumo region of Shimane, where Izumo-taisha draws millions of pilgrims and couples across Japan pray to him as the nation's matchmaker. The white hare of Inaba endures as the emblem of Tottori prefecture, and his son Kotoshironushi presides over the great pilgrimage shrine of Kotohira in Shikoku. The word kuni-yuzuri itself remains the standard term for the peaceful cession of sovereignty — the god's abdication absorbed into the political vocabulary of Japan.
lore.archaeology: Izumo-taisha (Taisha-machi, Izumo, Shimane) is among the oldest and grandest shrines of Japan; the present main hall dates to 1744, but excavations in 2000 uncovered massive clustered pillar bases confirming medieval records of a towering earlier hall — the 'high pillars' the kuni-yuzuri myth demands. The region's cultic antiquity is independently attested by the 1984 Kojindani discovery, a ritual cache of 358 bronze swords, the largest single find of its kind in Japan.
lore.syncretism: Japan's gods met no Roman pantheon; Ōkuninushi's later travels ran through Buddhism instead. Through the folk reading Daikoku-sama of the characters 大国, he was identified with Daikokuten, the Japanese form of Mahākāla, becoming the smiling god of wealth and the household hearth — one of the Seven Gods of Fortune. At Izumo the older identity survived intact: there he remains the great matchmaker of en-musubi, the binding of marriage fates, and in the month the rest of Japan calls Kannazuki, 'the godless month', Izumo calls it Kami-ari-zuki — 'the month the gods are here', when the eight million kami convene at his shrine.

entries.meaning: Hawaiian god symbolized by the squid or by the octopus, typically associated with Kāne

variants.note: Owned stylized form with conventional long-vowel marks; Pukui & Elbert and UH Mānoa write Kanaloa without kahakō

pronunciation.approximation: 'kah-NAH-loh-ah' — both 'a' vowels are long, and the name flows like a slow wave.
pronunciation.note: Kānāloa is Tier 1: the Hawaiian macrons on both ā's mark long vowels, the distinctive prosodic feature of the language. Without them the name collapses into a different rhythmic shape.

domains.title: Lord of the Vast Ocean
domains.subtitle: Sea, Underworld, and Healing
domains.lead: Kānāloa is the Hawaiian god of the deep ocean, the underworld, and healing. He is the companion and sometimes rival of Kāne, the creator; while Kāne governs fresh water and life, Kānāloa rules the salt sea and the mysteries beneath it. He is associated with the octopus, whose arms reach in all directions like ocean currents.

cards.name: Vast Ocean
cards.desc: The Pacific itself is his body, source of food, travel, and the unknown.

cards.name: Underworld
cards.desc: He receives the dead into the dark realm beneath land and sea.

cards.name: Healer
cards.desc: Kānāloa and Kāne together discovered medicinal plants and healing arts.

cards.name: Octopus Kin
cards.desc: The heʻe (octopus) is his animal, shape-shifting and intelligent.

symbols.name: Octopus (heʻe)
symbols.meaning: The many-armed creature of the deep, Kānāloa's kin or avatar.

symbols.name: Ocean waves
symbols.meaning: The visible movement of his vast body.

symbols.name: Kava plant
symbols.meaning: A plant of ritual and healing associated with him.

symbols.name: Dark depths
symbols.meaning: The mysterious underworld where souls and sea creatures dwell.

mythology.lead: Hawaiian myths present Kānāloa as a complementary power to Kāne, the creator. Their partnership structures much of traditional cosmology.

myths.title: Kāne and Kānāloa
myths.text: In Hawaiian cosmogony, Kāne and Kānāloa are paired creator gods. Together they travel across the primordial ocean, striking the earth with their staffs to create springs and bring forth life. Kāne is the fresh water and the sunlight; Kānāloa is the salt sea that surrounds and sustains the islands. Their partnership is not hierarchy but dynamic balance.

myths.title: The Discovery of Medicine
myths.text: Kānāloa fell ill, and no remedy could be found. Kāne prayed and was shown the healing plants of the forest and shore. After Kānāloa was cured, the two gods shared this knowledge with humankind, establishing the practice of lāʻau lapaʻau, traditional Hawaiian herbal medicine. Illness and cure both belong to Kānāloa's watery realm.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kānāloa's name survives in Hawaiian place names, in the scientific names of deep-sea creatures, and in the cultural revival movements that seek to restore indigenous relationships with the ocean. He is invoked in debates over marine conservation, deep-sea mining, and the rights of native Hawaiians to their waters. The octopus, his kin, has become an emblem of intelligent, adaptable life in the Pacific.
lore.syncretism: Kānāloa is clearly related to the pan-Polynesian Tangaroa / Taʻaroa, the great sea deity. In Hawaiian tradition, however, he is less a creator-from-void and more a partner of Kāne, a god of depth and healing. Christian missionaries sometimes identified him with Satan because of his underworld associations, but this identification distorts a figure who was primarily beneficent. Modern Hawaiian cultural revival has reclaimed Kānāloa as a symbol of oceanic sovereignty and ecological wisdom.
lore.originalScriptNote: Hawaiian had no indigenous writing system before European contact. The name is written in the Latin alphabet introduced by missionaries, with macrons added by modern scholars to mark long vowels. Kānāloa is composed of ka (article or intensifier) + nā (plural or intensifier) + loa ('long, vast, far'), together evoking vastness. PUNICODEX preserves both macrons because vowel length is phonemic in Hawaiian and the feature that makes the restoration Tier 1.
