pronunciation.approximation: SHOH-lotl, long ō on both syllables.
pronunciation.note: Xōlōtl carries two long ō vowels, both preserved in the restoration; the final -tl is Nahuatl's signature consonant cluster, released laterally — the sound every visitor learns on the name of the water-monster, the axolotl, that shares his name and, in myth, his skin. The final -tl is Nahuatl's lateral affricate, released to the side of the tongue — the sound that ends axolotl too.

domains.title: The Twin in the Dark
domains.subtitle: Venus's Evening Star, the Dog-Guide, and the Last Transformation
domains.lead: Xōlōtl is the twin who goes down with the sun: brother of Quetzalcōātl, guide of the dead across the underworld's river, and the god who turned himself into maize, maguey, and finally the axolotl rather than be sacrificed. He is the Aztec soul's ferryman — and the lake that still bears his name.

cards.name: The Dog
cards.desc: His animal: the guide that leads the dead across the ninefold river of Mictlān.

cards.name: The Evening Star
cards.desc: Venus at dusk — his station, twin to his brother's morning star.

cards.name: The Axolotl
cards.desc: His final disguise: the water-monster of Xochimilco, gilled and smiling, that shares his name.

cards.name: The Empty Sockets
cards.desc: The codices show him weeping his eyes out at the gods' sacrifice — grief itself, dog-eared.

symbols.name: The dog ears
symbols.meaning: His constant feature in every codex — the faithful guide's mark

symbols.name: The conch and crossbones
symbols.meaning: His lordship of death's roads, shared with Mictlāntēcutli

symbols.name: The maize stalk
symbols.meaning: His first transformation — the god hiding in the staff of life

mythology.lead: Xōlōtl's myths run on twoness: twin of the morning star, guide of the dying sun, the god who is always the second of a pair — and always the one who goes down into the dark.

myths.title: Across the Nine Waters
myths.text: The Aztec dead journeyed four years through Mictlān's nine levels, and at the deep river it was the dog — Xōlōtl's creature — who swam them across; a soul whose family had mistreated dogs in life found no ferryman. The funeral rite buried a red dog with the dead: the god's own form, sacrificed to carry its master home. Among the world's psychopomps, he is the only one who comes as a pet.

myths.title: The God Who Hid
myths.text: At the creation of the fifth sun the gods gathered at Teotihuacan to sacrifice themselves and set the new sun moving. Xōlōtl refused to die: he fled, weeping so hard his eyes fell from their sockets, and hid — as the twin-stalked maize, as the doubled maguey, and at last as the axolotl in the lake. They found him even there, and he died like the rest: the myth of the price of survival, and of the god who begged to live and serves death anyway.

lore.culturalLegacy: The axolotl — Ambystoma mexicanum, the salamander that never grows up, regenerating limbs and heart — took his name into every biology classroom on earth; its survival in Xochimilco's canals is now a national project. The xoloitzcuintli dog is Mexico's national breed, and Dante's Divine Comedy has, in the Mexican imagination, a local answer: the Xolo that carries you across. Frida Kahlo painted her xolos; the 2018 animated films gave him to the world's children.
lore.archaeology: Colima's ceramic dogs — plump, tumored, dancing, two thousand years old — are the west-Mexican ancestors of his cult, buried in shaft tombs to guide their masters. Aztec dog-effigy vessels and the Florentine Codex's account of the funeral dog detail the central-Mexican rite. Xochimilco's chinampa system — the floating gardens where the last wild axolotls hold on — is a UNESCO World Heritage site, the god's water-form's last stronghold, guarded by canals older than the Aztec state.
lore.syncretism: The friars identified him with the devil's lesser angels, but the people kept him closer to a saint of the road: the dog that guards the grave and guides the traveller survived in Mexican folk custom, and the hairless xoloitzcuintli — the national dog, named from his name — was never exorcised. Scholars pair him with every underworld canine from Cerberus to Anubis, and the Maya twins' underworld journey in the Popol Vuh runs on his same road. The axolotl, his water-form, became Mexico's ambassador-species: the smiling face of conservation itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: The codices write him as what he is: the dog-headed god, often shown twisted in transformation — half into maize, half into the water-beast — with the twin's ball-court and the Venus star in his glyphic entourage. The name and the animal (xōlōtl, "water monster," the axolotl) are one word: the god hiding inside his own spelling.

pronunciation.approximation: 'eets-pah-PAHL-ohtl' — the name crackles like obsidian breaking; hold the second 'a' and the final 'o' long.
pronunciation.note: The macrons on ā and ō mark reconstructed long vowels, making the restoration Tier 1. The name is onomatopoeic and lethal: a butterfly made of razor-sharp obsidian.

domains.title: Obsidian Butterfly
domains.subtitle: Stars, Tamoanchan, and the Cihuateteo
domains.lead: Itzpapālōtl is one of the most fearsome goddesses of the Nahua cosmos: a butterfly with wings of obsidian blades, mistress of Tamoanchan, and mother of the Cihuateteo. She is beauty that cuts, maternity that devours, and the star-demon who descends when the sun is darkened.

cards.name: Obsidian Wings
cards.desc: Her wings are edged with itztli, the black volcanic glass used for sacrifice and mirrors.

cards.name: Tamoanchan
cards.desc: The paradise of origins, where the gods created the first humans from ground bones.

cards.name: Mother of Cihuateteo
cards.desc: Women who died in childbirth became warrior spirits under her command, dangerous to the living.

cards.name: Eclipse Star
cards.desc: As a Tzitzimitl she leads star-demons against the sun, threatening cosmic collapse.

symbols.name: Obsidian butterfly
symbols.meaning: The union of delicate beauty and sacrificial cutting power.

symbols.name: Knife-edged wings
symbols.meaning: Instruments of war and childbirth, both forms of tearing that bring life or death.

symbols.name: Jaguar claws
symbols.meaning: Her taloned hands link her to the night hunters of the Mesoamerican forest.

symbols.name: Star headdress
symbols.meaning: Her identity as a Tzitzimitl, a stellar power that descends during eclipses.

mythology.lead: Itzpapālōtl belongs to the dangerous borderlands: between paradise and underworld, birth and death, daylight and eclipse. Her myths are preserved in fragments of the Florentine Codex and Borgia group codices.

myths.title: The Lady of Tamoanchan
myths.text: Tamoanchan is the mythical paradise of origins, a lush mountain of flowers and fruit where the creator couple dwelt. Itzpapālōtl rules there as both guardian and destroyer, her obsidian wings protecting the tree from which the first humans were fashioned. To approach her is to risk being flayed by the very beauty one admires.

myths.title: The Cihuateteo
myths.text: Women who died in childbirth were not ordinary dead. They became Cihuateteo, 'divine women', fierce spirits who accompanied the sun from zenith to sunset and prowled crossroads at night. Itzpapālōtl is their mother and queen. Because they had died bringing life, they had power over both: they could bless children or steal them away.

lore.culturalLegacy: Itzpapālōtl survives where Mesoamerican antiquity meets contemporary creativity. Her obsidian-butterfly form has inspired jewelry, tattoos, graphic novels, and installations that explore the beauty of the lethal. She is also a touchstone in studies of Nahua gender: the Cihuateteo show that childbirth was a battlefield as honoured as the warrior's, and that the dead women who fell in it were not victims but powers.
lore.syncretism: Colonial friars associated Itzpapālōtl with demons of the air and witches, flattening her complex identity into a Satanic figure. Modern scholars and artists have reclaimed her as an emblem of feminine ferocity, the dangerous side of motherhood, and the ecological violence of volcanic landscapes. Her image appears in Mexican feminist art and in celebrations of Día de los Muertos as a skeletal butterfly.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is composed of ītztli ('obsidian') and papālōtl ('butterfly'). Classical Nahuatl used macrons to mark vowel length, now reconstructed from colonial sources and comparative Uto-Aztecan evidence. The final -tl is a single lateral affricate. There is no surviving pre-contact alphabetic text of the name; it is known from alphabetic Nahuatl manuscripts produced under Spanish supervision, above all the Florentine Codex.

pronunciation.approximation: 'TLAH-lteh-KWEH-tlee' — begin with the single 'tl' sound, hold the first and second vowels long, and treat the final -tl as one release.
pronunciation.note: The name is a straightforward compound of tlālli ('earth') and tēcuhtli ('lord'). The honorific suffix is not gender-exclusive in Nahuatl; Tlāltēcuhtli is depicted as both male and female, and sometimes as a toad-like being. Tier 1: the macrons on ā and ē preserve reconstructed vowel length.

domains.title: Lord of the Earth
domains.subtitle: Chthonic Power and Cosmic Sustenance
domains.lead: Tlāltēcuhtli is the living earth beneath the feet of the Fifth Sun, the monster-toad whose body became the world and whose gaping mouth swallows the sun each evening. Unlike the sky gods who demand attention with thunder and light, Tlāltēcuhtli works in silence: receiving the dead, pushing up crops, and reminding mortals that every step is taken on a conscious being.

cards.name: The Earth as Body
cards.desc: Mountains rise from Tlāltēcuhtli's back; rivers flow from its folds; caves are its open mouth.

cards.name: Receiver of the Dead
cards.desc: The sun descends into Tlāltēcuhtli's jaws at sunset; corpses return to the earth that fed them.

cards.name: Agricultural Generosity
cards.desc: Maize, beans, squash, and cotton rise from its body; offerings of blood ensure the earth's continued fruitfulness.

cards.name: Devourer and Transformer
cards.desc: The earth consumes and renews; Tlāltēcuhtli is both tomb and womb, endings and beginnings.

symbols.name: Crouching toad
symbols.meaning: The common posture of Tlāltēcuhtli images, expressing the earth as a low, wide, waiting creature

symbols.name: Gaping jaws
symbols.meaning: The mouth that receives the setting sun and the bodies of the dead

symbols.name: Curved fangs and claws
symbols.meaning: Predatory features that mark the earth's power to destroy as well as nourish

symbols.name: Blood-red coloring
symbols.meaning: Aztec depictions often paint Tlāltēcuhtli red, the color of vitality and sacrifice

mythology.lead: Tlāltēcuhtli appears in several Mesoamerican creation accounts as the earth monster who must be defeated and dismembered before the present world can exist. The most detailed Nahuatl version is the Histoyre du Méchique, in which Quetzalcōātl and Tēzcatlīpōca split the earth monster in two; the K'iche' Maya Popol Vuh preserves a cognate tradition.

myths.title: The Dismemberment of the Earth Monster
myths.text: In the Nahua cosmogony preserved by colonial sources, the gods created the present earth from the body of a great monster. In some versions Quetzalcōātl and Tēzcatlīpōca seized Tlāltēcuhtli or a crocodilian earth-being and tore it in two: one half became the sky, the other the earth. From its body the mountains, rivers, and valleys were formed, and its hair became trees and plants. The story is cognate with K'iche' Maya accounts of the Hero Twins defeating the false sun Vucub-Caquix and his earth-giant sons Zipacna and Cabrakan. (Histoyre du Méchique; Leyenda de los Soles; Popol Vuh parallels.)

myths.title: The Sun's Nightly Journey
myths.text: Each evening the sun descends into the gaping mouth of Tlāltēcuhtli in the west. The earth devours the luminary, holds it through the night, and gives birth to it again in the east. This daily swallowing and rebirth mirrors the agricultural cycle and the human journey from death to afterlife.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tlāltēcuhtli entered global consciousness through the vivid monolith discovered during the Templo Mayor excavations in Mexico City — a massive red-painted stone slab showing the crouching, fanged earth lord. The image has become a staple of museum exhibitions on Aztec cosmology and a touchstone for discussions of ecological reciprocity in pre-Columbian thought. Contemporary Mesoamericanist artists and environmental writers invoke Tlāltēcuhtli to express the idea of the earth as a living, conscious, and hungry body.
lore.archaeology: The most spectacular find is the monolithic Tlāltēcuhtli sculpture uncovered in 2006 near the Templo Mayor, measuring more than 4 meters on a side and preserving red and yellow pigment. Templo Mayor excavations have located Tlāltēcuhtli shrines, offering caches, and sculptural reliefs showing the sun entering the earth's mouth. Postclassic and early colonial pictorial manuscripts such as the Codex Borgia and Codex Magliabechiano preserve ritual and iconographic details of the earth lord.
lore.syncretism: Tlāltēcuhtli overlaps with Cōātlīcue, Tōnantzin, and other female earth figures in Nahuatl religion; the gender and precise identity of the earth lord were fluid across regions and periods. In Maya traditions the cognate figure is often the crocodilian earth monster whose body supports the sky. Colonial Christian writers interpreted the earth devourer as a demonic figure, but the persistence of earth shrines and offerings suggests a deeper continuity of chthonic devotion.

variants.note: Fully tone-marked dictionary form with the initial low tone (Abraham). Written Yoruba routinely omits tone marks.

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks.
Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing.
The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-ROON-mee-LAH — low 'aw', high 'ROON', then low 'mee-LAH'.
pronunciation.note: Ọrúnmìlà is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute and grave accents that preserve Yoruba tones are distinctive features the ASCII form loses. The dot below ọ marks the open [ɔ] vowel.

domains.title: Witness at Creation
domains.subtitle: Wisdom, Divination, and the Ifá Corpus
domains.lead:
Ọrúnmìlà is the orixá of wisdom and the patron of Ifá, the Yoruba divination system that maps human destiny against the patterns of the cosmos. He was present at creation; he knows the day the world was made and the names that were spoken into it. Kings do not act without consulting him, and no orixá is said to understand the future as he does.

Unlike Ṣàngó or Ọya, he is not a warrior. His power is speech, memory, and the ability to read the signs hidden in the fall of sixteen palm nuts.

cards.name: Ifá Divination
cards.desc: Sixteen palm nuts and the divination chain reveal the odù that governs a situation.

cards.name: Sacred Knowledge
cards.desc: He remembers the verses, medicines, and sacrifices that restore cosmic balance.

cards.name: Witness of Creation
cards.desc: Only he saw the world being made; therefore only he can interpret its deepest laws.

cards.name: Babalawo
cards.desc: The father of secrets — the title of the priests who speak for him in divination.

symbols.name: Ikin palm nuts
symbols.meaning: The sixteen sacred nuts used in Ifá divination; they hold the signatures of the odù.

symbols.name: Ọpẹ̀lẹ̀ divination chain
symbols.meaning: The chain of eight half-shells that provides quicker access to Ifá wisdom.

symbols.name: Green and yellow beads
symbols.meaning: His sacred colours, associated with palm leaves, knowledge, and mature wisdom.

symbols.name: Staff of wisdom
symbols.meaning: The iron staff that grounds his authority and marks the babalawo in ceremony.

mythology.lead: Ọrúnmìlà's mythology is textual as much as narrative: it lives in thousands of Ifá verses (òdù Ifá) that record his journeys, judgments, and interventions.

myths.title: The Witness at the Foundation of the World
myths.text: According to Ifá tradition, Ọrúnmìlà was the only orixá present when Olódùmarè created the earth. He observed the placement of the rivers, the rising of the mountains, and the distribution of destinies. Because he witnessed the beginning, he can trace any present trouble back to its origin and prescribe the sacrifice that will set it right.

myths.title: The Sixteen Principals
myths.text: The Ifá corpus is organised around sixteen principal odù, each with sixteen sub-odù, generating 256 basic combinations. Each odù is a world of stories, proverbs, and medicines. Ọrúnmìlà is not merely the system; he is the living voice that speaks through it when the babalawo casts the chain or nuts.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọrúnmìlà's legacy is the Ifá corpus itself — one of the largest bodies of African sacred poetry, now recognised by UNESCO as an intangible cultural heritage of humanity. His influence reaches into literature, psychology, and ethics: the idea that wisdom is not possession but practice, that destiny can be read but must be met with sacrifice, and that the future is a conversation rather than a sentence. Contemporary African philosophers and diaspora theologians return to him as a model of disciplined, compassionate knowledge.
lore.archaeology: The Ifá corpus is preserved orally and in manuscript form across Yoruba-speaking regions, with archaeological evidence including divination implements such as carved palm nuts (ikin), brass chains (ọpẹ̀lẹ̀), and wooden divination trays (ọpọ́n Ifá). Diaspora collections hold beaded necklaces, iron staffs, and ritual texts that document the continuity of Ọrúnmìlà worship from West Africa to Cuba and Brazil.
lore.syncretism: Ọrúnmìlà travelled to the Americas as the patron of Ifá and the central figure of Santería's religious hierarchy. In Cuba, babalawos initiate devotees and divine through the dilogún shells or the full Ifá corpus. Catholic syncretism sometimes links him to Saint Francis of Assisi because of the Franciscan association with poverty, humility, and divine knowledge. In Brazil he is Orunmilá, less publicly prominent than in Cuba but still foundational to the Houses of Ifá.

entries.meaning: The hunter — orisha of the hunt, the forest, and deliberate strategy (standard Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì; Cuban Ochosi, Brazilian Oxóssi)

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The name Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì is the standard orthography of the hunter orisha known in Brazil as Oxóssi.
The underdots distinguish /ɔ/ and /ʃ/ from their plain counterparts; tone marks carry lexical tone (low–high–low–low).
The Unicode restoration Ọṣọọsì preserves the underdots and the final low tone; the ASCII form loses all of them.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-shaw-AW-sih — the dotted ọ is the open 'aw' of 'law'; ṣ is 'sh'; the tones run low-high-low-low.
pronunciation.note: The name in standard Yoruba orthography is Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì, fully tone-marked; the owned form Ọṣọọsì keeps the underdotted vowels (ọ, the open o) and the long double-o while following the diaspora convention that leaves tone marks implicit — the spelling carried across the Santería and Candomblé worlds. Abraham's Dictionary of Modern Yoruba lists him as the god of hunters; the etymology is debated, though the ọ̀ṣọ́ element suggests swiftness. Tier-1 by rule: the underdots and the ṣ are distinctive letters the ASCII "Ochosi" cannot carry.

domains.title: The Single Arrow
domains.subtitle: The Hunt, the Forest, and the Justice of the Patient Shot
domains.lead: Ọṣọọsì is the hunter orisha: lord of the forest, master of the bow, and patron of strategy — the one whose praise-poems say he kills with a single arrow, because he has learned what every hunter must learn: wait.

cards.name: The Single Arrow
cards.desc: One shaft, never wasted: his oríkì hail the hunter who does not need to shoot twice.

cards.name: The Bow (Ofá)
cards.desc: His emblem across three continents — the hunter's bow, carved on his shrines and sung in his names.

cards.name: The Forest (Igbó)
cards.desc: His cathedral and his larder: the deep bush where game, medicine, and danger all live.

cards.name: Justice
cards.desc: In the diaspora he stands with the accused: the orisha of right judgment and the patient case.

symbols.name: The bow and arrow
symbols.meaning: Skill married to patience: the whole doctrine of the hunt in one image

symbols.name: The forest
symbols.meaning: The realm of the provider — game, leaves, and the tests that make a tracker

symbols.name: The single shot
symbols.meaning: Strategy as worship: preparation so complete that one attempt suffices

mythology.lead: Ọṣọọsì's mythology lives in praise-poetry and divination verse — the oríkì that greet him, the Ifá corpus that ranks him among the orisha, and the itan, the sacred stories of the diaspora houses that still tell of the one arrow.

myths.title: The Hunter Who Kills Once
myths.text: His praise-poems are the hunt distilled: the oríkì greet Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì as the hunter who kills with a single arrow — the archer whose patience is so complete that the forest gives him what it denies the noisy and the hasty. In the Candomblé houses of Brazil the same idea opens his festivals: Oxóssi, rei das matas, king of the forest, the provider whose one shot feeds the whole town. The oríkì tradition is not ornament here; it is the liturgy of competence.

myths.title: The Orisha of the Odù
myths.text: In the Ifá divination corpus — the 256 odù and their thousands of memorized verses — the divine hunter walks as provider and strategist: the orisha who knows the paths of the bush as the babaláwo knows the paths of the palm nuts. Bascom's fieldwork in Ife and among Cuban practitioners recorded his place in the diviners' world; Idowu's theology of the orisha sets him among the ministers Olódùmarè appointed over creation's wild half. Wherever Ifá is consulted, the forest has a spokesman.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọṣọọsì is a living god, not a memory: his festivals still fill the terreiros of Bahia, his initiates still receive the Guerreros in Havana and Miami, and his oríkì are still sung in the tonal Yoruba that the written restoration tries to honor. The single arrow has become the tradition's own emblem of Afro-diasporic resilience — patience, precision, and provision against every odds. The spelling Ọṣọọsì keeps the marked vowels of the language the praise-poems were made in.
lore.archaeology: The hunter orisha's record is oral and liturgical rather than monumental: his corpus is the Ifá verse tradition, the oríkì preserved by praise-singers, and the ethnographies of Abraham, Idowu, Bascom, and Verger. His material culture is real but perishable — bows, iron implements, and forest shrines — and his oldest durable monuments are the diaspora's: the terreiros of Bahia, some a century and more old, the casa-templos of Havana, and the January streets of Rio on São Sebastião's day.
lore.syncretism: The diaspora rebuilt him with local materials and never lost the pattern. Cuba gave him the Guerreros and the courtroom; Brazil gave him São Sebastião's feast-day and the caboclos of Umbanda; Trinidad, Haiti, and the United States received the Lukumí lineages intact. Scholars from Bascom to Verger mapped the route: the Ketu nation's Oxóssi, the Oyo-heritage hunter, and the Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì of Abraham's dictionary are one figure wearing three orthographies. His closest cousins abroad are the other divine hunters — but none of them shoots only once.

pronunciation.approximation: ah-gah-NYOO — start low on 'ah', stay low on 'gah', then rise sharply to 'NYOO'.
pronunciation.note: Aganjú is Tier 1: the acute accent on ú preserves the high tone of the final syllable, a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. The dot below is absent from the lexical form because the stem vowel is plain /a/, not open /ɔ/ or /ɛ/.

domains.title: Lord of the Volcano
domains.subtitle: Wilderness, Desert, and Terrestrial Fire
domains.lead:
Aganjú is the orixá of the uninhabited places: volcanic earth, desert scrub, and the molten core beneath the mountain. Unlike Ṣàngó, whose fire crackles in the sky, Aganjú's fire moves slowly through stone. He is the son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá in many accounts, the giant whose strides once shook the earth and whose breath still steams from fissures in the ground.

In Afro-Atlantic ritual he appears as Aggayú Solá, the bearer of the world, a deity so tall that rivers reach only his ankles. To invoke him is to acknowledge that civilization rests on forces older and more patient than human law.

cards.name: Volcanic Earth
cards.desc: Magma, lava fields, and earthquakes are his body; he is the planet's slow, burning voice.

cards.name: Desert Wilderness
cards.desc: The uninhabited plain where no farm can take root; the place beyond the town's edge.

cards.name: World-Bearer
cards.desc: In the diaspora he becomes the giant who supports the earth on his shoulders.

cards.name: Terrible Strength
cards.desc: Force without malice; the power that does not negotiate because it does not need to.

symbols.name: Volcanic stone
symbols.meaning: His seat and his bones; cooled lava is placed on altars to ground his presence.

symbols.name: Palm frond fan
symbols.meaning: Used to cool and direct his immense heat during ritual possession.

symbols.name: Red and brown beads
symbols.meaning: The colors of iron-rich earth, dried blood, and scorched clay.

symbols.name: Giant's staff
symbols.meaning: The walking stick of the world-bearer, marking his stride across deserts.

mythology.lead: Aganjú's myths are less numerous than those of Ọṣun or Ṣàngó, but they centre on a single theme: the earth as a living, burning body that carries human life without belonging to it.

myths.title: Son of Odùduwà and Ọbatalá
myths.text: In Yoruba cosmogony, Aganjú is born from the union of the royal ancestor Odùduwà and the white-cloth creator Ọbatalá. The story makes him kin to both earthly kingship and heavenly craftsmanship, but his own domain remains the wild land that refuses cultivation. He is the child who left the palace to live in the volcano.

myths.title: Aggayú Solá Carries the World
myths.text: In Cuban Santería, Aggayú Solá is imagined as a giant so large that he wades through rivers and carries the earth itself. When he possesses a devotee in ceremony, the person's gait becomes heavy and swaying, as if the ground beneath them has gained consciousness. The myth turns geological force into a mythic person who walks among humans.

lore.culturalLegacy: Aganjú remains one of the less domesticated orixás. He is not the god of the marketplace or the bedroom; he is the god of what lies beneath and beyond. In an age of ecological awareness, his mythology reads like a warning: the ground we build on is alive, slow, and capable of overwhelming any city. His colors — red, brown, and iron — appear in Candomblé and Santería altars, and his giant stride survives in the heavy, deliberate dance of his possessed devotees.
lore.archaeology: Direct archaeological attestation of Aganjú is sparse because Yoruba orixá cults were transmitted orally and through ritual objects rather than temple inscriptions. Volcanic stone implements, iron slag, and boundary markers associated with wilderness orishas appear in Yoruba archaeological contexts, while diaspora altars preserve his colours and implements (palm fronds, stones, red beads) as material continuity of his cult.
lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Aganjú is syncretised with Saint Christopher, the giant who carries the Christ child across water. In Cuban Santería he becomes Aggayú Solá, often paired with the thunder-god Ṣàngó as complementary powers of sky-fire and earth-fire. The identification with Saint Christopher preserves the theme of colossal bearing strength, while the pairing with Ṣàngó maps the volcanic interior onto the stormy sky.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-bah-loo-ah-YEH — low on the first three syllables, then high on 'YEH'.
pronunciation.note: Ọbalúayé is Tier 1: the dot below ọ and the acute accents on ú and é are distinctive features the ASCII form loses, the acutes preserving high tones, while grave accents would mark low tones. The dot below ọ distinguishes open [ɔ] from close [o].

domains.title: Father of the World
domains.subtitle: Disease, Healing, and the Earth
domains.lead:
Ọbalúayé is the orixá who both strikes and heals. He governs infectious disease — especially smallpox — and the earth that receives the body after death. His name means 'king whose scourge is the world,' and his presence is feared because illness arrives without warning and leaves without explanation. Yet he is also the one who can lift what he has sent, and his devotees often become the most skilled healers.

In the diaspora he appears as an old man on crutches, wrapped in burlap, accompanied by dogs. He is poverty, affliction, and survival at once.

cards.name: Disease and Pestilence
cards.desc: Smallpox, leprosy, and epidemic illness walk in his shadow.

cards.name: Healing
cards.desc: The same hand that sends illness can remove it; his priests are herbalists and cleaners.

cards.name: Earth and the Grave
cards.desc: He rules the soil that receives the dead and the bacteria that break the body down.

cards.name: Survival
cards.desc: Those who survive his illness often become his children for life.

symbols.name: Crutches
symbols.meaning: His diaspora attribute, marking lameness and the limit of the human body.

symbols.name: Burlap or sackcloth
symbols.meaning: Poverty, humility, and the rough texture of illness and recovery.

symbols.name: Two dogs
symbols.meaning: His messengers and guardians at the boundary of sickness and health.

symbols.name: Earth-coloured beads
symbols.meaning: Brown, black, and purple beads that link him to soil and burial.

mythology.lead: Ọbalúayé's mythology is less a set of heroic adventures than a meditation on illness, marginality, and the earth's power to break and remake the body.

myths.title: The Scourge of the World
myths.text: Ọbalúayé is called 'Father of the World' not because he nurtures it but because his diseases touch everyone, high and low. In some accounts he was once a proud king who was brought low by sickness and learned compassion only after he himself had suffered. His myth teaches that the healer must know the body from the inside of affliction.

myths.title: The Dog and the Herb
myths.text: Stories of Ọbalúayé often involve a dog who leads a sufferer to a healing herb or a stream. The dog is his messenger, moving between the realm of disease and the realm of cure. The myth encodes the practical work of finding medicine: one must follow signs that do not speak in human language.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ọbalúayé's legacy is the theology of illness. In Yoruba and Afro-Atlantic thought, sickness is not mere biological accident; it is a message, a punishment, or a calling. Those who survive smallpox, HIV, or other epidemics often dedicate themselves to him. In the age of global pandemics, his mythology has gained new resonance: the earth can still send plagues, and the boundary between health and sickness remains thinner than modern medicine likes to admit. His image — old, limping, accompanied by dogs — is one of the most moving in Afro-Atlantic art.
lore.archaeology: Ọbalúayé's material culture includes earth-coloured bead necklaces, crutches, burlap garments, and dog imagery preserved in Candomblé and Santería altars. In West Africa, ritual objects associated with smallpox deities and earth cults appear in ethnographic collections; the deity's association with burial and epidemic illness means his traces are more often oral and performative than monumental.
lore.syncretism: In Brazilian Candomblé, Ọbalúayé became Obaluaiê, syncretised with Saint Lazarus (the beggar covered in sores) and Saint Roch (who shows the plague sore on his thigh). In Cuban Santería he is Babalú Ayé, often identified with Saint Lazarus. The Catholic saints of leprosy and plague mapped neatly onto the Yoruba deity of epidemic disease, and the image of the old man on crutches became a shared icon across the Atlantic.

steps: Spənta 'holy/bounteous' is written with schwa ə (𐬆).
The Avestan spelling matches the amesha spenta epithet in the Younger Avesta.
Mainiiu ends in the diphthongal sequence -iiu.
Vohu Manah is one of the Amesha Spentas praised in the Gathas.
The final -h in Vohu and Manah represents Avestan h (𐬵).
The vowel o in Vohu is written with the Avestan letter o (𐬊).
Aṣ̌a 'Truth' begins with the Avestan letter ṣ̌ (𐬴).
Vahišta shows the Avestan treatment of š (𐬱) and h (𐬵).
The phrase appears throughout the Gathas as the highest Asha.
The initial cluster xš- is written with x (𐬑) and š (𐬱).
The medial θ in Xšaθra corresponds to the Avestan letter θ (𐬚).
Vairiia writes the glide -y- with a doubled i (𐬌𐬌), a common Avestan orthography.
Spənta uses schwa ə (𐬆) before the n (𐬥).
Ārmaiti begins with long ā (𐬁).
The goddess is named in the Gathas as the personification of devotion.
Haurvatāt is one of the Amesha Spentas, associated with wholeness.
The long final āt is written with ā (𐬁) plus t (𐬙).
The sequence au is written with a (𐬀) followed by u (𐬎).

pronunciation.approximation: how-vuh-TAHT — begin with 'how' as in 'house,' glide through a light 'v,' and end with a long, emphatic 'tah.'
pronunciation.note: Haurvatāt is Tier-1: the macron on the long final ā is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. As an Amesha Spenta, her name is an abstract noun meaning 'wholeness' or 'health,' personified as a divine being.

domains.title: Wholeness and Health
domains.subtitle: Water, Integrity, and the Amesha Spenta
domains.lead: Haurvatāt is the Amesha Spenta of wholeness, health, and water in Zoroastrianism. Her name means 'every-ness' or 'completeness': she guards what is unbroken, undiminished, and life-giving. Waters — rivers, springs, rain, and the sea — are her domain, and health is her gift to those who live in harmony with Aša. With Amərətāt she forms a pair that promises the body and the earth restored.

cards.name: Guardian of Waters
cards.desc: Rivers, springs, rain, and the sea are sacred because they manifest Haurvatāt's wholeness.

cards.name: Health and Integrity
cards.desc: Her name names the state of being complete, sound, and free from the wounds of the lie.

cards.name: Pair with Amərətāt
cards.desc: Wholeness and immortality are worshipped together as the gifts that sustain body and soul.

cards.name: Purity of Water
cards.desc: Polluting water is a serious sin because it violates her domain and the cosmic order.

symbols.name: Water vessel or spring
symbols.meaning: The sacred waters that embody Haurvatāt's wholeness

symbols.name: Circle or ring
symbols.meaning: Completeness, integrity, and the unbroken cycle of health

symbols.name: Pairing with Amərətāt
symbols.meaning: The twin promise of health and eternal life in Zoroastrian devotion

symbols.name: Pure flowing water
symbols.meaning: The element most closely identified with her presence and blessing

mythology.lead: Haurvatāt, like the other Amesha Spentas, does not have a long heroic mythology. Her importance lies in cosmology and ritual: she is the divine principle that makes water pure, bodies whole, and the cosmos complete. Her myths are the myths of creation, purity, and final restoration.

myths.title: The Creation of Water
myths.text: In Zoroastrian cosmogony, AhuraMazdā creates water as one of the seven good creations and appoints Haurvatāt as its guardian. Angra Mainyu attacks water by bringing drought, pollution, and salt. The sacred duty of Zoroastrians to keep water pure — to avoid contaminating rivers and wells — flows directly from this mythic assignment.

myths.title: Water in the Yasna
myths.text: In the Yasna ritual, water is offered together with the Haoma plant. The rite unites Haurvatāt's domain (water) with Amərətāt's domain (plants) and the prayer of the priest. This triad — water, plant, and word — reconstitutes the original goodness of creation and asks the divine to restore wholeness to the worshipper.

lore.culturalLegacy: Haurvatāt remains central to Zoroastrian ethics of environmental purity, especially the protection of water from contamination. Her name survives in the Zoroastrian calendar and in prayers to the Amesha Spentas. In modern ecological readings of the tradition, Haurvatāt is invoked as the sacred dimension of clean water and holistic health. She reminds us that wholeness is not a private state but a cosmic condition that depends on how we treat the waters we share.
lore.archaeology: Haurvatāt is invoked in Avestan liturgical texts and in Sasanian inscriptions and seals naming the Amesha Spentas. Zoroastrian water rituals, including offerings at springs and the careful protection of wells, preserve her domain in practice. Manuscript illuminations and temple art associate her with flowing water and the paradisal garden. Archaeological sites near ancient water sources often show the material culture of these purification practices.
lore.syncretism: Haurvatāt is paired with Amərətāt in Zoroastrian worship and cosmology; their names passed into Middle Persian as Hordād and Amurdād and are preserved in the Zoroastrian calendar. The abstract noun haurvatāt is cognate with Vedic Sanskrit sarvatāt, 'all-ness,' showing the deep Indo-Iranian roots of the concept. In Greek and Roman contexts, the Amesha Spentas were sometimes compared to abstract virtues or to nymphs and water deities, though these comparisons are loose.

steps: Amərətāt pairs with Haurvatāt as the Amesha Spenta of immortality.
Both medial vowels are schwa ə (𐬆).
The ending -tāt uses long ā (𐬁) before final t (𐬙).

pronunciation.approximation: ah-muh-ruh-TAHT — the middle syllables are light and quick, while the final 'tah' is long and emphatic.
pronunciation.note: Amərətāt is Tier-1: the macron on the long final ā is a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses. As one of the Amesha Spentas, her name is an abstract noun meaning 'immortality' personified.

domains.title: Immortality in Bloom
domains.subtitle: Plants, Longevity, and the Amesha Spenta
domains.lead: Amərətāt is the Amesha Spenta of immortality and plants in Zoroastrianism. She embodies the divine promise that the soul endures and that the earth's vegetation sustains life. Where her sister Haurvatāt guards water and wholeness, Amərətāt guards the plant kingdom and the final victory over death. She is the green hope at the heart of Zoroastrian cosmology.

cards.name: Guardian of Plants
cards.desc: Every tree, herb, and grain falls under her protection as the divine patron of vegetation.

cards.name: Immortality
cards.desc: Her name means 'non-death'; she is the spiritual force that promises life beyond death.

cards.name: Pair with Haurvatāt
cards.desc: She and Haurvatāt (wholeness/health) are often worshipped together as complementary gifts.

cards.name: The Final Renovation
cards.desc: At Frashokereti, Amərətāt's domain will flourish in a world without death or decay.

symbols.name: Tree or branch
symbols.meaning: Vegetation, growth, and the plant kingdom under her guardianship

symbols.name: Fruit or grain
symbols.meaning: The sustenance that links earthly agriculture to divine immortality

symbols.name: Watered garden
symbols.meaning: The paradise-like setting where plants and water together manifest wholeness

symbols.name: Pairing with Haurvatāt
symbols.meaning: The two Amesha Spentas together symbolize health and eternal life

mythology.lead: Amərətāt does not have a long narrative mythology of her own. She is one of the seven Holy Immortals who surround AhuraMazdā and help govern the created world. Her stories are embedded in cosmology, ritual, and eschatology rather than in heroic adventure.

myths.title: The Creation of Plants
myths.text: In Zoroastrian cosmogony, AhuraMazdā creates the plant world — the fourth of the seven creations (sky, water, earth, plants, cattle, man, and fire) — and assigns its guardianship to Amərətāt. Angra Mainyu (Ahriman) responds by sending drought, locusts, and winter to wither the green world. The struggle between growth and decay is therefore a cosmic battle in which human agriculture participates.

myths.title: The Bodies of the Righteous
myths.text: At Frashokereti, the final renovation, the dead will be resurrected in perfected bodies that no longer age, sicken, or die. Amərətāt's gift of immortality will be realized not as escape from the body but as the body's transformation. The white Haoma, the paradisal plant, will be offered to the righteous to seal their eternal life.

lore.culturalLegacy: Amərətāt remains a focus of Zoroastrian devotion as the divine guardian of vegetation and the promise of eternal life. Her name survives in the Zoroastrian calendar and in the prayers offered to the Amesha Spentas. In ecological readings of Zoroastrianism, Amərətāt is invoked as the sacred dimension of plant life and the religious duty to protect the earth's green cover. She is a reminder that immortality in this tradition is not escape from the world but the world's final healing.
lore.archaeology: Amərətāt is invoked in Avestan liturgical texts and in Sasanian-era inscriptions and seals that name the Amesha Spentas. Zoroastrian ritual vessels, fire temples, and manuscript illuminations associate her with vegetation and the paradisal garden. The Haoma ritual, though now performed with substitutes in many communities, preserves the plant-offering at the center of her domain.
lore.syncretism: Amərətāt is one of a pair with Haurvatāt, and the two are often worshipped together as guardians of water/plants and health/immortality. Their names passed into Middle Persian as Amurdād and Hordād, and they are still commemorated in the Zoroastrian calendar. The Greek concept of ambrosia is closer than a loose parallel: Greek ambrotos, 'immortal', and ambrosia descend from the same Proto-Indo-European privative formation *n̥-mr̥-to-, 'undying', built on the root *mer-, 'to die' — the very root that, with the Iranian abstract suffix -tāt, produces Amərətāt; Sanskrit amṛta is the same formation again.

domains.title: Fire
domains.subtitle: Transformation, Purification, Cosmic Process
domains.lead: Pŷr is the Greek word for fire, an element that transforms, purifies, destroys, and illuminates. For Heraclitus it is the very substance of becoming; for cult it is the medium through which mortals communicate with gods.

cards.name: Heraclitean Flux
cards.desc: Heraclitus made fire the arche: all things are an exchange for fire, and fire for all things.

cards.name: Sacrificial Flame
cards.desc: Greek worship centered on altars where fire carried offerings upward to the gods.

cards.name: Purification
cards.desc: Fire cleanses metals, bodies, and cities; it is both punishment and renewal.

cards.name: Light in Darkness
cards.desc: The torch, the hearth, the beacon: fire as knowledge, safety, and communication.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: The visible, ever-moving form of fire itself

symbols.name: Hearth (hestia)
symbols.meaning: The sacred fire at the center of home and city

symbols.name: Torch
symbols.meaning: Carried fire, used in processions, war, and mystery rites

symbols.name: Phoenix pyre
symbols.meaning: The fire of self-renewal and transformation

mythology.lead: Pŷr is elemental and mythic at once. It appears in the theft of fire by Prometheus, the forge of Hephaistos, and the philosophical cosmos of Heraclitus.

myths.title: Prometheus Steals Fire
myths.text: Prometheus deceived Zeus over the division of sacrifice and then stole fire from heaven, hiding it in a fennel stalk to give to mortals. Zeus punished him with the torment of the Caucasus and sent Pandora as a counter-gift. Fire is thus the stolen technology that makes civilization possible.

myths.title: Fire as Cosmic Arche
myths.text: Heraclitus declared that 'all things are an exchange for fire, and fire for all things, as goods for gold and gold for goods.' Fire is the measure of transformation; it is war and peace, hunger and satiety. The cosmos is 'an ever-living fire, kindling in measures and going out in measures.'

lore.culturalLegacy: Pŷr is the element that made us human: cooking, metalworking, ceramics, glass, engines, electricity, and rockets all begin with controlled fire. It is also the element we most fear: conflagration, war, cremation, and climate change. The Greek word thus names both the origin of civilization and its potential end.
lore.archaeology: Fire was central to Greek sanctuaries: every altar maintained a sacred flame, and burnt offerings left ash and bone deposits. Hephaistos's forge and Prometheus's theft were depicted on vases. The eternal flame at Olympia and the hearth fires of cities like Athens (the prytaneion) were maintained by civic officials. Fire-management structures — kilns, furnaces, hearths — are common in Greek archaeological sites.
lore.syncretism: Pŷr became one of the four Aristotelian elements and the Stoic active principle (pneuma/fire). In Christian symbolism it represented the Holy Spirit, judgment, and hellfire. Zoroastrianism elevated fire as the purest symbol of Ahura Mazda. The word survives in English through 'fire,' 'pyre,' and scientific terms like 'pyrotechnics' and 'pyroclastic.' Modern chemistry identifies fire as rapid oxidation, but the cultural symbolism remains ancient.

pronunciation.approximation: 'GAY' — one long, level syllable, like the sustained note of a deep drum.
pronunciation.note: Gē is Tier 1 because the Greek Γῆ bears the circumflex, which marks both stress and the long vowel (eta) in a single accent — both features the ASCII form loses. It is the older cultic form of the earth goddess, later often called Gaîa in poetry.

domains.title: The Earth Itself
domains.subtitle: Motherhood, Fertility, Primordial Ground
domains.lead: Gē is the earth as goddess, the primordial ground from which gods, Titans, and mortals arise. She is not a distant creator but the very substance beneath our feet, venerated in every Greek city and invoked in oaths, harvests, and burials.

cards.name: Mother of All
cards.desc: From Gē spring the Titans, the Giants, the Erinyes, and — with Ouranos — the whole cosmos.

cards.name: Giver of Crops
cards.desc: Agricultural fertility and the annual return of grain depend on her body.

cards.name: Tomb and Womb
cards.desc: She receives the dead and regenerates life; grave and cradle are the same soil.

cards.name: Oracle of the Dead
cards.desc: Her chthonic power underlies oracles and dream-visions at sanctuaries of the underworld.

symbols.name: Cornucopia
symbols.meaning: The abundance that rises from her soil

symbols.name: Serpent
symbols.meaning: The earth-bound creature that glides through her body and guards her sanctuaries

symbols.name: Oak or olive tree
symbols.meaning: The rooted life that grows directly from her

symbols.name: Black stone
symbols.meaning: Aniconic representation of the earth goddess at numerous archaic shrines

mythology.lead: Gē is a primordial power whose myths are acts of generation and revenge. She creates without a mate, then conspires with her son Kronos against her husband Ouranos.

myths.title: Birth of the Cosmos
myths.text: After Chaos came Gē 'broad-breasted,' the ever-sure seat of all immortals. She gave birth to Ouranos, the mountains, and Pontos, the sea. Alone she is generative; with Ouranos she becomes the mother of the Titans and the origin of the Olympian order.

myths.title: The Castration of Ouranos
myths.text: Gē grew weary of Ouranos forcing her children back into her womb. She fashioned the adamantine sickle and persuaded Kronos to ambush his father. The blood from the wound produced the Erinyes, the Giants, and the ash-tree nymphs — new beings born from violence against the sky.

lore.culturalLegacy: The name Gē survives in English 'geo-' (geology, geography, geometry) and in the scientific Gaia hypothesis, which proposes that Earth functions as a self-regulating system. She is the oldest layer of Greek religion: not a specialist deity but the ground of all being. Every seed planted and every body buried returns to her, making her the most democratic of goddesses.
lore.archaeology: Gē was worshipped at numerous sites without always receiving monumental temples. The Athenian Agora preserves her altar and that of Gē Kourotrophos near the crossroads. Aniconic stones, pits for liquid offerings, and boundary markers attest her chthonic cult across Greece. The Pythion at Athens and the Eleusinion also honor her as the maternal earth underlying Demeter's mysteries.
lore.syncretism: Gē was identified early with the Minoan-Mycenaean earth mother and later with the Anatolian Cybele and the Roman Terra Mater. In Orphic cosmogonies she is sometimes preceded by Night or Water, but she remains the foundational maternal power. Neoplatonists interpreted her as the material substrate of the visible world, the 'receptacle' of becoming. Modern ecological movements have reclaimed Gaia/Gē as a symbol of the living planet.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-HAYR' — the second syllable is long, pitched high, and ends with a rolled or tapped r.
pronunciation.note: Aḗr is Tier 1 because the Greek ἀήρ contains both length (η) and stress (acute) on the same syllable. It is one of the elemental words of Greek philosophy and science.

domains.title: The Lower Air
domains.subtitle: Mist, Atmosphere, Breath of Life
domains.lead: Aḗr is the Greek word for the lower air, the misty atmosphere between earth and the bright aithēr above. For Anaximenes it was the arche, the fundamental substance from which all things arise by rarefaction and condensation.

cards.name: Elemental Air
cards.desc: One of the classical elements; the invisible medium of breath, weather, and life.

cards.name: Anaximenes' Arche
cards.desc: The Milesian philosopher made air the single substance underlying all change.

cards.name: Breath and Soul
cards.desc: Greek pneuma and psyche both connect life to the movement of air.

cards.name: Mist and Cloud
cards.desc: Aēr is not pure sky but the cloudy, breathable layer where mortals live.

symbols.name: Wind
symbols.meaning: The moving air that carries breath, weather, and omens

symbols.name: Cloud
symbols.meaning: Condensed air; the visible form of aēr

symbols.name: Lungs or breath
symbols.meaning: The biological medium in which life persists

symbols.name: Empty vessel
symbols.meaning: The philosophical symbol of aēr as the unseen substance filling space

mythology.lead: Aḗr has no mythic biography; its story is the history of Greek thought. From Homer to Aristotle, it moves from mere atmosphere to a recognized element of the cosmos.

myths.title: Aēr and Aithēr
myths.text: In Homer, aēr is the lower, misty air where mortals breathe and battle; aithēr is the bright upper air of the gods. The distinction sets up a cosmic hierarchy: the higher the air, the more divine it is.

myths.title: Air as Arche
myths.text: Anaximenes of Miletus (6th c. BCE) proposed that aēr is the arche, the fundamental stuff of the universe. When rarefied, it becomes fire; when condensed, it becomes wind, cloud, water, earth, and stone. This was one of the first monistic physical theories in the West.

lore.culturalLegacy: Aḗr is so ordinary that we forget it is sacred: every breath is a gift of atmosphere. The word survives in 'air,' 'aerial,' 'aerodynamics,' and 'aerospace.' Environmental science now treats air as a global commons, making the ancient element a political and ethical concern. To restore aḗr in Unicode is to name the invisible substance we share.
lore.archaeology: Aḗr has no cult sites, but its material trace is atmospheric and technological: ancient wind towers, pneumatic devices described by Hero of Alexandria, and the development of meteorology. The concept shaped Greek architecture, medicine, and philosophy, leaving its mark in texts rather than temples.
lore.syncretism: Aḗr entered Latin as āēr — the Greek loan Cicero and Lucretius use directly for the lower atmosphere — and from there through Old French into the Romance and Germanic languages (English 'air'). (Latin aura comes from a different Greek word, αὔρα, 'breeze'.) It was identified with the pneuma of Stoic physics and with the Holy Spirit in Christian theology, where 'spirit' and 'breath' share a root. Modern chemistry replaced the four-element theory, but 'air' remains the everyday name for Earth's atmosphere.

pronunciation.approximation: STEEX — one syllable, acute on the only vowel there is.
pronunciation.note: Greek Στύξ is monosyllabic — and Greek monosyllables carry the acute on their vowel in modern editions (as Πῦρ carries its circumflex, and φῶς its own). The restoration Stýx keeps that acute: the stress of the single syllable, the only mark the name can bear, exactly where the tradition places it.

domains.title: The River of the Oath
domains.subtitle: The Boundary, the Vow, and the Water the Gods Fear
domains.lead: Stýx is the river by which the gods themselves are bound: the underworld stream whose water makes an oath unbreakable even for Olympos, the eldest daughter of the Ocean, and the mother of Force, Rivalry, Power, and Victory.

cards.name: The Oath Water
cards.desc: Swear on her and the vow is iron — Zeús himself cannot break it.

cards.name: The Boundary
cards.desc: The river of the threshold: between the living and the dead, the world and the under.

cards.name: The Eldest Daughter
cards.desc: First-born of Ōkeanos and Tēthys — the river with seniority among all waters.

cards.name: Mother of Victory
cards.desc: Her children: Bía (Force), Zêlos (Rivalry), Krátos (Power), Níkē (Victory).

symbols.name: The dark water
symbols.meaning: The stream that chills even gods — oaths made absolute

symbols.name: The waterfall
symbols.meaning: Her plunge from the underworld cliff, seen by few and sworn by all

symbols.name: The four children
symbols.meaning: Force, Rivalry, Power, Victory — the engines of Zeús' reign, born of a river

mythology.lead: Stýx's myths are about the one thing stronger than the gods: the word you cannot take back — and the water that enforces it.

myths.title: The Water the Gods Swear By
myths.text: The Iliad's formula runs through the epic: "let this now be my inviolable oath, by the water of Stýx" — and even Zeús trembles at the breaking. When Hēra swears to Hypnos by that same water — promising him the Grace Pasithea in marriage for lulling Zeús to sleep (Il. 14.271) — the oath is the unbreakable currency between gods. Hesiod's Theogony (793–804) sets the penalty: a god who pours her water in libation and forswears lies one full year breathless, then nine years cut off from the gods' feasts, restored only in the tenth: the river punishes heaven itself.

myths.title: The Mother of the Reign
myths.text: Hesiod's Theogony makes her the hinge of Zeús' kingdom: Stýx, eldest daughter of Ōkeanos, brought her four children — Bía (Force), Zêlos (Rivalry), Krátos (Power), Níkē (Victory) — to Olympos at the start of the war with the Titans, the first immortal to side with Zeús. For this he honored her above all waters and set her children at his side forever. The king's throne, the poets say, is propped by a river and her brood.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Stygian" is her everyday immortality: the word for the unbreakably dark and the absolutely binding. Her children rule the modern vocabulary — force, zeal, power, victory — and her water gave literature its favorite contract: the deal you cannot exit, from Faust to fantasy. Every "swear on my life" and every oath of office is a small glass of her river, drunk in public.
lore.archaeology: The Greeks placed her water in Arcadia: the Styx waterfall near Nonakris in the northern Peloponnese — a cliff-plunge so cold it was said to be her true stream, and Pausanias reports the locals' oath by it. The gorge at Aroania (Kráthis river) is shown to visitors still as the legendary drop. Homer's and Hesiod's lines are her oldest attestations; the Roman poets from Virgil to Statius keep her darkly flowing in every underworld scene.
lore.syncretism: Rome kept her as the model of the binding vow — the jurists' "iusiurandum per Stygem" — and Dante lowered her to the fifth circle, the marsh of wrath, where the angry fight in her mud. Her name became the English adjective "Stygian" for anything dark, cold, and absolute; and her family — Force, Rivalry, Power, Victory — became the four imperial virtues Rome and every later empire borrowed for its own thrones.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-KHAY-rohn' — the middle syllable is pitched high; the final -ōn is long and sonorous.
pronunciation.note: Achérōn is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἀχέρων contains both stress (acute on έ) and length (ω). The name is at once a real river in Epirus and the mythic boundary of Hades.

domains.title: River of Woe
domains.subtitle: Underworld Boundary, Grief, Passage
domains.lead: Achérōn is the river of woe, one of the great boundary rivers of the Greek underworld. Real in Epirus and mythic in Hades, it marks the place where the living must stop and the dead begin their journey.

cards.name: Boundary of Hades
cards.desc: One of the rivers that separate the world of the living from the dead.

cards.name: River of Grief
cards.desc: Its waters are identified with ἄχος, the Greek word for pain and sorrow.

cards.name: Real and Mythic
cards.desc: The Thesprotian Acheron was believed to be an entrance to the underworld.

cards.name: Ferry and Guide
cards.desc: The dead must cross its waters, sometimes by Charon's boat.

symbols.name: Dark water
symbols.meaning: The boundary liquid that the dead must cross

symbols.name: Cypress and willow
symbols.meaning: Trees of mourning that grow along its banks

symbols.name: Charon's boat
symbols.meaning: The ferry that carries souls across the river

symbols.name: Reeds and marsh
symbols.meaning: The liminal landscape where solid ground dissolves into the underworld

mythology.lead: Achérōn is less a character than a place of passage. Its mythology is the geography of death: where the rivers flow, who ferries the dead, and what must be left behind.

myths.title: The Cosmic River
myths.text: Hesiod never gives the river a genealogy — the Theogony's catalogue of the sons of Oceanus and Tethys does not name Acheron. Plato's Phaedo (112e–113c) gives the fullest ancient map: Acheron flowing opposite Oceanus, under the earth, into the Acherusian Lake, where the souls of the dead gather and are purified. From this cosmic geography comes its status: it is not merely a local stream but a branch of the primordial waters.

myths.title: Odysseus at the Acheron
myths.text: In Odyssey 10, Circe sends Odysseus to the edges of Oceanus and the Acheron to summon the dead. There he digs a trench, pours libations, and calls up the shades of Tiresias, his mother Anticleia, and the heroines of old. The river is the membrane between epic and necromancy.

lore.culturalLegacy: Achérōn is the river whose name means grief. It appears in Dante's Inferno, in Romantic poetry, and in every metaphor that turns a dark stream into the threshold of death. The real Acheron in Epirus still carries the name, its waters a tourist route to an ancient oracle of the dead. The boundary between geography and myth remains thin there.
lore.archaeology: The Nekromanteion, an oracle of the dead, was located near the mouth of the Acheron in Thesprotia (modern Mesopotamos). Excavations revealed an underground labyrinth used for incubation and necromantic ritual. The river itself, with its springs and underground passages, reinforced the belief that this was an entrance to Hades. Roman travelers including Pliny and Pausanias noted the site.
lore.syncretism: The Greek underworld rivers were mapped onto real landscapes, especially the Thesprotian Acheron, where an oracle of the dead (Nekromanteion) operated. Roman poets Virgil and Ovid developed the river's role in the geography of Hades. Christian tradition transformed the Acheron into one of the rivers of hell, often conflated with the Styx. The name survives in modern Greek geography and in every reference to 'Acheron' as a symbol of sorrow.

pronunciation.approximation: gwahn-yin, high level tone on both syllables.
pronunciation.note: Guānyīn 观音 means "Perceiver of Sounds" — the one who hears the cries of the world, a rendering of Avalokiteśvara's name as the Chinese translators analyzed it. The level tone on guān and the falling-level yīn are among the most recognized syllables in East Asian devotion.

domains.title: The One Who Hears
domains.subtitle: Compassion, the Lotus Sūtra, and the Cries of the World
domains.lead: Guānyīn is the most beloved figure of East Asian Buddhism: the bodhisattva who vows to hear every cry of suffering in the world and answer it. Born in India as the male Avalokiteśvara, she became, in China, a mother — and compassion itself found its lasting face.

cards.name: The Lotus
cards.desc: Her seat and symbol: purity flowering unsullied from the mud of the world.

cards.name: The Vase
cards.desc: The pure vase with willow branch — the dew of compassion sprinkled on the suffering.

cards.name: A Thousand Eyes
cards.desc: The thousand-armed form: an eye in every palm — to see and to reach, without limit.

cards.name: Putuoshan
cards.desc: Her island mountain off Zhejiang: the Potalaka of the sūtras, anchored in the Chinese sea.

symbols.name: The willow branch
symbols.meaning: Gentleness that bends and does not break — sprinkled with the dew of mercy

symbols.name: The pure vase
symbols.meaning: The nectar of compassion, poured without end

symbols.name: The child in her arms
symbols.meaning: The Songzi Guānyīn — giver of children, mother of the vow

mythology.lead: Guānyīn's "myths" are vows and legends of response: the sūtra promises that whoever calls her name in danger will be heard — and Chinese legend supplies a thousand proofs.

myths.title: The Universal Gateway
myths.text: Chapter 25 of the Lotus Sūtra — circulated independently as the Guānyīn Sūtra — makes the vow explicit: if beings in danger from fire, flood, demons, or the executioner's blade call on the name of Guānshìyīn, the bodhisattva will at once perceive the sound and deliver them. It is the most recited chapter in East Asian Buddhism: compassion as a cosmic emergency line.

myths.title: Miàoshàn
myths.text: The Chinese legend that made her a daughter: Princess Miàoshàn refuses marriage to seek awakening, endures her father's destruction of her convent, and is executed — descending to hell, which her compassion turns to a paradise of flowers. When her father lies dying of a karmic illness, she gives her own eyes and arms for the medicine; revealed as the thousand-armed, thousand-eyed Guānyīn, she forgives him, and the king becomes her devotee.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her name is spoken daily by more people than perhaps any other divine name on earth: nāmó Guānshìyīn Púsà is East Asia's universal cry in fear and gratitude. Putuoshan draws millions of pilgrims yearly; her statues — from the Suma temple Kannon to the hundred-metre Guānyīn of the South Sea of Sanya — rank among the largest on earth. Vegetarian mercy, lifesaving charities, and countless hospitals across the Chinese world bear her vow.
lore.archaeology: Putuoshan's three great monasteries (Puji, Fayu, Huiji) preserve her island cult from its 10th-century founding, when a Japanese monk's Kannon image refused to sail on and stayed. Dunhuang's Mogao caves hold her earliest Chinese icons — the guide-of-souls Guānyīn leading the dead, the thousand-armed forms of the Tang. The Northern Song colossal bronze thousand-armed Guānyīn of Longxing Monastery in Zhengding, China, cast in 971 CE, and the Song-dynasty polychrome "Water-Moon Guānyīn" figures — of which the Nelson-Atkins example is the most celebrated — mark her iconography's golden age.
lore.syncretism: She is the great syncretist of East Asia: in Tibet she is Chenrezig, patron of the land, incarnate in the Dalai Lamas; in Japan Kannon, with temples from Asakusa to Kiyomizu; in Vietnam Quan Âm. Chinese folk religion fused her with the Queen of Heaven and associated her with Mazu the sea-goddess; Daoism canonized her as Cihang Zhenren; and she entered the Journey to the West as the pilgrimage's divine patron, who recruits the pilgrims and rescues them whenever heaven's bureaucracy fails.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 观音 in simplified, 觀音 in traditional characters: guān (to observe, with the seeing radical) plus yīn (sound). The fuller liturgical name 观世音 (Guānshìyīn, "Perceiver of the World's Sounds") preserves the whole Sanskrit sense.

pronunciation.approximation: TIE-SHUHNG — 'tai' like 'tie' with a sharp falling tone, 'shang' with a retroflex 'sh' and a falling tone.
pronunciation.note: 太上 means 'Supreme, Most Exalted.' In Daoist theology it is the title of the deified Laozi as Tàishàng Lǎojūn, one of the Sānqīng (Three Pure Ones). The Pinyin restoration Tàishàng preserves both citation tones.

domains.title: The Supreme Lord
domains.subtitle: Dao, Deification of Laozi, and Celestial Authority
domains.lead:
Tàishàng names the supreme station in Daoist cosmology. In its fullest form, Tàishàng Lǎojūn (Supreme Lord Lao) is the deified Laozi, the legendary author of the Dàodéjīng, elevated into one of the Three Pure Ones who stand at the summit of the Daoist pantheon. Where the historical Laozi taught wordless wisdom, the celestial Tàishàng Lǎojūn dispenses scriptures, elixirs, and revelations.

He is not a creator god in the Western sense. He is the personification of the Dao in its highest, most hidden aspect — the origin that cannot be named, named.

cards.name: The Dao Itself
cards.desc: He embodies the nameless source from which heaven and earth arise.

cards.name: Lord of Scriptures
cards.desc: Revealer of the Dàodéjīng and countless Daoist texts and talismans.

cards.name: Alchemy and Elixirs
cards.desc: Patron of internal and external alchemy, longevity, and the pursuit of immortality.

cards.name: Teacher of Emperors
cards.desc: Legendary instructor of sage-kings and source of imperial legitimacy.

symbols.name: Ruyi sceptre
symbols.meaning: The curved head-rest that signifies power, wish-fulfilment, and divine authority.

symbols.name: Gourd of elixir
symbols.meaning: The bottle that holds the medicine of immortality and the hidden medicine of the Dao.

symbols.name: Crane
symbols.meaning: Longevity and the celestial mount that carries the immortal to heaven.

symbols.name: Tàijí disc
symbols.meaning: The supreme polarity from which yin and yang unfold.

mythology.lead: Tàishàng's mythology moves between history and cosmology: the shadowy philosopher Laozi becomes the celestial teacher who reveals the Dao to emperors, hermits, and alchemists.

myths.title: Laozi Leaves the Pass
myths.text: According to tradition, Laozi grew weary of the Zhou court and rode west on a black ox. At the Hangu Pass the guard Yīn Xī recognised him and asked for a teaching. Laozi wrote the five thousand characters of the Dàodéjīng, then disappeared into the west. Later Daoism transformed this departure into an ascension: Laozi became Tàishàng Lǎojūn, the supreme immortal.

myths.title: The Conversion of the Barbarians
myths.text: Medieval Daoist apocrypha claimed that Tàishàng Lǎojūn travelled west and transformed himself into the Buddha in order to convert the barbarians. The myth was a polemical attempt to place Daoism above Buddhism by making the Buddha a manifestation of Laozi. Though historically tendentious, it reveals the prestige Tàishàng held in medieval Chinese religion.

lore.culturalLegacy: Tàishàng's legacy is inseparable from the Dàodéjīng, one of the most translated books in world literature. As Tàishàng Lǎojūn, he presides over Daoist temples, alchemical traditions, and popular practices of longevity and exorcism. His image appears in countless paintings, statues, and New Year prints, often riding a crane or holding a ruyi. Modern Daoist movements, martial-arts lineages, and global wellness culture all claim some connection to Laozi, though the sage would likely smile at the irony. The name Tàishàng has also become an adjective of highest rank, applied to emperors, elders, and even video-game bosses.
lore.archaeology: The deification of Laozi is attested in Han dynasty texts and inscriptions, with imperial cults developing under the Tang dynasty, which claimed Laozi as an ancestor. Archaeological finds include Dàodéjīng manuscripts from Mawangdui and Guodian, Daoist talismans, steles, and temple inscriptions honouring Tàishàng Lǎojūn. Temples dedicated to him survive across China and the Chinese diaspora.
lore.syncretism: Tàishàng Lǎojūn is the Daoist answer to the question of how a philosophy becomes a religion. The historical Laozi, if he existed, was a thinker; Tàishàng Lǎojūn is a god. This transition mirrors the broader Chinese pattern of deifying sages, from Confucius to Guān Yǔ. Buddhism influenced the structure of his cult — the Three Pure Ones parallel Buddhist trikāya theology — while popular religion absorbed him into a vast pantheon of immortals, city gods, and celestial bureaucrats. In the West, Laozi is often read as a purely philosophical figure, but in Chinese temples he is honoured with incense, images, and prayers for longevity.

pronunciation.approximation: LUHNG-WAHNG — two even syllables, each rising from mid to high pitch; the 'o' of the first is like the 'oo' in 'book', the 'a' of the second like the 'a' in 'father'.
pronunciation.note: 龍王 denotes the Dragon King, the crowned ruler of the waters in Chinese religion and literature. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Lóngwáng — both syllables in Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥) — as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) for 龍 and 王, and in standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese forms as *[m]-roŋ (龍, GSR 1193a) and *[ɢ]ʷaŋ (王). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Lóngwáng preserves the citation rising tones of both syllables; in connected speech the contours may be compressed, but the lexical tones remain Tone 2 throughout.

domains.title: Kings of the Four Seas
domains.subtitle: Crystal Palaces, Rain by Mandate, the Bureaucracy of Water
domains.lead:
Lóngwáng, the Dragon King, is not one god but a crowned office — four brothers who hold the Four Seas that ring the Chinese world, each enthroned in an underwater crystal palace with its own court, treasury, and army of shrimp soldiers and crab generals. Āo Guǎng 敖廣 of the East Sea is the most prominent; beside him rule Āo Qīn 敖欽 of the South, Āo Rùn 敖閏 of the West, and Āo Shùn 敖順 of the North. Beneath them, lesser dragon kings govern every river, lake, and well worth the naming.

In their world, rainfall is a bureaucratic act. The Jade Emperor issues the mandate — how much rain, where, and at what hour — and the Dragon King delivers it, down to the last tenth of an inch. It is the Chinese imagination at its most characteristic: the wild water of heaven brought under a seal, a ledger, and a chain of command. The novels and the village temples agree on the stakes — a king who edits the figures loses his head, and a village that loses the king's favour loses its harvest.

cards.name: The Four Seas
cards.desc: Four royal brothers divide the encircling oceans — East, South, West, and North — each ruling tides, storms, and every creature of his sea from a crystal palace below the waves.

cards.name: Rain by Mandate
cards.desc: Rainfall is paperwork: the Jade Emperor decrees the amount and the hour, and the Dragon King executes the order exactly — to alter either is treason against heaven.

cards.name: The Sea Treasury
cards.desc: The crystal palace hoards the wealth of the waters — pearls, coral, and the Rúyì Jīngū Bàng, the iron pillar that once pinned the seas, until the Monkey King claimed it for a staff.

cards.name: Kingship under Heaven
cards.desc: The Dragon King is sovereign in his own water and a subject above it — a king who kneels to the celestial bureaucracy and answers with his life for every misplaced drop.

symbols.name: Crystal palace
symbols.meaning: The underwater court (龍宮, Dragon Palace) — sovereignty, hidden wealth, and the ordered world beneath the chaos of the sea

symbols.name: Rúyì Jīngū Bàng
symbols.meaning: The compliant gold-banded staff, an iron pillar that once pinned the seas — the tameable measure of the waters, taken from the East Sea treasury by Sūn Wùkōng

symbols.name: Dragon robe and royal crown
symbols.meaning: Enfeoffed kingship within the celestial bureaucracy — the Dragon King rules as a peer of heaven's administration, not as a free lord

symbols.name: Rain clouds and tidal bore
symbols.meaning: The waters he commands — rain, rivers, lakes, and tides delivered by decree, withheld in drought, unleashed in flood

symbols.name: Shrimp soldiers and crab generals
symbols.meaning: The aquatic retinue of the Dragon Palace — the sea's own creatures enrolled as a court, a mirror of the imperial administration below the waves

mythology.lead: The Dragon Kings stand at the crossing of two Chinas: the literary China of the great Ming novels, where they are foils, creditors, and comic bureaucrats, and the living China of the village temple, where they were the address to which a drought-stricken county sent its prayers. The same figure is mocked in the novel and begged in the field.

myths.title: The Jìng River Dragon King's Wager
myths.text: The Journey to the West preserves the great cautionary tale of the celestial bureaucracy. The Dragon King of the Jìng River wagers with a mortal fortune-teller over the next day's rain; when the Jade Emperor's decree arrives matching the diviner's figures exactly, the king — unwilling to lose — secretly alters the amount and delays the timing. The difference is trifling, and it does not matter. For editing heaven's paperwork he is sentenced to death and executed, a reminder that in a cosmos run as an administration, the smallest forged figure is treason.

myths.title: Nézhā and the Third Prince
myths.text: In the Investiture of the Gods (Féngshén Yǎnyì), the boy Nézhā, bathing in the eastern stream, shakes the East Sea crystal palace to its foundations with his magic sash. Āo Guǎng sends his third son, Āo Bǐng, to subdue the child; Nézhā kills the prince and plucks out his sinews to make a belt. Faced with the Dragon King's wrath against his family and his town, Nézhā answers with the terrible arithmetic of filial duty — he cuts himself apart, returning his flesh to his mother and his bones to his father, so that the debt dies with him.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Dragon King never fully retired. His temples still stand along China's coasts and rivers, and rain-processions to the local king persisted in the countryside into the twentieth century. In literature and performance he is a permanent stock character: every adaptation of the Journey to the West — opera, film, television, animation — must eventually send someone down to the crystal palace, whether to borrow a weapon or to wreck the court. The feud with Nézhā alone has carried him through a century of Chinese animation, from the 1979 feature Nézhā Nào Hǎi (Nezha Conquers the Dragon King) to the 2019 blockbuster Ne Zha, where the dragon clan's grievance drives the plot. In the modern idiom the Dragon King's palace remains a byword for fabulous drowned wealth, and the figure himself endures wherever Chinese fantasy needs a throne beneath the sea.
lore.archaeology: The material cult behind the Dragon Kings is far older than the kings themselves. Shang oracle bones (c. 1250–1045 BCE) record rain sacrifices addressed to river and water powers, and Han texts describe rain-making rites performed with clay dragons — Dong Zhongshu's Chunqiu Fanlu gives the liturgy, and Wang Chong's Lunheng argues against it. Han mirrors and tomb reliefs show the older cosmic dragon of clouds and ascent, not yet a crowned bureaucrat. The named Dragon Kings of the Four Seas crystallize in medieval China under Buddhist influence: nāga kings with submarine palaces appear in translated sūtras from the early centuries CE, the Tang court formally enfeoffed the dragon kings of the Four Seas with royal titles, and by the Song their temples stood in the official register of sacrifices. The literary cycle reaches canonical form in the Ming novels Fengshen Yanyi and Xiyouji.
lore.syncretism: The Dragon Kings are among the clearest cases of Buddhism and native Chinese religion merging into a single figure. Native Chinese water-dragon and river-god cults are ancient, but the named kings with submarine palaces, retinues, and treasuries owe much to the Indian nāgarājas — serpent kings of the waters — carried into China with the translated sūtras; Chinese translators rendered nāga as lóng (dragon), and the eight nāga kings of Buddhist scripture became native sea-kings. The relative weight of the Indian import against the older Chinese cult remains a matter of scholarly debate. Taoism then absorbed the kings wholesale into its celestial administration as rain officials answerable to the Jade Emperor. From China the figure travelled with the culture: in Japan the dragon kings appear as ryūō, kin to the sea-god Ryūjin of the undersea palace; in Korea as Yongwang, propitiated by fishing and farming villages alike; in Vietnam as Long Vương, guardian of waters and of the nation's own dragon genealogy.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 龍王 in traditional Chinese and 龙王 in simplified. The Pinyin reading Lóngwáng — two Tone-2 (rising) syllables — is the Modern Standard Mandarin citation form, recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and standard dictionaries. The tone-marked restoration keeps both acute accents as the display form; the registrable domain maps the accented vowels to their ASCII base letters, giving longwang. No syllable-boundary apostrophe is required: the segmentation lóng·wáng is unambiguous, so the display and domain forms differ only in the tone marks. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese forms as *[m]-roŋ (龍) and *[ɢ]ʷaŋ (王).
