Each character is a logogram that encodes meaning and historical pronunciation.
Hanyu Pinyin with tone marks preserves Mandarin pronunciation; the ASCII form loses tone.
The Unicode restoration Bāguà is the registrable form because hanzi are outside the .com IDN table.

provenanceSources.title: Schuessler, ABC Etymological Dictionary of Old Chinese

pronunciation.approximation: BAH-GWAH — first syllable high and level, second syllable falling (high to low) like a command.
pronunciation.note: 八卦 (Bāguà) refers to the eight trigrams of the Yijing: 乾 qián, 坤 kūn, 震 zhèn, 巽 xùn, 坎 kǎn, 離 lí, 艮 gèn, and 兌 duì. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is bā (Tone 1) + guà (Tone 4), as recorded in the Unihan Database (kMandarin). For historical context, Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 八 as *pret (GSR 0281a) and 卦 as *[k]ʷre-s (GSR 0879s). The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Bāguà correctly shows the high level tone of 'eight' and the falling tone of 'trigram'.

domains.title: The Eight Trigrams
domains.subtitle: Yijing Cosmology and Divination
domains.lead:
Bāguà is the Chinese universe reduced to eight three-line figures. Each trigram — 乾 Qián, 坤 Kūn, 震 Zhèn, 巽 Xùn, 坎 Kǎn, 離 Lí, 艮 Gèn, 兌 Duì — stacks yin and yang lines in every possible combination of three, producing a complete symbolic alphabet for describing situations, forces, and transformations. From the trigrams come the sixty-four hexagrams of the Yijing, the oldest continuously used divination manual in the world.

Bāguà is not only a fortune-telling tool. It is a map of reality: directions, seasons, family roles, body parts, and moral qualities all attach to the eight figures.

cards.name: The Three Lines
cards.desc: A solid line is yang; a broken line is yin. Three lines yield 2³ = 8 trigrams, the elementary vocabulary of change.

cards.name: Heaven and Earth
cards.desc: Qián ☰, three solid lines, is heaven and creative power; Kūn ☷, three broken lines, is earth and receptive yielding.

cards.name: Cosmic Directions
cards.desc: The Later Heaven arrangement assigns each trigram to a direction, a season, and a domain of human life.

cards.name: Divination Method
cards.desc: Yarrow stalks, coins, and milfoil turn trigrams into hexagrams, turning a question into a reading of timing and transformation.

symbols.name: Qián ☰ (Heaven)
symbols.meaning: Creativity, strength, the father, the creative impulse

symbols.name: Kūn ☷ (Earth)
symbols.meaning: Receptivity, devotion, the mother, the power of bearing

symbols.name: Zhèn ☳ (Thunder)
symbols.meaning: Arousal, movement, the eldest son, sudden change

symbols.name: Xùn ☴ (Wind/Wood)
symbols.meaning: Gentle penetration, the eldest daughter, influence

symbols.name: Kǎn ☵ (Water)
symbols.meaning: The abyss, danger, the middle son, the testing flow

symbols.name: Lí ☲ (Fire)
symbols.meaning: Clarity, attachment, the middle daughter, brightness

mythology.lead: The Bāguà are surrounded by origin stories that credit culture heroes, sages, and even river creatures with their discovery. Whether these are history, legend, or mythic shorthand, they reveal how seriously the Chinese tradition took the trigrams as a key to cosmic order.

myths.title: Trigrams from the River
myths.text: Tradition says that the culture hero Fuxi observed the patterns on a dragon-horse that emerged from the Yellow River — the Hétú — and derived the eight trigrams. The Luoshu, a numeric diagram borne by a turtle from the Luo River, later supplied the magic-square arrangement used in feng shui.

myths.title: King Wen and the Sixty-Four Hexagrams
myths.text: King Wen of Zhou, imprisoned by the Shang king, stacked the eight trigrams into sixty-four hexagrams and composed the hexagram statements. His son, the Duke of Zhou, added line statements. Confucius or his school later wrote the Ten Wings, transforming a divination manual into a philosophical classic.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Bāguà are everywhere once you know how to look. The Korean flag places four of the trigrams at its corners; martial artists practice Baguazhang, the Eight Trigram Palm, walking in circles that map the directions; computer scientists and designers use the Unicode trigram block (U+2630–U+2637) as glyphs for menus and progress indicators. Feng shui consultants still lay the octagonal bagua over floor plans to diagnose relationships, wealth, career, and health. The I Ching itself has been translated into dozens of languages and consulted by everyone from Carl Jung to John Cage. The trigrams have proved durable because they are not answers; they are a grammar for asking better questions about change.
lore.archaeology: The Bāguà are rooted in the Shang dynasty practice of pyromancy on oracle bones and turtle plastrons, though the trigram system itself reaches written maturity in the Zhou period. The oldest Yijing manuscripts include the Mawangdui silk Zhouyi (c. 168 BCE) and the Warring States bamboo slips from Guodian and Shanghai Museum collections. Han dynasty commentaries, including the Xici, fixed the philosophical interpretation of the trigrams, while Song and Ming editions transmitted the diagrams that remain standard today.
lore.syncretism: Bāguà is shared by Confucian, Daoist, and folk-religious traditions, each giving the trigrams a different emphasis. Confucians read them as moral archetypes; Daoists use them in talismans and internal alchemy; feng shui masters arrange buildings by their directions. The arrangement called the Early Heaven sequence is associated with Fuxi and cosmogony, while the Later Heaven sequence is associated with King Wen and the flow of time. In Korea, the trigrams appear on the national flag; in Japan, they influenced Onmyōdō cosmology. Richard Wilhelm's 1923 German translation, rendered into English by Cary Baynes, introduced the I Ching to modern Europe and America, where it became a countercultural classic.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 八卦; traditional and simplified forms are identical. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Bāguà (Tone 1 + Tone 4). Bā means 'eight' and guà means 'trigram' or 'hexagram' in divinatory usage. The registrable form uses tone-marked Pinyin so the domain remains readable across scripts; the characters are displayed in the Original Script card. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 八 as *pret and 卦 as *[k]ʷre-s.

Each character is a logogram that encodes meaning and historical pronunciation.
Hanyu Pinyin with tone marks preserves Mandarin pronunciation; the ASCII form loses tone.

provenanceSources.title: Schuessler, ABC Etymological Dictionary of Old Chinese

pronunciation.approximation: TIE-JEE — 'tai' like 'tie' with a sharp falling tone (high to low), and 'ji' like 'gee' with a rising tone.
pronunciation.note: 太極 (Tàijí) means the 'Supreme Ultimate' or 'Great Extreme', the primordial source from which yin and yang differentiate in Neo-Confucian cosmology. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is tài (Tone 4) + jí (Tone 2), per the Hanyu Pinyin scheme (ISO 7098) and the Unihan Database (kMandarin). Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the component characters as 太 *l̥a[t]-s (GSR 0317d) and 極 *[g](r)ək (GSR 0910e). The Unicode restoration Tàijí preserves both citation tones.

domains.title: The Supreme Ultimate
domains.subtitle: Origin of Yin and Yang
domains.lead:
Tàijí is the moment before distinction. In Neo-Confucian cosmology it is the 'Supreme Ultimate' or 'Supreme Polarity' — not a god but a generative singularity from which yin and yang unfold. The famous opening of Zhou Dunyi's Taijitu shuo (c. 1073 CE) sets the sequence in motion: Wújí gives rise to Tàijí; Tàijí moves and generates yáng; at the limit of movement it becomes still and generates yīn.

This is not static monism. Tàijí is the axis of a cosmic breathing — the one that contains the two, the undivided source of all subsequent differentiation.

cards.name: The Undifferentiated One
cards.desc: Before heaven and earth separate, there is the circle of Tàijí: whole, self-contained, and pregnant with possibility.

cards.name: Movement and Stillness
cards.desc: Tàijí in motion produces yáng; Tàijí at rest produces yīn. The cosmos alternates between these two modes like a long, slow breath.

cards.name: Generative Cosmology
cards.desc: From the two modes come the four images, from the four images come the eight trigrams, and from the eight trigrams the ten thousand things.

cards.name: Taijiquan
cards.desc: The martial art named after Tàijí embodies the principle: soft overcomes hard, stillness defeats haste, and the center remains unmoved.

symbols.name: The taijitu circle
symbols.meaning: The whole that contains both yin and yang in dynamic interdependence

symbols.name: The empty circle of wuji
symbols.meaning: The limitless void from which Tàijí emerges

symbols.name: Solid and broken lines
symbols.meaning: Yang and yin as the two building blocks of all subsequent forms

symbols.name: Water
symbols.meaning: The softest thing that overcomes the hardest — the practical image of Tàijí's yielding power

symbols.name: The center
symbols.meaning: The still point around which all motion turns

mythology.lead: Tàijí has no body and no biography; its 'mythology' is the story Chinese thinkers told about how the one becomes many. The most influential telling is Zhou Dunyi's short prose poem, but it draws on much older Daoist and Yijing material.

myths.title: Wújí ér Tàijí
myths.text: Zhou Dunyi's Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate opens: 'Wújí ér Tàijí' — the limitless, and yet the supreme ultimate. From this arise movement and stillness, yang and yin, the five phases, and finally the moral order of the sage. The text became the cosmological charter of Song Neo-Confucianism and shaped Chinese state orthodoxy for centuries.

myths.title: The Dao Gives Birth to One
myths.text: Laozi describes a parallel cosmogony in Daodejing 42: 'The Dao gives birth to one; one gives birth to two; two gives birth to three; three gives birth to the ten thousand things.' The 'one' has often been read as Tàijí, the primordial unity that precedes the duality of yin and yang.

lore.culturalLegacy: Taijiquan is now practiced by millions worldwide and was added to UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2020. Hospitals prescribe it for balance, hypertension, and stress; parks from Beijing to San Francisco fill with slow, synchronized movement at dawn. The taijitu symbol appears on flags, album covers, tattoos, and corporate logos — a visual shorthand for equilibrium. Yet the most lasting legacy may be conceptual: Tàijí gave Chinese thought a vocabulary for describing how a single dynamic source can generate an ordered cosmos without recourse to a creator god.
lore.archaeology: Tàijí as a named cosmological term is textual rather than archaeological. Its locus classicus is Zhou Dunyi's Taijitu shuo, preserved in Song dynasty editions and woodblock prints. Earlier antecedents appear in Han commentaries on the Yijing and in the Mawangdui silk manuscripts, which transmit variant versions of the Daodejing and Yijing. The distinctive two-tone taijitu diagram itself becomes common only in Song and Ming visual culture, though the yin-yang pairing it encodes is far older.
lore.syncretism: Tàijí sits at the intersection of three Chinese traditions. For Daoists it is the cosmological stage just after the Dao; for Neo-Confucians it is the metaphysical foundation of ethics and natural order; for martial artists it is the physical principle of softness overcoming hardness. The symbol of the taijitu migrated into Korean Taoism, Japanese martial arts, and Vietnamese folk religion, often detached from Zhou Dunyi's text. In the modern West, Tai Chi is usually known as a health exercise, while the taijitu has become a generic emblem of balance and Eastern wisdom — sometimes stripped of its specific philosophical grammar but instantly recognizable.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 太極 in traditional Chinese and 太极 in simplified. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Tàijí (Tone 4 + Tone 2), per Hanyu Pinyin and the Unihan Database. The registrable form preserves the tone marks because the full hanzi cannot be used as an ASCII-compatible domain label; the temple displays the characters in the Original Script card. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct the component characters as 太 *l̥a[t]-s and 極 *[g](r)ək.

steps: The name is written with the Chinese characters 五行.
Each character is a logogram that encodes meaning and historical pronunciation.
Hanyu Pinyin with tone marks preserves Mandarin pronunciation; the ASCII form loses tone.
The Unicode restoration Wǔxíng is the registrable form because hanzi are outside the .com IDN table.

provenanceSources.title: Schuessler, ABC Etymological Dictionary of Old Chinese

pronunciation.approximation: WOO-SHING — 'wu' dips low and rises (or stays low in fast speech), and 'xing' rises like 'sheen' with a rising tone.
pronunciation.note: 五行 (Wǔxíng) denotes the 'Five Phases' or 'Five Agents'—wood, fire, earth, metal, and water—the cyclical modes of transformation in Chinese cosmology, medicine, and feng shui. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in this philosophical context is wǔ (Tone 3) + xíng (Tone 2), as given by the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and the Hanyu Pinyin scheme. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ (GSR 0058a) and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ (GSR 0748a). The Unicode restoration Wǔxíng preserves the citation tones; note that 行 is disyllabically distinguished from the reading háng ('row, profession').

domains.title: The Five Phases
domains.subtitle: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water
domains.lead:
Wǔxíng is often mistranslated as 'five elements,' but xíng means movement, conduct, or phase. Wood, fire, earth, metal, and water are not static substances but dynamic processes: wood grows, fire flames, earth ripens, metal contracts, water descends. Together they form a grammar of transformation that Chinese thinkers applied to seasons, organs, emotions, dynasties, and military strategy.

The system works through two main cycles: the generating cycle (wood feeds fire, fire makes earth, earth bears metal, metal carries water, water nourishes wood) and the controlling cycle (wood parts earth, earth absorbs water, water quenches fire, fire melts metal, metal chops wood).

cards.name: Generation Cycle
cards.desc: Each phase gives birth to the next in a circle of mutual nourishment and support.

cards.name: Control Cycle
cards.desc: Each phase checks another, preventing any one process from running to destructive excess.

cards.name: Correspondence System
cards.desc: Every phase maps to a direction, season, color, organ, emotion, taste, and musical note.

cards.name: Cosmic Calendar
cards.desc: The phases organize the year: wood/spring, fire/summer, earth/late summer, metal/autumn, water/winter.

symbols.name: Wood
symbols.meaning: Growth, spring, the east, the liver, the color green/blue, the wind

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: Flaming, summer, the south, the heart, the color red, heat

symbols.name: Earth
symbols.meaning: Ripening, late summer, the center, the spleen, the color yellow, dampness

symbols.name: Metal
symbols.meaning: Contracting, autumn, the west, the lungs, the color white, dryness

symbols.name: Water
symbols.meaning: Descending, winter, the north, the kidneys, the color black/dark, cold

mythology.lead: Wǔxíng has no divine biography, but its intellectual history is dramatic: it began as a description of natural processes, became a theory of state legitimacy, and ended as the diagnostic language of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

myths.title: The Great Plan
myths.text: The Hongfan chapter of the Shangshu presents the five phases as the first of the 'Nine Categories' revealed to Yu the Great. Water, fire, wood, metal, and earth each have their nature: water soaks and descends, fire blazes and ascends, wood bends and straightens, metal yields and changes, earth sows and gathers. This is the earliest systematic statement of Wǔxíng cosmology.

myths.title: The Yin-Yang and Five Phases School
myths.text: The philosopher Zou Yan (c. 324–250 BCE) applied the five phases to history, arguing that dynasties rise and fall according to which phase they embody. Each new dynasty was thought to possess the virtue of the next phase, giving cosmic legitimacy to political revolution.

lore.culturalLegacy: Wǔxíng is the hidden scaffolding of much that looks merely 'Chinese' on the surface. The five flavors, five colors, five notes, five grains, and five directions all derive from it. Traditional Chinese Medicine diagnoses in its terms; feng shui designs spaces by it; Xingyiquan organizes its five basic fists around it; Chinese astrology assigns each year an element. The system even colored imperial ritual: the Yellow Emperor claimed earth, the Qin chose black water to overcome Zhou red fire. Today Wǔxíng survives in video-game elemental mechanics, wellness branding, and martial-arts school names — sometimes faithfully, often trivially. Its deepest legacy is a habit of mind: the tendency to see nature not as a collection of things but as a field of interactive processes.
lore.archaeology: The textual foundation of Wǔxíng appears in the Shangshu's Hongfan chapter, transmitted through Warring States and Han manuscript traditions. The Mawangdui tomb library preserves early medical manuscripts that apply the five phases to diagnosis and treatment, while the Huangdi Neijing became the canonical medical synthesis. Han dynasty lacquerware, bronze mirrors, and tomb murals display the color-direction correspondences of the five phases. Unlike a deity, Wǔxíng has no temple, but its logic is inscribed across the material culture of state ritual, medicine, and calendrical science.
lore.syncretism: Wǔxíng was sometimes compared by Western observers to the Greek four elements, but the comparison is misleading. The Greek elements are building blocks of substance; the Chinese phases are patterns of change. A closer Indian analogue is the pañca mahābhūta, though the correspondences differ. Wǔxíng entered Japan as gogyō and Korea as ohaeng, shaping East Asian medicine, astrology, and martial arts. In modern times, Wǔxíng has been invoked — and sometimes distorted — in management theory, martial-arts branding, and popular spirituality, often reduced to a color-coded personality test. The medical tradition, however, continues to use the five phases as a sophisticated heuristic for pattern differentiation.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 五行; traditional and simplified forms are identical. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in the philosophical sense is Wǔxíng (Tone 3 + Tone 2), per Hanyu Pinyin and the Unihan Database. Note that 行 has a separate reading háng ('row, profession'); here it means 'movement, conduct, phase.' The registrable form preserves the tone marks; the characters are displayed in the Original Script card. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ.

pronunciation.approximation: foo-shee, rising tone on fu, high level on xi.
pronunciation.note: Fúxī 伏羲 carries the rising tone on fú and the high level tone on xī in Mandarin; older romanizations write Fu-hsi. The first graph 伏 suggests "to subdue, to prostrate," the second 羲 a sacrificial term — a name older than its etymologies, borne by the first of the Three August Ones. The older romanization Fu-hsi records the same syllables; pinyin's x is the alveolo-palatal fricative of modern Mandarin.

domains.title: The First Teacher
domains.subtitle: The Eight Trigrams, the Net, and the Marriage on the Mountain
domains.lead: Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.

cards.name: The Eight Trigrams
cards.desc: Bāguà: broken and unbroken lines in threes — the binary alphabet of the Yìjīng, attributed to his observation.

cards.name: The Net
cards.desc: He taught the people to knot cords into nets — fishing, hunting, and the technology of the snare.

cards.name: The Serpent Bodies
cards.desc: Han art shows him and Nǚwā as serpents intertwined — the primal pair, measuring square and compass in hand.

cards.name: Marriage
cards.desc: He instituted the rites of marriage and the bride-price of deer skins — order after the flood.

symbols.name: The trigrams
symbols.meaning: Pattern abstracted from nature — the seed of all Chinese correlative thought

symbols.name: The carpenter's square
symbols.meaning: His emblem in Han art: the earth-measurer's tool (Nǚwā holds the compass of heaven)

symbols.name: The dragon-horse
symbols.meaning: The creature from the Yellow River whose markings revealed the diagram

mythology.lead: Fúxī's myths are all acts of notation: he does not fight or flee — he observes, abstracts, and teaches. He is the culture-bringer as draftsman.

myths.title: Reading the World
myths.text: The Yìjīng's Great Treatise records the founding act: Fúxī looked up and contemplated the images of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth, contemplated the markings of birds and beasts and the order of the near at hand — and from all three made the eight trigrams, "to comprehend the powers of the spirits and to classify the natures of the ten thousand things." Writing, mathematics, and divination begin as one gesture of attention.

myths.title: The Dragon-Horse's Map
myths.text: Later tradition gives the revelation a courier: a dragon-horse rose from the Yellow River bearing on its back the Hétú, the River Chart — the arrangement of numbers and marks from which Fúxī drew the trigrams. Paired with the Luò River Writing that inspired the Great Plan, the Chart made the Yellow River itself the first text of Chinese civilization.

lore.culturalLegacy: Every reading of the Yìjīng — the book that shaped Confucian statecraft, Daoist alchemy, and Leibniz's binary arithmetic — begins with his act of looking. The eight trigrams appear on the flag of South Korea; the River Chart structures a millennium of cosmological diagrams; and "Fúxī" remains the standard icon for the inventor-ancestor in Chinese cultural memory, the answer to the question of where pattern-thinking began.
lore.archaeology: The Wu Liang shrine reliefs (2nd century CE, Shandong) show Fúxī and Nǚwā with serpent bodies entwined, square and compass raised — the canonical image, replicated across Han tomb art from Sichuan to Xinjiang (the famous Astana cemetery banner). The myth's textual archaeology runs from the Zhuangzi and Xunzi mentions to the Tang's flood-cycle records: a steady accretion from sage-king to cosmic progenitor, all preserved in the transmitted classics.
lore.syncretism: He heads most lists of the Three August Ones (Sānhuáng), paired inseparably with Nǚwā — their intertwined serpent forms in Han art echoing, scholars note, the union of measure and generation. Daoist tradition absorbed him as a revealer of the trigrams to the immortal lineages; Confucian tradition kept him as the first historian of pattern. The serpent-pair iconography has been compared by art historians with intertwined pairs from Egypt to India — diffusion debated, the resemblance celebrated.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 伏羲: fú (subdue; the man-radical with the hound) plus xī (the ancient graph for sacrificial breath). The compound is attested from Warring States texts onward — the name predates any agreed reading of it, which is itself a mark of antiquity.

pronunciation.approximation: nyoo-wah, low-dipping tone on Nǚ, high level on Wā.
pronunciation.note: Nǚwā 女娲 bears the third tone on nǚ — the vowel ü written with its two dots, which the restoration keeps and plain ASCII drops. Wā is the level-toned archaic graph for this goddess alone: a character invented for her name, used for nothing else in the language. The ü is the front rounded vowel — the sound French writes u — which plain ASCII loses to plain u.

domains.title: The Mender of Heaven
domains.subtitle: The Five-Colored Stones, the Clay, and the First People
domains.lead: Nǚwā is the great repairer: the goddess who melted five-colored stones to patch the broken sky, cut off the giant turtle's legs to prop the corners of the world, and — on a quieter day — knelt by the Yellow River and made the first human beings out of mud.

cards.name: The Five-Colored Stones
cards.desc: Melted and poured into the sky's wound — the world's first and greatest repair.

cards.name: The Serpent Body
cards.desc: Her form in Han art: human head, serpent body — earth's maker in earth's image.

cards.name: The Rope of Mud
cards.desc: The rich she shaped by hand, the poor she flung from a rope — humanity's two fortunes.

cards.name: The Marriage Rites
cards.desc: She instituted marriage and is prayed to for children — society's first legislator.

symbols.name: The five colors
symbols.meaning: The five phases (wood, fire, earth, metal, water) — the sky rebuilt in cosmic order

symbols.name: The compass
symbols.meaning: Her emblem in Han art, paired with Fúxī's square — heaven's measure in her hand

symbols.name: The turtle's legs
symbols.meaning: The four pillars she cut and set — sacrifice repurposed as architecture

mythology.lead: Nǚwā's two great myths answer the two great questions: where people came from, and why the sky holds. Both are told in the earliest strata of Chinese myth and never improved upon.

myths.title: The Mending of the Sky
myths.text: The Huáinánzǐ tells it: in high antiquity the four pillars snapped, the nine provinces split; fire raged unquenched, waters rose undrained; fierce beasts devoured the people. Nǚwā melted stones of five colors to mend the azure sky, cut the legs of the great turtle to set the four pillars, slew the black dragon to save Jì province, and heaped reed-ashes to dam the flood. Then — and only then — the world was habitable, and the beasts went quiet.

myths.title: People of Yellow Earth
myths.text: The later compendia preserve the gentler myth: Nǚwā, walking alone in the empty world, knelt by the river and shaped human beings from yellow clay. The work delighted but wearied her — so she trailed a rope through the mud and flung the drops, which became people too. The handmade figures became the rich and noble; the rope-flung drops, the poor and common — China's oldest reflection on how inequality began.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her stones became literature: the great novel Dream of the Red Chamber (Hónglóu mèng) opens with the one stone Nǚwā rejected for the sky — the stone that becomes the hero's jade and the book itself. "Nǚwā mends the sky" is the standing idiom for heroic repair; engineers, surgeons, and diplomats are all praised with it. Temples to her survive across North China — Shexian's cliff-hanging Wahuang Palace in Hebei is the grandest — where she is still prayed to for children.
lore.archaeology: The Wahuang Palace at Shexian — pavilions chained to a cliff above the Zhang River, founded in the Northern Qi dynasty (6th century) — is her principal surviving sanctuary and one of China's architectural marvels. Han pictorial stones pair her with Fúxī from Shandong to Sichuan; the Astana cemetery silk banner carried the image to the Silk Road's far end. Her myth's textual strata are mapped from the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE) backward into Warring States fragments and forward into the Tang flood-cycle accounts.
lore.syncretism: She pairs with Fúxī as sister-wife in the Han synthesis — their intertwined serpent bodies, compass and square in hand, form the canonical image of cosmic order — and she absorbs older creation figures as the myth spread south and north. Modern readers note her kinship with every world-mother from Gaia to the Navajo Changing Woman, but the Chinese tradition keeps her distinct signature: she is not just a mother but a repairer, the goddess of maintenance.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 女娲: nǚ (woman) plus wā — a graph so specific to her that dictionaries list almost no other word under it. The ü of the restoration is the sound itself; without it, the name is another word.

pronunciation.approximation: SHYEHN — a high, level tone held steady, with a light 'sh' that touches the palate.
pronunciation.note: 仙 denotes a transcendent being in Daoism, distinct from ordinary gods (shén) and from Buddhist arhats or bodhisattvas. The character combines 人 (person) with 山 (mountain), suggesting one who withdraws to the heights. The Pinyin restoration Xiān preserves the high level tone.

domains.title: The Immortal
domains.subtitle: Transcendence, Daoist Practice, and Celestial Freedom
domains.lead:
Xiān is the Chinese immortal: a human being who has refined body and spirit until death no longer applies. Unlike the gods of popular religion, who receive offerings and grant petitions, the xiān has escaped the bureaucracy of heaven and earth. He or she dwells in mountains, rides clouds or cranes, and appears unpredictably to those who have cultivated the Dao.

The path to becoming xiān is not faith but practice: meditation, breath control, diet, alchemy, and moral discipline. Immortality is an achievement, not a gift.

cards.name: Longevity
cards.desc: The xiān has overcome ageing and death through disciplined transformation of the body.

cards.name: Mountain Dwelling
cards.desc: Immortals withdraw to peaks and grottoes where the qi is pure and the world is far.

cards.name: Internal Alchemy
cards.desc: Neidan refines the three treasures — jīng, qì, shén — into an immortal embryo.

cards.name: Freedom from Bureaucracy
cards.desc: Unlike gods bound by celestial office, the xiān wanders freely between realms.

symbols.name: Crane
symbols.meaning: The mount and companion of immortals; a thousand-year lifespan.

symbols.name: Peach of immortality
symbols.meaning: The fruit of the Queen Mother of the West's garden, ripening every three thousand years.

symbols.name: Gourd
symbols.meaning: The bottle that holds elixirs, medicines, and the boundless space of the Dao.

symbols.name: Clouds and mist
symbols.meaning: The medium through which immortals travel and the boundary between mortal and transcendent realms.

mythology.lead: Xiān mythology is a vast gallery of individual adepts, each with a distinctive method of transcendence. They are less a pantheon than a community of perfected beings.

myths.title: The Eight Immortals (Bāxiān)
myths.text: The most famous xiān are the Eight Immortals, each representing a different social type and a different path to transcendence. Zhōnglí Quán was a general; Lǚ Dòngbīn a scholar; Hé Xiāngū a woman who nourished her spirit; Lán Cǎihé a gender-ambiguous beggar; and so on. Their collective journeys show that immortality is open to anyone who cultivates the Dao, regardless of birth.

myths.title: The Queen Mother of the West's Peach Banquet
myths.text: Every three thousand years, the peaches of immortality ripen in the garden of Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West. The xiān gather to feast and renew their transcendence. The myth links immortality to cosmic time: it is not a single event but a continual nourishment by celestial cycles.

lore.culturalLegacy: Xiān permeate Chinese culture. They appear in landscape painting as tiny figures on misty peaks, in New Year prints carrying peaches and gourds, and in countless novels, operas, and films. The aspiration to longevity shapes Chinese medicine, diet, and exercise practices such as tai chi and qigong. The word xiān is also used for extraordinary people: a great cook is a 'food immortal,' a beautiful woman a 'fairy.' In global spirituality, the xiān offers an alternative to Western heaven: not a reward after death but a transformation of life itself, achieved through sustained practice.
lore.archaeology: The xiān tradition is attested in Warring States and Han dynasty texts, tomb art showing feathered immortals ascending to heaven, and the Mawangdui tomb manuscripts on longevity and breath cultivation. Medieval Daoist caves and temple murals depict the Eight Immortals and other transcendent figures. Alchemists' stoves, elixir recipes, and neidan manuals survive in the Daozang and in archaeological contexts from the Han through the Song dynasties.
lore.syncretism: The xiān tradition absorbed many influences. Indigenous Chinese quest for longevity merged with shamanic flight, alchemical experimentation, and Buddhist meditation techniques. The figure of the wandering immortal influenced Chan Buddhism, Confucian self-cultivation, and Chinese poetry and painting. In popular religion, local spirits and historical figures were posthumously enrolled as xiān. The West knows the xiān chiefly through the Eight Immortals and martial-arts films, where they appear as eccentric sages with superhuman powers. Modern Daoist lineages continue to practice neidan in pursuit of the same goal.

pronunciation.approximation: MAH-tsoo — level tone, then a dip-and-rise.
pronunciation.note: Māzǔ 媽祖 — "Maternal Ancestor" — carries the first tone on mā and the dipping third tone on zǔ; the restoration keeps both tone marks. Her personal name was Lín Mòniáng ("Silent Maiden"), but the world prays to the title: Grandmother of the sea. The third tone on zǔ dips and rises — the small valley in the name that Mandarin speakers sing without noticing.

domains.title: The Mother of the Sea
domains.subtitle: Sailors, Storms, and the Red Lantern
domains.lead: Māzǔ is the most-worshipped sea goddess on earth: the fisherman's daughter who became the guardian of everyone who works the water, whose temples line every coast of the Chinese world, and whose red lanterns guide sailors home through a thousand years of storms.

cards.name: The Sailors' Guardian
cards.desc: The goddess of everyone who goes to sea — the busiest answering voice on the water.

cards.name: The Red Lantern
cards.desc: Her signal in the storm — the light sailors pray to see.

cards.name: The Two Generals
cards.desc: Qiānlǐyǎn and Shùnfēng'ěr — her thousand-mile eyes and wind-sharp ears.

cards.name: Meizhou
cards.desc: Her island home off Fujian — the Nazareth of the sea-faith.

symbols.name: The red robe
symbols.meaning: Her temple color — protection worn bright against the grey sea

symbols.name: The lantern
symbols.meaning: The guide-light of the storm-tossed

symbols.name: The two generals
symbols.meaning: Sight and hearing deified — vigilance in both directions

mythology.lead: Māzǔ's myth is a life, not a legend: the historical Lín Mòniáng of 10th-century Meizhou, whose silence, visions, and early death became the sea's own religion.

myths.title: The Silent Girl of Meizhou
myths.text: Lín Mòniáng was born on Meizhou island in 960 CE, and tradition says she did not cry at birth — hence "Silent Maiden." She learned to read the weather on her father's fishing boat, stood on the shore watching for lost sails, and was seen in dreams guiding drowning sailors home. Dead by twenty-eight, she rose, the fishermen said, straight to the sky on a cloud of incense — and the sea was never without her again.

myths.title: From Daughter to Empress of Heaven
myths.text: The dynasties out-titled each other: the Song made her Consort of Heaven, the Yuan made her Princess, the Ming made her Holy Mother, the Qing made her Tiānhòu — Empress of Heaven. The historical woman is buried in the titles: the fishing daughter became, by twelve centuries of gratitude, the highest-ranked goddess of the Chinese sea, outranking every god the bureaucracy could promote her past.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her temples number in the thousands — over 1,500 in Taiwan alone; her birthday (23rd of the 3rd lunar month) shuts down the island's coasts; her Dajia procession is a national institution watched by millions more online. Fishermen, sailors, the navy, and migrants all claim her: the goddess who was once a girl watching the sea is now the sea's own government, elected annually by the crowds who walk behind her statue.
lore.archaeology: The Meizhou Ancestral Temple on her home island — rebuilt repeatedly from the Song original, crowded with imperial plaques — is her Nazareth; the Dajia Jenn Lann Temple and Taipei's grand Tianhou temples are her living capitals. Macau's A-Ma Temple (15th c., older than the Portuguese) marks her oldest colonial-era shore, and the Mazu statues of the Taiwan Strait's temples document eight centuries of her iconography.
lore.syncretism: She absorbs the coast's other sea-powers: associated with Guānyīn (who is sometimes her patron in the legends), honored in Daoist and Buddhist temples alike, and worshipped as Tin Hau in Hong Kong and A-Ma in Macau — whose very name, some say, comes from her ("A-Ma-Gau," Bay of A-Ma). The diaspora carried her to every Chinese port from San Francisco to Sydney: wherever junks and container ships anchor, her shrine overlooks the harbor.

entries.domain: War, Justice, Nephew of Jade Emperor

pronunciation.approximation: NUH-jah — the first syllable rises like a question, the second stays high and level; keep the 'zh' retroflex, tongue curled back, closer to 'dr' than to 'j'.
pronunciation.note: 哪吒 is the settled transcription of a name that entered Chinese through Buddhist transmission from Sanskrit Nalakūvara, son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Nézhā: 吒 zhā (Tone 1) is the value recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard dictionaries, while 哪 carries here its special proper-name reading né (Tone 2), preserved only in this name and recorded as such in the standard dictionaries (Xiandai Hanyu Cidian, Hanyu Da Cidian); its ordinary interrogative reading is nǎ (Tone 3), the value given under kMandarin in the Unihan Database. Because the name is a medieval transcription of a foreign theonym rather than a native Chinese word, Old Chinese reconstruction does not apply.

domains.title: The Lotus-Born Rebel
domains.subtitle: Filial Sacrifice, Divine Weaponry, Unconquerable Youth
domains.lead:
Nézhā is the child who would not stay born. Third son of the garrison commander Li Jing, he came into the world after three and a half years of pregnancy — not as an infant but as a ball of flesh, which his father split with a sword to reveal a walking, talking boy. The immortal Taiyi Zhenren took him as a disciple and armed him as no child has ever been armed: the Universe Ring, the Red Armillary Sash, the Fire-Tipped Spear, and the Wind Fire Wheels on which he rides the sky.

What follows is one of the most harrowing arcs in Chinese myth: a boy who kills the Dragon King's son, returns his flesh to his father and his bones to his mother to spare them heaven's vengeance, and is rebuilt from lotus roots and blossoms — a body owed to no one. From there he becomes the vanguard of Jiāng Zǐyá's Zhou army in the Investiture of the Gods and, in Journey to the West, the celestial marshal sent to battle Sūn Wùkōng.

cards.name: The Universe Ring
cards.desc: Qiánkūnquān, the golden ring of heaven and earth, first of the weapons Taiyi Zhenren bestowed — a cosmic bracelet that strikes with the weight of the world it names.

cards.name: The Eastern Sea
cards.desc: Bathing in the sea, Nézhā stirred the waters with his sash until the Dragon King's palace shook — the act that killed Āo Bǐng and set the cycle of debt and sacrifice in motion.

cards.name: The Lotus Rebirth
cards.desc: His soul rebuilt from lotus roots and blossoms by Taiyi Zhenren, Nézhā returns in a body owing flesh to no parent — purity, renewal, and freedom from the debt of birth.

cards.name: The Wind Fire Wheels
cards.desc: Fēnghuǒlún, the paired wheels of wind and flame beneath his feet — the mount that carries the celestial vanguard faster than storm across the three realms.

symbols.name: Universe Ring (乾坤圈)
symbols.meaning: Cosmic sovereignty in miniature — heaven and earth bound into a single striking weapon

symbols.name: Red Armillary Sash (混天綾)
symbols.meaning: The seven-chi silk that churns seas and binds foes; the instrument of the East Sea upheaval

symbols.name: Fire-Tipped Spear (火尖槍)
symbols.meaning: Martial fire and unrelenting advance, the spear of the vanguard who never retreats

symbols.name: Wind Fire Wheels (風火輪)
symbols.meaning: Unstoppable motion — the storm itself harnessed as a vehicle for the young marshal

symbols.name: Lotus (蓮花)
symbols.meaning: Rebirth without debt: purity rising from the water, a body remade beyond blood and bone

mythology.lead: The Nézhā cycle is the great Chinese myth of the filial rebel — a story in which the most radical act of disobedience and the most extreme act of filial piety turn out to be the same act. Its canonical form was fixed in the Ming dynasty, above all in the Investiture of the Gods.

myths.title: The Flesh Ball
myths.text: Lady Yīn carries her third child for three years and six months. When the birth finally comes, what emerges is not an infant but a ball of flesh, and Li Jing, garrison commander of Chéntānguān, strikes at it with his sword, certain it is a demon. The ball splits open — and out steps a boy already able to walk and speak, a divine embryo sent down as the disciple of the immortal Taiyi Zhenren. The wrongness of the birth is the point: Nézhā enters the world already owing nothing to ordinary nature.

myths.title: The Dragon King's Third Son
myths.text: Bathing in the Nine-Bend River where it meets the East Sea, the boy dips his Red Armillary Sash in the water — and the sash, an instrument of cosmic order, churns the sea until the palace of the Dragon King Āo Guǎng trembles on its foundations. When the Dragon King's third son, Āo Bǐng, rises to punish the offender, Nézhā kills him. A child has bloodied the bureaucracy of the waters, and the Dragon King of the East Sea will have justice from heaven itself.

lore.culturalLegacy: No Chinese deity has had a stronger twenty-first century. Nézhā's cult thrives in Taiwan and the diaspora, where the Marshal of the Central Altar dances in temple processions — in recent decades to electronic music, the 'techno Nézhā' of modern festival culture. On screen, the 2019 animated feature Ne Zha became the highest-grossing animated film in Chinese history, its defiant reading of the myth — fate is a rumor the child refuses — resonating with a generation; Ne Zha 2 (2025) went further, breaking global box-office records for animation. The rebel child who returned his body to his parents has become, arguably, the most popular Chinese deity of the modern era: an emblem of youth that will not be told what it owes.
lore.archaeology: Nézhā is a textual rather than an archaeological figure, and his attestation history tracks the Buddhist transmission itself. The name first appears in Tang-dynasty Buddhist translations as 那吒 (Nata), a transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa, whose cult flourished in Tang China and whose iconography — armor, spear, and reliquary pagoda — later passed to Nézhā's literary father, Li Jing. By the Song dynasty the flesh-and-bone-returning motif was current in Chan literature, and Yuan-era drama gave the child a stage life. The canonical narrative was fixed in the Ming novels: the Investiture of the Gods supplied the full cycle from flesh ball to lotus rebirth, and Journey to the West installed him as a marshal of the celestial court. Material attestation is chiefly cultic — temple statuary of the Marshal of the Central Altar, a wheel-riding, ring-bearing youth, across southeastern China, Taiwan, and the diaspora.
lore.syncretism: Nézhā is himself a product of transmission: the name enters Chinese through Buddhism as a transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, a son of the guardian king Vaiśravaṇa, and the earliest Chinese forms (那吒, read closer to Nata) preserve that foreign sound. As the figure was naturalized, the genealogy was rewritten — his father became the historical-flavored general Li Jing, who absorbed Vaiśravaṇa's iconography wholesale and became the pagoda-bearing Heavenly King (托塔天王) of the Chinese celestial court. Taoism then claimed the child outright: under the title Zhōngtán Yuánshuài, Marshal of the Central Altar, Nézhā became one of the most vividly worshipped protectors in the Chinese ritual pantheon. The figure traveled with the Chinese world — to Korea, Vietnam, and Japan (where he is Nataku) — but it is in the Sinitic ritual tradition, and above all in the temples and processions of Taiwan and the southeastern diaspora, that the lotus-born marshal remains a living god rather than a literary memory.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 哪吒, identical in traditional and simplified Chinese. Pinyin Nézhā combines the special proper-name reading né (Tone 2) of 哪 — preserved only in this name, the ordinary interrogative reading being nǎ — with 吒 zhā (Tone 1), as recorded in the standard dictionaries and the Unihan Database. The name is a medieval transcription of Sanskrit Nalakūvara, so no Old Chinese reconstruction applies. The tone-marked restoration Nézhā maps directly to the registrable domain form: the display keeps both diacritics (é and ā, both registrable IDN characters), and no apostrophe is required anywhere in the name.

entries.meaning: The Moon goddess who drank the elixir of immortality

pronunciation.approximation: CHAHNG-UH — both syllables rise in tone, as in a questioning intonation; 'ch' is an aspirated retroflex with the tongue curled back, and 'é' is close to the vowel of 'her' with the r removed.
pronunciation.note: 嫦娥 denotes the Chinese goddess of the moon. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Cháng'é — cháng (Tone 2) and é (Tone 2) — as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. The goddess's earlier name was 姮娥 Héng'é; under the Han it was altered to Cháng'é to observe the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor Wen (Liú Héng 劉恆), the graph 常 cháng ('constant') replacing the tabooed homophone 姮 héng. The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Cháng'é preserves the citation rising tone on both syllables; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tones remain Tone 2.

domains.title: Goddess of the Cold Moon
domains.subtitle: Immortality, Exile, Reunion
domains.lead:
Cháng'é is the woman who swallowed forever and paid for it with the earth. Wife of the archer Hòuyì, who shot nine suns out of the sky, she came into possession of the elixir of immortality — a gift of the Queen Mother of the West, Xīwángmǔ — and drank it. Whether she acted to keep the drug from a treacherous disciple or out of her own longing, the sources divide; what they agree on is the result: her body grew light, the ground let go of her, and she rose through the night until the moon received her. There she remains, the goddess of the cold luminary, in the Guǎnghán Palace — the Palace of Vast Cold.

She is not alone up there. The Jade Rabbit stands beside her, pounding the elixir with mortar and pestle, and the woodcutter Wú Gāng swings his axe at a cassia tree that heals each wound as it is struck. Once a year, at the full moon of the eighth month, all of China looks up at her: the Mid-Autumn Festival, when families reunite, mooncakes are cut, and the distance between heaven and earth is measured in shared light.

cards.name: The Moon
cards.desc: Her dwelling and her domain; the full moon of Mid-Autumn is read as her face, brightest and roundest when mortal eyes seek reunion.

cards.name: The Archer Hòuyì
cards.desc: Her husband, who shot down nine of the ten suns and received the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ — the gift that divided them forever.

cards.name: The Palace of Vast Cold
cards.desc: The Guǎnghán Palace (廣寒宮), her luminous and solitary court on the moon, shared with the Jade Rabbit and the woodcutter Wú Gāng.

cards.name: Reunion under the Full Moon
cards.desc: The Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋節): mooncakes, moon-gazing, and the gathering of families — the night her separation sanctifies mortal togetherness.

symbols.name: The full moon
symbols.meaning: Her dwelling and her face; completeness, distance, and the reunion it mirrors

symbols.name: The Jade Rabbit
symbols.meaning: Her companion (玉兔), who pounds the elixir of immortality with mortar and pestle — labor without end in her service

symbols.name: Mortar and pestle
symbols.meaning: The ceaseless preparation of the elixir she carried to heaven

symbols.name: The cassia tree
symbols.meaning: The self-healing tree Wú Gāng chops forever beside her palace — punishment and persistence in a single image

symbols.name: The mooncake
symbols.meaning: The round pastry of Mid-Autumn, cut and shared as an edible likeness of the moon she rules

mythology.lead: Cháng'é's story is short and inexhaustible: one ascent, endlessly retold. The early sources preserve a bare skeleton — an elixir, a flight, a moon — and two thousand years of poets, painters, and festival-goers have hung their longing on it.

myths.title: The Elixir of Immortality
myths.text: The core myth, fixed in the Huáinánzǐ (c. 2nd century BCE), begins with the archer Hòuyì, who had shot down nine of the ten suns and so received from Xīwángmǔ, Queen Mother of the West, the elixir of immortality. Cháng'é took it and floated up to the moon, where she became its goddess. The sources divide on her motive: in some versions she drinks to keep the elixir from Féngméng, Hòuyì's treacherous disciple; in others she drinks out of her own longing for deathlessness. Scholarship preserves both strands rather than adjudicating between them — the myth holds theft and sacrifice in suspension.

myths.title: From Héng'é to Cháng'é
myths.text: The goddess was originally 姮娥 Héng'é. Under the Han, her name was altered to avoid the naming taboo on the personal name of Emperor Wen, Liú Héng 劉恆: the graph 姮 was replaced by the synonymous 常, and Héng'é became Cháng'é. It is a rare case where imperial censorship is legible inside a divine name itself — a goddess renamed so that a mortal emperor's name could remain unspoken.

lore.culturalLegacy: Cháng'é has been China's shorthand for beautiful distance since the poets claimed her. Sū Shì's Mid-Autumn lyric closes with the wish that, though a thousand miles apart, we may share chánjuān 嬋娟 — the lovely one, the moon, her. The Mid-Autumn Festival remains one of the great holidays of the Chinese world, and the mooncake its edible emblem. In 2020 the animated film Over the Moon carried her to global audiences as a pop-diva goddess still waiting for Hòuyì. Most remarkably, she has gone back: China's lunar exploration program is named for her, and the probes Cháng'é 1 through 6 (2007–2024) orbited the moon, landed on it, achieved the first landing on its far side (Cháng'é 4), and returned samples to earth (Cháng'é 5 and 6). No other deity in this lexicon has been so literally restored to her own heaven.
lore.archaeology: The flight to the moon is attested remarkably early. An early version of the story circulated in the Guǐcáng (歸藏), a divination text known from medieval quotations and from Qin-dynasty bamboo slips excavated at Wangjiatai in Hubei (tomb closed c. 3rd century BCE), in which Héng'é takes the elixir and ascends. The Huáinánzǐ (c. 139 BCE) gives the first full surviving account. Pictorial evidence is nearly as old: the painted silk funeral banner from Mawangdui Tomb 1 (sealed 168 BCE) depicts the moon disk with its toad and rabbit, and Han pictorial stones — notably from the Nanyang region — show Cháng'é in flight toward the moon, her robes streaming. Later dynasties rendered her on mirrors, ceramics, and festival prints, and moon-gazing scenes became a staple of Ming and Qing painting.
lore.syncretism: The rabbit in the moon is older than any single nation's telling of it. Buddhist tradition carried the śaśajātaka — the tale of the rabbit who offered itself as food and was set in the moon as a reward — from India into East Asia, and scholars commonly link the Chinese moon rabbit to this transmission, though the Jade Rabbit's elixir-pounding is China's own elaboration. Taoist religion absorbed Cháng'é into its celestial bureaucracy, where she is often identified with the sovereign of the yin luminary (太陰). Japan received the moon rabbit without the elixir: there he pounds mochi instead, and the autumn moon-viewing custom (tsukimi) echoes Mid-Autumn without keeping its goddess. Korea's harvest festival Chuseok and Vietnam's Tết Trung Thu share the same full-moon night of cakes, lanterns, and family gathering — the festival traveled further than the myth, and in each harbor took local form.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 嫦娥, written identically in traditional and simplified Chinese; the earlier form of the name is 姮娥, altered under the Han naming taboo on Emperor Wen's personal name. Pinyin Cháng'é (Tone 2 + Tone 2) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The apostrophe is part of standard Hanyu Pinyin orthography, separating the two syllables so the name cannot be misread as a single syllable or wrongly divided; the display form Cháng'é keeps it, while the registrable domain label drops it, since IDN labels cannot contain an apostrophe — the tone-marked vowels alone carry the restoration into the domain system.

entries.meaning: The divine archer who shot down nine suns

pronunciation.approximation: HOH-yee — two crisp syllables, each spoken with a sharp falling tone, like a decisive command: 'HOE! YEE!'
pronunciation.note: 后羿 names the divine archer: 后 is an archaic title meaning 'lord, sovereign' (not the later sense 'empress', for which 皇后 is used), and 羿 is the archer's given name. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Hòuyì (both syllables Tone 4), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese reading of 羿 as *N-ŋ(r)ik-s. The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Hòuyì preserves the citation falling tone of both syllables; in connected speech the contour may be compressed, but the lexical tones remain Tone 4.

domains.title: Archer of the Nine Fallen Suns
domains.subtitle: Precision, Deliverance, the Spared Light
domains.lead:
Hòuyì is the divine archer of Chinese myth, the hero who stood between heaven's excess and the earth's survival. In the age of the sage-emperor Yáo, the ten suns — three-legged crows, sons of Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé — rose all at once instead of taking their appointed turns. Rivers dried, crops failed, and monsters crawled out of the scorched wilderness. Hòuyì drew his great bow and shot nine suns from the sky, sparing one so that day and night, sowing and harvest, could keep their order.

His story is a hinge between worlds: the same bow that cleared the earth of monsters also won him the elixir of immortality from Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West — the elixir his wife Cháng'é would ultimately take, fleeing to the moon. The archer who saved the earth lost heaven, and Chinese myth has never stopped telling both halves of that story.

mythology.lead: The cycle of Hòuyì is the great Chinese myth of cosmic correction: a heaven that gives too much, an earth that suffers for it, and one archer whose arrows restore the mean. Its episodes run from the scorched world of the ten suns to the cold moon where his wife still dwells.

myths.title: The Shooting of the Nine Suns
myths.text: In the reign of Emperor Yáo, the ten suns — three-legged crows roosting in the Fusang tree, sons of Dìjùn and the sun-mother Xīhé — abandoned their orderly rotation and rose together. The earth burned: rivers dried, crops withered, and the people starved. Yáo called on Hòuyì, the divine archer, who climbed to the heights and loosed his arrows. One by one nine suns fell from the sky in their crow forms, and the tenth — spared — resumed its solitary, lawful journey. The myth is told across the Shān Hǎi Jīng tradition and given its fullest early form in the Huáinánzǐ.

myths.title: The Clearing of the Monsters
myths.text: The drought had loosed terrors on the world, and the Huáinánzǐ lists the archer's second labor: he slew Yàyǔ, the man-eating beast of the wilds; Záochǐ in the waters of Chouhua; Jiǔyīng, the nine-headed monster of the Xiong river; the great wind-bird Dàfēng in the marshes of Qingqiu; the giant serpent Xiūshé at Lake Dongting; and the monstrous boar Fēngxī in the mulberry groves of Sanglin. Only when the last beast fell could the people plow in peace.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hòuyì never left the Chinese imagination. The shooting of the suns is among the first myths Chinese children learn, retold in primers, animated films, and television dramas, and the Cháng'é sequel anchors the Mid-Autumn Festival, when families gaze at the moon where the archer's wife is said to dwell. Modern China has written the pair onto the sky itself: the national lunar exploration program is named Cháng'é, and its missions are spoken of as the moon goddess finally receiving visitors — a deliberate bridal of myth and engineering. The idiom of 'shooting the suns' survives as a metaphor for cutting down excess and correcting what has grown monstrous. In art, from Han dynasty tomb reliefs to contemporary illustration, the archer drawing his bow against a wheel of suns remains one of the most recognizable images in the Chinese visual canon.
lore.archaeology: Hòuyì's deeds are textual before they are pictorial. The earliest witnesses are Warring States literature: the Shān Hǎi Jīng preserves the ten-suns framework and the suns' parentage, the Chǔ Cí poem Tiān Wèn (Heavenly Questions, c. 4th–3rd century BCE) interrogates Yì's shooting of the suns and his tangled fate, and the Mèngzǐ records the Féngméng betrayal. The fullest surviving narrative is the Huáinánzǐ (139 BCE), which sets the archer in Emperor Yáo's reign and catalogs the slain monsters. In Han dynasty art the cycle became a staple of funerary iconography: tomb reliefs and painted stones at sites such as the Wu Liang shrines (Shandong, 2nd century CE) show the archer drawing against crow-bearing suns, while Mawangdui funerary art (168 BCE) depicts the solar crow and the moon's toad-and-hare company that would gather around Cháng'é. Han mirrors and later pictorial stones continued the imagery, fixing the bow, the crows, and the moon as the archer's permanent attributes.
lore.syncretism: Hòuyì's myth traveled with Chinese civilization itself. In Japan the story of the archer and the ten suns was known through Chinese texts and pictorial art, where it informed depictions of solar catastrophe alongside native Amaterasu lore; Korea received the cycle through the same classical canon, and its own founding archer figure Jumong — whose very name is glossed as 'skilled archer' — shows how deeply the archer-hero type resonated on the peninsula. Vietnamese tradition likewise absorbed the ten-suns narrative through Chinese literature. Within China, Taoist tradition folded Yì into its cosmology of solar regulation and immortality elixirs, while the Queen Mother of the West, his benefactor, rose to become one of the highest deities of the Taoist pantheon. The myth also furnished Buddhist and popular writers with a ready vocabulary for speaking of cosmic excess and karmic reversal, though Yì himself remained a figure of the native classical tradition rather than a Buddhist convert. Scholars have long noted the parallel with other great archers — Apollo's plague-bringing arrows in Greece, Rama's bow in India — but the Chinese version is distinctive: the archer's target is not a rival god but disorder itself.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 后羿, identical in traditional and simplified Chinese (the character 后 'sovereign' must not be confused with 後 'after', which simplifies to 后 — in the archer's name it is the archaic title, 'lord'). Pinyin Hòuyì (both syllables Tone 4) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries. The registrable Unicode restoration uses the tone-marked Pinyin Hòuyì rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original characters in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable; the name carries no apostrophe, so the display form and the domain form differ only in the tone marks. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct the Old Chinese reading of 羿 as *N-ŋ(r)ik-s.

pronunciation.note: Tier 1: the Greek original Χείρων carries both stress (the acute on ει) and long vowels (ει and ω). The restored form Cheírōn preserves both marks — the accent and the macron — that plain ASCII 'Cheiron' erases.

domains.title: The Most Just of Centaurs
domains.subtitle: Wisdom · Teaching · Heroes
domains.lead: Cheírōn is the exception among the wild κένταυροι: the immortal son of Kronos who dwells in a cave on Mount Pelion and turns raw princes into heroes. Where his kin are drunkards and rapine, Homer calls him δικαιότατος Κενταύρων — the most just of centaurs. He is the teacher: medicine for Asklepios, the lyre and the remedies for Achilles, the whole heroic craft for Iason and Herakles.

cards.name: The Tutor's Craft
cards.desc: He reared Achilles, Iásōn, and Asklepios on Mount Pēlion — “the most just of the Centaurs” (Iliad 11.832).

cards.name: The Healing Hand
cards.desc: He taught Asklepios the art of drugs, and was himself struck by Herakles’ hydra-venomed arrow that no healing art could cure.

cards.name: The Hunter's Art
cards.desc: From him the heroes learned the chase itself — tracking, coursing, and spear-work in the mountain wilds.

symbols.name: The Pelian Ash Spear
symbols.meaning: The great spear of ash wood that Cheírōn cut on Pelion's peak and gave to Peleus at his wedding — the same spear Achilles alone could wield (Iliad 16.143–144). The teacher's gift that arms the hero.

symbols.name: The Cave on Mount Pelion
symbols.meaning: His dwelling and school, the legendary academy of heroes where the gods themselves celebrated the wedding of Peleus and Thetis (Pindar, Pythian 9.29–30).

symbols.name: The Lyre
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the education he gave Achilles, who in Iliad 9 (186–189) is found in his hut singing the glories of heroes to the lyre.

symbols.name: Herbs and Remedies (φάρμακα)
symbols.meaning: The healing lore he taught Asklepios and gave to Peleus's line; Achilles treats wounds with remedies 'that Cheiron gave his father' (Iliad 4.219, 11.831–832).

symbols.name: The Hydra-Poisoned Arrow
symbols.meaning: Herakles's stray arrow, dipped in the Lernaean hydra's venom, that struck his knee and gave the immortal an unhealable wound (Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).

symbols.name: The Stars
symbols.meaning: Zeus set him in the sky — remembered as Centaurus or Sagittarius — after he surrendered his immortality and died (Ovid, Fasti 5.379–414; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38).

mythology.lead: Cheírōn stands at the hinge of two orders: Titan-born yet honored by the Olympians, beast-bodied yet the very image of wisdom. His myths are the myths of transmission — what one generation hands to the next.

myths.title: Son of Kronos and Philyra
myths.text: Kronos lay with the Oceanid Philyra in the shape of a horse, and from that union was born a child of double nature — half god, half horse: Apollodorus, Library 1.2.4. Pindar likewise names him the son of Philyra and Kronos, making Cheírōn the half-brother of Zeus (Pythian 4.102–103). Abandoned by his mother, who in shame was changed into a linden tree in later telling, he was reared by Apollo and Artemis, from whom he learned the arts he would pass on. Thus the wisest of teachers begins as the child of deception and rejection.

myths.title: Tutor of the Heroes
myths.text: Pindar gives the roll of his pupils: in his cave Cheírōn reared Iason, gentle-handed Asklepios, whom he taught the craft of remedies, and Achilles, whom he fed on the marrow of lions and wild boars to make him fierce (Nemean 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the bond: Achilles carries remedies 'that Cheiron gave to his father in friendship' (Iliad 4.218–219), and is the man 'whom Cheiron taught, the most just of the centaurs' — δικαιότατος Κενταύρων (Iliad 11.831–832). Actaeon and Herakles also passed through his tutelage. In Pindar's grief for Hieron, the poet wishes Cheírōn still lived in his cave, that another healer might come to Sicily (Pythian 3.1–7).

lore.culturalLegacy: His name lives in the sky: the minor planet 2060 Chiron, discovered in 1977 between Saturn and Uranus, was named for him and gave its class of objects — the centaurs, bodies orbiting among the giant planets — their collective name. Modern astrology adopted him as the emblem of the wounded healer, the one whose incurable hurt becomes the source of healing for others. Ancient herbalists named the plant centaury (κενταύριον, Centaurium) after the centaur's healing lore. And the old association of his name with χείρ, the hand, echoes — though by the word's own root, not by his name — in 'surgery,' from χειρουργία, 'hand-work.'
lore.archaeology: No great temple of Cheírōn is known; he is a daimonic tutor, not an Olympian with a state cult, though a cave above Portaria on Mount Pelion is traditionally identified as the Cheironeion, his school. His real monument is the art: Attic black- and red-figure vases repeatedly show Peleus handing the infant Achilles into the centaur's arms, and Roman sarcophagi of the 'education of Achilles' (2nd–3rd c. CE) show him teaching the lyre. The sculpted centauromachies — the Olympia west pediment and the Parthenon south metopes — preserve the wild centaur type against which his justice was defined.
lore.syncretism: Rome changed Cheírōn least of all the Greek figures: he keeps his name as Chiron in Latin, too singular to be merged with any Italian power. What Rome absorbed was his catasterism — Latin poets and star-cataloguers fixed him in the sky, debating whether the Centaurus or the Sagittarius was his (Ovid, Fasti 5; Hyginus, Astronomica 2.38). In later tradition he remains the named exception among his kind: Dante makes him chief of the centaurs who guard the violent in Inferno 12, still 'Chiron, who nursed Achilles.' The word 'centaur' (κένταυρος) traveled into every European language, but Cheírōn travels as himself.

domains.title: The Vedic Lord of Creatures
domains.lead: Prajāpati is not a god of thunder or war. He is the slow, patient power of generation itself — the one who broods over the waters, performs tapas (ascetic heat), and brings forth creatures by sacrifice. In the Brāhmaṇas he becomes the supreme creator; in the Purāṇas, he passes his crown to Brahmā.

cards.name: Creation by Tapas
cards.desc: He heats himself by ascetic ardor until the cosmos condenses from his sweat and seminal emission.

cards.name: Lord of Sacrifice
cards.desc: The ritual fire altar is his body; every sacrifice reconstructs the world from his dismembered form.

cards.name: Father of the Veda
cards.desc: He produces the triple Veda from himself so that gods and humans may speak the language of order.

cards.name: Cosmic Egg
cards.desc: From the waters an egg develops; its shell becomes earth, its inner fire becomes sun and life.

symbols.name: Fire altar

mythology.lead: Prajāpati's mythology is cosmogonic speculation cast as narrative. He is the One who becomes many, the undifferentiated whole who divides himself so that time, space, and species can exist.

myths.title: From Tapas to Cosmic Egg
myths.text: In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Prajāpati exists first as the nonmanifest unity-totality. Desire (kāma) moves him to reproduce, so he heats himself by ascetic ardor (tapas) until he creates the triple Veda, then the Waters, and finally enters them. An egg develops; from it he is born as the year, the sacrifice, and the ordered cosmos. Exhausted by creation, he must be restored through ritual — which is why every sacrifice is said to be Prajāpati.

myths.title: The Puruṣa Sūkta
myths.text: Ṛgveda 10.90 hymns the Puruṣa, the Cosmic Man whose body is the whole universe. The gods sacrifice him, and from his parts arise the four varṇas, the sun, moon, and earth, and all creatures. In the Brāhmaṇas this Puruṣa is identified with Prajāpati: 'Puruṣa is Prajāpati; Puruṣa is the Year.' Creation is therefore not manufacture but self-sacrifice — the deity giving himself to become the world.

lore.culturalLegacy: Prajāpati never became a popular devotional deity with mass temples, but his influence is foundational. The Puruṣa Sūkta remains one of the most recited hymns in Hindu ritual, used in weddings, housewarmings, and temple consecrations. The varṇa imagery derived from the cosmic body has shaped Indian social theory for millennia — debated, resisted, and reinterpreted, but never ignored. In modern India, 'Prajāpati' is a common surname and a title of honor. The idea that creation is a sacrifice rather than a manufacture continues to inform Hindu ecological and ritual thinking: the world is not raw material but a living body.
lore.archaeology: Prajāpati's archaeology is ritual rather than sculptural. The Agnicayana fire-altar construction, documented by Frits Staal among Kerala Nambudiri Brahmins in 1975, preserves the śrauta technology in which the altar is Prajāpati's body. The Puruṣa iconography appears in Gupta relief, notably at Deogarh's Dashavatara temple (6th century CE). Satavahana, Gupta, and Chola royal consecration inscriptions invoke Prajāpati as the source of kingship and cosmic generation.
lore.syncretism: Prajāpati is the bridge between Vedic impersonality and Purāṇic theism. His identification with Puruṣa links him to cosmic-sacrifice theology; his absorption into Brahmā links him to the later Trimūrti. The Atharvaveda already calls him the first physician, connecting creation with healing. In some strands of Vedānta, Prajāpati becomes a name for the personal god who presides over the lower Brahman, while the higher Brahman remains unnamed. His absence of cultic statues in the Vedic period makes him a pure concept: the generative ground before the gods take shape.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Devanagari form is प्रजापति. IAST marks the long ā in the second syllable. The compound is transparent: prajā ('offspring, creatures') + pati ('lord, master'). In Vedic sandhi the initial pra- often carries a sense of forward motion or emergence.

domains.title: Avenger of Baldr
domains.subtitle: Vengeance, Inevitability, and the Binding of Loki
domains.lead: Váli is the son of Óðinn by the giantess Rindr, born to avenge Baldr's death. He grows to adulthood in a single day, kills the blind Höðr, and survives Ragnarök to inherit the new world. His life is compressed into a single mythic function: the necessary violence that follows an unforgivable killing.

cards.name: One-Day Warrior
cards.desc: Born, armed, and grown to manhood in a single day to fulfil vengeance.

cards.name: Slayer of Höðr
cards.desc: He kills the blind god who, tricked by Loki, shot the mistletoe at Baldr.

cards.name: Namesake in the Binding
cards.desc: Loki's son Váli, not Óðinn's, is turned into a wolf in the binding of Loki; the namesake confusion is as old as the manuscripts.

cards.name: Survivor of Ragnarök
cards.desc: Unlike most gods, Váli lives through the twilight to inhabit the renewed earth.

symbols.name: Bow
symbols.meaning: The weapon with which he avenges Baldr.

symbols.name: Mistletoe
symbols.meaning: The plant that killed Baldr and set Váli's vengeance in motion.

symbols.name: Wolf
symbols.meaning: Loki's son Váli is transformed into a wolf to tear his brother Nari (Narfi) — a namesake of Óðinn's son.

symbols.name: Bonds
symbols.meaning: The fetters made from Narfi's entrails, holding Loki until Ragnarök.

mythology.lead: Váli appears briefly but decisively in the Norse corpus. His myths are episodes in the larger tragedy of Baldr and the doom of the gods.

myths.title: Born for Vengeance
myths.text: After Baldr is slain, the gods cannot simply kill Höðr, for he is one of their own and acted in blindness. Óðinn therefore fathers Váli on Rindr, a reluctant giantess. Váli grows to full strength in a single day, takes up his bow, and slays Höðr in the holy place. The killing is ritually necessary and morally ambiguous: it rights one wrong with another.

myths.title: The Binding of Loki
myths.text: When Loki flees Asgard after engineering Baldr's death, the gods capture him in a riverside house. They seize his sons Váli and Nari (or Narfi): Váli is turned into a wolf and tears his own brother Nari apart, and the Æsir bind Loki with Nari's entrails to three stones beneath the earth (Gylfaginning 50). This wolf-Váli is Loki's son, not Óðinn's; Óðinn's Váli plays no part in the binding. A snake drips venom on Loki's face until Ragnarök, when he will break free and steer the ship of the dead against the gods.

lore.culturalLegacy: Váli remains a minor but haunting figure in modern retellings of Norse myth. He embodies the idea that some violence is inescapable, that vengeance can be both righteous and tragic. His one-day childhood has made him a symbol of compressed destiny, and his namesake's part in binding Loki keeps the name alive whenever the cycle of revenge is told.
lore.syncretism: Váli has no clear non-Germanic counterpart, but his function resembles the Indo-European avenger figure: a youthful warrior born to settle a blood-debt. He is sometimes confused with Váli, the son of Loki and Sigyn, a much less prominent figure. Romantic-era scholars and Wagnerian opera tended to ignore him, preferring the more dramatic figures of Baldr, Loki, and Sigyn.
lore.originalScriptNote: Old Norse was written in runes (Younger Futhark) centuries before the Latin alphabet was adopted in the medieval period. Váli is written in the runic alphabet (Younger Futhark) as ᚢᛅᛚᛁ (u-a-l-i). The acute accent on á in modern editions marks a long vowel; in manuscripts the distinction between long and short vowels was not consistently written. PUNICODEX uses the accented Latin form Váli as the registrable scholarly restoration.

pronunciation.note: Old Norse Hermóðr is a transparent compound: herr ("host, army") + móðr ("spirit, mood, courage" — the same word as English "mood" and German "Mut"), whence the standard rendering "war-spirit." The restoration Hermóðr keeps the two things the ASCII form "Hermod" erases: the long ó and the letter ð (eth), the voiced dental fricative Old Norse wrote with its own character. Tier-1 by rule: two distinctive features preserved.

domains.title: The Rider of the Nine Nights
domains.subtitle: The Errand, the Bridge of Gold, and the Ransom of Baldr
domains.lead: Hermóðr is Óðinn's son and the boldest rider of the Æsir: the god who volunteered, when Baldr lay dead, to mount Sleipnir and ride nine nights through darkness to the halls of Hel, to ransom the light of the world back from the land of the dead.

symbols.name: The ring Draupnir

mythology.lead: Hermóðr has essentially one story, and it is the noblest errand in the Edda: the ride to ransom Baldr, told in Gylfaginning with the plainness of a chronicle and the weight of a funeral.

myths.title: The Errand of the Nine Nights
myths.text: When Baldr fell to the mistletoe dart and the gods' grief had spent itself, Frigg asked who among the Æsir would ride the road to Hel and offer a ransom. Hermóðr the Bold, called Óðinn's sveinn — his lad, his attendant — stood up. They brought him Sleipnir, and he rode nine nights through valleys so dark and deep that he saw nothing until he reached the river Gjöll and the Gjallarbrú, the bridge roofed with glowing gold. There the maiden Móðguðr asked his name and lineage, and told him the bridge had thundered less under five companies of the dead the day before than under him alone.

myths.title: The Gate and the Hall
myths.text: He rode on to Helgrindr, the barred gate of the dead, tightened the stirrups, and spurred Sleipnir — and the horse leapt the gate with room to spare. In the hall he found his brother Baldr seated in the high seat, and he stayed the night. In the morning he begged Hel to let Baldr ride home with him, telling how great the weeping was among the Æsir. Hel's answer became the condition on which the whole ending turns: if all things in the world, living and dead, weep for Baldr, he may return; if anything refuses, Hel keeps him.

lore.culturalLegacy: Hermóðr left few traces outside the texts — no cult, no toponyms securely his — but the ride itself became one of the defining images of Norse myth: the nine nights, the golden bridge, the gate leapt in the dark. Modern retellings from Victorian mythographies to present-day novels and games cast him as the North's answer to Orpheus, the one who goes down to bargain with death and nearly wins. His name survives in the Icelandic given name Hermóður, and in scholarship as the standing example of the Edda's gift for making a minor god carry the grief of the whole world.
lore.archaeology: Hermóðr is a textual figure: his attestations are the Codex Regius and its sister manuscripts of the Prose Edda (13th-14th c.) and the Hyndluljóðr preserved in the Flateyjarbók. No cult sites, toponyms, or inscriptions name him securely. The Gotland picture stones are his nearest material kin: the rider on the eight-legged horse on stones such as Ardre VIII is conventionally read as Óðinn or a hero on Sleipnir, and scholars have long wondered whether the image tradition knew the descent-ride that Gylfaginning tells.
lore.syncretism: The temptation to compare Hermóðr with Hermēs is as old as philology itself — the divine messenger riding between worlds looks like the Greek god's portrait. The comparison has been argued and abandoned for a century: the name is transparently Germanic (herr + móðr), not a borrowing, and the errand-rider is a role the North could grow on its own. What the comparison gets right is the shape of the job: where Hermēs is a psychopomp by office, Hermóðr becomes one for a single night, by courage. His cognate in the heroic record is Beowulf's Heremōd, and his kin in the pantheon are the other sons Óðinn spends on impossible errands — none of whom rode farther.
