pronunciation.approximation: 'man-ah-WIH-dan' — stress the third syllable (the Welsh penult); the w is a quick glide and the y is the Welsh central vowel [ɨ], a sound with no English equivalent, closest to a tight, short 'ih'.
pronunciation.note: Manawydan is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, and only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input. The lexicon's gloss is 'Manannán (Welsh form)', and that is the defensible line: Ifor Williams derived the name from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, and the Old Irish Manannán is its cognate. The brief that sometimes floats around — *man-, 'mind' — is not the derivation the handbooks print, and this temple does not use it.

domains.title: The Wise Survivor of Dyfed
domains.subtitle: Sea, Craftsmanship — the Son of Llŷr who outwitted an enchantment
domains.lead: Manawydan fab Llŷr is the Mabinogi's counselor and craftsman: a son of the sea-named Llŷr and brother of Brân the Blessed, one of the seven who came home from Ireland with the wondrous head — and the man who, when Dyfed was stripped bare by enchantment, kept his patience, took up the saddler's, the shield-maker's, and the shoemaker's trades, and unmade the spell without a sword-stroke, by hanging a mouse and refusing three ransoms.

cards.name: Son of Llŷr
cards.desc: Brother of Brân and Branwen, of the house whose very name is the sea — the Welsh face of the figure Ireland calls Manannán mac Lir.

cards.name: The Golden Shoemaker
cards.desc: In exile at Hereford he made shoes so fine the triads remember him among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain.

cards.name: Gorsedd Arberth
cards.desc: The mound above Arberth where the thunder came and the mist fell — and where Manawydan later built a gallows for a mouse.

cards.name: The Tried Mouse
cards.desc: The fattest of the wheat-thieves, caught and judged as a felon — the lever that finally pried the whole enchantment open.

symbols.name: The golden bowl
symbols.meaning: The enchanted vessel on the marble slab — the snare that took Pryderi and Rhiannon by their own reaching

symbols.name: The white boar
symbols.meaning: The Otherworld lure that leads men out of the world they know, shining and wrong

symbols.name: The mouse on the gallows
symbols.meaning: Patience armed with procedure — the smallest catch that bought back a kingdom

symbols.name: The shoemaker's last
symbols.meaning: Craft as survival: the trades a dispossessed prince practiced better than the guildsmen

symbols.name: Gorsedd Arberth
symbols.meaning: The mound of wonders, where sitting is never safe and where the case was finally tried

mythology.lead: Manawydan's dossier is the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi: Branwen ferch Llŷr, where he is one of the seven who bring the head home, and Manawydan fab Llŷr, the branch that bears his name — the quietest and most perfectly built of the Four, a tale in which an entire kingdom is stolen by silence and won back by patience.

myths.title: The Seven Who Brought the Head Home
myths.text:
Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the whole catastrophe. When the insult of the mutilated horses has festered into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host that crosses with him comes home as seven men: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life.

At Harlech they feast seven years with the head, the three songs of the birds of Rhiannon singing to them, and time does not move. At Gwales in Penfro they find a royal hall with two doors open and one shut — toward Cornwall — and there they pass eighty years in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head, forgetting every sorrow, until Heilyn fab Gwyn says 'shame on my beard if I do not open the door' — and opens it, and all their losses come back at once like a tide. Then they do as the head had commanded: they carry it to London and bury it in the White Mount, facing France, and the triads count that burial among the Three Fortunate Concealments of the Island of Britain. Manawydan, who had counseled the wedding, survives its end — the pattern of his whole life in one branch.

myths.title: The Counsel and the Marriage
myths.text: While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London. Pryderi, lord of Dyfed and son of Pwyll and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], would have fought him; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war. It is the most characteristic speech in the whole Mabinogi — a man with the best claim to vengeance declining it out of arithmetic and mercy. Pryderi yields, and gives Manawydan the fairest compensation the tale can imagine: his mother's hand and the seven cantrefs of Dyfed. Manawydan and Rhiannon wed, and the four — Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi, and Pryderi's wife Cigfa — live at Arberth in unbroken fellowship.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried Manawydan into English, and the Third Branch has held a special place ever since: critics from Ifor Williams onward have called it the most perfectly constructed of the Four Branches, and the trial of the mouse — the courtly ransomers, the miniature gallows, the terms exacted one by one — is the anthology piece of Welsh prose comedy and wisdom in one. Scholarship gave the name its modern standing: Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text and the Manaw etymology, and Mac Cana's The Mabinogi made the branch's architecture a set text of Celtic studies. Modern Druid and pagan practice honors Manawydan as a patron of craft, patience, and the sea-kinship; in Wales the name survives as a rare literary given name, carried less by folk memory than by the sheer durability of the Third Branch, which has never gone out of print since Guest.
lore.archaeology: Manawydan is a textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the epigraphic record of pre-Christian Wales — Latin and ogham memorial stones of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — records personal names, not theonyms. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented — Ifor Williams placed them in the later eleventh century, and current scholarship generally holds a range around 1060–1120. The geography of the Third Branch is real and visitable: Dyfed is the historic kingdom of southwest Wales; Arberth is Narberth in Pembrokeshire, and the gorsedd is traditionally located on the hill above it; the seven cantrefs of Dyfed were still an administrative reality when the tales were written. The nearest linguistic trace of the sea-kinship is onomastic rather than archaeological: Manaw survives in the Welsh name of the Isle of Man and in Manaw Gododdin, the district of the old North remembered in place-names such as Clackmannan and Slamannan.
lore.syncretism: Manawydan's one great comparison is also the deepest fact about him: he is the Welsh form of the figure Ireland knows as [[manannan|Manannán mac Lir]], the sea god and guardian of the Otherworld. The names are cognates — Ifor Williams derived both from Manaw, the Welsh name of the Isle of Man, so that 'Manawydan' and 'Manannán' each mean, in effect, the Manxman — and the fathers match exactly, Welsh Llŷr against Irish Lir, each a personification of the sea. What the Welsh tradition did with the inheritance is the interesting part: where Manannán strides through Irish myth as a god of mist, ships, and wonder-working treasure, the Mabinogi keeps only the sea-kinship and the uncanny craft, and makes its Manawydan mortal, patient, and wise — a euhemerized sea god filed down to a counselor. Whether the Welsh figure is descended from the Irish, or both from a lost common sea god, is debated (Mac Cana; Koch); the handbooks register the kinship and leave the direction open. In Manx folklore the same figure survived as Mannan beg mac y Leir, first man of the island, and gave the Isle of Man its name. No Gaulish counterpart has ever been convincingly proposed; the comparison is an insular affair, Irish Sea water on both sides of it.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Manawydan — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi, with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover, which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: manawydan.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/manawydan/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: ma-THOL-ukh — stress the middle syllable; 'th' as in 'thin'; the w is a short 'oo'-like vowel; the final ch is the rough, breathy ch of Scottish 'loch', as in modern Welsh.
pronunciation.note: Matholwch is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — Welsh writes its distinctive sounds with Latin digraphs (th, ch) and the vowel-letter w, none of which carries a diacritic or a letter the ASCII alphabet lacks. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the king's standing in the tale is beside the point.

domains.title: The King Across the Sea
domains.subtitle: The Thirteen Ships, the Maimed Horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth
domains.lead: Matholwch is the king of Ireland in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr: the bridegroom who came with thirteen ships to Harlech to ask for Branwen's hand, the wronged man appeased with gold and a cauldron that raises the dead, and the husband who could not shield his queen when the insult of the maimed horses came home to his court — the man whose marriage laid two islands waste.

cards.name: The Thirteen Ships
cards.desc: The fleet that brought him to Harlech to ask for Branwen — Ireland arriving as a suitor, and sailing home as a husband.

cards.name: The Maimed Horses
cards.desc: Efnisien's insult — lips, ears, tails, and eyelids cut to the bone — the wound no compensation could make Ireland forget.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
cards.desc: Given to Matholwch in recompense: the slain cast in at evening rise fighting-fit by morning — all but their speech.

cards.name: The Starling
cards.desc: Branwen's tamed messenger, taught to speak, carrying her letter across the sea to Brân when no ship could sail.

symbols.name: The thirteen ships
symbols.meaning: Sea-borne kingship — the power that comes across the water to ask, and can always sail away

symbols.name: The maimed horses
symbols.meaning: An insult done to property but felt in honor — the wound that recompense could not close

symbols.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
symbols.meaning: Resurrection without speech: the body restored, the voice withheld

symbols.name: The starling
symbols.meaning: The smallest thing in the tale that crosses the sea — a tamed bird against a kingdom's embargo

symbols.name: The house of a hundred pillars
symbols.meaning: Peace built as a trap: a pillar for every beam, a bag on every pillar, an armed man in every bag

mythology.lead: Matholwch has essentially one story — but it is the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, the tale medieval Welsh literature remembers as its national tragedy: a marriage between the two islands that ends with the hosts of both destroyed.

myths.title: The Thirteen Ships at Harlech
myths.text: Bendigeidfran — Brân the Blessed, crowned king of Britain — was seated on the rock of Harlech above the sea, with his brother Manawydan and his half-brothers Nisien and Efnisien, when they saw thirteen ships coming from the south of Ireland, fair and swift, their shields above their gunwales. It was Matholwch, king of Ireland, come to ask for Branwen, Brân's sister, fairest maiden in the world, so that Ireland and the Island of the Mighty might be joined by marriage and grow stronger together. Brân consented, and the wedding was held at Aberffraw — and because no house had ever been built that could contain Brân, they slept in tents.

myths.title: The Maiming of the Horses
myths.text:
Efnisien, the half-brother whose gift was quarreling, had not been consulted, and he took the omission as an insult to his honor. Coming on Matholwch's horses stabled apart, he asked whose they were, and hearing, he fell on them in a rage: he cut their lips back to the teeth, their ears back to their heads, their tails to the skin, and their eyelids back to the bone. Matholwch's men could make no sense of it — a king given a bride and mutilated horses in the same week. They armed for home in silence, which Brân read rightly as the beginning of a war.

Brân sent an embassy led by Manawydan to ask what recompense would content him. Matholwch was offered the full replacement of the horses, a silver staff as tall as himself, a golden platter as broad as his face — and, beyond all price, the Cauldron of Rebirth. The tale is exact about the transaction: the honor-price was paid, the peace was sworn, and neither was ever real again.

lore.culturalLegacy: Matholwch entered the world's reading with Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49), which carried the Second Branch into English and made the maimed horses and the Cauldron of Rebirth part of the general inheritance of fantasy literature. Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) fixed the text for scholarship, and Sioned Davies's translation (2007) is the modern English standard. The branch's sentences have never left Welsh letters — 'a fo ben, bid bont' is quoted wherever leadership is discussed — and Evangeline Walton's The Children of Llyr (1971) retells the whole catastrophe as a novel. The cauldron motif, transmitting through the Welsh tradition, stands behind every modern cauldron that raises armies of the dead; Lloyd Alexander's Prydain chronicles drew freely on the Mabinogion's world. On Anglesey, the Bronze Age cairn beside the river Alaw still answers to the name Bedd Branwen, Branwen's grave — the tale's one fixed point in the landscape of two islands.
lore.archaeology: Matholwch is a textual figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or place-name in Ireland names him, and his kingship exists entirely within the Welsh tale. His manuscript witnesses are exact — the Second Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 4, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425), the two great codices on which Williams's edition rests. The tale's one fixed point in the landscape is Welsh: Bedd Branwen, the cairn beside the river Alaw on Anglesey where the branch says Branwen was buried, is a genuine Bronze Age burial monument — cremation urns were recovered when the cairn was opened in the early nineteenth century, and later excavations confirmed its prehistoric date. The name attached to it is medieval folklore, not prehistory — but it proves the story was already rooted in Welsh ground centuries ago. The nearest epigraphic kin of his name-element are the Gaulish personal names in Matu- (Matugenos and kin): comparative evidence only, never identification.
lore.syncretism: Matholwch is a Welsh invention wearing an Irish crown, and the tradition knows it: no Irish-language tale names him, and his kingship of Ireland exists only inside Branwen ferch Llŷr. The honest comparisons are structural, and Proinsias Mac Cana's monograph Branwen Daughter of Llŷr mapped them: Brân's sea-crossing against the Voyage of Bran mac Febail (Immram Brain), the children of Llŷr against the Irish family of Lir, and above all the Cauldron of Rebirth against the cauldron-lore of Ireland — the Dagda's cauldron from Murias, from which no company went away unsatisfied, is the standard parallel for the Celtic vessel of inexhaustible power. The Welsh and Irish cauldrons divide the two ends of the motif between them: Ireland's feeds the living, Wales's revives the dead — and takes their speech as payment. Arthurian scholarship, from Loomis onward, has long set the cauldron and the carried head beside the Grail procession of Peredur; the comparison is illuminating and unprovable, and this temple registers it as such.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Middle Welsh form is Matholwch — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet, and its distinctive sounds are carried by digraphs (th, ch, ll) and the vowel-letter w, none of which the ASCII set lacks. The earlier monumental scripts of the two islands — the ogham stones of Ireland and Wales — predate the manuscript tradition, but no attestation of this name has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: matholwch.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ev-NIS-yen' — the f sounds as v, the stress lands on the middle syllable, and the last syllable is a quick, light 'yen'.
pronunciation.note: Efnysien is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the Middle Welsh manuscript form is written in plain Latin letters, and normalized Welsh orthography attaches no diacritic to the name — there is nothing for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the figure's weight in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: Trouble, Mischief
domains.subtitle: The Strife-Maker of the Second Branch, and the Cauldron He Died Breaking
domains.lead: Efnysien is the destroyer of the Mabinogi: the man the Second Branch introduces in a single balanced sentence — his brother Nisien could make peace between two armies at their most embittered; Efnysien could make two brothers quarrel when they loved each other best. One act of his, the maiming of the Irish king's horses, sets two kingdoms on the road to ruin; his last act, the breaking of the Cauldron of Rebirth, costs him his heart and ends the slaughter he began.

cards.name: The Maimed Horses
cards.desc: At the wedding feast of Aberffraw, in a rage that no one had asked his consent, he cuts the lips, ears, tails, and eyelids of Matholwch's horses — the insult that compensation could not bury.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth
cards.desc: Pair Dadeni — the vessel Brân gives in compensation: a slain man thrown in today rises tomorrow a fighting man, but speechless. Efnysien dies stretching it to pieces.

cards.name: The Hundred Bags
cards.desc: In the great house the Irish built for Brân, a hundred armed men hide in flour-bags hung on the pillars. Efnysien walks the row, asks what is in each bag, and crushes a skull through the sacking with his fingers.

cards.name: The Boy in the Fire
cards.desc: At the peace feast his nephew Gwern — Branwen's child, newly made king — goes from lap to lap; at Efnysien's lap he is seized and thrown into the flames. After that there is no peace to be made.

symbols.name: The mutilated horses
symbols.meaning: Pride made visible — an insult so literal that no payment could make the injured king forget it

symbols.name: The Cauldron of Rebirth (Pair Dadeni)
symbols.meaning: War stripped of death's limit — the gift that became a weapon, until the one who broke it broke himself

symbols.name: The flour-bags on the pillars
symbols.meaning: Treachery hidden in hospitality — seen through only by the man whose own mind worked that way

symbols.name: Gwern cast into the flames
symbols.meaning: The murder of the heir at the moment of his investiture — the point past which the tale permits no return

symbols.name: The broken heart
symbols.meaning: His only death-wound: he stretched himself inside the cauldron until it burst into four pieces, and his heart broke with it

mythology.lead: Efnysien belongs to one tale and fills it: the Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr. The branch is the story of a compensation that failed, and Efnysien is the reason — twice over the author of the injury, and at the end the author of the only sacrifice that stopped the ruin.

myths.title: The Two Brothers
myths.text: The tale introduces him by contrast. Penarddun ferch Beli, mother of Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan by Llŷr, bore two sons to Euroswydd: Nisien and Efnysien. Of Nisien the branch says he was a good man and a gentle youth, who could bring peace between two armies at their most embittered; of Efnysien it says he would set two brothers at strife when they loved each other most. The whole Second Branch is the working-out of that one sentence.

myths.title: The Maiming of the Horses
myths.text: When Brân gave his half-sister Branwen to Matholwch, king of Ireland, the wedding feast was held at Aberffraw, and the horses of the Irish king were stabled for the night. Efnysien asked why they were there, and was told they belonged to Matholwch, who had married his sister. 'Is this what they have done with a maiden as fine as her, my own sister — given her away without asking me?' In his rage he went under the horses and cut off their lips to the teeth, their ears to the head, their tails to the rumps, and their eyelids to the bone. Matholwch rose in silence and made for his ships; only Brân's embassy — Manawydan among them — and the offer of honour-price brought him back: a silver staff as tall as himself, a gold plate as broad as his face, fresh horses, and the Cauldron of Rebirth, which Brân had from Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid and Cymidei Cymeinfoll, wanderers who had fled to his court out of Ireland.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the Second Branch into the English-speaking world, and Efnysien's maiming of the horses and death in the cauldron became set-pieces of the Victorian Celtic revival. Evangeline Walton retold the branch at full length in The Children of Llyr (1971), the second volume of her Mabinogion tetralogy, and gave him the modern novel's inside view without softening him. His widest-reaching legacy is the cauldron itself: Lloyd Alexander drew the deathless cauldron-born warriors of his Prydain chronicles — The Black Cauldron (1965), filmed by Disney in 1985 — directly from the Welsh matter, where a cauldron that returns the slain to silent service is broken at terrible cost. In Welsh memory the branch left two landmarks: the proverb 'A fo ben, bid bont' — he who would be a leader, let him be a bridge — and Bedd Branwen, the grave by the Alaw where the tradition buried the sister his acts helped kill.
lore.archaeology: Efnysien is an entirely literary figure: no inscription, cult site, or votive deposit names him, and the Welsh theonymic record of the period survives in literature rather than stone. His evidence is manuscript evidence — the Second Branch complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with the tales' composition argued to the later eleventh or early twelfth century. The geography of his story is real and walkable: Aberffraw, the royal court of Gwynedd where the horses were maimed; Harlech, where Brân's court sat; and the shore of Anglesey where the survivors landed. The tradition's one material anchor is Bedd Branwen, a cairn on the bank of the Afon Alaw in Anglesey identified since the Middle Ages with Branwen's 'four-sided grave' — excavated by Frances Lynch in 1967–68 and found to hold Early Bronze Age cremations, far older than any Mabinogi event: the identification is the folklore, not the archaeology, and it is precisely that honesty the record keeps.
lore.syncretism: The comparison that follows Efnysien everywhere is with [[loki|Loki]]: the malice inside the house, the sworn kin whose mischief costs the gods their peace, the trickster the tale can neither spare nor save. MacKillop and the handbooks register the parallel as typological rather than genealogical — the Mabinogi's strife-maker is a human prince of the Children of Llŷr, not a god, and his story answers to Welsh concerns: the honour-price, the insult remembered, the compensation that fails. The truer Celtic company is the cauldron-complex: the Cauldron of Rebirth belongs to the same deep stock as the Dagda's cauldron from Murias in the Lebor Gabála Érenn, from which no company went away unsatisfied, and the branch itself gives the vessel an Irish provenance through the fugitive Llasar Llaes Gyfnewid. Within the corpus his closest kin are [[nisien|Nisien]], the brother he was written as the opposite of, and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the king his pride destroyed; [[manawydan|Manawydan]] and [[taliesin|Taliesin]] are among the seven who carried Brân's head home.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as Efnisien — Middle Welsh (Brythonic Celtic), attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), recording material composed centuries earlier. The normalized form writes plain Latin letters with no diacritic, so the restoration Efnysien differs from the ASCII input only in the capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: efnysien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'NISS-yen' — stress the middle syllable, keep every vowel short, and never let the s soften into a z.
pronunciation.note: Nisien is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The manuscripts write Nissyen; the modern standard writes Nisien; only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The traditional gloss 'peaceful one' suits the character exactly, but the philology behind the name is honestly uncertain, and the handbooks record rather than resolve it.

domains.title: Peace, Brother of Efnysien
domains.subtitle: The Gentle Twin of the Second Branch
domains.lead: Nisien is one half of the strangest doublet in the Mabinogi: twin brothers, sons of Euroswydd, whom the Second Branch introduces with a single matched sentence — Nisien, the good man who would make peace between two armies when they were most furious; Efnysien, who would set two loving brothers fighting to the death. The tale then gives the whole war to the cruel twin and keeps the gentle one as its standing might-have-been: peace personified, present at the court that marches to Ireland, and never once allowed to prevail.

cards.name: The Peace Between Hosts
cards.desc: The tale's whole dossier in one clause: he would bring two armies to peace at the very height of their rage.

cards.name: The Twin
cards.desc: Son of Euroswydd and Penarddun, twin of Efnysien — the gentle half of a pair the tradition built as peace and strife in one cradle.

cards.name: Euroswydd's Line
cards.desc: Half-brother to Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan — kin to the children of Llŷr by his mother's side.

cards.name: The Road Not Taken
cards.desc: Wherever the Second Branch's counsel is weighed, Nisien is the standing alternative: the peace that was in the house and was not chosen.

symbols.name: The paired sentence
symbols.meaning: The Second Branch's balanced character note — peace and strife defined as twin brothers, one clause each

symbols.name: The twin's shadow
symbols.meaning: Efnysien's cruelty measured against Nisien's gentleness — each brother the other's definition

symbols.name: The house of Euroswydd
symbols.meaning: The second father-line of Penarddun's children — the gentler inheritance beside the children of Llŷr

symbols.name: The mutilated horses
symbols.meaning: His brother's unprovoked outrage against Matholwch's team — the act of strife that no peace in the tale can undo

symbols.name: The silent presence
symbols.meaning: The peace-maker carried with the host to Ireland and given no scene — the might-have-been that haunts the branch

mythology.lead: Nisien has the smallest dossier in the Mabinogi and the clearest definition: he exists as one half of an antithesis. The Second Branch of the Mabinogi, Branwen ferch Llŷr, names him exactly once as a character and then spends its whole length on the war his brother kindles. What survives of him is a sentence, a lineage, and a presence — and the Welsh tradition built an entire moral pole out of that spareness.

myths.title: The Two Sons of Euroswydd
myths.text:
The Second Branch introduces the twins in a single balanced construction, the most quoted sentence either brother ever gets. Nisien, the tale says, was a good man: he would bring about peace between two armies when they were at the height of their fury. Efnysien would bring about a quarrel between two brothers when they loved each other most. They are twins, sons of Euroswydd by Penarddun — and so half-brothers to Brân the Blessed, Branwen, and Manawydan, Penarddun's children by Llŷr.

The construction is the whole point: Welsh prose has no other pair like it. The tradition does not describe two temperaments; it defines two forces — peace and strife — as brothers born in one hour, and then sets them loose in the same household. Every reader of the branch knows, before the horses are harmed, exactly which twin will act and which will stand by.

myths.title: The Horses at Aberffraw
myths.text:
When Brân consents to give Branwen in marriage to Matholwch, king of Ireland, and the wedding is held at Aberffraw, it is Efnysien — insulted that the match was made without his leave — who takes revenge on the groom's horses: he cuts off their lips to the teeth, their ears to their heads, their tails to their backs, and the eyelids to the bone. The outrage becomes the war's first cause, patched over with reparation and the gift of the Cauldron of Rebirth, and reopened in Ireland when Branwen is made a scullion and struck daily in the kitchen.

Nisien's place in all this is the tale's deliberate emptiness: the peace-maker is there, kin to all parties, gifted by his own description with the one power the crisis needs — and the text never once shows him using it. The mutilation stands unappeased from its author; no embassy of Nisien's is ever recorded. The Second Branch's tragedy is written so that the reader supplies the missing twin.

lore.culturalLegacy: Nisien's afterlife is as quiet as his dossier. Lady Charlotte Guest's translation of the Mabinogion (1838–49) carried the twins into English, and every retelling of Branwen since has kept the paired sentence — it is the one line of the Second Branch that anthologies quote whole. The scholarly tradition made the antithesis canonical: Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi and MacKillop's dictionary fixed the reading of the twins as personified peace and strife, and the pair now serves Celtic studies as the standard example of the Welsh redactor's art of definition-by-contrast. Nisien himself never became a cult figure, a comic-book antihero, or a given name in the way louder Mabinogi figures did — Efnysien, the interesting twin, took all of that. The gentle brother's legacy is the sentence itself: in a tale about a war no one could stop, Welsh literature wrote its peace-maker in one clause and let the silence around him say the rest.
lore.archaeology: Nisien is a purely textual figure: no inscription, votive deposit, or cult site names him, and the early inscribed stones of Wales — the Latin and ogham memorials of roughly the fifth to seventh centuries — record personal names in funerary formulae, not theonyms or tale-figures. His evidence is manuscript evidence. The Four Branches survive complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; the tales' date of composition is argued rather than documented, with current scholarship generally holding a range around 1060–1120. The geography of his branch is real: Aberffraw, where the wedding and the outrage are set, was the historic principal seat of the kings and later princes of Gwynedd on Anglesey, and the Alaw, where Branwen dies of her broken heart, is an Anglesey river. The giant who wades the sea and the cauldron of revival belong to the tale's mythic furniture; the courts and the crossings are drawn from the Welsh world the redactor knew.
lore.syncretism: Nisien has no counterpart anywhere, and the honesty of that fact is part of his record. No Irish figure bears his name or his office: the Irish cycles know war-goddesses and peace-breaking satirists in abundance, but no personified peace-twin, and Sims-Williams's survey of Irish influence on Welsh literature — which finds deep Irish strata in the Second Branch itself, from the giant king who wades the sea to the cauldron of revival — supplies no Irish original for the sons of Euroswydd. The twins look like the Welsh redactor's own construction. The nearest comparisons are structural, drawn from inside the lexicon: his brother [[efnysien|Efnysien]], the necessary other half of the antithesis; [[manawydan|Manawydan]], his half-brother, whose own branch turns on patience and forbearance rather than force; and [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the wronged king whose horses his brother maimed. Beyond the Mabinogi the antithesis device has famous analogues — the paired forces of other traditions — but the Welsh pair needs no borrowing to explain: peace and strife as twin brothers is the sort of idea a mature prose tradition can invent in a single sentence, and the Second Branch is exactly that tradition.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Middle Welsh form is Nisien (manuscript Nissyen) — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Middle Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet in the medieval Welsh bookhand; the earlier epigraphic scripts of Britain, the Latin and ogham memorial stones, name no figure of the Mabinogi. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way long ago: nisien.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'blo-DEH-weth' — three syllables with the weight on the middle one; the final dd is the soft th of 'this', and the eu slides like the vowel of 'say' pulled toward a rounded close.
pronunciation.note: Blodeuwedd is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: Middle Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet and the manuscript spelling carries no diacritic or distinctive letter for ASCII to lose, so the restored form differs from the input only by the capital. The name is a transparent Welsh compound — blodau 'flowers' + gwedd 'face' — and its history runs in a circle: coined in the tale for a woman made of blossoms, it survives in modern Welsh as the everyday word for the owl she became.

domains.title: Flower Bride, Betrayal
domains.subtitle: The domain of Blodeuwedd
domains.lead: In the celtic tradition, Blodeuwedd is the flower-bride of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi: the fairest woman ever seen, made by [[gwydion|Gwydion]] and [[math|Math]] from the blossoms of oak, broom, and meadowsweet to defeat the destiny that barred Lleu Llaw Gyffes from every wife on earth — and the bride who loved Gronw Pebr of Penllyn, drew her husband's death-secret out of him, and was judged into the shape of the owl.

cards.name: Oak, Broom, and Meadowsweet
cards.desc: The three blossoms Math and Gwydion took up with their wands and fashioned into the fairest woman anyone had seen — a wife made by craft for the man no earthly wife was allowed.

cards.name: The Impossible Conditions
cards.desc: Neither in a house nor out of one, neither on horseback nor on foot — the death-terms Blodeuwedd drew from Lleu for Gronw: one foot on a cauldron's rim, one on a goat, a spear a year in the forging.

cards.name: The Owl
cards.desc: Gwydion's sentence — 'I will not kill you': the bird-shape hated by all birds, never to show its face by day, and the name Blodeuwedd kept as the mark of shame.

cards.name: Llyn y Morwynion
cards.desc: The Lake of the Maidens, where Blodeuwedd's attendants, looking backward as they fled through the mountains by night, walked into the water and drowned.

symbols.name: Oak, broom, and meadowsweet
symbols.meaning: The three flowers of her making — beauty assembled by enchantment, with no childhood and no kin

symbols.name: The spear a year in the forging
symbols.meaning: Worked only during Mass on Sundays — the weapon shaped by the stolen secret of an impossible death

symbols.name: The cauldron and the billy-goat
symbols.meaning: The two footings of the fatal stance: one foot on the rim, one on the beast — neither indoors nor out, neither mounted nor afoot

symbols.name: The owl
symbols.meaning: The shape of the sentence: the face that must not be shown by day, mobbed by every other bird

symbols.name: Llyn y Morwynion
symbols.meaning: The Lake of the Maidens — the backward glance in the dark that drowned her whole retinue

symbols.name: Mur Castell
symbols.meaning: Her court in Ardudwy, the bridal seat from which the hunter of Penllyn was welcomed in

mythology.lead: Blodeuwedd exists in exactly one witness, and it is enough: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi, 'Math uab Mathonwy', the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose. She enters the tale as its most beautiful artefact and leaves it as its most haunting sentence — a woman made from flowers, a bride who chose her own lover, and an owl that still bears her name in modern Welsh.

myths.title: Made of Flowers
myths.text:
When Arianrhod, shamed by the birth the wand had forced from her, laid her third destiny on her son — that he should never have a wife of any race then on earth — Math the king took counsel with [[gwydion|Gwydion]]: 'Let us try, by charms and enchantment, to conjure a wife for him out of flowers.' They took the flowers of the oak, the flowers of the broom, and the flowers of the meadowsweet, and from them made the fairest and most beautiful woman anyone had ever seen; they baptized her in the manner of the time, and named her Blodeuwedd, Flower-face.

The wedding sealed the counter-spell: Lleu was given the cantref of Dinoding to rule, and the pair settled at his court in Ardudwy, at the place called Mur Castell. The Fourth Branch gives the marriage one sentence of happiness — everyone was content — before it sets the trap the whole tale has been building toward: a king's nephew with a destiny, and a wife who was never born of woman at all.

myths.title: Gronw of Penllyn
myths.text:
Lleu went to Caer Dathyl to visit Math, and while he was away Gronw Pebr, the lord of Penllyn, came hunting into the country. At nightfall Blodeuwedd welcomed the hunter into the court — the hospitality owed to a guest — and the tale says simply that that night they talked, and she conceived a love for him, and he for her. Three nights they lay together while her husband sat at his uncle's court.

The Fourth Branch wastes no breath condemning them; it reports desire with the same flat care it gives to flower-making. But the lovers' question is the tale's hinge: how can they be together for good? Blodeuwedd's answer is to learn what only a wife can learn — the manner of her husband's death — and the text lets her do it in his own trust, 'in the guise of concern', asking how a man so strangely fated could ever be killed.

lore.culturalLegacy: Blodeuwedd's afterlife is carried in two forms: a word and a novel. The word is blodeuwedd itself — in modern Welsh simply 'owl', so that every Welsh speaker who names the bird repeats her sentence, a folk-etymology the Fourth Branch deliberately installed. The novel is Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967), winner of the Carnegie Medal, which takes the Fourth Branch's triangle as a pattern that replays down the generations of a Welsh valley: a dinner service whose painted flowers resolve into owls, and three young people cast again as the flower-bride, the lord, and the hunter. The tale has become a set text of Welsh education and a touchstone of Welsh-language letters — retold for children, staged, and argued over by critics who read her as traitor, as sovereignty figure, or as the literature's first portrait of a made thing demanding a will of its own. In scholarship she holds a fixed place: Ifor Williams's edition, Mac Cana's study of the Mabinogi, and Koch's encyclopedia all treat her episode as the Fourth Branch's tragic heart.
lore.archaeology: Blodeuwedd is a literary figure with no material cult record: no inscription, image, or votive object names her, and her witnesses are the two Mabinogion codices — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400). What she has instead of temples is topography, and the Fourth Branch's map is still walkable. Mur Castell, her bridal court, is traditionally placed at Tomen y Mur in Ardudwy, beside the Roman fort; Llyn y Morwynion, the Lake of the Maidens where her retinue drowned, is pointed out above Ffestiniog; and on the bank of the river Cynfael stands a holed stone locally called Llech Ronw, 'Gronw's stone', the slab Lleu's spear pierced. These are local identifications rather than proof, but they show how early and how firmly the tale was staked into the landscape of Gwynedd — medieval hearers, like modern walkers, could be taken to the places where it happens.
lore.syncretism: Blodeuwedd's closest comparative kin is the made bride. Greek tradition offers [[pandora|Pandora]], the woman the gods fashion as a gift that is also a trap — beauty assembled by divine craft and given to a man, with ruin in the giving. The parallel holds at the level of motif, not borrowing: both figures are manufactured women whose makers intend one destiny and whose own desires rewrite it, though Pandora's makers send her as the trap while Blodeuwedd's makers are her undoing's victims. Within Celtic scholarship she has been read in the sovereignty frame — Mac Cana and others note the pattern by which the woman's favour carries the land, since Gronw takes Lleu's rule with his wife — and her triple flowers have drawn the attention of the tree-calendar speculation around Robert Graves, which the handbooks do not accept. The honest verdict is that she belongs to the international faithless-bride and made-woman complexes, with a sentence that is the Mabinogi's own: no other tradition punishes a woman by letting her keep her name forever.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Blodeuwedd (also written Blodeuedd), in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1400), the two codices of the Mabinogion. The normalized spelling is plain ASCII, so the restoration recovers no diacritic or distinctive letter — hence Tier 2, and the capital alone marks the temple form. The plain-ASCII domain blodeuwedd.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release; no form of the name is owned, and this temple claims none, standing at its canonical lexicon address in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tal-YES-in' — three syllables, the weight squarely on the middle one, the first a soft tap; exactly the living Welsh name.
pronunciation.note: Taliesin is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: medieval Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name's fame vastly outruns its orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Poet, Shapeshifter
domains.subtitle: The Radiant Brow, Chief of Bards
domains.lead: Taliesin is the supreme bard of Welsh tradition — twice-born master of the awen, the flowing spirit of poetic inspiration. As Gwion Bach he stirred Ceridwen's cauldron and caught the three drops meant for her son; as the grain the black hen swallowed he was reborn from the water with a brow so radiant that Elffin ap Gwyddno named him for it. Before Maelgwn Gwynedd's court he silenced the assembled bards with a puff of breath and freed his foster-father from thirteen locks; and behind the legend stands a historical poet of sixth-century Rheged, whose praise-songs to Urien the Historia Brittonum already knew. Poet and shapeshifter, child of the cauldron and voice of all he has ever been, Taliesin is the Welsh tradition's own answer to what a name is: a brow made radiant by what has passed through it.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Awen
cards.desc: Ceridwen's cauldron, boiled a year and a day for her son Afagddu, from which the whole science of poetry was to distill — the vessel of inspiration at the root of the legend.

cards.name: The Three Drops
cards.desc: The three drops of the cauldron's liquor that flew onto Gwion Bach's thumb as he stirred: all the awen there was, spent at once, and the reason everything after belongs to him.

cards.name: The Grain and the Hen
cards.desc: The last shape of the pursuit: Gwion as a single grain on the winnowing floor, Ceridwen as a black hen who swallowed him — the meal that became a womb.

cards.name: The Weir of Gwyddno
cards.desc: Elffin's salmon weir where the coracle came to rest: the luckless boy lifting from the water a child with a radiant brow, and giving Welsh poetry its name.

symbols.name: The cauldron of inspiration
symbols.meaning: The vessel Ceridwen set to boil for a year and a day — the awen made material, the source from which all poetry in the legend flows

symbols.name: The three drops
symbols.meaning: The sum of the cauldron's virtue, caught on a boy's thumb — inspiration as a finite, transferable grace

symbols.name: The black hen
symbols.meaning: Ceridwen's final shape in the chase — the goddess as the mother who must swallow to give birth

symbols.name: The coracle in the weir
symbols.meaning: The skin boat Elffin found among the salmon — the poet's second arrival, from the water like every gift of Annwn

symbols.name: The silenced bards
symbols.meaning: Maelgwn's court poets reduced to droning 'blerwm blerwm' by a child's breath — the power of true song over mere office

mythology.lead: Taliesin's dossier divides into two figures the Welsh tradition never quite separated: the historical poet of sixth-century Rheged, and the wonder-child of the cauldron whose story is medieval but survives whole only in sixteenth-century manuscripts. The first is attested within three centuries of his life; the second is the fullest legendary biography any Celtic poet ever received. Between them the name becomes a theory of poetry itself.

myths.title: The Poet of Urien
myths.text:
The Historia Brittonum (c. 829) names five poets famed in the days of Ida of Bernicia, in the mid-sixth century: Talhaearn Tad Awen, Aneirin, Cian, Blwchfardd — 'and Taliesin, who is renowned in British poetry'. The Book of Taliesin preserves the substance behind the notice: a core of praise-poems to Urien of Rheged and his son Owain, court verse of the Old North, singing the wars of Rheged against the Bernician Angles. Ifor Williams's scholarship established the canon: a dozen poems of the Book stand as plausibly the work of a real Taliesin, court bard of Urien in the generation before Rheged fell.

This is the oldest Taliesin the record offers — not a wonder-child but a professional of the northern courts, remembered three centuries later as the very type of the famed poet. The legend did not invent him; it annexed him, and gave the court bard of Rheged a second birth out of a goddess's cauldron.

myths.title: The Cauldron and the Chase
myths.text:
Ceridwen, dwelling by Lake Tegid in the land of Gwynedd, had two children: Creirwy the fairest of maidens and Afagddu, called Morfran, the most ill-favored of men. To compensate her dark son she set a cauldron of inspiration and science to boil for a year and a day, put blind Morda to tend the fire, and set the boy Gwion Bach to stir. On the last day three drops of the charmed liquor flew from the cauldron onto Gwion's thumb; scalded, he put it in his mouth — and at once knew all things past and to come. The cauldron split, and all its virtue was spent on the wrong child.

What follows is the great transformation chase of Celtic literature. Gwion fled as a hare; Ceridwen pursued as a greyhound. He became a fish in the river; she came after as an otter. He rose as a bird; she stooped as a hawk. At last he dropped as a single grain onto a winnowing floor, and she came as a black hen and swallowed him. Nine months she bore him, and could not kill so fair a child when he was born; she sewed him in a skin coracle and cast him into the sea on the eve of May Day.

lore.culturalLegacy: Taliesin entered the modern world with Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion (1838–49), which first printed the Hanes Taliesin from Elis Gruffydd's sixteenth-century chronicle and made the cauldron story a classic far beyond Wales. Twentieth-century scholarship restored the historical poet: Ifor Williams's Canu Taliesin (1960) separated the Urien corpus from the legendary Book and set the standard for all later work. Robert Graves's The White Goddess (1948) built a famous and much-contested mythology on Cad Goddeu — scholars reject his tree-alphabet, but he carried the poem to a vast new readership. Modern Druidry took the awen for its own: the three rays are its emblem and the word its name for inspiration. The name itself passed into architecture — Frank Lloyd Wright named his Wisconsin home and school Taliesin — and in Wales it never needed reviving: Taliesin remains a living given name, and Swansea's arts centre bears it. Few figures in the lexicon bridge a sixth-century court and a modern concert hall so completely.
lore.archaeology: Taliesin is a wholly textual figure: no inscription names him, no ogham stone or cross-slab invokes him, and the Welsh epigraphic record — Romano-British memorial stones and the ogham stones of the Irish settlers in Dyfed — belongs to other names entirely. His witnesses are manuscripts of unusually late but exact pedigree. The Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century) preserves both the sixth-century praise-poems to Urien of Rheged and the legendary cycle in a single hand. The Black Book of Carmarthen (mid-thirteenth century) holds the Ymddiddan Myrddin a Thaliesin. The Historia Brittonum's notice travels in its ninth-century recensions, Harley MS 3859 chief among them. And the full legendary biography, the Hanes Taliesin, survives entire only in the sixteenth-century chronicle of Elis Gruffydd — a late witness to a story whose own materials (the Triads, the Book's persona-poems) prove medieval. Between Peniarth and Gruffydd stands the whole transmission: a poet who is historical, legendary, and manuscript all at once.
lore.syncretism: Taliesin's closest kin is Irish. The Song of Amairgen — 'I am the wind on the sea, I am the wave of the sea, I am the stag of seven tines' — speaks in the same grammar of self-predication as Cad Goddeu, and Sjoestedt set the two side by side as the Celtic poet's native form: the boast that is a cosmology, the claim that the inspired singer has been all things and so may speak of all. The awen itself has its Irish counterpart in imbas, the 'great knowledge' of the filid, and the transformation chase of the Hanes belongs to the international tale-type of the flight in shifting shapes. Within Wales, Taliesin was paired from early on with Myrddin: the Black Book of Carmarthen's Ymddiddan Myrddin a Thaliesin stages the two prophets in dialogue over the battle of Arfderydd — the two great names of Welsh poetry reading each other's grief. The Christian scribes needed no euhemerism for him: a poet, however marvelous, was safe to keep, and they kept him whole.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in medieval Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet — the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2) for the poems, and the sixteenth-century chronicle of Elis Gruffydd for the full legend — and the spelling Taliesin is already plain ASCII: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, so the restoration is a matter of canonical reference rather than rescued orthography. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: taliesin.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MUR-thin' — stress the first syllable (the Welsh penult); the dd is the soft 'th' of 'this', and the whole name takes two short beats, never 'MER-lin'.
pronunciation.note: Myrddin is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Middle Welsh form is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose, and the digraph dd is an orthographic convention, not a lost character. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the prophet's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The Wild Prophet of the Forest
domains.subtitle: Seer, Wild Man
domains.lead: Myrddin is the original Welsh form of the name the world knows as Merlin: the prophet who went mad at the battle of Arfderydd in 573, fled into the Caledonian forest, and lived there as a wild man — lamenting his dead lord Gwenddolau, sheltering beneath an apple tree, and uttering the prophecies that made him the canonical voice of Welsh vaticination before Geoffrey of Monmouth made him the wizard of the Arthurian world.

cards.name: The Apple Tree
cards.desc: The sweet apple tree that shelters Myrddin in the Afallennau — his only house in the forest of Celyddon, addressed like a friend.

cards.name: Arfderydd
cards.desc: The northern battle of 573 where his lord Gwenddolau son of Ceidio fell; grief and slaughter drove Myrddin mad, says the Welsh Triad.

cards.name: The Threefold Death
cards.desc: The death Myrddin prophesies in the Vita Merlini — from a rock, in a tree, and in the water — fulfilled to the letter; the wild prophet's own end in the northern tale.

cards.name: The Brud
cards.desc: The prophetic poems gathered under his name — the Black Book's Afallennau and Oianau, and Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini, the most copied political prophecy of the Middle Ages.

symbols.name: The apple tree
symbols.meaning: The wild man's shelter and confidant — prophecy spoken from hiding, sweet and bitter at once

symbols.name: The forest of Celyddon
symbols.meaning: The Caledonian wood — madness, exile, and second sight in one landscape

symbols.name: The stag
symbols.meaning: The wild mount he rides to court in the Vita Merlini, driving the forest's herds before him

symbols.name: Rock, tree, and water
symbols.meaning: The three elements of the foretold death — prophecy that cannot miss, however it is guarded against

symbols.name: Gwenddydd's questions
symbols.meaning: The sister's dialogue — prophecy as the speech left between the mad and those who loved them

mythology.lead: Myrddin's dossier divides in two, and the tradition itself knew it: the northern prophet who went mad at Arfderydd and fled to Coed Celyddon, preserved in the Welsh Triads, the Annales Cambriae, and the Black Book poems; and Geoffrey of Monmouth's Merlinus, who carried the wild man into Latin and grafted him onto the Arthurian world. Gerald of Wales already separated them in the twelfth century: Merlinus Ambrosius, the boy prophet of Vortigern's tower, and Merlinus Celidonius — Sylvester — the wild man of the Caledonian forest.

myths.title: The Battle of Arfderydd
myths.text:
The Annales Cambriae enter under the year 573 the battle of Arfderydd, fought in the north between the sons of Eliffer and Gwenddolau son of Ceidio — a historical-seeming conflict of the British Old North. The Welsh Triads count it among the futile battles of the Island of Britain, brought about, in the triad's famous understatement, for a lark's nest; and the triad records the consequence that matters here: Gwenddolau fell, and Myrddin became mad.

From that seed the whole legend grows. Myrddin son of Morfryn, his lord dead and his side defeated, flees the world of the mead-hall into Coed Celyddon, the Caledonian forest, and becomes Myrddin Wyllt — the Wild — living from the forest's gifts and speaking only in verse and prophecy.

myths.title: The Apple Trees and the Oianau
myths.text:
The earliest Welsh manuscript, the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), preserves the poems that give the wild man his own voice. In Yr Afallennau, 'The Apple Trees', Myrddin addresses the sweet apple tree that shelters him: he laments Gwenddolau, slain in the bloodshed of Arfderydd; he grieves that he endures want while once he rode at the head of warriors; he hides from Rhydderch's men; and the refrain returns to the tree, his one companion and hiding-place.

The companion poem, Yr Oianau, keeps the same voice — the outcast prophet calling his mournful 'oian' through the forest, mourning his dead, marked out by madness as the gods' or fate's chosen sufferer. These are not narrative poems but laments with prophecy threaded through them; together they made Myrddin the patron and mouthpiece of the whole Welsh prophetic genre.

lore.culturalLegacy: No Celtic figure has had a stranger second life. Geoffrey's Prophetiae Merlini — the seventh book of the Historia — circulated separately for centuries and became the most copied political prophecy of the Latin Middle Ages, mined for omens by kings and rebels alike; the romances then turned the prophet into the enchanter, and by the thirteenth-century Vulgate cycle Merlin is Arthur's maker: arranger of Uther's night at Tintagel, keeper of the Round Table's founding, and prisoner of the Lady of the Lake. Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion (1838–49) and the nineteenth-century Arthurian revival carried the Welsh roots back into English view, and modern scholarship — Jarman above all — rebuilt the northern prophet behind the wizard. In Welsh memory the original never disappeared: Caerfyrddin, 'Myrddin's fortress', still bears the folk etymology Geoffrey loved, and the Myrddin of the Black Book remains the patron of Welsh prophecy — the figure every later brud quietly pretended to be. The name now means the wizard worldwide; the temple's task is to hand the name back to the wild man it began with.
lore.archaeology: Myrddin is a textual figure, and his witnesses are among the most precisely identified in Welsh letters. The Afallennau and Oianau stand in the Black Book of Carmarthen (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250), the earliest surviving manuscript in Welsh; the Cyfoesi Myrddin a Gwenddydd stands in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410); Geoffrey's Vita Merlini survives complete in a single manuscript (British Library, Cotton Vespasian E.iv, thirteenth century). The landscape behind the texts is real and partly recoverable: Arfderydd is traditionally identified with Arthuret near Longtown in Cumbria, in the Old North the poems remember; Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen) overlays the Roman fort of Moridunum, 'sea-fort', attested in the Antonine Itinerary and confirmed by excavation — the place-name from which, on the scholarly account, the prophet's name derives; and Dinas Emrys, the hillfort in Gwynedd where Nennius sets the fatherless boy and the dragons, yielded post-Roman occupation material in Savory's excavations of 1954–56. No inscription names Myrddin, and none would be expected: the early stones of Wales record the dead, not prophets.
lore.syncretism: Myrddin's comparisons run north, not east. The twelfth-century Life of St Kentigern by Jocelyn of Furness knows a mad prophet at the court of Rhydderch Hael named Lailoken, who foretold his own threefold death; a fragmentary Latin life of 'Merlin the Wild' preserved in the Cotton collection tells the same penitence, conversion by Kentigern, and triple end — stoned, fallen on a stake, drowned in the Tweed. Nikolai Tolstoy's Quest for Merlin argued that Lailoken and Myrddin Wyllt are two records of one north-British wild-man figure, and the modern handbooks treat the kinship as real, its exact shape unproven. The Irish tradition offers no namesake — the wild men of the Irish tales, Suibhne Geilt above all, share the type rather than the name: the king driven mad by battle who lives in trees, speaks in verse, and is watched by the court he left. Within the Welsh corpus his truest kin is [[taliesin|Taliesin]], the other great prophetic poet, with whom the Vita Merlini pairs him in discourse; and his own tradition split him in two, as Gerald of Wales records — Merlinus Ambrosius of Dinas Emrys and Merlinus Celidonius of the Caledonian forest, the tower-boy and the wild man the romances later fused.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Myrddin — attested in the Black Book of Carmarthen (NLW Peniarth MS 1, c. 1250, the earliest Welsh manuscript) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1382–1410), and in the Welsh Triads. Middle Welsh writes the name in plain ASCII letters: there is no diacritic and no distinctive atomic letter for the restoration to recover — the digraph dd for the soft 'th' is orthography, not a lost character — which is why the name stands in Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: myrddin.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: GWALH-my — the gw of 'Guinevere', the ch of Scottish 'loch', and 'my' like the month of May. The later English form Gawain runs 'guh-WAYN', stress on the second syllable.
pronunciation.note: Gwalchmai is a transparent Welsh compound: gwalch ('hawk') + Mai ('May'), whence the standard scholarly rendering 'hawk of May' (Bromwich, Trioedd Ynys Prydein; Koch); the PuniCodex lexicon keeps the traditional English gloss 'little falcon' for the same root-image. The temple form Gawain is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the English name is already plain ASCII — there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input.

domains.title: The Courteous Knight
domains.subtitle: The Hawk of May, the Quest Completed, and the Girdle of the Green Chapel
domains.lead: Gawain — Welsh Gwalchmai, Arthur's nephew — is the courteous knight of the Welsh and continental cycles: the one who never came home without the quest he went to seek, the measure against whom Chrétien ranks every other knight of the Round Table, and the man the Green Knight chose to test, at the turning of a year, for the one virtue the pentangle guards — truth.

cards.name: The Hawk of May
cards.desc: Gwalch + Mai: the name itself is a raptor and a season — the spring hawk of the Welsh court.

cards.name: The Pentangle
cards.desc: The five-pointed star Solomon set on Gawain's shield in the Green Knight poem — five fives, and truth at the center of them all.

cards.name: The Green Girdle
cards.desc: The lace of silk and gold kept back from the exchange — worn home as the 'token of untruth' the court turned into a badge of honor.

cards.name: Gringolet
cards.desc: Gawain's horse from Chrétien onward — the mount that carries him, in the Green Knight poem, through the winter forest to the Green Chapel.

symbols.name: The hawk
symbols.meaning: The name made image: gwalch, the raptor of the Welsh genealogies — swift sight, swift return

symbols.name: The pentangle
symbols.meaning: The endless knot of five fives: senses, fingers, wounds, joys, and the five knightly virtues bound by truth

symbols.name: The green girdle
symbols.meaning: The kept-back token: one small failure of truth worn openly, until shame becomes the court's badge

symbols.name: The waxing strength
symbols.meaning: The romancers give him a power that rises with the sun to noon and fails after — the trace the scholars read as a faded solar hero

symbols.name: The nick in the neck
symbols.meaning: The single cut of the third stroke: the wound that is also a judgment, and a verdict he refuses to forget

mythology.lead: Gawain's dossier runs from a Welsh triad to a fourteenth-century masterpiece: in every century someone is testing him, and the test is always the same — not whether he can fight, but whether he will keep faith.

myths.title: The Knight Who Finished the Quest
myths.text: The oldest Arthurian tale in Welsh names him in its great muster at Arthur's court: Gwalchmei mab Gwyar — Gwalchmai son of Gwyar — 'because he never returned home without achieving the quest he had gone to seek; he was the best of walkers and the best of riders; he was nephew to Arthur, the son of his sister, and his first cousin.' In a catalogue of hundreds of warriors, giants, and wonders, that is the whole of his entry, and it is the whole of his character: the Welsh tradition remembers him not for a single exploit but for completion itself — the errand that always comes home.

myths.title: One of the Three Well-Endowed Men
myths.text: The Welsh Triads — the medieval memory-system that files the Island of Britain's heroes in threes — name Gwalchmai son of Gwyar among the Three Well-Endowed Men of the Island of Britain, beside Llacheu son of Arthur and Rhiwallawn Broom-Hair (Triad 4). Rachel Bromwich's edition of the Triads is also the standard witness for his name: Gwalchmai, gwalch 'hawk' + Mai 'May', the 'hawk of May' — a name that stands in Welsh before any French romance ever sang of Gauvain.

lore.culturalLegacy: Gawain is the Arthurian figure with the longest continuous critical life. Chrétien made him the definition of cortoisie; the Gawain-poet made him the test-case of truth; Malory made him the tragedy of loyalty. Tennyson split him in two, taking his courtesy for the early idylls and his Orkney darkness for the last; the twentieth century gave him back to the scholars — Weston and Loomis argued his solar and Celtic pedigrees, and the Tolkien–Gordon edition of 1925 made Sir Gawain and the Green Knight a fixed star of the English canon. Harrison Birtwistle's opera Gawain (1991) set the Green Chapel to music, and the twenty-first century has filmed the poem twice. Through it all the Welsh name never went anywhere: Gwalchmai still stands in the Triads, the hawk of May, waiting at Arthur's court for the quest to be finished.
lore.archaeology: Gawain is a textual figure with one famous epigraphic witness. The Modena Archivolt — the carved portal relief of Modena Cathedral, dated c. 1120–1140 — depicts an Arthurian rescue scene with the figures labeled in stone: Artus de Bretania, Che (Cei), and GALVAGIN(VS), Gawain himself — the earliest Arthurian image in medieval art, carved a generation before Geoffrey of Monmouth finished the Historia. William of Malmesbury (c. 1125) adds the tradition's one grave: the tomb of Walwen, he reports, was found in his own time on the seashore at Rhos in Pembrokeshire, fourteen feet long. His manuscript witnesses are exact: Culhwch ac Olwen survives in the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410); Sir Gawain and the Green Knight survives uniquely in British Library MS Cotton Nero A.x (c. 1400), the small quarto it shares with Pearl, Cleanness, and Patience.
lore.syncretism: Gawain's deepest comparative file is Irish. The beheading game itself has its classic Celtic witness in Fled Bricrenn, Bricriu's Feast, where the giant Uath — 'Horror' — offers the Ulster heroes exactly the Green Knight's bargain: strike off my head today, and I strike yours tomorrow. Only Cúchulainn takes the axe twice and kneels for the return stroke; the giant brings the blade down blunt, and the champion's portion is judged his. Kittredge's Study of Gawain and the Green Knight (1916) made the Irish episode the standing source-analogue of the English poem, and the comparison has been refined, never abandoned. The loathly-lady strand of Gawain's story — Dame Ragnelle, whose riddle is answered with sovereignty — has its own Irish kin in the sovereignty-goddess tales, where a hag by a well becomes a queen when a king will kiss her. Within the pantheon his standing kin are [[kai|Cei]] and [[bedwyr|Bedwyr]], the two companions Culhwch pairs beside him, and [[cuchulainn|Cúchulainn]], the only other hero in Celtic story who knelt under the return stroke. The Welsh tradition itself never made him a god; it made him something rarer — the knight every other knight is measured against.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is transmitted in the Latin alphabet throughout: Middle Welsh writes Gwalchmei in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, Geoffrey of Monmouth writes Walganus, and the Cotton Nero manuscript writes Gawayn. The name's single epigraphic witness is the carved label GALVAGIN(VS) on the Modena Archivolt (c. 1120–1140) — the earliest Arthurian image in art. There is no non-Latin original script to restore, and the canonical English form Gawain is plain ASCII: because the name needs no diacritic, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way — gawain.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release. No form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.
