pronunciation.approximation: 'BED-weer' — stress the first syllable; read the w as the vowel 'oo' and the final y as a vowel between 'i' and 'u', with the r lightly rolled.
pronunciation.note: Bedwyr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: medieval Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters — w and y are vowel-letters in Welsh, but ordinary characters of the Latin alphabet, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII form to lose. Only the capital distinguishes the temple form from the input. The name's meaning is recorded as unknown; Koch's derivation from bedw, 'birch trees', is the standard proposal and remains debated.

domains.title: Knight, One-handed
domains.subtitle: The One-Handed Spearman of Arthur's War-Band
domains.lead: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc is the great companion-hero of the oldest Welsh Arthurian tradition: the warrior who never shrank from any enterprise on which [[kai|Cei]] was bound, the one-handed spearman whose single thrust made a wound equal to nine, and the one man the triads crown with a battle-diadem above the three they name. Before French romance gave Arthur his Lancelot, the Welsh tradition gave him Bedwyr.

cards.name: The Lance of Nine Wounds
cards.desc: His one strange property in Culhwch ac Olwen: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances — one arm doing the work of nine.

cards.name: The Battle-Diadem
cards.desc: The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed names Drystan, Hueil, and Cei — then adds that one was battle-diademed above all three: Bedwyr son of Bedrawc.

cards.name: Cavall the Hound
cards.desc: In the hunting of Twrch Trwyth, the greatest boar-hunt in Welsh literature, Bedwyr led Cavall — Arthur's own hound.

cards.name: The Wooden Tweezers
cards.desc: On the summit of Pumlumon he and Cei plucked the beard of Dillus the Bearded alive with wooden tweezers — for dead, the bristles would have been brittle, and no other leash could hold the hound Drudwyn.

symbols.name: The one-handed lance
symbols.meaning: A single arm doing the work of nine — prowess measured by what remains, not what is missing

symbols.name: The battle-diadem
symbols.meaning: The triad's crown above the crowned — the one name set over Drystan, Hueil, and Cei

symbols.name: Cavall, Arthur's hound
symbols.meaning: The king's own dog entrusted to his hand in the Twrch Trwyth hunt — trust made visible

symbols.name: The wooden tweezers
symbols.meaning: The impossible instrument for the impossible task — craft serving the quest on Pumlumon

symbols.name: The sword cast back to the water
symbols.meaning: In the later Malorian tradition, Bedivere is the last knight, who returns Excalibur to the lake — loyalty outliving the kingdom

mythology.lead: Bedwyr belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian tradition: the Welsh heroic material that predates Geoffrey of Monmouth and the whole romance edifice. His dossier is compact and precise — a poem's roster, a tale's three great episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes, and the one-handed man is never the lesser of the pair.

myths.tag: Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen
myths.title: The War-Band Remembered
myths.text:
The poem known from its opening line as Pa gŵr yv y porthaur? — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh: preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen, and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. In it Arthur, halted at a fortress gate by the porter Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr, recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names Arthur speaks to prove his company.

The poem is fragmentary — it breaks off mid-recitation — but its testimony matters beyond its length: it shows a Welsh Arthurian war-band whose heroes had their own deeds long before Geoffrey of Monmouth drew Arthur into Latin history, and Bedwyr is fixed in that founding generation.

myths.title: The One-Handed Spearman
myths.text:
Culhwch ac Olwen, the earliest full Arthurian prose tale, gives Bedwyr his formal introduction when Arthur calls the companions for the quest of Olwen: Arthur called Bedwyr, 'who never shrank from any enterprise upon which Kai was bound. None was equal to him in swiftness throughout this Island except Arthur and Drych Ail Kibddar. And although he was one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle. Another property he had: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.'

The great court-list earlier in the tale quietly extends the household: Amren son of Bedwyr stands among Arthur's huntsmen, and Eneuawc daughter of Bedwyr among the golden-chained maidens of the Island — the one-handed spearman with a son and daughter woven into the fabric of the court.

lore.culturalLegacy: Bedwyr's afterlife runs under a French name. Wace's Roman de Brut and Layamon's Brut carried Geoffrey's Beduerus into the vernacular chronicles; the French romances made him Bedivere, one of the first and last of the Round Table; and Malory gave him the role the whole world now knows — the last knight alive with Arthur after the day of destiny, commanded to cast Excalibur into the water, twice hiding it for its worth and twice rebuked, until at the third throw an arm clothed in white samite rose from the lake, caught the sword, brandished it thrice, and vanished. Tennyson's Idylls of the King sealed the image: it is to Bedivere that the dying Arthur speaks the great consolation — 'The old order changeth, yielding place to new' — before the barge bears him away. Twentieth-century scholarship brought the Welsh original back into view: Bromwich's edition of the triads restored the battle-diadem to Bedwyr son of Bedrawc, and the standard handbooks now present the romance Bedivere as what he is — a Welsh heroic companion who had served Arthur in Welsh for perhaps three hundred years before French poetry ever heard of him. In Wales itself the name never left: Bedwyr remains a living Welsh given name.
lore.archaeology: Bedwyr is a textual hero: no inscription names him, and Welsh tradition offers no relic or shrine. His manuscript witnesses are exact. The poem Pa gŵr? survives uniquely in the Black Book of Carmarthen (Aberystwyth, National Library of Wales, Peniarth MS 1), copied in the mid-thirteenth century and the oldest surviving manuscript wholly in Welsh. Culhwch ac Olwen survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and, in a fuller recension, in the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, late fourteenth century), which also carries the great collection of the triads. The one landscape witness is genuine: Pumlumon (Plynlimon) in Ceredigion, the mountain whose summit cairns the tale makes the lookout of Cei and Bedwyr in the Dillus episode, is a real massif of the Cambrian Mountains crowned with prehistoric cairns. Geoffrey of Monmouth's burial of Beduerus at Bayeux belongs to his Norman pseudo-history, not to any Welsh memory.
lore.syncretism: Bedwyr's transmission is the clearest case in the Arthurian corpus of a Welsh hero passing whole into the continental tradition: Welsh Bedwyr becomes Geoffrey's Latin Beduerus, then the Bedivers and Bedoier of Old French romance, and at last Malory's Sir Bedivere — one continuous name-line from the Black Book of Carmarthen to Caxton's print shop. Within Celtic comparison the one-handed warrior who loses nothing of his worth has tempted scholars toward the Irish parallel of [[nuada|Nuadu]] of the Silver Hand, the king who lost his arm at Mag Tuired and ruled again by means of a silver one; the handbooks treat this as a shared Celtic motif of the maimed-but-undiminished champion, not a derivation of one figure from the other. What the Welsh tradition keeps distinct is the pairing: Cei and Bedwyr are a fixed couple — the tradition names them in that order, never the reverse — as elemental a bond in early Welsh Arthurian lore as any kinship.
lore.originalScriptNote: Medieval Welsh was written in the Latin alphabet, and the manuscripts write the name Bedwyr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; Welsh w and y are vowel-letters, but ordinary Latin characters. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: bedwyr.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'KAY' — one syllable, exactly the English name Kay; the diphthong glides from a neutral 'uh' to 'ee' inside a single beat.
pronunciation.note: Kai is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: Middle Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters, so there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the hero's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The Steward of Arthur's Hall
domains.subtitle: The Nine Days' Breath, the Fire in His Hands, and the Sword No Physician Can Heal
domains.lead: Cei son of Cynyr is the first companion Arthur assigns to Culhwch: the tall man of the Mabinogion's oldest Arthurian tale, who could hold his breath nine nights and nine days under water, go nine nights and nine days without sleep, deal a wound no physician could heal, grow as tall as the tallest tree in the forest, and carry so much heat in his body that rain dried a handbreadth above and below his hand and his companions lit their fires from him in the cold. Centuries of romance would remember him as the steward of the court — the seneschal Kay.

cards.name: The Nine Days' Breath
cards.desc: Nine nights and nine days under water; nine nights and nine days without sleep — the Mabinogion's measure of the tall man's endurance.

cards.name: The Fire in His Hands
cards.desc: His heat kept his hand dry a handbreadth in the hardest rain; in the bitterest cold he was fuel for his companions' fire.

cards.name: The Unhealable Sword
cards.desc: A wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal — and the sword of Wrnach the giant came into Arthur's hand by Cei's trickery.

cards.name: The Seneschal's Office
cards.desc: Geoffrey of Monmouth's Caius dapifer — steward of Arthur's household, given Anjou, buried at Chinon: the office the later romances never let him leave.

symbols.name: The nine days' breath
symbols.meaning: Endurance past the human limit — the hero who outlasts water and sleep alike

symbols.name: The fire in his hands
symbols.meaning: Heat as provision: the companion who keeps the whole company warm, dry, and fed with fire

symbols.name: The unhealable sword
symbols.meaning: A stroke beyond remedy — the oldest stratum's mark of the warrior, before romances made him a steward

symbols.name: The beard of Dillus
symbols.meaning: The quest accomplished by cunning — and Arthur's mocking englyn that ended the fellowship

symbols.name: Cei Hir, 'the Tall'
symbols.meaning: Tall as the tallest tree in the forest when it pleased him — stature as the visible sign of the older, larger hero

mythology.lead: Kai's mythology lives in the oldest stratum of Welsh Arthurian tradition: Culhwch ac Olwen gives him the tale's largest dossier after Arthur himself, and the fragmentary dialogue poem Pa Gur remembers exploits the prose never told. The later Latin and French traditions kept the man and quietly spent the magic.

myths.title: The First Companion
myths.text: When Culhwch comes to Arthur's court to win Olwen daughter of Ysbaddaden Chief Giant, Arthur grants him help, and the first companion named is Cei son of Cynyr. The warrior-list fixes his peculiarities in one breath: nine nights and nine days he could be under water; nine nights and nine days he could go without sleep; a wound from Cei's sword no physician could heal. Cei the Tall — when it pleased him he could make himself as tall as the tallest tree in the forest. And the list adds the attribute the whole fellowship depended on: when the rain was heaviest, whatever he carried in his hand stayed dry for a handbreadth above and below, so great was his heat; and when the cold was hardest on his companions, he was fuel to them to light their fire. The list also preserves his mother's prophecy that his heart would be cold — the oldest trace of the coldness the later romances turned to mockery.

myths.title: The Salmon and the Sword
myths.text: Two of the hardest anoethau — the 'things hard to get' that Ysbaddaden sets as the bride-price — fall to Cei. To free Mabon son of Modron from his prison at Caer Loyw, the company follows the oldest animals to the Salmon of Llyn Llyw, and Cei and Bedwyr ride up the Severn on the salmon's shoulders; while Arthur's men assault the fort from the front, Cei carries Mabon away on the salmon's back. And when Arthur's band comes to the hall of Wrnach the giant, whose sword is needed to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth — no guest had ever left that hall alive — Cei claims to be a master polisher of swords. Admitted, he burnishes the giant's blade, asks to hold it to test the work, and strikes Wrnach's head off with his own sword; the company destroys the fortress. The wonder-hero's greatest feats in the tale are won with a craftsman's hands, not a charge of horse.

lore.culturalLegacy: The steward outlived the giant-killer. Malory's Sir Kay — the foster-brother who claims he drew the sword from the stone, confesses, and is made seneschal at Arthur's coronation — fixed the English image: blunt, envious, brave enough, and indispensable to the household. Chrétien's Keu had already made him the court's satirist, and the romances of every language kept that register. T. H. White's The Sword in the Stone made Kay the human counterweight to the Wart, the brother who gets the crown's shadow instead of the crown. In Welsh the name never left: Cai remains a living given name, and the Mabinogion's Cei Hir is still the tall man of the oldest Arthurian tale. Modern scholarship treats the arc from wonder-hero to comic steward as one of the great case-studies in how the Arthurian legend domesticated its oldest figures.
lore.archaeology: Kai is a literary figure: no inscription, ogham stone, or Romano-British dedication names him, and Welsh tradition generally left texts rather than cult monuments for its heroes. His manuscript witnesses are exact and early. The dialogue poem Pa Gur survives in the Black Book of Carmarthen (c. 1250), the oldest substantial manuscript of Welsh verse; Culhwch ac Olwen survives in a fragmentary copy in the White Book of Rhydderch (Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and complete in the Red Book of Hergest (Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1425); and the Otherworld-raid poem Preiddeu Annwn, the companion witness to this stratum, is preserved in the Book of Taliesin (Peniarth 2, early 14th c.). Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) and Lifris of Llancarfan's Vita Cadoci (c. 1100) carry the Latin attestations. The places of the tales — Caer Loyw on the Severn, the Anglesey of Cath Palug — remain on the map, but the tall man himself left nothing in stone.
lore.syncretism: Kai is less a figure who absorbed other gods than one whom each retelling rewrote. The Welsh stratum gives a wonder-hero: the tall, fire-handed, sleepless companion whose attributes belong to the oldest legendary stock of Britain. Geoffrey of Monmouth euhemerizes him into Caius dapifer, a duke and steward of recognizable twelfth-century type; Chrétien de Troyes turns the steward's sharpness into Keu's venomous tongue, the court's mocker who is always wrong; and Malory resolves the long arc into Sir Kay, Arthur's foster-brother — loyal, loud, and forever outmatched. Scholars have long paired him with Bedwyr, his constant companion in Culhwch ac Olwen, as the two oldest members of Arthur's band; and Mac Cana and others note that the tale-patterns around the pair — the raid on a giant's stronghold, the hunt of the enchanted boar — have close Irish analogues, though no Irish cycle preserves Cei himself. The transformation of the tall man into the seneschal is the tradition's own syncretism: one name, four costumes, and the office outlasting the magic.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Cei, with the spelling variants Kei and Kai — plain Latin letters in Insular script, c. 12th–14th c. CE, in the Black Book of Carmarthen, the White Book of Rhydderch, and the Red Book of Hergest. No diacritic and no distinctive letter is involved: the normalized form is already ASCII, and the restoration Kai differs from the input only by its capital. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: kai.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: 'DOHN' — one syllable, one long pure 'oh' held steady, like English 'dawn' with the vowel kept clean and simple.
pronunciation.note: Don is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple follows the Middle Welsh manuscript spelling Don — three plain ASCII letters, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Modern Welsh scholarship writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign, not a letter the manuscripts carry; the normalized temple form preserves it only in the pronunciation record, not the spelling. The etymology is honestly uncertain: derivation from Common Celtic *dēwā 'goddess' — the root the Welsh still hear in Dyfrdwy, the Dee — is the traditional reading, while a river-name origin is also argued; the handbooks mark the question open.

domains.title: Mother of Gods
domains.subtitle: Plant Dôn — the children named for the mother
domains.lead: Dôn is the matriarch of the Mabinogi's magical house: sister of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd, and mother of the great kindred the Welsh tradition called Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn — Gwydion the enchanter, Gilfaethwy his brother, Arianrhod of the star-castle, Gofannon the smith, and Amaethon the ploughman. She is the only major figure of the Four Branches who never speaks, acts, or appears: the whole of the Fourth Branch happens among her children and her brother, and she is present only in the names they carry — uab Dôn, son of Dôn; uerch Dôn, daughter of Dôn.

cards.name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy
cards.desc: The sister-sons at Math's court: Gwydion the enchanter, 'the best teller of tales in the world', and Gilfaethwy his brother — named, always, as sons of Dôn.

cards.name: Arianrhod ferch Dôn
cards.desc: The daughter proposed for Math's footholder, tested by the wand, mother of Dylan and Lleu — and the proudest, most wounded figure of the Fourth Branch.

cards.name: Gofannon and Amaethon
cards.desc: The craftsman-sons of Culhwch ac Olwen: Gofannon the smith and Amaethon the ploughman, without whom the giant's impossible tasks cannot be done.

cards.name: Plant Dôn
cards.desc: The Children of Dôn — the Welsh divine kindred named for its mother, the standing parallel to Ireland's Túatha Dé Danann.

symbols.name: The matronymic (uab Dôn)
symbols.meaning: 'Son of Dôn' — the mother-name standing at the head of every child's name, her whole presence in the text

symbols.name: Math's wand
symbols.meaning: Her brother's instrument of testing and transformation, laid across her children's fates — the power of the uncle's house over the mother's

symbols.name: Plough and anvil
symbols.meaning: Amaethon's plough and Gofannon's smithy — the crafts of cultivation and making that her sons carry into the oldest tale

symbols.name: The Dee (Dyfrdwy)
symbols.meaning: The river the Welsh still call 'the goddess' — *Dēwā, the name's closest living relative, flowing through the real landscape

symbols.name: The star-castles
symbols.meaning: Caer Arianrhod and Caer Gwydion — her daughter's and her son's halls written into the Welsh night sky by later tradition

mythology.lead: Dôn has no myth of her own — no tale, no speech, no deed the sources record. What she has is a family, and the family is the mythology: the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi unfolds among her children and her brother Math, and the oldest Arthurian tale cannot finish its tasks without two more of her sons. Every witness names her the same way — as the mother in the matronymic — and the Welsh tradition built its northern divine house around exactly that: Plant Dôn, the Children of Dôn.

myths.title: The Sister-Sons at Math's Court
myths.text:
The Fourth Branch opens at the court of Math fab Mathonwy, lord of Gwynedd — who cannot live unless his feet rest in a virgin's lap, except when war is in the land — and it introduces the great men of that court by their mother's name: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy, sons of Dôn, Math's own sister-sons, his nephews and his company. Gwydion is 'the best teller of tales in the world'. It is these two who set the branch's whole tragedy in motion: Gilfaethwy desires Goewin, the maiden of the foothold, and Gwydion engineers the remedy — a war against Pryderi of Dyfed, bought with conjured stallions, hounds, and shields that vanish after a day, so that the king marches south and the rape can happen.

Through all of it — the war, the crime, the three years of animal-shape punishment — the mother never appears. Dôn is present in the text exactly as a name inside other names: uab Dôn, son of Dôn, the matronymic the tale attaches to her children every time it introduces them. The most consequential family in Welsh prose walks the stage under her name, and she never once walks it herself.

myths.title: Arianrhod ferch Dôn and the Wand
myths.text:
When Math needs a new footholder after Goewin, Gwydion proposes his own sister: 'Seek for you a maiden... here is Arianrhod daughter of Dôn.' The maiden is summoned and asked if she is a virgin; she answers that she does not know but believes she is. Math makes her step over his magic wand, and as she steps she drops a fine yellow-haired boy — Dylan, who at once makes for the sea and takes the sea's nature, Dylan Eil Ton, son of the wave — and, all but unnoticed, 'something small' that only Gwydion marks, wraps in a cloth, and hides in a chest at the foot of his bed. From the chest comes the boy who will be Lleu.

Arianrhod, shamed before the whole court, refuses the boy and lays upon him the three tynghedau — the fated destinies — that he shall have no name until she names him, no arms until she arms him, and no wife of any race then on earth. The rest of the branch is Gwydion undoing his sister's curses by craft. Dôn's daughter is the Fourth Branch's proudest and most wounded figure — and Dôn is present, once again, only in the patronymic: uerch Dôn, daughter of Dôn.

lore.culturalLegacy: Dôn rode into English on the same wagon as the rest of the Mabinogi: Lady Charlotte Guest's translation (1838–49) first carried the Fourth Branch into print, and the antiquarian mythography that followed made Plant Dôn the standard label for the northern divine kindred — the house of Gwydion, set beside the house of Llŷr, in every Victorian account of the Welsh gods. Twentieth-century scholarship fixed her place with precision: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi (1930) established the text, Mac Cana's The Mabinogi read the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of Welsh prose, and the great encyclopedias — Koch's Celtic Culture and MacKillop's Dictionary — gave the matriarch her standing head-words, Danu comparison and all. Her widest modern audience came through a children's classic: Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain (1964–68) made 'the Sons of Don' the ruling house of Prydain, with Math son of Mathonwy and Prince Gwydion at Caer Dathyl — her name on the throne of the best-loved Welsh-derived fantasy ever written. Modern Druid and pagan practice honours her as the Welsh mother-goddess and mother of the magical line, and the Welsh sky keeps her children's names: Caer Gwydion, the Milky Way, and Caer Arianrhod among the stars.
lore.archaeology: Dôn is a textual figure: no temple, votive deposit, or inscription names her, and the epigraphic record of early Wales — the Latin and ogham memorial stones catalogued by Nash-Williams — records personal names in funerary formulae, not theonyms. Her evidence is manuscript evidence. The Fourth Branch survives complete in the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth MSS 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1375–1420), with earlier fragments in Peniarth 6; Culhwch ac Olwen is preserved in the same two codices; the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century) holds Kat Godeu. The tales' date of composition is debated, most often placed in the later eleventh or twelfth century. The geography of her house is real — Gwynedd and Arfon in the north-west of Wales, where Math's court and Arianrhod's castle stand in the tale — but no sanctuary of hers is known. The closest thing to a material trace of the name is a river: Dyfrdwy, the Welsh name of the Dee, continues Common Celtic *Dēwā, 'the goddess', and keeps the matriarch's name-element flowing through the landscape to this day.
lore.syncretism: Dôn's great comparison is Irish, and it is as old as modern Celtic studies: [[danu|Danu]] (or Dana), the equally shadowy mother after whom the Túatha Dé Danann — the peoples of the goddess Danu — are named. A Welsh divine kindred called the Children of Dôn and an Irish one called the peoples of Danu look like two faces of one inheritance, and MacKillop and Koch both register the comparison as standard. But it is a comparison, not an equation: no Welsh text identifies the two names, and the philology is genuinely disputed. The traditional reading derives Dôn from Common Celtic *dēwā, 'goddess' — the very word the Welsh language keeps in Dyfrdwy, its name for the River Dee — while a river-name origin, matching the continental Dānuvius (Danube) and the English Don, is also argued; the handbooks leave the question open rather than resolve it. Inside the Welsh corpus her closest kin are the tradition's other mothers and queens: [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], the Great Queen of Dyfed, and, in later genealogical speculation, her pairing with [[beli|Beli Mawr]] as father of her children — a marriage the genealogies assert and the Mabinogi never mentions. Her husbandless, speechless sovereignty has no exact parallel anywhere in Celtic literature: she is the matriarch reduced to pure name.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is preserved in Middle Welsh in the Latin alphabet as Don — attested in the White Book of Rhydderch (c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (c. 1375–1420), the two great manuscripts of the Mabinogi. Modern Welsh orthography writes Dôn with a circumflex, but that mark is a modern length-sign for the long vowel, not a letter any manuscript carries; the project therefore follows the manuscript form, and the name stands in Tier 2 by the mechanical rule — no diacritic, no distinctive letter, nothing for ASCII to lose. Because the name is pure ASCII — and also an ordinary English word and river-name — its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: don.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none. The temple is served at /sites/don/ in the meantime.

pronunciation.approximation: BEL-ee — two syllables, stress on the first; the e is the open e of 'bed', never the long ay of 'bailey'.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Beli (Beli mawr uab Manogan, 'Beli the Great, son of Manogan') is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The traditional gloss 'bright, shining' reaches the name through its long-proposed connection with the Celtic god Belenos — conventionally derived from the root *bhel-, 'to shine' — but the etymology of Belenos itself is debated, and the handbooks record the link as a possibility, not a proof.

domains.title: The Root of the Pedigrees
domains.subtitle: The Island of Britain, the Four Sons, and the Question of the Bright One
domains.lead: Beli mawr — Beli the Great, son of Manogan — is the deep ancestor of British kingship: the king of the Island of Britain whom the Mabinogion sets at the head of its dynasties, father of Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw, and Llefelys, and the name to which the medieval Welsh royal pedigrees climb. Behind the king, scholarship has long glimpsed a god — the continental Belenos, the 'bright, shining' one — but the texts give us the ancestor, and the ancestor is what the record can defend.

cards.name: The Island of Britain
cards.desc: Beli's realm in Lludd a Llefelys: the whole island, 'the crown of London' its seat — the deep past of a single British kingship.

cards.name: The Four Sons
cards.desc: Lludd, Caswallawn, Nynniaw — and, 'as the story tells', a fourth, Llefelys: the branches of the house the whole tradition descends from.

cards.name: The Pedigree
cards.desc: The Harleian genealogies carry the royal houses of Wales back to Beli Mawr — the name at the root of the British family trees.

cards.name: The Bright One
cards.desc: The proposed god behind the king: Belenos, 'bright, shining' — the continental name Tertullian and the Aquileia altars attest, linked to Beli by a long scholarly tradition.

symbols.name: The Island of Britain
symbols.meaning: The single realm Beli held and his sons inherited — kingship imagined whole before it was ever divided

symbols.name: The family tree
symbols.meaning: The pedigrees of the Welsh dynasties growing back to one root — ancestry as the ground of legitimacy

symbols.name: The veil of illusion
symbols.meaning: Caswallawn's invisible cloak in Branwen — the house of Beli taking the crown unseen

symbols.name: The walled city
symbols.meaning: Lludd's rebuilding of London — Lud's town, the memory of the dynasty fixed in stone and street-names

symbols.name: The sun's brightness
symbols.meaning: The traditional gloss of the name — 'bright, shining' — carried from the Belenos inscriptions into the Welsh ancestor

mythology.lead: Beli has no adventure of his own: his story is his house. The Mabinogion knows him as the dead king whose four sons inherit Britain, France, and the quarrels of the next generation; the pedigrees know him as the root; and Geoffrey of Monmouth knows him as Heli, father of the builder of London.

myths.title: The Four Sons of Beli
myths.text:
The tale of Lludd and Llefelys opens with the settlement of the island: Beli the Great, son of Manogan, was king of this island, and he had three sons — Lludd, Caswallawn, and Nynniaw — and, as the story tells, a fourth son called Llefelys. When Beli died, the kingdom of the Island of Britain fell to Lludd as the eldest, and Lludd ruled it prosperously, rebuilding the walls of London and living there for most of the year. Llefelys, the youngest, went to France, won the love of the old king's only daughter, and inherited that kingdom in his turn.

What follows — the three plagues that fall on Britain, and Llefelys's counsel from the middle of the Channel — belongs to the sons' temples. Beli's part is finished in the opening lines, and that is precisely his function: he is the point from which legitimacy flows, the dead father whose reign makes his sons' divided world one family.

myths.title: Caswallawn's Veil
myths.text:
The Second Branch remembers Beli's house at the moment it takes the crown. While Brân the Blessed marched into Ireland to avenge Branwen, he left seven men as regents in Britain, his son Caradog at their head. Caswallawn son of Beli marched against them wearing a veil of illusion, so that no one could see him — only his sword killing. He slew the seven, and Caradog died of a broken heart at the sight of the slaughter and the knowledge of who held the island now.

Caswallawn son of Beli became king in London. The branch never explains or excuses the usurpation; it simply registers that while the children of Llŷr spent themselves overseas, the children of Beli took the island — the two great houses of Welsh tradition passing the crown between them without a battle anyone could see.

lore.culturalLegacy: Beli's afterlife is genealogical before it is literary. The medieval pedigrees made descent from Beli Mawr the deepest claim a British dynasty could print, and the convention outlived the Middle Ages: Tudor and Stuart antiquaries, eager to trace the crown to British and Trojan roots, found Beli waiting at the root of the trees Geoffrey had Latinized. Through Geoffrey's Heli he fathered the legend of London itself — Lud's town, Lud's gate, the name written into the city's streets — and through his son Cassibelaunus he stands two generations above Shakespeare's Cymbeline, whose Britain is still Beli's island. In modern Wales the name persists quietly: Beli remains a Welsh personal name, and Beli Mawr keeps his place in the national memory as the grandfather of kings. Modern Celtic pagan and Druid practice honors the ancestral Belenus beside him, keeping the old question — king or bright god — alive rather than answered.
lore.archaeology: Beli is a textual figure: no inscription, image, or votive object from Britain names him, and no cult site is his. His witnesses are codices — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1382–1410) for the Mabinogion tales, and British Library Harley MS 3859 (c. 1100) for the genealogies that root the Welsh dynasties in him. The material evidence belongs to his proposed continental cognate: the dedications Belino Augusto sacrum from Aquileia and the eastern Alps are real stones with a real theonym — the strongest archaeological fact in the whole dossier, and the reason the 'bright, shining' gloss will not go away. Comparative evidence only: no altar can be read as addressed to the Welsh ancestor-king himself.
lore.syncretism: Beli's whole cross-cultural argument is the Belenos question. The continental god is attested from Aquileia to Noricum, glossed by the ancients as a Celtic Apollo, and derived by tradition from *bhel-, 'to shine'. Welsh Beli Mawr matches the name nearly perfectly, and from O'Rahilly onward scholars have set the Irish ancestor-god Bile beside both, proposing a single Celtic 'bright one' dimmed into three literatures as three ancestors. Mac Cana and Koch record the comparison; neither certifies it. The distinction worth keeping is Geoffrey's other Belinus — the son of Dunvallo, brother of Brennius — a different figure who shares nothing with Beli Mawr but the name. Within the Welsh corpus, Beli's closest kin are the other fountainheads of dynasty: [[don|Dôn]], mother of the Children of Dôn, and Llŷr, father of the house of Llŷr, whose sons Brân and [[manawydan|Manawydan]] lose the island's crown to Beli's son Caswallawn in the Second Branch.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Beli (Beli mawr uab Manogan) in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: beli.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

pronunciation.approximation: MAATH — a long, open 'ah', held like the a of 'father', closing on the soft voiceless th of English 'thin'. One syllable; the whole weight of the name sits on the length of the vowel and the hush at the end.
pronunciation.note: Middle Welsh Math (Math uab Mathonwy) is already written in the Latin alphabet, so the ASCII form loses nothing: the name is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule, since the restoration preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that ASCII drops. The standard etymology derives the name from Proto-Celtic *matu- 'bear' — compare Old Irish math 'bear' (attested in the compound mathgamain), the Irish name Mathgen borne by the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish Matugenos 'bear-born'. The father's name, Mathonwy, is built on the same root, and the handbooks treat the bear-derivation as the best-supported reading.

domains.title: Magic, Kingship
domains.subtitle: The domain of Math
domains.lead: In the celtic tradition, Math governed magic, kingship. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

cards.name: The Wand of Office
cards.desc: Math's hutlath — the magic wand that tested Arianrhod, turned his nephews into beasts for three years, and helped fashion a woman out of flowers.

cards.name: The Footholder's Geas
cards.desc: The strange condition of his kingship: Math could not live except with his feet in the lap of a virgin, unless the turmoil of war released him.

cards.name: The Threefold Sentence
cards.desc: His justice wore animal skins: Gwydion and Gilfaethwy spent a year each as deer, boars, and wolves — and their beast-children were baptized at his court.

cards.name: The Flower Bride
cards.desc: With Gwydion he took oak, broom, and meadowsweet and made Blodeuwedd — the wife no earthly race could supply for the nephew fated to have none.

symbols.name: The virgin's lap

symbols.name: Goewin ferch Pebin

symbols.name: The swine of Annwfn

mythology.lead: Math fab Mathonwy is the king at the still centre of the Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi — the branch that bears his name: lord of Gwynedd, master of the magic wand, uncle of Gwydion and Gilfaethwy. His rule hangs on the strangest condition in Welsh literature — he cannot live except with his feet in a virgin's lap, unless war calls him out — and around that geas the whole plot turns: the theft of the swine, the wrong to Goewin, the justice of the three animal years, and the making of a bride from flowers.

myths.title: The Geas of the Footholder
myths.text:
Math son of Mathonwy was lord over Gwynedd, and the tale's first fact about him is the condition of his life: except when the turmoil of war prevented it, he could not live unless his feet lay in the lap of a virgin. The office of footholder went to Goewin daughter of Pebin of Dôl Pebin in Arfon, the fairest maiden of her generation; and while Math kept the lap, his sister's sons Gwydion and Gilfaethwy ruled the realm in his stead.

The arrangement is neither joke nor luxury: it is the Fourth Branch's picture of sacral kingship, a rule whose life is bound by taboo. When Gilfaethwy sickened with desire for Goewin, Gwydion read the geas like a statute. The king may leave the lap for one thing only — war. Therefore there would be a war.

myths.title: The War for the Swine
myths.text:
Pryderi of Dyfed held the hobeu, the swine sent him from Annwfn by its king Arawn — the first pigs ever brought to Wales. Gwydion went south in the guise of a poet, conjured twelve stallions with golden harness, twelve greyhounds with golden collars, and twelve golden shields, traded the day's glamour for the herd, and was gone before the illusion faded. Pryderi mustered and came north, and Math led Gwynedd out to meet him — out of the lap, exactly as the condition required.

At the parley Pryderi demanded single combat, for it was because of him that the hosts had come; at the maenor of Penardd Gwydion slew him 'by strength and valour and by magic and enchantment', and Dyfed gave hostages and went home under tribute. But while Math marched, Gwydion and Gilfaethwy forced Goewin in the king's own chamber. The war had only ever been the key, and the lap the lock.

lore.culturalLegacy: Math's afterlife is quieter than his nephews', but the Fourth Branch carried him far. In the twentieth century the branch was remade twice over: Evangeline Walton's The Virgin and the Swine (1936) retells his story as a tragedy of old religion and new, with the geas and the three animal years as its moral engine, and Lloyd Alexander's Chronicles of Prydain made Math son of Mathonwy the aged High King of Prydain for a generation of young readers — the geas laid aside, the grave authority kept. Alan Garner's The Owl Service (1967) drew its haunting from the Blodeuwedd strand that Math's wand set in motion, the branch repeating itself down the generations of a Welsh valley. In scholarship he stands at the centre of the Mabinogi industry: Ifor Williams's Pedeir Keinc y Mabinogi fixed the text, Sioned Davies's Oxford translation carries it to the world's readers, and Mac Cana's and Koch's handbooks treat the Fourth Branch as the masterpiece of medieval Welsh prose, with the footholder geas among the most-discussed cruxes in Celtic studies.
lore.archaeology: Math is a textual figure with no pre-Christian material attestation: no inscription, votive object, or image names him. His witnesses are manuscripts — the White Book of Rhydderch (Aberystwyth, NLW Peniarth 4–5, c. 1350) and the Red Book of Hergest (Oxford, Jesus College MS 111, c. 1400), the two codices in which the Fourth Branch survives. The epigraphic witness belongs to the root rather than the man: Gaulish personal names such as Matugenos, 'bear-born', attest the *matu- element in the onomastics of the continental Celts. The tale's own geography is real Gwynedd terrain — Dôl Pebin in Arfon, where Goewin's father held his land — and the branch's southern war-road runs to the maenor of Penardd, where Pryderi fell.
lore.syncretism: Math is the Welsh reflex of a pan-Celtic institution: the sacral king whose rule is bound by taboo. Irish tradition gives the condition its clearest grammar — the gessi of kings, the network of prohibitions whose slow breaking dooms Conaire Mór in Togail Bruidne Da Derga — and Math's footholder geas is the same machinery in Welsh dress, a kingship valid only while its condition holds. Mac Cana reads the Children of Dôn as the Welsh counterpart of the Túatha Dé Danann, and the name itself crosses the water on its own root: Cath Maige Tuired names Mathgen as the seer of the Túatha Dé Danann, and Gaulish epigraphy attests Matugenos — both 'bear-born', from the *matu- that names the king and his father. Within the Mabinogi the root echoes across the branches: [[matholwch|Matholwch]], the Irish king of the Second Branch, carries the same Math- element. His closest kin are the members of his own house — his sister [[don|Dôn]]'s children, above all [[gwydion|Gwydion]], whose plots the geas licences and whose punishments the king's wand performs — and the co-made bride [[blodeuwedd|Blodeuwedd]], his one act of creation.
lore.originalScriptNote: Welsh is written in the Latin alphabet; the name is attested in Middle Welsh manuscripts as Math (Math uab Mathonwy), in the White Book of Rhydderch and the Red Book of Hergest, and the ASCII spelling loses nothing — hence Tier 2. The plain-ASCII domain math.com is registered to a third party and held outside the collection; it is watched for release. Until then this temple stands without a domain of its own.

pronunciation.approximation: 'uh-MEE-tah-bhuh' — the 'bh' is aspirated like 'b-huh' in one sound; the 'tā' is held long.
pronunciation.note: Amitābha is Tier 1 because the medial ā is long. The name is a standard Sanskrit bahuvrīhi compound: a-mita ('unmeasured') + ābha ('light, splendor'). In East Asian Buddhism he is also known as Amitāyus, 'Infinite Life,' the two names emphasizing light and longevity.

domains.title: Buddha of Infinite Light
domains.subtitle: Pure Land, Compassion, and Other-Power Salvation
domains.lead:
Amitābha is the Buddha whose light has no limit and whose compassion refuses no one. In Mahāyāna Buddhism, especially the Pure Land traditions of East Asia, he presides over Sukhāvatī, the Blissful Land, a paradise where rebirth guarantees progress toward Buddhahood. He did not attain this realm for himself alone; as the monk Dharmākara he made forty-eight vows, promising that anyone who called his name with sincere faith would be welcomed into his land.

His cult transformed Buddhism from a primarily monastic path of self-cultivation into a devotional religion accessible to laypeople, sinners, and the spiritually exhausted. For many millions, the name Amitābha is itself the practice.

cards.name: Sukhāvatī
cards.desc: The Pure Land of Bliss, a paradise of gold trees, jeweled ponds, and ceaseless Dharma teaching.

cards.name: The Forty-Eight Vows
cards.desc: As Dharmākara he vowed that even those with heavy karma could be reborn in Sukhāvatī through faith and name-recitation.

cards.name: Nembutsu / Niànfó
cards.desc: The invocation of his name — 'Namo Amitābhāya' or 'Namo Amituofo' — becomes the central practice of Pure Land devotion.

cards.name: Welcoming Descent
cards.desc: At death he descends with bodhisattvas to escort the faithful to Sukhāvatī, a scene painted and meditated upon across East Asia.

mythology.lead: Amitābha's mythology is the story of a vow. Long ago, as the monk Dharmākara, he stood before the Buddha Lokeśvararāja and promised to create a Buddha-field so perfect that any being who trusted in him would be reborn there and swiftly attain enlightenment.

myths.title: The Vows of Dharmākara
myths.text: The Larger Sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra describes how the monk Dharmākara, after five aeons of contemplation, formulated forty-eight vows. The eighteenth vow became the foundation of Pure Land practice: any being, even one who had committed the five grave crimes, if they trusted in him and recited his name even ten times, would be reborn in Sukhāvatī. Having made the vows, Dharmākara fulfilled them and became the Buddha Amitābha, whose Pure Land now welcomes beings from every direction.

myths.title: The Contemplation of Sukhāvatī
myths.text: The Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra was addressed to Queen Vaidehī, imprisoned by her cruel son Ajātaśatru. In her despair she asked the Buddha to show her a land without sorrow. The Buddha taught her sixteen meditations, culminating in a vision of Amitābha and his Pure Land. The sutra insists that even the worst sinner, if they sincerely call Amitābha's name at the moment of death, will be received by him.

lore.culturalLegacy: Amitābha is one of the most widely invoked names in religious history. The phrase Namo Amituofo or Namu Amida Butsu has been recited billions of times across East Asia, and Pure Land Buddhism remains one of the largest forms of Buddhist practice worldwide. His image dominates temple halls from Kyoto to Xi'an, and the Raigo paintings of his descent to meet the dying are among the masterpieces of Japanese art. In the West, Zen and Tibetan Buddhism have received more scholarly attention, but Pure Land devotion remains the Buddhism of ordinary households across East Asia. The Unicode restoration Amitābha preserves the long ā and aspirated bh that distinguish the Sanskrit name from its East Asian pronunciations.
lore.archaeology: The earliest artistic representations of Amitābha appear in Gandhāran and Mathuran Buddhist sculpture from the early centuries CE. His cult flourished along the Silk Road, leaving magnificent cave-temple murals at Kizil, Dunhuang, and Bingling. In East Asia, colossal Amitābha images were carved at Longmen and Dazu in China, and the great Amida halls of Hōryūji, Byōdōin, and Zenkōji in Japan became centers of Pure Land devotion. Tibetan thankas and mural cycles depict him in red, surrounded by the bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, preserving his iconography across Himalayan Buddhism.
lore.syncretism: Amitābha became the central figure of Pure Land Buddhism in China, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, where he is known as Ēmítuófó, Amit'a, Amida, and A Di Đà Phật. The Japanese schools founded by Hōnen and Shinran made exclusive devotion to Amida the path of the 'evil person' who cannot achieve enlightenment through self-power. In Tibetan Buddhism, Amitābha presides over the red Buddha family and the realm of Padmasambhava; the phowa practice transfers consciousness to his Pure Land at death. The cult of Amitābha also influenced Manichaean and Nestorian art in Central Asia, and his imagery — especially the welcoming descent — shaped East Asian Buddhist painting, sculpture, and mortuary culture for over a millennium.

pronunciation.approximation: mah-hah vai-ROH-chuh-nuh — mahā is "great"; the c is the soft 'ch' of 'church.'
pronunciation.note: The lexicon takes the full canonical form, Mahāvairocana: mahā, "great," + vairocana, "the Shining One," from vi-√ruc, "to shine forth" (Monier-Williams) — "the Great Illuminator." The Avataṃsaka tradition also knows the short form Vairocana, which the lexicon preserves as the plain variant; the esoteric schools prefer the full name. Monier-Williams records the word's older life as a solar epithet — and even as the name of a Dānava king, the father of Bali — before Buddhism made it the name of the cosmic Buddha. Tier-1 by rule: the macron and the long vowels are distinctive features the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: The Great Sun
domains.subtitle: The Avataṃsaka Cosmos, the Two Maṇḍalas, and the Preaching of the Dharmakāya
domains.lead: Mahāvairocana is the cosmic Buddha: the Great Sun whose body is the universe itself, the center of the Avataṃsaka's jeweled cosmos and of the Shingon maṇḍalas — the Buddha who does not merely teach the Dharma but whose every mountain, river, and star is the teaching.

cards.name: The Great Sun

cards.name: Indra's Net

mythology.lead: Mahāvairocana's mythology is cosmology recited as liturgy: the universe telling itself the story of its own enlightenment.

myths.title: The Buddha Whose Body Is the Cosmos
myths.text: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the Flower Garland, opens on a scale no other scripture attempts: Vairocana enthroned not in a grove but in the dharmadhātu itself, every pore of his body a world-system, every atom of every world containing all the others. The Huayan masters drew the sūtra's vision as Indra's net — an infinite web with a jewel at every crossing, each jewel mirroring every other. It is the largest picture of interdependence ever painted: nothing exists alone, and the Great Sun is the name for the whole net seen at once.

myths.title: The Sun That Preaches Without Words
myths.text: The esoteric tradition's own charters, the Mahāvairocana Sūtra and its twin the Tattvasaṃgraha, present the cosmic Buddha not as a person among persons but as the dharmakāya — the Dharma-body — whose sermon is reality's ongoing act of existing. Kūkai gave this its boldest formula: hosshin seppō, the dharmakāya itself preaches. Mountains, rivers, the sound of rain — for Shingon these are not metaphors for the teaching but the teaching in progress, and the maṇḍala is the lesson read as a map.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Nara Daibutsu remains Japan's most visited Buddha, and Kōya-san's temple-cemetery complex — grown around Kūkai's mausoleum, where the master is held to sit in meditation still — is among the great sacred landscapes of Asia. The Avataṃsaka's jeweled net has become a standing metaphor far beyond Buddhism, borrowed by ecologists and systems theorists for interdependence itself. And the name keeps its grammar: every Dainichi temple and every Rushana image is still conjugating vi-√ruc, the verb "to shine forth," in bronze and wood.
lore.archaeology: The monuments are enormous and intact. Tōdai-ji's Daibutsu (dedicated 752; head and hands recast) still anchors Nara; Kōya-san (vowed 816, consecrated 819) and Tō-ji (granted 823, its five-story pagoda the tallest wooden tower in Japan) preserve Kūkai's school entire — all UNESCO-listed. On Java, Borobudur's five-jina program culminates in the Vairocana series of its upper terraces, the Avataṃsaka cosmos walked as a mountain of stone, and its relief galleries unfold the Gaṇḍavyūha's pilgrimage of Sudhana panel by panel. Dunhuang's cave murals give the Flower Garland assemblies in pigment, the same cosmos painted on silk-road walls.
lore.syncretism: The name itself is an old loan from the sun: Monier-Williams lists Vairocana as a solar epithet and even as a Dānava king, the son of Prahlāda and father of Bali — Buddhism took the word for light and made it the light-source of the Dharma. In Japan the identification ran the other way as well: medieval honji-suijaku thought read Dainichi as the true face of Amaterasu, the sun goddess of Ise, fusing the two great suns of the archipelago's religions. In Tibet he is the center of the five tathāgatas and the white crown of the system; in China his Avataṃsaka became the Huayan school, whose Indra's-net teaching is still the standard Buddhist answer to the question of how everything relates.

domains.lead: Akṣobhya is the Buddha who cannot be shaken: lord of Abhirati, the eastern Land of Delight, blue as the vajra family he heads, seated in the earth-touching gesture — the one of the five tathāgatas who turns the poison of hatred into the mirror-like wisdom that reflects everything and is disturbed by nothing.

mythology.lead: Akṣobhya's mythology is the story of a single vow kept without a crack: the monk who resolved never to be angry, and became the Buddha of the unshakable land.

myths.title: The Vow Against Anger
myths.text: His sūtra — the Akṣobhya-tathāgatasya-vyūha, among the earliest pure-land scriptures translated into Chinese, carried over by Lokakṣema in the second century CE — tells how a monk of a past age stood before a Buddha and vowed that until his own awakening he would never give rise to anger or malice toward any being. From that vow came his name: Akṣobhya, the Unshakable. The text then shows the vow fulfilled: the monk is now the Buddha of Abhirati, and beings who aspire to his land are promised rebirth where anger finds no purchase.

myths.title: The Land of Delight
myths.text: Abhirati, "the Delightful," is the east's answer to Sukhāvatī: a Buddha-field without the evil rebirths, level and fragrant, beautiful beyond the worlds men know. The sūtra lavishes detail on its gentleness — no lower destinies, no sickness as we know it, and women, the text takes care to say, bear children there without pain. It is the pure land of moral steadiness: not escape from the world, but a world where steadiness is finally possible.

lore.culturalLegacy: Akṣobhya's legacy is the mirror itself: the image of mind as a reflecting surface that needs only to stay still became one of the deep metaphors of East Asian Buddhism, from Huayan to Zen. His earth-touching gesture — assigned to him among the five — is the most reproduced Buddha pose on earth, the seal of the historical awakening reassigned to the unshakable one. And his vow remains the tradition's standing definition of patience: not slowness, but a stillness no insult can reach.
lore.archaeology: His oldest document is textual: Lokakṣema's second-century Chinese translation of his sūtra, among the first pure-land scriptures rendered into any language. In stone he belongs to the five-jina program that matured in the eighth and ninth centuries: the eastern niches of Borobudur carry his series in the earth-touching gesture, and the crowns of Nepalese paubhā and Tibetan sculpture place him on the east petal of the jina-mandala. East Javanese bronzes and stone Akṣobhyas — dark, right hand to the earth — are among the finest small Buddhist images in the world.
lore.syncretism: China received him early as Āchù and later rendered him "the Immovable" — a name he shares as a near-doublet with Acala, the blazing Fudō Myōō of Japan, whose wrathful immovability is the mirror image of his serene one. Tibet made Mi bskyod pa central to the highest tantras and to the rites of death and purification, and the five-Buddha system that enthrones him traveled from the Indian universities to every Himalayan valley. Scholars have noted the quiet irony: the least-known of the five in the West is, liturgically, among the most invoked — every vajra-family rite is his household.

His other names are a litany of the same music: Mañjughoṣa, "Gentle Voice"; Vāgīśvara, "Lord of Speech." domains.title: The Gentle Glory
domains.subtitle: The Flaming Sword, the Book on the Lotus, and the Mountain of Five Terraces
domains.lead: Mañjuśrī is the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom: the ever-youthful prince who raises the flaming sword that cuts ignorance and bears the book of the Perfection of Wisdom on a blue lotus — the mind of every Buddha made visible as a sixteen-year-old with a blade.

cards.name: The Flaming Sword
cards.desc: The khadga that does not wound but severs: ignorance cut at the root, wisdom flaming at the edge.

cards.name: The Book on the Lotus
cards.desc: The Prajñāpāramitā volume resting on a blue utpala — the text the sword serves.

cards.name: The Lion Mount
cards.desc: He rides the lion of the teaching — wisdom's roar that no argument withstands.

cards.name: A Ra Pa Tsa Na
cards.desc: Oṃ A Ra Pa Tsa Na Dhīḥ — the Arapacana syllabary as mantra, recited for a sharp mind.

symbols.name: The flaming sword
symbols.meaning: Discrimination that liberates: the cut that ends confusion, not the one that starts it

symbols.name: The blue lotus and the book

symbols.name: The seed syllable Dhīḥ
symbols.meaning: The sound of insight itself, traced on children's tongues in the Himalaya

mythology.lead: Mañjuśrī's mythology is the biography of wisdom itself: he appears wherever the sūtras need the hardest question asked — and answered without a flicker.

myths.title: The Debate of Non-Duality
myths.text: When the layman Vimalakīrti feigned illness to teach, every bodhisattva found an excuse not to visit — each remembered being corrected by him once. Mañjuśrī alone went, leading the whole assembly, and their exchange is the sūtra's summit: asked how a bodhisattva enters non-duality, Vimalakīrti answered Mañjuśrī's courtesy with silence, and Mañjuśrī pronounced the silence itself the teaching. It is the most famous consultation in Buddhist literature — the wisdom bodhisattva certifying that the highest truth declines to be phrased.

myths.title: The Nāga King's Daughter
myths.text: In the Lotus Sūtra's twelfth chapter, Mañjuśrī returns from the nāga palace under the sea and reports that the dragon king's daughter — eight years old — has attained full awakening. The elder Śāriputra objects on every ground the age could supply; the girl appears, offers a jewel to the Buddha, and demonstrates her enlightenment before the assembly. The chapter is Mañjuśrī's brief for the universality of awakening: wisdom, taught well, does not check credentials.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mañjuśrī is the patron saint of students across half the world: Himalayan children still have the syllable Dhīḥ traced on their tongues for a quick mind, and his Arapacana mantra is murmured before examinations from Ladakh to Lhasa. His iconography — sword in the right hand, book on the lotus at the left — is the universal Buddhist shorthand for the two halves of wisdom, cutting and knowing. Mount Wutai, his earthly seat, is a UNESCO landscape where a dozen languages still call on Wénshū.
lore.archaeology: His mountain is the monument: Wǔtái shān preserves the Nanchan temple (782) and the Foguang temple's East Hall (857) — the two oldest surviving timber halls in China — on the terraces pilgrims have climbed for fifteen centuries. The Kathmandu valley keeps his founding stroke in stone and water: the Chobhar gorge through which the lake drained, and the Svayambhū stūpa on its hill, eyes painted and sword remembered. His certain images emerge in the early centuries CE and multiply along the Silk Road; by the Pāla period the sword-and-book type was fixed, and it has not changed since.
lore.syncretism: He is the most portable of the great bodhisattvas: Wénshū in China, Monju in Japan, 'Jam dpal in Tibet — and in Tibet his cult became inseparable from scholarship itself, Tsongkhapa venerated as his emanation and the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, "Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī," recited as the daily liturgy of the monasteries; Wayman's translation made the text a classic in the West. With Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi he forms the lords of the three families — wisdom, compassion, and power — the triad painted over a thousand Himalayan doorways. His sword-and-book traveled the sea routes as well: his images stand in the temples of Buddhist Java.

domains.title: The Earth-Womb
domains.subtitle: The Great Vow, the Six-Ringed Staff, and the Hells Emptied One Being at a Time
domains.lead: Kṣitigarbha is the bodhisattva of the greatest vow ever sworn: not to attain Buddhahood until the hells are emptied — the monk-robed guardian of the dead, the traveler, and the child, who accepted the loneliest commission in Buddhism: to fill the age between one Buddha's passing and the next one's coming.

cards.name: The Great Vow
cards.desc: "Until the hells are empty, I shall not become a Buddha" — the pledge that defines him.

cards.name: The Khakkhara
cards.desc: The six-ringed monk's staff: its jingle warns the small creatures, and its point opens the gates of hell.

cards.name: The Wish-Fulfilling Jewel
cards.desc: The cintāmaṇi in his hand: the light he carries into the darkest of the six realms.

cards.name: The Six Jizō
cards.desc: One for each realm of rebirth: the six forms in which he patrols the whole wheel of existence.

symbols.name: The monk's robe and shaven head

mythology.lead: Kṣitigarbha's mythology is the story of a vow repeated across lifetimes — a brahmin daughter, a king — each life renewing the same impossible promise.

myths.title: The Commission in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven
myths.text: The Sūtra of the Past Vows of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva is set in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, where the Buddha preaches for his mother's sake before his passing. There he recounts Kṣitigarbha's long record of vows and formally entrusts to him all beings of the coming age — the interval between Śākyamuni's parinirvāṇa and Maitreya's arrival. The sūtra's most quoted line is the vow itself: until the hells are empty, he shall not become a Buddha; only when every being is saved will he accept awakening. The Sanskrit original is lost; the text survives chiefly in Chinese and Tibetan, and its promise survived everything.

myths.title: The Brahmin Daughter
myths.text: The sūtra's most beloved past life is a daughter's. A pious brahmin girl's mother died slandering the Dharma, and the daughter, selling all she had to make offerings, was granted a vision of the Avīci hell — where she learned that her merit had already lifted her mother toward heaven. Seeing the legions of the damned who had no daughter to save them, she vowed to deliver them all: the vow was born of filial piety and outgrew the family in a single act. In East Asia this story fused his cult with the Ghost Festival itself, the season of the dead.

lore.culturalLegacy: Kṣitigarbha is the working religion of grief in East Asia: the mizuko kuyō services in which Japanese parents memorialize lost pregnancies are held before him; the bibbed stone Jizō is Japan's commonest roadside sight; and Dìzàng's temples anchor the Chinese underworld's moral map. His vow has become the Mahāyāna's most quoted sentence — the standard against which every other pledge of compassion is measured — and his monk's robe the proof that the highest bodhisattva need not look like a king.
lore.archaeology: His surviving landscape is vast: Jiuhuashan's temple-mountain, with the flesh-body hall of the Silla prince, remains an active pilgrimage city; the Dunhuang caves preserve banner-paintings of Dìzàng enthroned among the Ten Kings of hell, the earliest great cycle of his iconography. Japan's material record is the stone Jizō itself — uncounted thousands of carved figures at village edges, crossroads, and temple yards, from medieval stelae to today's bibbed statues — the densest distribution of any Buddhist image in the archipelago.
lore.syncretism: East Asia rebuilt him in its own image without touching the vow: China seated him over the Ten Kings of the underworld bureaucracy and wove him into the Ghost Festival's calendar; Korea's Jijang shares the Jiuhua inheritance; Japan fused Jizō with the roadside protector-deities of the old highways and the cult of dead children. Tibet received him as Sa yi snying po among the eight great bodhisattvas, though without the underworld portfolio. Comparatists place him among the great psychopomps — but note the difference: he does not guide the dead out; he goes in and stays until the last one leaves.

pronunciation.note: Vajrapāṇi is a bahuvrīhi: vajra, "thunderbolt, diamond," + pāṇi, "hand" (Monier-Williams) — "the one with the vajra in hand." The name is older than Buddhism: Monier-Williams lists it first as an epithet of Indra, the thunderbolt-wielder, and the lexicon preserves that gloss. domains.lead: Vajrapāṇi is the power of the Buddhas in person: the thunderbolt-bearer who walks at the Buddha's shoulder in the earliest Gandhāran panels, the enforcer who once held a blazing club over a liar's head in the Pāli canon, and the Lord of Secrets to whom the tantras themselves were entrusted.

cards.name: The Buddha's Shadow

cards.name: The Lord of Secrets

mythology.lead: Vajrapāṇi's mythology runs from the Pāli canon to the highest tantras without a break: the same thunderbolt, passed from Indra's hand to the Buddha's bodyguard to the Lord of Secrets.

myths.title: The Yakkha with the Blazing Club
myths.text: His earliest certain appearance is already dramatic. In the Dīgha Nikāya's Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the proud young brahmin Ambaṭṭha twice evades the Buddha's direct question about his lineage; and there appears above his head the yakkha Vajirapāṇi, holding aloft a great blazing iron club, ready to split his skull into seven pieces if he refuses a third time. Ambaṭṭha answers. The episode is the whole doctrine in miniature: the thunderbolt exists not to strike but to make truth the easier choice.

myths.title: Heracles at the Buddha's Side
myths.text: When Gandhāran sculptors of the early centuries CE carved the Buddha's life in stone, they needed a protector — and they found him in the Greek hero their patrons already knew. The muscular attendant at the Buddha's shoulder, sometimes bearded and lion-skinned, is Heracles with his club swapped for a vajra: Vajrapāṇi in the dress of the strongest man the Mediterranean could imagine. It is the most candid syncretism in ancient art — the thunderbolt-bearer wearing another culture's power, because power was the job description.

lore.culturalLegacy: Vajrapāṇi gave the third turning of Buddhism its very name: Vajrayāna, the diamond-thunderbolt vehicle, is the way of his implement. The paired Niō still loom in the gates of Japanese temples — the colossal guardians of Tōdai-ji's Nandaimon, set up in 1203 by the studios of Unkei and Kaikei, are national treasures — and the wrathful krodha protectors of Himalayan art inherit his stance, his serpents, and his color. His is the oldest continuously-employed job in Buddhist art: someone has to hold the thunderbolt.
lore.archaeology: His material record begins with Gandhāra: schist panels of the second and third centuries CE — now divided among Peshawar, Lahore, the British Museum, and the Musée Guimet — show the Heracles-bodied attendant at the Buddha's shoulder, the first datable images of a bodhisattva-protector. The type traveled: the paired gate-guardians descend from him — the Niō or Heng-Ha pairs of Japan and the Korean Geumgang yeoksa, mouths open and closed, culminating in the Nandaimon colossi of Tōdai-ji (1203, Unkei and Kaikei workshops). Himalayan art fixed his wrathful blue form by the Pāla period, and the three-lords triad became the standard threshold of Tibetan sacred painting.
lore.syncretism: His lineage is a relay of weapons: Indra's vajra — the name is first Indra's epithet, as Monier-Williams records — passed to the Buddha's yakkha enforcer, then to the bodhisattva of power; and in East Asia the single figure split into the paired gate-guardians of every great temple: the Kongōrikishi or Niō of Japan, mouths open and closed, the alpha and omega of the spoken world. The Heracles parallel runs in both directions: as the Greeks lent him a body in Gandhāra, so scholarship reads him as the Buddha's answer to every culture's strong-armed god — Zeus's bolt, Indra's club, Thor's hammer — reassigned to the protection of awakening.
