Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: SHAH-kyuh-moo-nih — ś is the soft palatal 'sh'; the ā of Śākya is long.
pronunciation.note: Śākyamuni is a title, not a personal name: śākya, of the Śākya clan of Kapilavastu, + muni, "sage, silent one" (Monier-Williams) — "the sage of the Śākyas." His personal name was Siddhārtha (Pāli Siddhattha), his clan name Gautama (Pāli Gotama); the tradition itself connects Śākya with the śāka (teak) tree of the clan's founding legend. The restoration keeps the palatal ś and the long ā that the ASCII "Shakyamuni" only approximates. Tier-1 by rule.

domains.title: The Sage of the Śākyas
domains.subtitle: The Renunciation, the Awakening, and the Turning of the Wheel
domains.lead: Śākyamuni is the historical Buddha: Siddhārtha Gautama of the Śākya clan, who left a palace at twenty-nine, awoke under the Bodhi tree at thirty-five, taught for forty-five years across the Ganges plain, and died at eighty between two sāla trees — the one teacher of antiquity whose birthplace an emperor certified in stone.

cards.name: The Bodhi Tree
cards.desc: The aśvattha at Uruvelā under which the ascetic became the Buddha — Bodh Gayā to this day.

cards.name: The Wheel
cards.desc: The Dhammacakra set turning at Sarnath: the first sermon, the middle way, the four noble truths.

cards.name: The Footprints
cards.desc: Buddhapāda — the earliest art dared not show him; his footprints stood for the one who had gone.

cards.name: The Twin Sāla Trees
cards.desc: The couch between two sāla trees at Kusinārā, where the teaching ended in flowers out of season.

symbols.name: The Bodhi tree
symbols.meaning: The axis of the awakening: the tree a whole religion still calls by one name

symbols.name: The earth-touching hand
symbols.meaning: Bhūmisparśa: the gesture that called the earth to witness against Māra

symbols.name: The begging bowl
symbols.meaning: The middle way in an object: neither the palace's gold nor the ash of the fire-ascetics

mythology.lead: The life of Śākyamuni is the best-attested sacred biography of the ancient world — told in the Pāli Nikāyas, versified by Aśvaghoṣa, expanded in the Nidānakathā and the Lalitavistara, and anchored in the ground by Aśoka's own inscriptions.

myths.title: The Birth at Lumbinī
myths.text: Queen Māyā, traveling to her father's house, gave birth standing in the grove at Lumbinī, holding the branch of a sāla tree; the child took seven steps and declared this his last birth. The legends multiplied — the shower of blossoms, the two streams of water, the prophecy of the sage Asita — but the place is fixed in stone: Aśoka's pillar at Rummindei, raised in his twentieth regnal year, reads in plain Prakrit, hida budhe jāte sakyamuni — "here the Buddha Śākyamuni was born." It is the only birthplace of a world teacher certified by a contemporary emperor.

myths.title: The Four Sights and the Going Forth
myths.text: Sheltered in three palaces, the young Śākyan saw what his father had fenced out: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — the four sights the later tradition makes the hinge of his life. In the Majjhima Nikāya's Ariyapariyesanā Sutta (MN 26) he tells it himself: he shaved his hair, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from home into homelessness while still young, in the prime of life, with his parents weeping. The great renunciation — the night ride on Kaṇṭhaka with the groom Channa — became Buddhist art's first epic scene.

lore.culturalLegacy: A third of Asia orders its calendar by him: Vesak keeps his birth, awakening, and death in one full-moon festival; the Buddhist Era counts from his parinibbāna; India's national emblem is the lion capital of the pillar Aśoka raised at his first sermon. The English word "Buddha" is his epithet — "the Awakened" — and Śākyamuni remains the name that ties the cosmic teacher back to a clan, a grove, and a date: the sage of the Śākyas, a man of one valley whose refusal to accept decay as final became a world religion.
lore.archaeology: No sacred biography of antiquity is better grounded. Lumbinī's Rummindei pillar (Aśoka's twentieth year, c. 249 BCE) names the birthplace in words; Kapilavastu's candidate sites (Piprahwa, with its inscribed relic vase of 1898, debated but famous) anchor the clan; Bodh Gayā preserves the seat itself, marked by Aśoka's shrine and the Mahābodhi temple of later centuries; Sarnath holds the Dhāmekh stupa and the lion capital that India took as its national emblem; Kusinārā (Kushinagar) keeps the parinirvāṇa temple and the cremation stupa. The eight original relic stupas of DN 16 began the tradition that Aśoka multiplied, by the later legend, to eighty-four thousand.
lore.syncretism: Every Buddhism is his daughter: the Theravāda of the Pāli canon, the Mahāyāna that set him among countless Buddhas yet kept his biography as the pattern of all awakening, the Vajrayāna that read his life as an already-enlightened being's demonstration. East Asia naturalized the name itself — Chinese Shìjiāmóuní, Japanese Shakamuni, Korean Seokgamoni — and Southeast Asia made his earth-touching gesture the single most common Buddha image on earth. Modern scholarship from Rhys Davids onward has treated him as history's first fully-documented founder: a reformer of the Gangetic plain whose dates, places, and words can be argued from evidence, not legend alone.

entries.meaning: ‘death, the tempter’, the personification of death and desire who assailed the Buddha under the Bodhi tree (from √mṛ ‘to die’), MW.

steps: Sanskrit Māra is written in Devanagari as मार
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: MAH-ruh — the ā is long; two syllables, no ornament.
pronunciation.note: Māra derives from √mṛ, "to die" (Monier-Williams): "death, the killer" — the personification of everything that kills the spiritual life, from desire to death itself. The Pāli canon also knows him as Namuci (an old Vedic name), Pāpimā, "the Evil One," and Kaṇha, "the Dark One." The restoration's whole content is the long ā: the difference between "Mara" and Māra is the difference between a name and the word for death. Tier-1 by rule.

domains.title: The Tempter
domains.subtitle: The Ten Armies, the Three Daughters, and the Defeat of Being Seen
domains.lead: Māra is Death wearing every disguise the mind can manufacture: the lord of the desire-realm who marched his ten armies against the Buddha under the Bodhi tree, sent his three daughters when the armies broke, and lost — not to a weapon, but to being recognized.

cards.name: The Ten Armies
cards.desc: Lust, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth, fear, doubt, obstinacy, glory, and self-praise — the Sutta Nipāta's catalog.

cards.name: The Three Daughters
cards.desc: Taṇhā, Aratī, Rāgā: Craving, Aversion, Passion — the last seduction, sent when the army fled.

cards.name: Girimekhala
cards.desc: His war-elephant, Mountain-high — which knelt, the commentaries say, when the earth itself bore witness.

cards.name: The Flower-Arrowed Bow
cards.desc: Borrowed from Kāma, the love-god: the weapons of desire — beautiful, flowered, and aimed.

symbols.name: The tenfold army
symbols.meaning: The taxonomy of temptation: every assault on resolve sorted by battalion

symbols.name: The flower arrows
symbols.meaning: Desire's camouflage: the shafts that arrive looking like gifts

symbols.name: The shadow at the seat
symbols.meaning: His claim on the Bodhi throne: the ego's final argument, "this place is mine"

mythology.lead: Māra's mythology is the dark half of the Buddhist biography: wherever the teaching advances, the texts station him at the next bend — and his defeats chart the whole path from striving to parinibbāna.

myths.title: The Ten Armies
myths.text: The Sutta Nipāta's Padhāna Sutta gives his order of battle, and it is a psychology textbook in disguise: sensual pleasure is his first army, discontent the second, hunger and thirst the third, craving the fourth, sloth and torpor the fifth, fear the sixth, doubt the seventh, hypocrisy and obstinacy the eighth, gains, fame, and honor the ninth, and the tenth is self-exaltation joined with contempt for others. The Buddha's answer is the template of every later victory: he sees each army for what it is. The tradition's whole art of temptation is this catalog — and its whole defense is recognition.

myths.title: The Night Under the Tree
myths.text: The full assault is told in the Nidānakathā and versified in Aśvaghoṣa's Buddhacarita, whose canto on the Defeat of Māra is Sanskrit poetry's great set-piece: whirlwinds that cannot stir his robe, a rain of rocks that falls as flowers, darkness that will not spread. Mounted on the elephant Girimekhala, Māra advances his final claim — the seat of awakening is his — and calls his army as witness. The bodhisattva answers with the gesture that defines Buddhist art: he touches the earth, and the earth itself thunders witness to his perfections. The elephant kneels; the army scatters; the dawn comes up on an undefeated man.

lore.culturalLegacy: Māra gave Buddhism its psychology of the inner adversary: modern teachers from forest masters to mindfulness clinicians read the ten armies as the mind's own defenses against stillness, and "the Blessed One knows me" as the moment every compulsion loses power — when it is seen. His assault is the most-painted scene in Buddhist art, from Gandhāran panels to the murals of a thousand Thai wats, where the earth-goddess Thoranī wrings a flood from her hair to drown his host. And his name still does its original work: in the teaching languages of three continents, māra remains the common noun for what kills.
lore.archaeology: The assault on the Bodhi seat is among the oldest narrative scenes in Buddhist art: Gandhāran schist panels of the first centuries CE — now in Peshawar, Lahore, and Western collections — show the demon host shrinking from the seated figure, and the Pāla-period steles of the eight great events put the Māra-vijaya at the center of the sacred biography. The bhūmisparśa image that records the victory became the default Buddha of mainland Southeast Asia; Thai, Lao, and Khmer temple murals added the earth-goddess Thoranī wringing the flood from her hair; and Bodh Gayā itself — the vajrāsana, the "diamond throne" beneath the descendant of the very tree — remains the one site on earth where his defeat has a postal address.
lore.syncretism: His oldest document is Vedic: Namuci, the asura of the Ṛgveda whom Indra slew with the foam of the waters, survived in the Pāli canon as Māra's other name — a borrowing as old as the texts themselves. Indian religion lent him Kāma's iconography, the sugarcane bow and flower arrows of the love-god, for desire was his first army. The scholastics then multiplied him: the Mahāyāna handbooks count four Māras — the aggregates, the defilements, death, and the god — turning the tempter into a complete theory of bondage. And the comparison with Satan, inevitable since the first missionaries, is inexact in the instructive way: Māra is no eternal adversary but a god of the highest desire-realm heaven, the Vasavattī, himself mortal, himself subject to the wheel — the ceiling of samsāra, not its enemy.

pronunciation.approximation: 'LAOW-dzuh' — 'lao' like 'loud' without the final 'd', with a dipping tone (down then up); 'zi' like 'dzuh' with the same dipping tone.
pronunciation.note: Lǎozǐ is Tier 1: the tone marks on both syllables preserve the Mandarin citation tones — diacritics the ASCII form loses. The name means 'Old Master,' an honorific rather than a personal name. Whether Lǎozǐ was a historical figure, a composite, or a symbolic founder remains debated among scholars.

domains.title: The Old Master
domains.subtitle: Dao, Wuwei, and the Art of Ruling by Not Ruling
domains.lead:
Lǎozǐ is the legendary author of the Dàodé Jīng, the founding text of Daoism and one of the most translated books in world literature. His name means simply 'Old Master,' and the figure behind it is as elusive as the philosophy he teaches. Whether he was a real archivist of the Zhou court, a constellation of early Daoist teachers, or a literary creation, Lǎozǐ gave classical Chinese thought its most radical statement: the way that can be told is not the eternal way.

His teaching centers on dào (the way), wúwéi (non-coercive action), zìrán (spontaneity), and the return to an uncarved simplicity that precedes all names and schemes.

cards.name: The Dao
cards.desc: The unnamable source of all things; empty yet inexhaustible, it gives birth to heaven and earth.

cards.name: Wuwei
cards.desc: Acting without forced interference, like water that wears down stone by yielding.

cards.name: Uncarved Block
cards.desc: The pǔ, primal simplicity before society carves people into roles, names, and desires.

cards.name: Sage Ruler
cards.desc: The ideal leader governs by emptying hearts and filling bellies, keeping people simple and content.

symbols.name: Ox or water buffalo
symbols.meaning: His legendary mount on which he rode westward out of China, leaving the Dàodé Jīng at the pass

symbols.name: The empty circle
symbols.meaning: The Dao as void and source, the womb from which the ten thousand things emerge

symbols.name: Water
symbols.meaning: The supreme image of wúwéi: soft, yielding, low, yet able to overcome the hard and strong

symbols.name: The uncarved block (pǔ)
symbols.meaning: Primal simplicity; the state before social and linguistic differentiation

symbols.name: The gate (guān)
symbols.meaning: Hán Gǔ Guān, the pass where Lǎozǐ is said to have composed the Dàodé Jīng at the request of Yīn Xī

mythology.lead: Lǎozǐ's mythology is inseparable from the biography invented for him by later tradition and from the enigmatic poems of the Dàodé Jīng. The sage is less a character in narrative than the voice of a teaching, but stories gathered around him to give that teaching a body.

myths.title: The Departure at Hán Gǔ Guān
myths.text: Sīmǎ Qiān's Shǐjì records the most influential biography of Lǎozǐ. Weary of the Zhou court's decay, the old sage mounted a water buffalo and rode west toward the frontier. At Hán Gǔ Guān, the gatekeeper Yīn Xī recognized him and asked him to leave a record of his wisdom before disappearing into the wilderness. Lǎozǐ wrote the five thousand characters of the Dàodé Jīng and then passed beyond the pass, never to be seen again. The story turns the text into a gift given at the edge of the known world.

myths.title: The Nameless Origin
myths.text: The opening of the Dàodé Jīng is not a myth in the usual sense but a cosmogonic statement: 'The Dao that can be told is not the eternal Dao; the name that can be named is not the eternal name.' From the nameless comes the origin of heaven and earth; from the named comes the mother of the ten thousand things. This framing dissolves the distinction between creator and creation, offering a process cosmology in which all things arise and return to the Dao.

lore.culturalLegacy: Lǎozǐ's influence is woven into the texture of East Asian civilization. The Dàodé Jīng is studied, memorized, and quoted from childhood to old age; its aphorisms inform Chinese calligraphy, painting, martial arts, medicine, and governance. Daoist temples honor him as a deity, while scholars continue to debate the date, authorship, and meaning of his book. In the global marketplace of ideas, Lǎozǐ represents an alternative to Western activism and dualism: the sage who wins by yielding, who acts by not acting, and who finds power in emptiness. The Unicode restoration Lǎozǐ preserves the Mandarin tones that distinguish his name from the ordinary words for 'old' and 'master.'
lore.archaeology: The earliest manuscripts of the Dàodé Jīng were discovered at Mawangdui (c. 168 BCE) and Guodian (c. 300 BCE), predating the received text and showing the fluidity of the tradition. These silk and bamboo manuscripts are among the most important archaeological finds for early Chinese thought. Images of Lǎozǐ appear in Han tomb art and in later Daoist iconography as an aged sage riding an ox. Major Daoist temples and palace complexes preserve steles with imperial prefaces to the Dàodé Jīng, and the supposed site of Hán Gǔ Guān remains a place of pilgrimage.
lore.syncretism: Lǎozǐ and his text shaped not only Daoism but Chinese Buddhism, Confucianism, aesthetics, medicine, and statecraft. Early Chinese Buddhists used Daoist terms to translate Indian concepts, a process that permanently colored East Asian Buddhism. Neo-Confucian thinkers like Zhōu Dūnyí and Zhū Xī absorbed Daoist cosmology even while criticizing its quietism. In the modern West, Lǎozǐ became an icon of ecological thinking, anarchism, and mystical spirituality, though these readings often detach him from his political and ritual contexts. The Dàodé Jīng has been translated into more languages than any other Chinese text, making Lǎozǐ a global symbol of wisdom beyond words.

pronunciation.approximation: shee-WAHNG-moo — Xī held high and level like a sustained note, wáng rising from mid to high as in a question, mǔ dipping low and turning up again.
pronunciation.note: 西王母 means 'Queen Mother of the West' — xī (west), wáng (king, sovereign), mǔ (mother). The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Xīwángmǔ (Tones 1-2-3), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Xīwángmǔ preserves the citation tones of all three syllables; in connected speech the third tone on mǔ is often realized as a low half-third tone, but the lexical tone remains Tone 3.

domains.title: The Western Paradise
domains.subtitle: The Peaches of Immortality, Mount Kūnlún, and the Taming of a Wilderness Goddess
domains.lead:
Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West, has the strangest biography of any great goddess in the Chinese tradition. Her oldest portrait, in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, is fearsome: a figure with a tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail, her hair wild, wearing the shèng headdress, presiding over plague and calamity from Mount Kūnlún at the western edge of the world. She is not yet the serene sovereign of later ages — she is the numinous power of the untamed west itself.

Across the Han dynasty she was refined, age by age, into the great goddess of the western paradise: keeper of the Peaches of Immortality, which ripen once every three thousand years; host of the Peach Banquet; bestower of the elixir that lifts Cháng'é to the moon; and, in the fullness of Taoist theology, the sovereign of yin and the west, balanced against Dōngwánggōng, the King Father of the East. The wilderness was never banished from her — it was enthroned.

cards.name: Mount Kūnlún
cards.desc: Her paradise stands on Mount Kūnlún at the western edge of the world, the axis where heaven leans down to meet the wild earth.

cards.name: The Peaches of Immortality
cards.desc: The pántáo ripen once every three thousand years; to taste one is to step outside death's jurisdiction — which is why the Monkey King could not resist them.

cards.name: Tiger's Teeth, Leopard's Tail
cards.desc: Her archaic form keeps its claws: the Shān Hǎi Jīng gives her a tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail, the regalia of a mistress of plague and calamity.

cards.name: Sovereign of Yin and the West
cards.desc: In mature Taoist theology she rules yin, the west, and all goddesses, balanced against Dōngwánggōng's yang and east — the two poles of a complete cosmos.

symbols.name: The shèng headdress
symbols.meaning: Her ancient insignia of authority — the distinctive headdress she wears even in her oldest, wildest images

symbols.name: Tiger's teeth and leopard's tail
symbols.meaning: The zoomorphic vestiges of her primordial form, marking her dominion over plague and calamity

symbols.name: The Peaches of Immortality
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over death itself — fruit that ripens once in three thousand years and frees the eater from mortality

symbols.name: Mount Kūnlún
symbols.meaning: The western paradise at the edge of the world, where her palace and orchards stand

symbols.name: The tallies
symbols.meaning: The tokens her Han-era devotees carried from commandery to commandery as pledges of her protection and long life

mythology.lead: Xīwángmǔ's myths trace an arc no other Chinese deity matches: from wilderness terror to the most gracious sovereign of the Taoist heavens. Each age kept something of the last, so that the serene hostess of the Peach Banquet still carries the teeth and tail of the mountain power she once was.

myths.title: The Fearsome Portrait
myths.text: In the Classic of Mountains and Seas, the oldest surviving description, the Queen Mother is not a queen at all in the courtly sense. She has a tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail, her hair unbound beneath the shèng headdress, and she presides over plague and calamity from Mount Kūnlún. She is the personified danger of the far west — the lands beyond the pale of the settled world, where the sun goes down into mystery. Later ages would clothe her in silk, but the earliest text keeps her wild.

myths.title: The Elixir for Hòuyì
myths.text: It is the Queen Mother who holds the elixir of immortality, and it is she who grants it to Hòuyì, the archer who shot down the nine excess suns. The gift does not stay in his hands: it becomes Cháng'é's ascension to the moon. The versions differ — in some tellings Cháng'é takes the elixir unbidden, in others to keep it from unworthy hands — but the constant is the source: immortality flows from the Queen Mother's store, and no one rises to the heavens except through her treasury.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Queen Mother never retired from the heavens. In Taoist temples across Taiwan and the diaspora she is venerated still, often under the title Golden Mother of the Jasper Pool, and her birthday is kept with festival observance. In art she rides phoenixes and cranes through centuries of painting, lacquer, and embroidery, and the immortal peach she tends became the standard emblem of longevity, pressed into birthday buns and painted onto porcelain as a wish for long life. The Journey to the West made her banquet immortal in another sense: every screen adaptation of the Monkey King's career — film, television, animation, games — must sooner or later raid her orchard. She remains what she has been since the Han mirrors first invoked her for blessing: the great goddess at the western edge of the world, holding the one treasure every mortal wants and no one may take uninvited.
lore.archaeology: The Queen Mother's earliest textual portrait is in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, compiled from Warring States through Han materials (roughly 4th–1st centuries BCE), where she appears with tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail on Mount Kūnlún. Her great material flourishing is Han: bronze mirrors invoke her by name for blessing and long life, and tomb reliefs and murals — most famously the Wu Liang shrine of the 2nd century CE — show her enthroned in the west, increasingly paired with Dōngwánggōng in the east. The Book of Han preserves the documentary trace of her popular cult in the millenarian movement of 3 BCE, when her tallies passed through the commanderies. By the medieval period, Taoist scriptures and liturgical texts had raised her to the summit of the goddess hierarchy, the form in which she has been worshipped ever since.
lore.syncretism: The Queen Mother travelled with Chinese letters and liturgy across East Asia. In Japan she is read Seiōbo, appearing in painting, garden imagery, and the literary imagination as the hostess of the western orchard; in Korea she is Seowangmo, present in folklore and shamanic song; in Vietnamese she is Tây Vương Mẫu, her name borne into the southern reception of the Taoist pantheon. Within China her deepest transformation was her absorption into organized Taoism, where she rose to the summit of the celestial hierarchy as sovereign of yin and the west, paired with Dōngwánggōng, the King Father of the East, as the balanced poles of the cosmos. Buddhist storytellers did not so much absorb her as borrow her orchard: the immortality peaches and the great banquet pass freely between Taoist and popular-Buddhist narrative worlds, and it is in that shared space that the Journey to the West stages her most famous scene.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 西王母, written identically in traditional and simplified characters — none of the three graphs was altered in the twentieth-century simplification. Pinyin Xīwángmǔ (Tones 1-2-3) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries: xī (west, Tone 1), wáng (sovereign, Tone 2), mǔ (mother, Tone 3). The registrable Unicode restoration uses the tone-marked Pinyin rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original characters in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable; the tone marks ī, á, and ǔ carry the citation tones that plain ASCII drops.

entries.domain: Storm God, Lord of the Heavens

variants.note: Ugaritic/Phoenician ʿayin (ʿ) is the ideal consonant, but is rejected by the DNS root zone

etymology.derivation: From Common Semitic baʿlu, "lord"; the pharyngeal is written with Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) as the only registrable Unicode workaround

steps: The name is written 𐎁𐎓𐎍 in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet.
Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability.
Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons.
The Unicode restoration Baꜥal is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-ahl' — the middle consonant is a deep, throaty 'ʿ' (like Arabic ع), not a glottal stop or silent letter.
pronunciation.note: Baꜥal is technically a title ('Lord') that became a name. The ideal form includes Semitic ʿayin, which is blocked at the DNS root; the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) is the registrable compromise. The name is Tier 1 because it preserves the ʿayin as a distinctive phoneme — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses. In texts he is often 'Baꜥlu-Haddu' or simply the 'Rider on the Clouds.'

domains.title: Rider on the Clouds
domains.subtitle: Storm, Fertility, and Divine Kingship
domains.lead: Baꜥal is the storm made king. In a land where rain is life and drought is death, he is the deity who rides the clouds, shatters the sea-monster, and opens his palace windows so that the rains may fall. He is young, vigorous, and hungry for a throne — yet even his kingship depends on the older god Ēl. The Baꜥal Cycle is the great myth of his rise, death, and return.

cards.name: Storm and Thunder
cards.desc: His voice is thunder, his weapon lightning; he gathers clouds, wind, and rain around his chariot.

cards.name: Lord of Mount Zaphon
cards.desc: His cedar palace stands on the mountain of the north, the axis mundi from which he governs the cosmos.

cards.name: Fertility of Field and Flock
cards.desc: When he lives, bread, wine, and oil abound; when he descends to Mot, the land withers.

cards.name: Divine Warrior
cards.desc: He defeats Yamm, the primordial Sea, and shatters the seven-headed serpent Lotan.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: His father's animal and a sign of fertility and storm power

symbols.name: Lightning club
symbols.meaning: The divine weapon forged by Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs

symbols.name: Window
symbols.meaning: The palace window through which Baꜥal's thunder and rain go forth to the world

symbols.name: Cloud chariot
symbols.meaning: His vehicle, the storm cloud itself

mythology.lead: The Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle (KTU 1.1–1.6) is the central myth of Canaanite religion. It tells how Baꜥal wins kingship from the chaotic Sea, builds his palace, confronts Death, and returns to bring back the rains. The cycle is a seasonal drama of drought and renewal, but also a political statement about divine legitimacy.

myths.title: Baꜥal and Yamm
myths.text: Ēl grants kingship to Yamm, the Sea, who sends messengers demanding that Baꜥal be delivered as a slave. Baꜥal refuses. The craftsman god Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs forges two clubs, Yagrush ('Chaser') and Ayamur ('Driver'). With them Baꜥal strikes Yamm on the skull and scatters the chaotic waters, claiming the throne for himself (KTU 1.2 iv).

myths.title: The Palace on Zaphon
myths.text: Victorious, Baꜥal still has no palace. He sends ꜥAnat to petition Ēl, but it is Asherah who finally secures permission. Kothar-wa-Ḫasīs builds a cedar palace on Mount Zaphon. Baꜥal hesitates over a window — it will let his voice out, but it may also let Death in. He opens it, and his thunder resounds across the earth (KTU 1.3–1.4).

lore.culturalLegacy: No Canaanite name was more reviled or more enduring than Baꜥal. The prophets of Israel spent generations attacking his cult, yet his imagery — the storm god who rides the clouds, defeats the sea, and sends rain — was quietly absorbed into the figure of Yahweh. In the New Testament, Beelzebub ('Lord of the Flies,' probably a distortion of Baꜥal-Zebul, 'Prince Baꜥal') becomes a name for Satan. In modern fantasy and occult literature, Baal persists as a demon-king. But beneath the polemic remains the old Levantine truth: a god of storm and fertility whose absence means drought and whose return means life.
lore.archaeology: The Temple of Baal at Ugarit, excavated by Claude Schaeffer, yielded stelae, votive anchors, and the Baʿal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6). The Karatepe bilingual pairs Baʿal with King Azatiwada in Phoenician and Luwian. At Palmyra the great Temple of Baal-Shamin dominated the city; at Carthage, Baʿal-Hammon received child sacrifice in the tophet sanctuary. Hazor, Megiddo, and Mount Carmel provide Levantine cultic contexts attacked by biblical polemic.
lore.syncretism: Baꜥal is inseparable from the older West Semitic storm god Hadad/Haddu; in texts and inscriptions the two names are often combined as Baꜥal-Haddu. In Mesopotamia he was equated with Adad (dIM), and in Egypt he influenced the Levantine storm god imported during the New Kingdom. The Greeks saw in him a Near Eastern Zeus, a sky-storm king, though they did not directly worship him. In the Hebrew Bible, Baꜥal became the archetype of apostasy, the 'false god' opposed by Elijah on Mount Carmel. Later Jewish and Christian tradition demonized the name, turning 'Baal' into a byword for idolatry and, in medieval occultism, for a class of demons.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (b-ʿ-l), literally 'lord.' The middle sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative. Because Semitic ʿayin is blocked at the DNS root, PUNICODEX renders it with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724). In many contexts the name is an appellative rather than a personal name; at Ugarit the storm god is often called Baꜥlu-Haddu.

entries.meaning: The high god of the Canaanite pantheon; the common Semitic word for "god" and a divine name

variants.note: Lowercase display form of the owned domain

etymology.derivation: From Common Semitic ʾil-/ʾēl, with long /ē/ preserved by the macron

steps: The name is written 𐎛𐎍 in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet.

Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons.
The Unicode restoration Ēl is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AYLE' — like 'ale' with a long vowel and a slight glottal catch at the beginning; the name is short and resonant.
pronunciation.note: Ēl is both a proper name and the common Semitic word for 'god.' The macron marks the long vowel inferred from Hebrew אֵל and Ugaritic spellings. As a Tier-1 name it preserves length (macron) — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: Father of Years, Bull of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Supreme God, Creator, and King of the Divine Assembly
domains.lead: Ēl is the ancient one at the center of the Canaanite pantheon. He is the father of gods and men, the Bull whose creative power generates the divine assembly, and the king whose distant authority nonetheless settles every dispute. Unlike Baꜥal, who acts, Ēl decrees. His throne is at the source of the rivers; his tent is where the gods come to receive judgment.

cards.name: Creator of Creatures
cards.desc: His epithet bny bnwt, 'Creator of Creatures,' marks him as the ultimate source of all life.

cards.name: Bull El
cards.desc: The bull is his animal: strength, fertility, and patriarchal authority concentrated in one image.

cards.name: King and Judge
cards.desc: The divine assembly gathers before him; kingship is conferred by his word, whether for Baꜥal or for Athtar.

cards.name: Father of Gods and Men
cards.desc: He is 'ab ʾilm, 'father of the gods,' and 'ab ʾadmi, 'father of man' — the origin of all genealogies.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: Strength, fertility, and the patriarchal authority of the high god

symbols.name: Grey beard
symbols.meaning: His venerable age and wisdom; he is the 'father of years'

symbols.name: Source of rivers
symbols.meaning: The cosmic freshwater spring where his tent stands

symbols.name: Winged sun or throne
symbols.meaning: His exalted kingship over the divine council

mythology.lead: Ēl appears in almost every major Ugaritic myth, yet he rarely takes center stage. He is the one appealed to, the one who gives or withholds blessing, the one whose laughter signals cosmic assent. His mythology is the mythology of authority itself — distant, benevolent, sometimes foolish, always final.

myths.title: The Divine Kingmaker
myths.text: In KTU 1.2 iii, Ēl initially grants kingship to Yamm, the Sea. Later, persuaded by Asherah, he approves Baꜥal's palace and kingship (KTU 1.3 v 36; 1.4 iv 48). Even Baꜥal's triumphant reign depends on the old king's word. Ēl is not the warrior; he is the source from which warrior-kingship flows.

myths.title: Father of Years
myths.text: When messengers approach Ēl, they find him at the source of the rivers, in the midst of the divine assembly. His epithet ab šnm, 'father of years,' emphasizes that he is older than the seasons themselves. Yet he is also approachable, even convivial: in KTU 1.114 he gets drunk at a banquet and must be helped home.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ēl did not disappear; he was subsumed. His name lives in the word 'God' itself across the Semitic languages, in countless theophoric personal names, and in the biblical title El Shaddai. The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is partly shaped by the old Canaanite high god: distant, paternal, creator, judge. In modern religious studies, Ēl has become a test case for how monotheism emerged not by inventing a new deity but by elevating and narrowing an old one. To name Ēl is therefore to name a ancestor shared by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — and by the Canaanite religion they eventually superseded.
lore.archaeology: At Ugarit the Baʿal Cycle tablets (KTU 1.1–1.6) and the Epic of Keret (KTU 1.14–1.16) name ʾil as supreme judge and royal patron. The Karatepe bilingual invokes El as creator of the earth. Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions preserve El names in an Israelite religious context, while Tel Arad ostraca, Shechem, and Jerusalem temple texts show his continued prestige. His name underlies Biblical ʾĒl, ʾĒl ʿElyôn, and theophoric names such as Israel and Gabriel.
lore.syncretism: Ēl is the common Semitic god par excellence. His name underlies Hebrew ʾĒl and its compounds (Israel, Gabriel, Michael), and it survives in Arabic Allāh (< al-ʾilāh, 'the God'). In the Greek world, the Phoenician high god was identified with Kronos, the aged father of Zeus, while Baꜥal was compared to Zeus himself. In Hurrian and Hittite treaties, Ēl appears as Elkunirša, paired with Asherah/Ašertu. The biblical tradition eventually absorbed Ēl into Yahweh: many of Israel's oldest poems use ʾĒl as a name or title for their own god, and the epithet ʾĒl Shaddai may preserve a Canaanite title of the high god.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎛𐎍 (ʾ-i-l), the common word for 'god' as well as the proper name of the high god. Phoenician writes 𐤀𐤋 (ʾ-l). The macron over ē in Ēl marks the long vowel inferred from Hebrew אֵל and from comparative Semitic evidence. The name is both appellative and proper name, a fact that makes Ēl uniquely elusive and foundational.

entries.meaning: Canaanite warrior goddess, sister and ally of Baꜥal
entries.domain: Goddess of War and the Hunt

variants.note: Ugaritic/Phoenician ʿayin (ʿ) is ideal but not registrable at the DNS root

etymology.derivation: From Ugaritic ʿnṯ/ʿnt; the initial pharyngeal is rendered with Egyptian Ain (ꜥ) as the registrable workaround

steps: The name is written 𐎓𐎐𐎚 in the Ugaritic cuneiform alphabet.
Ugaritic ʿayin is rendered with Egyptological Ain (ꜥ) for DNS registrability.
Long vowels are reconstructed from Hebrew and Akkadian cognates and marked with macrons.
The Unicode restoration ꜥAnat is registrable in .com; the Ugaritic cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-naht' — start with a rough, throaty 'ah' (like Arabic ع), then 'naht' with a crisp final t.
pronunciation.note: The ideal spelling would use Semitic ʿayin (ʿ), but that character is rejected by the DNS root zone. We therefore render the pharyngeal with the Egyptological Ain (ꜥ, U+A724), the only registrable Unicode workaround that signals the original consonant. The name is Tier 1: it preserves the ʿayin (a distinctive phoneme) — a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: Maiden of Battles
domains.subtitle: War, Hunt, and Ferocious Loyalty
domains.lead: ꜥAnat is the maiden who refuses to grow up into the domestic sphere. In the Ugaritic texts she is neither wife nor mother but a singular force: a warrior who wades knee-deep in the blood of her enemies, a huntress who ranges the wilderness, and the most faithful ally of Baꜥal. Her title btlt — "maiden" — marks her as marriageable in social terms, yet mythologically she remains unattached, unpredictable, and absolutely devoted to her brother.

cards.name: Divine Warfare
cards.desc: She fights both armies and cosmic foes, wielding bow, spear, and sword; KTU 1.3 ii describes her battle fury in graphic detail.

cards.name: The Hunt
cards.desc: She ranges mountains and heights in search of game or vengeance; her pursuit of Aqhat turns the hunt into tragic myth.

cards.name: Loyal Sister
cards.desc: Baꜥal's most passionate advocate; she confronts El, avenges Baꜥal's death, and restores the storm to the world.

cards.name: Unbound Feminine Power
cards.desc: A young woman operating in male-coded spheres without condemnation — a figure of autonomous, even terrifying, agency.

symbols.name: Bow
symbols.meaning: Her favored weapon and the cause of the Aqhat tragedy

symbols.name: Spear and sword
symbols.meaning: Instruments of her martial rage against divine and human armies

symbols.name: Lion
symbols.meaning: Her leonine ferocity; she is linked to the Mistress of Animals tradition

symbols.name: Dew and rain
symbols.meaning: After battle she is purified by the dew of heaven and the rain of the Cloud-Rider

mythology.lead: ꜥAnat's mythology is preserved chiefly in the Ugaritic Baꜥal Cycle and the Epic of Aqhat. She is not a fertility goddess in the usual sense; she is force itself, concentrated in a young woman's body, and her stories turn on violence, loyalty, and the refusal to accept limits.

myths.title: Wading in Blood
myths.text: In KTU 1.3 ii, ꜥAnat returns from battle in exultation: 'Heads rolled beneath her like balls, hands flew over her like locusts.' She fastens severed heads to her back and hands to her belt, then washes herself clean in the dew sent by Baꜥal, the Rider on the Clouds. The scene is shocking not because she is evil but because she is unrestrained — war as ecstasy, not duty.

myths.title: Avenger of Baꜥal
myths.text: When Mot, Death, swallows Baꜥal and the rains fail, ꜥAnat searches the wilderness for her brother. Finding Mot, she attacks him with a sword, winnows him like grain, burns him, grinds him, and scatters him in a field (KTU 1.6 ii 30–35). Her violence is the engine of Baꜥal's return and the renewal of fertility.

lore.culturalLegacy: The name ꜥAnat echoes across millennia in unexpected ways. The Israelite town of Anathoth (Jeremiah's birthplace) carries her name. Medieval Jewish folklore remembered her in the figure of the warrior woman, and modern Levantine archaeology has recovered countless amulets and plaques bearing her image. In contemporary literature, film, and Neopagan practice, Anat resurfaces as an icon of untamed female power — a goddess who will not be domesticated, who fights for those she loves, and who makes the boundaries between love and violence uncomfortably thin.
lore.archaeology: The Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU 1.3, 1.6, 1.17–19) preserve her warrior mythology in alphabetic cuneiform. In Egypt, bronze figurines and scarabs from Tanis, Memphis, and the eastern Delta identify her as ꜥnt(t), a Levantine war goddess absorbed into the New Kingdom pantheon. The stela from Beth-Shean and Israelite place names such as Anathoth and the epithet Shamgar ben-Anath attest her cult west of the Jordan.
lore.syncretism: In Egypt, ꜥAnat was worshipped as a war goddess alongside her sister Aštart, especially at Tanis and Memphis; she appears on scarabs and in the Egyptian pantheon as ꜥnt(t). Greeks and Romans later identified her with Athena/Minerva in her martial aspect. Some scholars have argued for an early equation with the Mesopotamian Ishtar/Inanna, since both are young, autonomous warrior goddesses, but the Ugaritic texts treat ꜥAnat as a distinct Levantine figure. In the Hebrew Bible, place names such as Anathoth preserve her memory without endorsing her cult.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is written in Ugaritic alphabetic cuneiform as 𐎓𐎐𐎚 (ʿ-n-t). The first sign is ʿayin, a voiced pharyngeal fricative absent from English and from standard Latin transcription. Because the standard IPA ʿ is blocked at the DNS root, PUNICODEX represents it with the Latin Capital/Small Letter Egyptological Ain (ꜥ / U+A724), preserving visual recognition while remaining registrable.

entries.meaning: She who treads on the sea

steps: The name is written 𐤀𐤔𐤓𐤕 in the Phoenician abjad.
Phoenician writing records consonants only; vowels are supplied by modern scholars from cognate languages.
The final vowel markings in the transliteration are inferred from older Northwest Semitic case endings.
The Unicode restoration Ašeratu is registrable in .com; the Phoenician form is not in the .com IDN table.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ah-she-RAH-too' — begin with a slight catch in the throat, then 'she' with a crisp sh, roll or tap the r, and end with 'rah-too'.
pronunciation.note: Reconstruction follows the Phoenician/Ugaritic nominative form ʾAšeratu. The initial consonant is a glottal stop (aleph), not a pharyngeal, so the PUNICODEX form uses plain A rather than Egyptological Ain. The medial š marks the Canaanite/Phoenician reflex of Proto-Semitic *ṯ, while Ugaritic retains the older ṯ (probably [θ]); the final -u is the case vowel, dropped in Hebrew Asherah. Tier 1: the caron on š preserves a distinctive Semitic phoneme — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses. Sources: KTU, CIS/KAI, Smith The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Day Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan.

domains.title: She Who Treads the Sea
domains.subtitle: Mother of the Gods, Consort of Ēl
domains.lead: Ašeratu is the great mother of the Canaanite pantheon, the consort of Ēl and the goddess whose footsteps quiet the sea. Her full Ugaritic title rbt ʾaṯrt ym — “Lady Ašeratu of the Sea” — and the Phoenician form ʾšrt name her as both cosmic navigator and divine ancestress. Where Ēl is the distant father, Ašeratu is the active queen mother who knows how to approach him.

cards.name: Mother of the Gods
cards.desc: Called qnyt ʾilm, 'Creatress of the Gods'; the seventy sons of Ašeratu populate the divine council (KTU 1.4 vi 46).

cards.name: Lady of the Sea
cards.desc: Her epithet rbt ʾaṯrt ym links her to the Mediterranean, to fishing, and to the cosmic waters tamed by her presence.

cards.name: Royal Intercessor
cards.desc: In KTU 1.4 she travels to Ēl's tent, petitions on Baꜥal's behalf, and secures permission for the storm-god's palace.

cards.name: Domestic Sovereignty
cards.desc: Spindle, weaving, and nursing imagery mark her as the divine model of women's labor raised to cosmic scale.

symbols.name: Sea
symbols.meaning: The waters she treads and tames, source of fertility and commerce for coastal Ugarit

symbols.name: Tree or pole
symbols.meaning: The biblical ʾăšērâ, a wooden cult object that represents or embodies her presence

symbols.name: Spindle
symbols.meaning: Her attribute in Ugaritic and Hittite iconography; symbol of feminine labor and cosmic order

symbols.name: Donkey
symbols.meaning: The beast she rides when approaching Ēl's tent in the Baꜥal Cycle

symbols.name: Nursing breast
symbols.meaning: The nourishment she gives to gods and kings; kings may be called her nurslings

mythology.lead: Ašeratu's mythology is the mythology of influence. She does not fight; she intercedes. Her journeys to Ēl's tent, her titles as creatrix and nurse, and her treading of the sea all mark her as the figure who turns raw divine power into ordered legitimacy.

myths.title: The Queen Mother's Journey
myths.text: In KTU 1.4, Baꜥal longs for a palace but cannot win Ēl's approval directly. He turns to Ašeratu. She prepares herself with care, harnesses her donkey, and travels to the source of the divine rivers. There she prostrates before Ēl, praises his wisdom, and asks that Baꜥal be granted a house 'like the gods'. Ēl laughs, welcomes her, and consents. Without her diplomacy, Baꜥal would remain homeless.

myths.title: Creatress of the Gods
myths.text: Ašeratu is repeatedly called qnyt ʾilm, 'Creatress of the Gods' (KTU 1.3 v 25–26; 1.4 i 23; iii 26). The seventy sons of Ašeratu (KTU 1.4 vi 46) are the divine council itself; when Baꜥal disappears into Mot's realm, it is she who is asked to choose a successor from among her sons.

lore.culturalLegacy: Ašeratu is the divine feminine the Hebrew Bible tried to erase and failed. Her tree, her pole, and her cakes survived in folk religion; her name survived in place names and theophoric roots; her image survived, some argue, in the Shekhinah and in the maternal iconography of the Virgin Mary. Modern feminist theologians and Canaanite- and Goddess-oriented movements have reclaimed her as a symbol of the sacred feminine suppressed by later monotheism. To restore her name with the Phoenician š and the Ugaritic nominative -u is to recover a sound that once rang in temples from Ras Shamra to Jerusalem.
lore.archaeology: The Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU 1.3–1.4, 1.23) preserve Ašeratu's titles and intercessory role in alphabetic cuneiform. The Hittite Elkunirša myth from Boğazköy-Hattusa adapts her as Ašertu, consort of Elkunirša and a weaver of divine children. Phoenician inscriptions (CIS/KAI) attest ʾšrt in theophoric names. In Israel and Judah, the Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom inscriptions, the Taanach cult stands, and the Jerusalem temple asherah (2 Kings 23) provide material and textual witnesses to her contested cult.
lore.syncretism: Ašeratu's reach extended across the ancient Near East. In Hittite treaties she appears as Ašertu, the consort of Elkunirša and a weaving goddess with dozens of divine children. In Egypt she was identified with Hathor and venerated as Qudšu, 'Holiness.' In Israel and Judah she became the Bible's most controversial goddess: the Asherah, the Queen of Heaven, perhaps the consort of Yahweh in inscriptions from Kuntillet ʿAjrud and Khirbet el-Qom. The Deuteronomistic reformers condemned her wooden pole and the women who baked cakes for her, but the very polemics testify to her persistent hold.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎀𐎘𐎗𐎚 (ʾ-a-ṯ-r-t), while Phoenician writes 𐤀𐤔𐤓𐤕 (ʾ-š-r-t). The caron on š marks the Canaanite/Phoenician reflex of the consonant; Ugaritic retains the older ṯ, probably [θ]. The final -u of Ašeratu is the nominative case vowel of the divine name, dropped in Hebrew אֲשֵׁרָה. The initial consonant is a glottal stop (aleph), not a pharyngeal, so the PUNICODEX form uses plain A. Tier 1: the š preserves a distinctive Semitic phoneme — a distinctive diacritic the ASCII form loses.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MOHT' — one syllable with a long, drawn-out o (or oo) and a crisp final t.
pronunciation.note: The name is the Canaanite word for 'death.' The macron on the registrable Mōt signals vowel length, not a fixed quality: Phoenician has mūt, Hebrew māwet, and Ugaritic mt gives no vowels. Sources: KTU, CIS/KAI, Smith The Ugaritic Baal Cycle, Day Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan.

domains.title: The Devouring King
domains.subtitle: Death, Drought, and the Underworld
domains.lead: Mōt is the personified appetite of death in Canaanite myth — not a reaper with a scythe but a being whose throat is a chasm and whose jaws grind gods and mortals alike. In the Baꜥal Cycle he is the necessary opposite of the storm-god: where Baꜥal brings rain, Mōt brings the parched season when growth stops and the world turns to dust.

cards.name: Personified Death
cards.desc: The name itself is the Canaanite word for death; in Ugaritic he is a god, not merely an abstraction.

cards.name: Insatiable Hunger
cards.desc: KTU 1.5 i describes a throat like a lion's, a gullet like a whale's, and an appetite that swallows armies.

cards.name: Seasonal Drought
cards.desc: His victory over Baꜥal brings years of barrenness; his defeat restores the rains and the fertility of the land.

cards.name: Underworld Sovereign
cards.desc: He rules the arṣ, the land of death to which every living thing must eventually descend.

symbols.name: Devouring mouth
symbols.meaning: His throat is the underworld itself; his jaws crush gods and mortals

symbols.name: Dust and dry earth
symbols.meaning: The landscape of his kingdom and the sign of his victory over Baꜥal

symbols.name: Sword and winnowing fan
symbols.meaning: The tools ꜥAnat uses to split, scatter, and destroy him

symbols.name: Seven portions
symbols.meaning: The meal Mōt demands; he eats by double handfuls and drinks a river

symbols.name: Desert wasteland
symbols.meaning: The parched country where death's rule is felt most keenly

mythology.lead: Mōt's mythology is the dark season of the year made personal. His stories are preserved in the Baꜥal Cycle, where he confronts Baꜥal, kills him, and is in turn destroyed and reborn in a cycle that explains drought, death, and the return of fertility.

myths.title: The Summons
myths.text: In KTU 1.4 vii–viii, Mōt sends word to Baꜥal: because he was not invited to the storm-god's feast, he will feast on Baꜥal himself. His messengers describe a throat like a lion's, a gullet like a whale's, and an appetite that devours by the double handful. Baꜥal's own envoys are warned not to come too close, 'lest he make you like a lamb in his mouth' (KTU 1.4 viii 17–20).

myths.title: The Descent and Death
myths.text: In KTU 1.5, Baꜥal submits. He descends into Mōt's mouth and dies. Ēl mourns on the ground, cutting himself with stones; the rains fail and the earth grows dry. Even the high god cannot reverse Mōt's claim — at least, not directly. The cosmos enters the season of death.

lore.culturalLegacy: Mōt's name survives in Hebrew māwet, Arabic mawt, and the Semitic root for death itself. His myth helped shape later personifications of death in biblical and apocalyptic literature, and the Baꜥal-Mōt cycle has long fascinated scholars of ancient religion as a Near Eastern parallel to — and a warning against facile equations with — later dying-and-rising god traditions. In modern fantasy, games, and Neopagan reconstructions, Mōt appears as the Canaanite lord of the underworld, a reminder that every pantheon must make room for the figure who says, 'All feasting ends here.'
lore.archaeology: The Baꜥal Cycle tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU 1.4–1.6) are the principal witnesses to Mōt's mythology, preserving his threats, his swallowing of Baꜥal, and his dismemberment by ꜥAnat in alphabetic cuneiform. The Hellenistic Phoenician cosmogony survives only in the excerpts of Philo of Byblos transmitted by Eusebius. No distinct sanctuary of Mōt has been identified, but the widespread West Semitic word for death — Ugaritic mt, Phoenician mūt, Hebrew māwet, Akkadian mūtu — testifies to the concept's deep cultural reach.
lore.syncretism: The Hellenistic Phoenician account preserved by Eusebius of Caesarea — quoting Philo of Byblos, who summarized Sanchuniathon — makes Mōt (Muth) a son of El and Rhea, deified after death and identified by the Phoenicians with the Greek Thanatos and Pluto. A more speculative cosmogonic strand in the same tradition makes Mōt arise from primal mud or putrefaction, the source from which the seeds of creation emerge. In the Hebrew Bible the common noun māwet ('death') sometimes appears almost personified, especially in Hosea 13:14, suggesting that the Canaanite figure lingered in Israelite imagination even where he was no longer worshipped.
lore.originalScriptNote: Ugaritic writes the name 𐎎𐎚 (m-t), Phoenician 𐤌𐤕 (m-t), and Hebrew מות (m-w-t). The macron over ō in Mōt marks a reconstructed long vowel; the actual quality differs by dialect (Phoenician mūt, Hebrew māwet), while Ugaritic mt is vowelless in writing. The name is the common Canaanite word for 'death,' here personified as a god. Tier 1: the macron preserves a reconstructed long vowel.

pronunciation.note: Šāpšu is Tier-1: the caron on š and the macron on ā are distinctive features the ASCII form loses. The Ugaritic name is conventionally vocalized Šapšu or Šāpšu; the final u reflects the nominative case ending common in scholarly transliteration.

domains.title: Torch of the Gods
domains.subtitle: Sun, Justice, and the Messenger of El
domains.lead: Šāpšu is the sun goddess of Ugarit and Phoenicia, the brilliant torch that travels across the sky and descends into the underworld at evening. Unlike the Egyptian male sun god Ra, Šāpshu is female, a daughter of El who sees everything and carries messages between gods and mortals. Her light exposes lies, guides the dead, and warms the fields of the Levant.

cards.name: The Solar Torch
cards.desc: She is called 'Šāpšu the Torch' and 'the Luminary of the Gods' in Ugaritic hymns.

cards.name: All-Seeing Eye
cards.desc: Her light reveals hidden crimes and exposes those who break oaths before the gods.

cards.name: Guide of the Dead
cards.desc: She descends into the underworld and leads the shades of the dead to their rest.

cards.name: Messenger of El
cards.desc: She carries the decrees of the high god across heaven, earth, and the realm below.

symbols.name: Solar disk with rays
symbols.meaning: The sun's body and the light that penetrates every hidden corner

symbols.name: Torch or lamp
symbols.meaning: Her epithet 'torch of the gods' and her role as divine messenger

symbols.name: Upraised hand or winged sun
symbols.meaning: The protective solar presence common in Phoenician and Aramaean iconography

symbols.name: Boat or chariot
symbols.meaning: The vehicle that carries her across the day sky and through the underworld at night

mythology.lead: Šāpshu's mythology is woven through the Baal Cycle and Ugaritic ritual texts. She does not fight like Anat or Baal; she illuminates, witnesses, and transmits divine will. Her descent into the underworld marks the boundary between day and night, life and death.

myths.title: Šāpshu Warns Baal
myths.text: In KTU 1.4, when Baal's enemies plot against him, Šāpshu sees their schemes and warns the storm god. Her all-seeing light makes her the divine intelligence network of the pantheon: nothing done in darkness escapes her. She is loyal to Baal and helps preserve the order he establishes after defeating Yām.

myths.title: The Sun's Descent into the Underworld
myths.text: Ugaritic and later Phoenician texts describe Šāpshu descending at evening to the land of the dead, lighting the way for the rpum (shades or ancestors). Her nightly journey links her to the Mesopotamian sun god Shamash and the Greek Helios, though she remains distinctively Levantine and female.

lore.culturalLegacy: The name Šāpshu survives in scholarly discussions of Canaanite religion and in the Phoenician inscriptions that mention her. She is less visible in popular culture than Anat or Asherah, but her role as a female sun goddess and divine witness challenges the common assumption that sun deities are always male. Modern feminist scholarship and Neopagan practice have reclaimed her as a symbol of clarity, justice, and the luminous feminine.
lore.archaeology: Šāpshu is attested in the Ugaritic tablets from Ras Shamra (KTU corpus) and in Phoenician inscriptions across the Mediterranean. Her solar disk and winged sun imagery appear on Phoenician seals, ivories, and stelae. The Ugaritic texts preserve hymns and ritual references that show her importance in royal cult and daily religion, though no temple exclusively dedicated to her has been securely identified.
lore.syncretism: Šāpshu corresponds to the Mesopotamian Shamash and the later Aramaic/Achaemenid Mithra as a solar deity of justice and oath. She also overlaps with the Egyptian Hathor in her role as a cow or sun-goddess who guides the dead. In the Hebrew Bible, the common noun šemeš ('sun') is never personified as a goddess, but the Ugaritic evidence shows that Northwest Semitic peoples once knew the sun as female. The winged sun disk of Phoenician and Israelite iconography may carry echoes of her protective radiance.

pronunciation.approximation: DAH-ghan — both the first 'a' is long like 'father,' and the second 'a' is short; stress falls on the long first syllable.
pronunciation.note: Dāgan is a Tier-1 restoration because the long vowel ā is preserved. The name is common Semitic but its precise etymology is uncertain; it has been connected with 'grain' (Hebrew dāgān) and with 'fish' (Hebrew dāḡ), though the former is more widely accepted for the Northwest Semitic grain god.

domains.title: Lord of Grain
domains.subtitle: Fertility, Agriculture, and Divine Fatherhood
domains.lead: Dāgan is the grain god of the ancient Levant, the divine power who fills the storehouses and makes the fields fertile. In Ugaritic myth he is the father of Baal and the patron of the agricultural cycle; in Philistine religion he is the national god whose temple Samson pulls down. His domain is not the storm on the mountain but the quiet miracle by which seed becomes bread.

cards.name: God of Grain
cards.desc: His name and cult center on wheat, barley, and the harvest that sustains city and village alike.

cards.name: Father of Baal
cards.desc: In Ugaritic texts Dāgan is Baal's father, grounding the storm god's power in the agricultural cycle.

cards.name: Temple at Ugarit
cards.desc: A major temple dedicated to Dāgan stood in the city of Ugarit, receiving royal offerings.

cards.name: Philistine Dagon
cards.desc: Worshipped by the Philistines as a national god, his temple at Gaza is destroyed by Samson.

symbols.name: Sheaf of wheat or barley
symbols.meaning: The grain that is Dāgan's gift and the basis of Levantine agriculture

symbols.name: Plowed field

symbols.name: Bull or ram

mythology.lead: Dāgan is a father figure rather than a warrior. In the Ugaritic texts he receives offerings and grants blessings; in the Hebrew Bible he is a foreign god whose temple symbolizes Philistine power. His myths are few, but his cultural importance is immense: he is the god of the staple crop on which every Near Eastern society depended.

myths.title: Dāgan's Blessing
myths.text: Ugaritic ritual texts record sacrifices and offerings to Dāgan, especially at the time of planting and harvest. In KTU 1.12 and related texts, Baal is called 'son of Dāgan,' and the grain god's favor is sought for the fertility of the land. Dāgan does not ride the clouds; he sits in his temple and receives the first fruits of the field.

myths.title: Samson and the Temple of Dagon
myths.text: Judges 16:23–30 describes the Philistine nobility gathering in the temple of Dagon at Gaza to offer a great sacrifice. They bring Samson to entertain them, but he prays for strength, seizes the two central pillars, and pulls the temple down upon himself and his captors. The story marks Dāgan/Dagon as the defeated god of Israel's enemies.

lore.culturalLegacy: Dāgan survives in the Bible as the Philistine god toppled by Samson, and his name echoes in the Hebrew word for grain. In modern fantasy and role-playing games, 'Dagon' often appears as a tentacled or fish-like sea monster, a distortion of the ancient grain god produced by medieval iconographic confusion. For scholars of religion, Dāgan is a key example of how an agricultural deity could become a national patron and a symbol of ethnic identity.
lore.archaeology: A major temple to Dāgan has been identified at Ugarit, and references to his cult appear throughout the Ugaritic tablets. The Mari archives from the Euphrates valley record royal offerings and divine messages involving Dāgan. In the Levant, Philistine sites such as Tel Miqne (Ekron) and Gaza preserve material culture associated with his cult, though the biblical story of Samson's destruction of Dagon's temple cannot be verified archaeologically. The later 'fish-god' Dagon is a medieval iconographic development without ancient Near Eastern support.
lore.syncretism: Dāgan's cult spread from Mesopotamia to the Levantine coast and was adopted by the Philistines after their settlement in Canaan. His name may underlie the Hebrew word for grain, dāgān, though some ancient interpreters connected him with fish (dāḡ), producing the tradition that Dagon was half-man, half-fish. This fish-god image became popular in medieval and early modern art but is not supported by the older Northwest Semitic evidence. In Ugarit, Dāgan was the father of Baal, linking agricultural and storm fertility in a single divine family.

pronunciation.approximation: 'OOP-sah-lir' — three beats, the double p held a fraction long, the final r trilled; modern Swedish Uppsala ('OOP-sah-lah') has shed the old plural ending.
pronunciation.note: Uppsala is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The holiest documented place in the Norse world carries a name of seven ordinary letters; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Temple, Freyr, Sacred Grove
domains.subtitle: The Upper Halls of the Swedish Kings
domains.lead: Uppsalir — 'the Upper Halls' — is the one sanctuary of the Norse world the medieval record describes beam by beam and tree by tree. Adam of Bremen, writing about 1075 from the reports of the Danish court, gives us the golden temple where [[thor|Þórr]] sat enthroned between Wodan and Fricco; the sacred grove beside it, every tree made divine by the offerings hung in its branches; and the nine-day festival, renewed every ninth year, at which nine males of every living kind were given to the gods. Snorri's Ynglingasaga makes the place the seat of [[freyr|Freyr]] himself — the god who built the temple, endowed it with the Uppsala wealth, and lies in a mound beside it. Below the ridge the three royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala still stand, the largest barrows in Sweden, the graves of kings the poems call the Scylfings.

cards.name: The Golden Temple
cards.desc: The temple at Uppsala that Adam of Bremen describes as entirely decked with gold, a golden chain hanging from its gable — the cult house of the Swedish commonwealth.

cards.name: The Sacred Grove
cards.desc: The grove adjoining the temple, every tree held sacred because of the death and decay of the victims — men, horses, and dogs hung among the branches.

cards.name: The Nine-Year Festival
cards.desc: Every ninth year, nine days of sacrifice at the turn of the cycle, one offering each day, nine of every male creature — a rite from which no Swede could absent himself without paying a price.

cards.name: The Royal Mounds
cards.desc: The three great barrows of Gamla Uppsala, cremation graves of sixth- and seventh-century kings; Ynglingasaga buries Freyr himself in such a mound on the same ground.

symbols.name: The gilded temple
symbols.meaning: The gold-decked hall where the triad sat enthroned — the sacral core of Swedish kingship, visible wealth offered to the gods

symbols.name: The enthroned triad
symbols.meaning: Þórr central with his sceptre, Wodan armed like Mars, Fricco shaped for peace and pleasure — sovereignty, war, and fertility enshrined in one room

symbols.name: The sacred grove
symbols.meaning: Trees made divine by sacrifice — the boundary where offering becomes landscape and the forest itself turns temple

symbols.name: The hanging offerings
symbols.meaning: Men, horses, and dogs suspended in the branches, nine of every kind — the commonwealth renewed at the price of nine-year blood

symbols.name: The royal mound
symbols.meaning: The barrow of kings and, by Snorri's account, of Freyr himself — dynasty made continuous with the god who endowed it

mythology.lead: Uppsala's dossier is not a god's biography but a sanctuary's record — and it is the fullest any Norse holy place receives. Adam of Bremen describes the temple and its rites from the testimony of the Danish court a generation before the old religion died in Sweden; Snorri gives the site its founding god and its dynasty; the saga of Hrólfr kraki sets a famous treasure-flight on the plain below it. Between the four witnesses, the Upper Halls emerge as the one place where the whole northern religion can be watched at prayer.

myths.title: The Golden Temple
myths.text:
Adam of Bremen, archbishop's scholar at Hamburg-Bremen, sets down about 1075 the most exact account of Norse cult that survives. Near Sigtuna, he writes, stands a famous temple called Ubsola, entirely decked with gold, and in it the people worship the statues of three gods: the most powerful, Thor, occupies the throne in the middle of the hall; on either side stand Wodan and Fricco. Thor, Adam explains, governs the air, thunder, lightning, winds, rains, fair weather and crops, and holds his sceptre like Jove; Wodan, 'that is, Frenzy', rules war and gives men strength against enemies, carved in the likeness of an armed man as Mars is shown; Fricco, bestower of peace and pleasure on mortals, is shaped with an immense phallus. Each god has his priests, and the people's vows follow need: in plague or famine they sacrifice to Thor, for war to Wodan, for weddings to Fricco.

Adam worked from the reports of the Danish king Sven Estridsen, 'who retained all these facts in his memory', and the scholia added to the text fill in further colour — the temple ringed by a golden chain hanging from the gable, the feasting within. What the account gives the record is irreplaceable: a working temple of the Æsir described in its last generation, by a churchman who wanted it abolished and could not help seeing it clearly.

myths.title: The Nine-Day Sacrifice
myths.text:
Adam's second chapter on the site records the great communal rite. It is customary, he writes, to hold a solemn assembly of all the provinces of Sweden at Uppsala every nine years, from which no one may purchase exemption; every man sends his offerings. The sacrifice is of this kind: of every living creature that is male, nine head are offered, by whose blood it is the custom to placate the gods. The bodies are hung in a grove adjoining the temple, a grove so sacred to the heathens that each tree is believed divine because of the death and putrefaction of the victims. Dogs and horses hang there with the men, and one of the Christians told Adam he had seen seventy-two bodies hanging together. The incantations sung at the rite, Adam adds, are so disgraceful that it is better to say nothing of them.

A scholion adds the spring beside the temple in which a living man was drowned; if he was not found again, the people's wish would be granted. Every element — the nine-year cycle, the nine of each kind, the grove, the hanging — belongs to the deep grammar of Germanic sacrifice: Thietmar of Merseburg records a parallel nine-year rite at Lejre in Denmark, and Tacitus had described the sacred groves of the continental Germans a thousand years before. Uppsala is where that grammar has its fullest surviving page.

lore.culturalLegacy: Uppsala never stopped being the stage on which Sweden remembers itself. The old cult centre became the church's: Gamla Uppsala was the seat of Sweden's first archbishopric from 1164 until the see moved to Östra Aros — the modern city of Uppsala — in 1273, and the medieval church still stands on the artificial plateau where Adam's temple is sought. Nineteenth-century romantic nationalism made the mounds the nation's Westminster; their excavation in 1846–47, ordered to still public argument about what they contained, yielded the cremated kings of the Vendel era and made Old Uppsala the birthplace of Swedish archaeology. The university at Uppsala, founded in 1477, gave the name a second, learned fame that now outruns the temple's. For modern scholarship the site remains the test case for the union of cult and kingship in the North — Olof Sundqvist's Freyr's Offspring is built on its ground — and for modern Heathen and Ásatrú communities the grove and the mounds are the north's most numinous standing landscape, the one address where the old religion can still be visited rather than merely read about.
lore.archaeology: Uppsala is the rare Norse holy place where the texts can be tested against the ground. The three royal mounds of Gamla Uppsala — the largest barrows in Sweden — were opened in 1846–47 under Bror Emil Hildebrand: beneath each lay a cremation of the sixth or seventh century, burned in its finery and sealed under birch bark, with weapons, game-boards, and sacrificed animals, the graves of the dynasty the poems call Ynglings or Scylfings. Beside them the medieval church — seat of Sweden's first archbishop from 1164 — stands on a great artificial plateau of levelled terraces, the one construction on the site that matches Adam's scale; Sune Lindqvist's excavation beneath the church floor in 1926 revealed the postholes of a very large wooden building, and the argument whether it was the pagan temple, a royal feasting hall, or both has run ever since — Olof Sundqvist's work on the Svea cult-and-kingship complex is the standard modern frame. The surrounding landscape is dense with the dynasty's furniture: boat-graves at Valsgärde a few miles north, the Vendel graves across the river, hundreds of smaller mounds on the Fyris plain. No runestone carves the place-name itself; the Younger Futhark rendering ᚢᛒᛒᛋᛅᛚᛅ (ubbsala) is a normalized reconstruction, though Uppland is the richest runestone province in Scandinavia.
lore.syncretism: Uppsala's closest kin are not gods but holy places. Thietmar of Merseburg, writing two generations before Adam, describes the nine-year sacrifice at Lejre in Denmark — ninety-nine men, horses, dogs and cocks offered to placate the gods — the Danish counterpart of the Uppsala rite and the proof that Adam's nine-year cycle was pan-Scandinavian grammar, not local invention. Behind both stands the deepest stratum: Tacitus' Germania records the sacred grove of the Semnones, entered bound and widened by human sacrifice, and the grove and wagon of Nerthus — the goddess whose name is the feminine counterpart of Njörðr, father of the Freyr whose seat was Uppsala. The enthroned triad itself has been read since Dumézil against the archaic Roman triad of Jupiter, Mars and Quirinus — sovereignty, war, and the fertile commons — though Adam's own glosses (Thor as Jove, Wodan as Mars, Fricco as peace and pleasure) show the comparison began with the medieval churchman, not the modern comparatist. Modern handbooks urge the same caution they urge for Adam's secondhand testimony: Simek, Orchard, and Lindow treat the account as the fullest and most dangerous source for Norse cult — a Christian observer describing the rite he wanted abolished, through informants a kingdom away. What remains undisputed is the place: no other site in the North is so continuously written about, from the royal mounds' century to the last generation of the old religion.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Uppsalir — a nominative plural, genitive Uppsala, already plain ASCII with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚢᛒᛒᛋᛅᛚᛅ (ubbsala), a normalized phonetic reconstruction, since the sixteen-rune row distinguishes neither b from p nor long from short vowels. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: uppsala.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

The name shares yama, "twin": she is the twin of death's lord, and the twin of Gaṅgā at the sangam — the name tells both stories.

domains.title: The Twilight River
domains.subtitle: Devotion, the Sangam, and Kṛṣṇa's Own Water
domains.lead: Yamunā is the second of India's great river-goddesses and the first of Kṛṣṇa's loves: daughter of the sun-god, sister of death, the dark-blue water on whose banks the cowherd god danced, battled the serpent, and made an entire land his memory.

cards.name: The Sangam
cards.desc: Her meeting with Gaṅgā at Prayāgrāj — the trivenī, the holiest confluence in India.

cards.name: Kāliya
cards.desc: The poison-serpent she hosted until the child-god danced on its heads — the river cleansed by dance.

cards.name: Daughter of Sūrya
cards.desc: The sun's daughter, Yama's twin — light and death sharing one water.

cards.name: Vṛndāvana
cards.desc: The pastoral heartland where Kṛṣṇa's līlā plays out on her banks.

symbols.name: The dark-blue water
symbols.meaning: Her twilight color — the river of the blue god

symbols.name: The tortoise
symbols.meaning: Her patient mount — the current that carries everything slowly

symbols.name: The confluence
symbols.meaning: Her union with Gaṅgā — twilight meeting clarity

mythology.lead: Yamunā's myths bind the solar and the pastoral: the sun's daughter flowing through the cowherd's land, purifying and purified by the god who plays in her.

myths.title: The Sun's Twin Daughter
myths.text: Born of Sūrya and Saṃjñā, twin sister of Yama — death and the river as siblings, the tradition's quiet pairing. The Purāṇas rank her beside Gaṅgā in holiness and ahead in intimacy: if Gaṅgā is the mother, Yamunā is the beloved — the river whose water Kṛṣṇa drank as a child and blessed as a god, making her, alone of rivers, "the co-wife of the Lord."

myths.title: The Dance on Kāliya
myths.text: The serpent Kāliya poisoned her water at Vṛndāvana until the child Kṛṣṇa dived in, wrestled him, and danced on his hundred heads — the serpent's wives begging mercy for their husband. He spared it and banished it to the sea, and her water ran clean: the myth every pilgrim to Kāliya-ghāṭa hears, and the river's own story of being made pure.

lore.culturalLegacy: Delhi stands on her bank; the Taj Mahal reflects in her backwater; the Kumbh Mela is partly hers. Yamunā Jayanti (her descent-day) and Bhai Dooj (the sibling festival she shares with Yama) are national observances. Her pollution crisis — Delhi's stretch among the world's most contaminated urban rivers — makes her the central case of India's river-restoration debate: the goddess whose water pilgrims now filter before the ritual.
lore.archaeology: Yamunotri, her glacier source in the Garhwal Himalaya, keeps her temple (rebuilt after earthquakes, hot springs beside it). Mathurā and Vṛndāvana preserve the Kṛṣṇa-ghāts — Vishram Ghāt where the god rested after killing Kaṃsa — and Prayāgrāj's sangam fort and akshayavata tree mark the confluence. The medieval ghāt architecture of the Braj country documents five centuries of Krishna-pilgrimage on her banks.
lore.syncretism: Her cult runs parallel to Gaṅgā's but more intimate: the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition of Bengal holds her highest of all rivers because of Kṛṣṇa; Southeast Asian Krishnaism keeps her in the same narratives; and the Yamunā-Gaṅgā pairing became India's standard metaphor for complementary holiness — the two waters every pilgrim needs both of.
