symbols.name: The haka
symbols.meaning: The war-dance: the body made into the angry face of the god

symbols.name: The feather cloak
symbols.meaning: The kahu huruhuru of the war-chief — honour worn on the shoulders

mythology.lead: Tūmatauenga's cycle is the Polynesian account of how humanity got its arts: not by gift but by conquest — the war-god subduing his elemental brothers and distributing the spoils to his mortal children.

myths.title: The Sons of Rangi and Papa
myths.text: In the beginning the Sky Father (Ranginui) and the Earth Mother (Papatūānuku) lay locked together, and their sons lived crushed in darkness between them. Tūmatauenga, fiercest of the brothers, urged that the parents be killed; the gentler counsel of Tāne prevailed — they would be forced apart. Rongo, Tangaroa, Haumia, and Tāne each tried and failed to push them; then Tāne set his head on the earth, his feet against the sky, and tore the parents open. Light came into the world — and war came with it.

myths.title: The One Who Stood
myths.text: Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, had opposed the separation, and now he attacked his brothers in revenge: Tangaroa fled to the sea, the gods of food hid in the earth and the forest — but Tūmatauenga alone stood fast against the storm, unbowed on the open plain. When the tempest spent itself, the war-god turned on his fleeing brothers: he made nets and took Tangaroa's fish, snared Tāne's birds, and dug up Rongo's and Haumia's crops. His standing made humanity heir to every domain.

lore.culturalLegacy: The haka — performed by the All Blacks before every match and by the army at every farewell — is his face in modern life: the widened eyes and out-thrust tongue are the literal mata anga of his name. Ngāti Tūmatauenga, the army's Māori designation, makes him the only ancient god officially patron of a modern state's armed forces. His cycle — the standing against the storm, the conquest that feeds the people — remains the charter myth of Māori resilience, quoted in land-march speeches and waiata alike.
lore.archaeology: New Zealand's ridgelines keep his monuments: thousands of pa — terraced, ditched, and palisaded hill-forts — from the classic period, with sites like Maungakiekie (One Tree Hill) among the largest earthworks of the Pacific. The greenstone mere and the carved taiaha of the museum collections (Te Papa's among them) are his regalia; the Auckland War Memorial Museum — itself a cenotaph to the fallen — houses the war-canoes and the martial taonga of his people. The kumara storage-pits beside every pa tie his war-and-garden cycle into the ground itself.
lore.syncretism: He is one face of a Polynesian-wide god: Hawaiian Kū — the great war-god of the feathered helmets and the luakini temples — Tahitian Tū, and the Cook Islands' war deities share his name and his office, the deepest layer of pan-Polynesian religion. In New Zealand his worship ran through the war-parties and their tohunga; the 19th-century Māori military genius (the gunfighter pa of the New Zealand Wars) applied his standing to musket and trench, and the New Zealand Army today bears his name as its own: Ngāti Tūmatauenga, "the tribe of the war-god."
lore.originalScriptNote: Te reo Māori writes him with the macron as the vowel-length it is: Tūmatauenga. The oral text is the truer scripture — the whakataukī "Ka mate kāinga tahi, ka ora kāinga rua" and the karakia of war and planting carry his name in the living language, and the New Zealand Army's Māori name, Ngāti Tūmatauenga, writes it into the state itself.

entries.meaning: "Emperor Guan" — the deified general Guān Yǔ, god of war, loyalty, and righteousness

pronunciation.approximation: gwahn-DEE — level tone, then a firm falling tone.
pronunciation.note: Guāndì 關帝 — "Emperor Guan" — carries the first tone on guān and the falling fourth on dì. The name is a title, not a personal name: the deified Guān Yǔ of the Three Kingdoms, raised by eight centuries of imperial investitures to the rank of Emperor. The restoration keeps the macron that marks his tone.

domains.title: The General Who Became a God
domains.subtitle: War, Loyalty, Righteousness, and the Brotherhood of the Peach Garden
domains.lead: Guāndì is China's god of the kept oath: the historical general Guān Yǔ (d. 220 CE) whose loyalty outlasted his dynasty, deified by emperors, merchants, and triads alike until his red-faced statue stood in more temples than any other figure in the Chinese world.

cards.name: The Crescent Blade
cards.desc: Qīnglóng Yǎnyuèdāo — the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, his legendary weapon and temple attribute.

cards.name: The Peach Garden Oath
cards.desc: The brotherhood sworn with Liú Bèi and Zhāng Fēi — China's founding myth of loyalty.

cards.name: The Red Face
cards.desc: His temple image: crimson countenance of righteous wrath, green robe, long beard.

cards.name: The God of Commerce
cards.desc: Merchants worship him as the enforcer of contracts — loyalty monetized into trust.

symbols.name: The crescent halberd
symbols.meaning: Martial honor wielded with precision — war in service of the oath

symbols.name: The red face
symbols.meaning: Righteousness made visible; loyalty that cannot hide

symbols.name: The green robe
symbols.meaning: The gift he refused to surrender to Cáo Cāo — fidelity to the old lord

symbols.name: The long beard
symbols.meaning: The beautiful beard he protected with a silk bag — dignity kept

mythology.lead: Guāndì's myth is history sanctified: the Records of the Three Kingdoms gave him a life, the Romance gave him a legend, and eight dynasties gave him a godhood.

myths.title: The Peach Garden
myths.text: The Romance of the Three Kingdoms opens with the oath: in a peach garden, Guān Yǔ swore with Liú Bèi and Zhāng Fēi to die on the same day as brothers. He kept it past reason — through capture, through Cáo Cāo's gold and titles, riding a thousand miles back to his sworn lord with the general's seal hung on his gate. Loyalty, in China, has a face, and it is his.

myths.title: Lord of the Beautiful Beard
myths.text: Held by Cáo Cāo, he accepted three conditions only: he surrendered to the Han, not to Cáo; his brother's wives would be protected; and he would leave the moment Liú Bèi was found. He kept all three, repaying Cáo Cāo's courtesy by beheading the enemy general Yán Liáng — honor answering honor, the episode the temples never tire of carving.

lore.culturalLegacy: His temples outnumber Confucius' in the Chinese world; his birthday (24th day of the 6th lunar month) is a national observance from Shanxi to Singapore. The "Guān Gōng" of business is the unwritten clause of every contract; his image guards mahjong parlors, restaurants, and police stations alike. The Romance's peach-garden oath remains East Asia's template for sworn brotherhood, quoted in films, games (Dynasty Warriors made him a global icon), and every oath of office sworn with a hand on his name.
lore.archaeology: The Guān Lín tomb-temple at Luoyang (where Cáo Cāo buried his head with honors) and the Guān Dì Miào at his birthplace in Yuncheng, Shanxi — the largest Guandi complex, repeatedly rebuilt since the Sui — anchor his cult geography. Ming-Qing Guandi temples survive in every southern port city; Yokohama's Kanteibyō (1862) preserves the diaspora form. His statues' iconography — red face, green robe, crescent blade, the beard-bag — is among the most standardized in world religion.
lore.syncretism: He is the one deity all three teachings claim: Taoism's Guān Shèng Dì Jūn (Holy Emperor), Buddhism's Sānghārāma, Confucianism's co-Sage. The diaspora carried him everywhere — his altar stands in Yokohama's Kanteibyō, in San Francisco's oldest Chinatown temples, and in every Hong Kong police station, where officers and triads bow to the same red face: the god both sides trust because both sides fear to lie before him.

entries.meaning: "The Golden One" — the radiant form of the Great Goddess, mother of the universe

steps: Sanskrit Gaurī is written in Devanagari as गौरी
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: GOW-ree — the diphthong of "cow," then a long ee.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit gaurī — "the golden, the radiant" — carries the long ī of the feminine epithet, which the restoration keeps. The same word is the adjective "golden-complexioned": her name is her skin, the color of turmeric, ripe wheat, and morning light. The diphthong au is inherent and unmarked in IAST, like e and o — her name needs no further marks to be read exactly.

domains.title: The Golden Mother
domains.subtitle: Beauty, Austerity, Marriage, and the Gentle Śakti
domains.lead: Gaurī is the Great Goddess at her most benevolent: the golden-skinned Mother whose austerity won Śiva himself, whose festivals celebrate marriage and motherhood. Her name — "the radiant one" — in the Ṛgveda simply means a female gaura, the wild ox; the goddess's first secure appearance comes later, as the Kena Upaniṣad's Umā.

cards.name: The Golden Skin
cards.desc: Her color: turmeric and dawn — the glow that names her.

cards.name: The Austerity
cards.desc: The tapas by which she won Śiva — devotion as fierce as any warrior's.

cards.name: The Festivals
cards.desc: Gaurī Pūjā and the Tṛtīyā fasts — the mother's days kept by millions of women.

cards.name: Mother of Heroes
cards.desc: Mother of Gaṇeśa and Kārttikeya — the goddess behind the gods.

symbols.name: The golden complexion
symbols.meaning: Radiance as nature — beauty without artifice

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Her seat and offering — purity of the household goddess

symbols.name: The bilva leaf
symbols.meaning: Her austerity — the tree of Śiva she tended in penance

mythology.lead: Gaurī's myths are the Great Goddess's domestic epic: the mountain-daughter who becomes the universe's mother through patience.

myths.title: Daughter of the Mountain
myths.text: Born as Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat, the mountain-king, she was Satī reborn — the goddess returned after her first death to reclaim her lord. The Purāṇas call her Gaurī from the start: the golden girl of the peaks, destined from birth for the ash-covered wanderer who had forgotten how to love.

myths.title: Winning the Unwinnable
myths.text: When beauty failed to move Śiva in his grief, she chose tapas: years of austerity in the forest — leaves for food, rain for bath, standing on one leg through seasons — until the ascetic god himself came disguised as a young brahmin to test her. She would not be dissuaded, and Śiva, conquered by patience, married her at Kailāsa with the whole pantheon as guests: the wedding the Purāṇas tell as the universe's own.

lore.culturalLegacy: The Gaurī festivals — Gaṇeśa's mother welcomed for three days before her son's own ten — anchor the Maharashtrian religious year; the phrase "gaurī kā vivāha" (the ideal marriage) is everyday Hindi. Turmeric, her color, remains the ritual substance of Indian womanhood. She is the Śākta answer to the question of what a goddess of the home looks like when she also happens to be the energy of the universe.
lore.archaeology: Her temples stand with Pārvatī's: the great Śiva-Pārvatī shrines from Elephanta's marriage-panel to the Kailāsa of Ellora — where the wedding of Gaurī and Śiva fills the whole south wall — document her in stone. The Gaurī Shankar temples of the Kathmandu valley and the festival-images of Maharashtra (made annually in the potters' quarters) carry her golden form into the present.
lore.syncretism: She is the gentle face of the same goddess who is Durgā in battle and Kālī in wrath — the Śākta tradition's proof that power has a domestic form. Her golden form travels: as the benevolent mother of Balinese Hinduism (Mā Gaurī), and into the syncretic Devi temples of the diaspora from Fiji to Trinidad, where her immersion-festivals (Gangā-snan of the image) kept the homeland's calendar across two oceans.

entries.meaning: "The Slow One" — Saturn as the lord of karma, justice, discipline, and time

steps: Sanskrit Śani is written in Devanagari as शनि
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: SHUH-nee — soft palatal sh, short and even.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit śani — "the slow one" — begins with the palatal ś (IAST's acute-accented s) and the short a and i. The restoration keeps the ś that English writes "sh": Śani, the slow planet, whose very name is a warning about haste. The ś is the palatal sibilant, made at the roof of the mouth farther forward than sh — the sound English approximates but never quite keeps.

domains.title: The Slow Reckoning
domains.subtitle: Saturn, Karma, Justice, and the Seven-and-a-Half Years
domains.lead: Śani is the most feared of the nine planets: Saturn as the auditor of karma, whose slow passage through the zodiac delivers every deed's return — never early, never late, and never, ever argued with. India loves him exactly as much as it fears him, which is to say, enormously.

cards.name: Sade Sati
cards.desc: The seven-and-a-half years of his transit over your moon — India's most-dreaded astrological season.

cards.name: The Auditor
cards.desc: Karma's bookkeeper: no bribe, no appeal, no clerical error — only the account.

cards.name: Son of the Sun
cards.desc: Sūrya's estranged son — the shadow the light itself begot.

cards.name: The Crow
cards.desc: His vāhana: the dark bird that sees what others will not look at.

symbols.name: The crow
symbols.meaning: The dark mount — witness of the unavoidable

symbols.name: The iron
symbols.meaning: His metal — hard, cold, unglamorous, indispensable

symbols.name: The slow orbit
symbols.meaning: Twenty-nine-and-a-half years — time as the measure of justice

mythology.lead: Śani's myths are about the impossibility of escaping consequence — even for gods, and especially for kings.

myths.title: The Shadow of the Sun
myths.text: Born of Sūrya and Chhāyā — "Shadow," the substitute-wife the sun's true wife left in her place — Śani was the son the light refused to look at. His gaze fell so baleful that his own father's skin darkened at the meeting. The Purāṇas make the estrangement permanent: the planet of justice is the sun's shadow-child, and no amount of brilliance exempts the family from audit.

myths.title: Even the Gods Are Judged
myths.text: His stories form a single syllabus: when Śani's gaze fell on Śiva, the great god was made to wander as a beggar; on Rāma's line, even the righteous king's fortune bowed. The Hanumān legend adds the one counter: when Śani pressed Hanumān, the mighty one crushed him instead — and Śani, begging release, vowed never to afflict Hanumān's devotees. Devotion freely given is the only shield Śani honors — the one god who bows to bhakti.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Śani chal raha hai" (Saturn is upon us) is the everyday explanation for every run of bad luck from Mumbai to Trinidad. His Saturday fast, his black-and-blue colors, his iron-and-sesame remedies constitute the largest planetary cult in the world. The fear is genuinely democratic: billionaires and bus-drivers check the same ephemeris, and Shingnapur's donations fund entire towns. Jyotiṣa, India's living astrology, centers on his slow clock.
lore.archaeology: Shani Shingnapur's open-air black boulder — the village with famously doorless houses, trusting his protection — is his great shrine; the queue on Saturdays runs for kilometers. Navagraha temples across the South (the Kumbakonam circuit) install him among the nine planets in fixed order, and his bronze from the Chola period shows the stiff, dark, crow-mounted figure unchanged.
lore.syncretism: Saturn's malefic reputation is Indo-European common ground — the Greek Kronos' devouring shadow and Rome's cold planet carry the same dread — but India alone made the planet a judge to be appeased weekly. His temple at Shingnapur (Maharashtra), where the god is an unwalled black stone under open sky, is the anti-temple: no roof over the planet, as if architecture itself feared to constrain him.

entries.meaning: "Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world

pronunciation.approximation: aw-ROON — open o (dot-below), low-high melody.
pronunciation.note: Ọrun is Yoruba for "heaven": the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form — the full tone marks (Ọ̀run, low-high) cannot be registered as a domain, so the temple preserves the tone in text while the address bar carries what the DNS allows. The dot-below is the open-mid vowel — the open aw of law — distinct from the close o; the tone is low-high, rising from the grave to the acute.

domains.title: The Heaven Above the Heavens
domains.subtitle: Sky, Destiny, and the Realm of Olódùmarè
domains.lead: Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.

cards.name: Ọrun and Ayé
cards.desc: Heaven and earth: the two halves of reality, with the soul commuting between them.

cards.name: Orí
cards.desc: The inner head — the personal destiny each soul chooses (or receives) in Ọrun before birth.

cards.name: Olódùmarè
cards.desc: The Owner of Heaven — the supreme being whose realm Ọrun is.

cards.name: The Descent
cards.desc: Every birth is an emigration from heaven; every death, the return journey.

symbols.name: The white cloth
symbols.meaning: Heaven's color — purity and the unblemished sky

symbols.name: The palm nuts
symbols.meaning: Ifá's instruments — heaven's messages read on earth

symbols.name: The head
symbols.meaning: Orí, the chosen destiny — heaven carried inside the skull

mythology.lead: Ọrun's myths are the architecture of Yoruba cosmology: how heaven was made, and how souls travel its road to earth.

myths.title: The Chain to Earth
myths.text: In the beginning there was only Ọrun above and the waters below. Olódùmarè sent Odùduwà down with a chain, a hen, and a handful of earth: the hen scattered the soil on the water, and the land of Ilé-Ifẹ̀ spread — earth founded beneath heaven, the two realms joined by the road of the orisha. Every Yoruba city thereafter is a point on that first chain's route.

myths.title: The Choosing of Orí
myths.text: Before birth, each soul kneels in Ọrun before Olódùmarè and receives its orí — its inner head, its portion of destiny. The Ifá corpus teaches that the choice, once made, is erased from memory but not from life: every fortune and misfortune on earth is the heaven-chosen head working out its own plot. To pray for a good orí is to negotiate with one's own prenatal self.

lore.culturalLegacy: The word lives in a thousand names: Ọrunmila (heaven-knows-salvation), Ọlọrun (owner-of-heaven), Ọrúnmìlà, Ọba-Ọrun. Ifá divination — UNESCO-listed — is its daily news service, and the Egúngún festivals keep the ancestors' visits on the calendar. Every Yoruba funeral says the same thing in ten thousand voices: "the journey to Ọrun is well-traveled" — heaven as home, not as hope.
lore.archaeology: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city Odùduwà founded on the scattered earth, keeps the creation-site shrines: the Oke Itase hill and the palace of the Ọọni, whose crown descends from heaven's own. The bronze heads of Ifẹ̀ (12th–15th c.), among Africa's supreme artworks, are the faces of heaven's first citizens. The Ifá corpus — the great oral archive — is preserved by the babaláwo lineages of Yorubaland and the diaspora.
lore.syncretism: The Ọrun-ayé structure traveled with the diaspora: Candomblé's Oxalá-realm, Santería's heaven of Olófin, and Haiti's lwa-cosmology all keep the two-world map. Christian heaven merged with Ọrun in the New World without ever absorbing it: the Yoruba sky remains a realm of traffic and traffic-officers (the orisha), not of distant thrones — heaven as the next city over, not the next world.

entries.meaning: "Fire Lord" — the Aztec fire god, lord of the hearth and of the year

pronunciation.approximation: shee-oo-TEH-kwtlee — the kʷtɬ cluster released as one, no extra vowel; the final -tl sideways.
pronunciation.note: Xiuhtēcuhtli — "Fire Lord" — takes the long ē of tēcuhtli (lord) in Nahuatl; the domain keeps the plain ASCII form xiuhtecuhtli.com, which the temple explains: the canonical form bears the macron, the address bar carries what the registrar allows.

domains.title: The First Fire
domains.subtitle: Hearth, Year, and the New Fire Ceremony
domains.lead: Xiuhtēcuhtli is the Aztec fire itself: first and last of the gods, the hearth at the center of every home and of the universe, and the god whose great ceremony — the drilling of the New Fire — restarted time itself every fifty-two years.

cards.name: The Hearth
cards.desc: The three stones of every Aztec kitchen — his throne in every house.

cards.name: The New Fire
cards.desc: Every 52 years, all fires died and one was drilled anew — the cosmos restarted.

cards.name: Huehueteotl
cards.desc: "The Old God" — his other name: the ancient of days, wrinkled with a brazier on his back.

cards.name: The Center
cards.desc: The axis mundi: fire as the pillar between the levels of the world.

symbols.name: The fire drill
symbols.meaning: The instrument of the New Fire — time kindled by friction

symbols.name: The brazier
symbols.meaning: His back-mounted bowl — the old god carrying the hearth

symbols.name: The butterfly
symbols.meaning: The fire-moth drawn to his flame — the soul seeking the light

mythology.lead: Xiuhtēcuhtli's myths are the calendar's: the fire that must be renewed, and the darkness that waits if it is not.

myths.title: The Drilling of the New Fire
myths.text: At the close of each 52-year cycle (xiuhmolpilli), the Aztec world extinguished every flame: households went dark, debts were settled, and the priests climbed Huixachtlan — Hill of the Star — to watch for the Pleiades' midnight passage. On a captive's chest the fire-priest drilled the new flame; if it caught, the runner carried it to the Templo Mayor, and every hearth in the empire was relit from it. If it failed, the stars said, the sun would not rise — and the world would end in the dark.

myths.title: Huehueteotl, the Old One
myths.text: Under his other name he is the oldest thing in the cosmos: Huehueteotl, the wrinkled god who carries the brazier on his bent back, present before the suns. The Aztecs put him at the center of the universe's four directions — the fire-pillar of the world — and every domestic hearth was his shrine: the smallest and the greatest cult at once, the god of the kitchen who is also the god of the calendar.

lore.culturalLegacy: The 52-year cycle's shadow falls on Mexico's calendar still; Huixachtlan's hill is in today's Mexico City sprawl, and the last New Fire was drilled in 1507 — the empire fell before the next. His wrinkled, brazier-backed figure is one of the most-recognized images of Aztec art (the great stone Huehueteotl of the Museo Nacional), and the fire-drill remains the emblem of renewal ceremonies across Mexican civic culture.
lore.archaeology: The Templo Mayor's excavations found his shrine among the precinct's gods; the great Huehueteotl brazier-figures — stone elders carrying the fire-bowl — survive from Teotihuacan to Tenochtitlan, making him the longest-documented god-image in Mesoamerica (a thousand years of the same bent back). Huixachtlan's summit is preserved within Mexico City, and the Florentine Codex's New Fire account is the fullest ritual description from the pre-Columbian world.
lore.syncretism: The friars saw him as the devil's furnace — and the people quietly kept lighting the hearth: the vigil-candle of Mexican folk Catholicism and the copal-smoke of Day of the Dead altars are his continuing liturgy. The Maya fire-lords and the Zapotec coquihani are his southern cousins; the New Fire concept — the cosmos rekindled by human hands — has no closer parallel than the Vedic agni-liturgies on the other side of the world.

entries.meaning: "The Rich One" — Roman lord of the underworld and of buried wealth

steps: Epigraphic Latin wrote V for u: Pluto appears as PLVTO

pronunciation.approximation: PLOO-toh — both vowels long.
pronunciation.note: Latin Plūtō carries two long vowels, both marked by the restoration. His name is Rome's calque of the Greek Πλούτων — "the Rich One" — the underworld god whose buried wealth made death and riches share a single name. Both vowels are long in the classical scansion; Lewis & Short print the macrons that the restoration keeps.

domains.title: The Rich One Below
domains.subtitle: Underworld, Wealth, and the Doors of the Deep
domains.lead: Plūtō is Rome's underworld god in his own right — not merely Hádēs renamed, but the Latin "Rich One" who rules the dead and the buried treasure together: the god in whose name the ground gives up both its wealth and its silence.

cards.name: The Doors
cards.desc: The Plutonia — the underworld gates, of which Rome kept its own at the Aventine.

cards.name: Plūtus
cards.desc: His twin-name: the wealth-god Plutus — cornucopia from below.

cards.name: Cerberus
cards.desc: The three-headed hound of the threshold — the deep's own border guard.

cards.name: Proserpina
cards.desc: The queen he took by force and kept by season — Rome's Persephonē.

symbols.name: The bident
symbols.meaning: His two-pronged staff — the scepter of the depths

symbols.name: The cornucopia
symbols.meaning: Wealth rising from the earth — his benign face

symbols.name: The cypress
symbols.meaning: The underworld's tree — the dark column of the graveyard

mythology.lead: Plūtō's Roman myths retell the Greek cycle with a merchant's accent: the underworld as a treasury as much as a tribunal.

myths.title: Proserpina in the Meadow
myths.text: Ovid tells the Roman version of the oldest underworld story: Plūtō rose through the earth of Henna's meadow as Proserpina gathered flowers, and carried her down through the lake's opening to be his queen. Cerēs searched the world with torches; the famine followed her grief; and the settlement — half the year above, half below — made the seasons. Rome read it as agriculture's charter-myth: seed descends, grain returns.

myths.title: Plūtus the Giver
myths.text: Under the name Plūtus he was the benign twin: the wealth that comes from under the earth — grain, metal, the harvest itself. Aristophanes' comedy made him a blind old man who, healed, gives riches to the just; Rome's poets used him for the moral that wealth, like the grave, is no respecter of persons. The two names stayed one god: the Rich One below is also the Giver below.

lore.culturalLegacy: The dwarf planet demoted in 2006 bears his name — and the irony is his: the richest name in the sky, given to the smallest body. "Plutocracy" is his grammar of wealth; "plutonic" his geology. In the Renaissance his image became Fortune's dark twin, and modern finance still speaks of the "underworld" of markets — the Rich One below, invoked daily by people who have forgotten him.
lore.archaeology: The Plutonium site on the Aventine is text-attested (Livy) though not certainly located; the great painted tombs of the Etruscan underworld — Aita and Phersipnai at Tarquinia — show his Italian face two centuries before Rome's. His richest monument is negative space: the absence of any grand Plūtō-temple in Rome itself, the city preferring to worship the giver (Plūtus, with Cerēs) and wall the taker out.
lore.syncretism: His Greek equation with Hádēs was total and early, but Rome kept the distinction of names: Hádēs the Unseen, Plūtō the Rich — the wealth-emphasis Roman. Etruria's Aita stood behind him on the Piacenza liver; Gaul's Dis Pater, claimed by Caesar as the Gauls' ancestor, absorbed his worship northward; and the alchemists kept "plutonic" for all deep-earth fire, whence the element plutonium takes its name from his planet.

entries.meaning: Goddess of grain and growth — the source of the word "cereal"

steps: Roman inscriptions wrote in monumental capitals; CERES needs no V-for-U substitution

pronunciation.approximation: KEH-rehs — hard c, long second vowel.
pronunciation.note: Latin Cerēs carries the long ē of the second syllable — Cĕ-rēs — the same root that gives "create" and "grow" (crescere): the goddess named for growth itself. Her name is the ancestor of the word "cereal," which is why her temple's bread is etymological. The hard c of the classical period later softened in Italian mouths; the temple keeps the older, harder reading.

domains.title: The Grain Mother
domains.subtitle: Agriculture, Bread, Law, and the People's Goddess
domains.lead: Cerēs is Rome's oldest working goddess: the power of grain and growth, patron of the plebeians who eat it, and the deity whose Greek sister's myth (Dēmētēr and Persephonē) she borrowed so completely that Rome's religion of the field became one with the mystery of the seasons.

cards.name: The Sheaf
cards.desc: The wheat-sheaf she carries — the staff of civilization.

cards.name: The Torches
cards.desc: Her search for Proserpina by torchlight — the mother who would not stop.

cards.name: The Plebeian Triad
cards.desc: Cerēs, Liber, Libera — the Aventine trinity of the common people.

cards.name: The Grain Fleet
cards.desc: Rome's annona: the wheat-ships of Sicily and Egypt under her protection.

symbols.name: The wheat-sheaf
symbols.meaning: The gift that made agriculture — and law — possible

symbols.name: The torch
symbols.meaning: The search that never ends — maternal persistence as cosmic order

symbols.name: The poppy
symbols.meaning: Sleep and renewal — the flower of the fallow field

mythology.lead: Cerēs' myths are Rome's double helix: the Greek mother-goddess woven into the Italian grain-god, until the field and the mystery were one.

myths.title: The Teaching of the Furrow
myths.text: Before Cerēs, the poets say, humanity ate acorns and called it food. She taught the cutting of the furrow, the keeping of seed, the harvest's measure — and with grain came surplus, and with surplus came law: Ovid and Cicero both note that Rome's oldest laws guarded the field and its boundaries, because the goddess who invented agriculture also, necessarily, invented property. Her temple was the archive of the plebeians' laws: grain and statute, one house.

myths.title: The Torches of Cerēs
myths.text: When Plūtō took Proserpina, Cerēs lit torches at Aetna's crater and searched the world for nine days, fasting and raging. Finding her daughter queen of the underworld, she refused the compromise until the earth starved with her; the settlement — Proserpina's year divided between the realms — is the myth that explains why the field sleeps and wakes. Rome told it as the charter of the Cerealia, her April festival of the grain's return.

lore.culturalLegacy: "Cereal" is her everyday immortality: every breakfast bowl in the West carries her name. Her statue sits atop the Chicago Board of Trade — the grain market's own goddess, uncrowned by any myth but the price of wheat. State seals (New Jersey's, North Carolina's) put her beside Liberty; the dwarf planet Ceres, first-discovered and largest of the asteroids, is NASA's probe Dawn's destination — the grain mother, honored in orbit.
lore.archaeology: Her Aventine temple's platform survives beside the Circus Maximus; the Enna sanctuary in Sicily — her mythic meadow — preserves its rock-cut shrines. The Cerealia's games are documented in the fasti; her bronze and terracotta votives from the grain-districts of Sicily and Latium fill the museums, and the Plebeian Games' theater-temple complex on the Aventine marks the political grain-cult's ground.
lore.syncretism: Her equation with Dēmētēr was total by the 5th century BCE — the Sibylline Books themselves prescribed the merger — but Rome added its own stresses: the plebeian politics, the annona grain-supply, and the Cerealia's games. Sicily, her mythic homeland and Rome's first granary, kept her temples as the island's patron (Enna, her meadow); and through the grain-fleet she became the one goddess every province ate with daily, the most-consumed deity in the empire.

entries.meaning: "Cloud Serpent" — god of the hunt, of clouds, and of the starry road

pronunciation.approximation: meesh-KOH-ahtl — long o, lateral finish.
pronunciation.note: Mixcōātl is Nahuatl for "cloud serpent" (mixtli + cōātl); the macron on the ō marks the long vowel of the serpent-word, the same one in Quetzalcōātl and Xōlōtl. The restoration keeps it — the serpent is always long. The x of Nahuatl is the sh-sound, not ks: meesh, not mix — the single most misread letter in the language.

domains.title: The Serpent in the Clouds
domains.subtitle: Hunting, Stars, and the Milky Way
domains.lead: Mixcōātl is the Aztec god of the hunt and the starry road: the cloud-serpent who slides along the Milky Way, patron of the nomadic hunters who became the Aztecs' ancestors — the oldest god of the road that leads to the empire.

cards.name: The Milky Way
cards.desc: His body in the sky: the star-serpent, the road of the night.

cards.name: The Hunt
cards.desc: Patron of hunters — his bow and net, the Chichimec tool-kit.

cards.name: The Cloud
cards.desc: The weather-serpent: rain and sky in motion.

cards.name: Camaxtle
cards.desc: His other name — the ancient hunting god of the Chichimecs.

symbols.name: The bow and arrows
symbols.meaning: The hunt — his gift to the wandering tribes

symbols.name: The star-serpent
symbols.meaning: The Milky Way as a living road

symbols.name: The white stripes
symbols.meaning: His hunting-paint, cloud on dark sky

mythology.lead: Mixcōātl's myths are the Aztec origin-story in one figure: the wilderness god who taught the city-builders how to hunt, and whose star-road they followed south.

myths.title: The Serpent of Stars
myths.text: The Chichimec tribes who became the Aztec nobility followed his road: the Milky Way, which the Nahuatl called Mixcōātl, the Cloud Serpent, slithering nightly across the sky. The migrating peoples read their path in his body — the desert crossed by the serpent's light — and when they founded Tenochtitlan, they enthroned the wilderness-guide among the city's great gods, the god of where they had come from.

myths.title: The Bow of the Chichimecs
myths.text: As Camaxtle, he gave the wandering tribes the bow and the fire-drill — the two technologies of the road. The Aztec coronation rites remembered: the new Tlatoani dressed as Mixcōātl for the warrior's investiture, and the festival of Quecholli ("the precious feather") honored him with the hunt's own weapons laid on his altar — the city's annual thanks to the god who fed it before it had fields.

lore.culturalLegacy: His name survives in the Milky Way's Nahuatl name itself; the Quecholli weapons-festival is documented in the Florentine Codex's fullest ritual detail; and the Chichimec hunting mythology is the standard account of the Aztecs' own self-image: the empire that began as wanderers following a serpent of stars. The Mexican National Museum of Anthropology's Mixcōātl figures — striped, netted, bowed — are his standing portraits.
lore.archaeology: Teotihuacan's hunting-god precedes him; the Toltec-Aztec Camaxtle cult at Tula and the Templo Mayor's offerings (his arrows among the buried gifts) anchor his archaeology. The Florentine Codex's Quecholli chapter — weapons, dance, and the hunt's liturgy — is the fullest record, and the rock-art of the northern deserts (the bowmen of the Sierra Madre) keeps his people's original ground.
lore.syncretism: The hunt-gods of North America stand in his lineage: the Huichol's Kauyumari (the blue deer-guide) and the Maya hunting-lords share his road-and-prey theology. Colonial chroniclers merged him with Santiago and with Nimrod (the hunter-king of the missionaries' Genesis); the people kept the star-serpent — and hunters in rural Mexico still note the sky's deer-road on the way to the field.

entries.meaning: The river orisha Ọba — co-wife of the thunder god, lady of the sacred waters

variants.note: Previous owned form; the current primary adds the final low tone (Ọbà)

steps: Yoruba has been written in the Latin alphabet since the 1840s, with diacritics for tone and vowel quality.
The underdot marks the open vowels /ɛ, ɔ/ and the postalveolar fricative /ʃ/; these are the obligatory phonemic marks.
Tone marks (grave low, acute high) are fully written in dictionaries but routinely omitted in everyday Yoruba writing.
The owned Unicode form preserves the underdots and the tone marks the domain could carry; the fully tone-marked dictionary form is documented in the variants and here.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-bah — open o, low-low melody.
pronunciation.note: Ọba names the river orisha of the Ọba River; the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form (tone marks cannot be registered), and the fuller tone-marked Ọ̀bà is preserved in the temple's display text. The dot-below marks the open-mid vowel.

domains.title: The River that Endures
domains.subtitle: Devotion, Jealousy, and the Lake of the Co-Wife
domains.lead: Ọba is the river orisha who loved and lost: the senior wife of Ṣàngó, whose jealousy cost her an ear and whose grief became a lake. She is the Yoruba study of endurance — the quiet river that outlasts the storm-god's louder wives.

cards.name: The Ọba River
cards.desc: Her water in Yorubaland — the stream that bears her name and her temperament.

cards.name: The Hidden Ear
cards.desc: The ear she lost to Ṣàngó's rage — hidden under her crown and her hair.

cards.name: The Senior Wife
cards.desc: The senior wife — and last to be believed.

cards.name: The Lake
cards.desc: Her grief made geography: the lake where the faithful mourn with her.

symbols.name: The covered ear
symbols.meaning: Wounds hidden and endured — dignity after injury

symbols.name: The brass bracelet
symbols.meaning: Her marriage-token from the thunder-king

symbols.name: The red parrot feather
symbols.meaning: Her sign beside the other wives' red

mythology.lead: Ọba's myths are domestic tragedy told as hydrology: the co-wife's war that became a river and a lake.

myths.title: Three Wives, One Storm
myths.text: Ṣàngó, the thunder-king, took three river-wives: Ọba the senior, Ọṣun the beloved, and Ọya the storm-sharer. The oríkì tell how Ọba, seeing her husband's love flow to Ọṣun, schemed — and how Ọṣun, learning of it, tricked her in return: she told Ọba the king loved the ear of a woman in his soup, and Ọba, desperate to be loved, cut her own ear and cooked it for him.

myths.title: The Ear in the Soup
myths.text: When the trick was revealed, Ṣàngó's disgust and rage drove her from the palace; the co-wives laughed, and Ọba fled north, weeping. She hid her maimed head under her crown and her hair — which is why her images cover the ears — and the thunder-king, in the later tellings, never stopped regretting the day. Her myth is the Yoruba warning about jealousy: not the villain's punishment, but the victim's endurance.

lore.culturalLegacy: Her image — the crowned figure hiding her ears — is one of Yoruba art's most intimate: the wound as regalia. The co-wives' cycle structures the orisha households of two continents; her river in Yorubaland keeps her shrines active; and the "Obá" of Cuban Santería is beloved as the most patient of the female orisha — the one who teaches that endurance is also a form of power.
lore.archaeology: Her river rises in the hills of the Ọyọ country, and her cult-centers at Ọṣogbo and the Ọba lake preserve her shrines and her priests; the brass and terracotta figures of the covered-ear goddess are documented in the museum collections from Ifẹ̀ to Havana. The oríkì of the three wives, recorded by Bascom and others, is among the finest domestic myth-cycles in the Yoruba corpus.
lore.syncretism: In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría (Saint Catherine, whose wheel she shares) — her cult strong in Matanzas; in Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, the devotee-dancers' hair arranged to hide what the king did. The three-wife cycle (Ọba-Ọṣun-Ọya) is the diaspora's standard parable of the polygamous household, told wherever the orisha went.

entries.meaning: "Best Truth" — the Amesha Spenta of cosmic order (Aša), guardian of the sacred fire and the moral law

steps: Written aṣ̌a vahišta in the Avesta; the Aṣ̌əm Vohū prayer gives the oblique forms aṣ̌əm… vahištəm
ṣ̌ is written 𐬴 (SSHE) and š 𐬱 (SHE)

pronunciation.approximation: ah-shah-vah-HISH-tah — two sharp š sibilants, even vowels.
pronunciation.note: Avestan aša vahišta — "Best Truth/Righteousness" — is written in the scholarly transliteration with the palatal š of the Avestan alphabet, twice: Ašavahišta. The restoration keeps both sibilants exactly where the Gathas put them; English "Asha Vahishta" softens what the Avesta writes sharp.

domains.title: The Best Truth
domains.subtitle: Righteousness, the Sacred Fire, and the Moral Order
domains.lead: Ašavahišta is the Amesha Spenta of Aša — "Best Righteousness": the Bounteous Immortal who is cosmic order itself, the truth the universe is built to run on, and the sacred fire that tests every soul and every word against it.

cards.name: The Sacred Fire
cards.desc: His element: the altar-flame of the Avesta, purifier and witness.

cards.name: Aša
cards.desc: Cosmic order as a person — the truth against which all thought, word, and deed is measured.

cards.name: The Six
cards.desc: One of the Amesha Spentas — the Bounteous Immortals who form Ahura Mazda's council.

cards.name: The Ordeal
cards.desc: Fire as the test: the Avestan ordeal that proves the truthful from the deceitful.

symbols.name: The altar flame
symbols.meaning: The fire of the Avesta — his presence in every Zoroastrian temple

symbols.name: The ašem-vohū verse
symbols.meaning: The oldest prayer in the faith: "aša is the best, it is happiness"

symbols.name: The winged sun
symbols.meaning: The fravašis' symbol he shares with the whole order

mythology.lead: Ašavahišta's mythology is the Gathas' own theology: truth not as an idea but as an immortal who must be fed, fought for, and kept alight.

myths.title: The Bounteous Immortals
myths.text: The Avesta's great hymn-names them: Vohu Manah (Good Mind), Aša Vahišta (Best Truth), Xšathra Vairya (Chosen Power), Spenta Ārmaiti (Holy Devotion), Haurvatāt (Wholeness), Amərətāt (Immortality) — the Amesha Spentas, the Bounteous Immortals who are at once Ahura Mazda's powers and persons. Ašavahišta is the second: the Truth the Good Mind thinks, and the Fire that proves it. In the Gathas, Zaraθuštra meets each as a presence, not a principle.

myths.title: The Fire of Aša
myths.text: His element is fire — not the destroyer but the tester. The Avesta gives fire to Aša Vahišta as his domain: the altar-flame through which prayers rise, and the ordeal-fire through which innocence is proven. Every Zoroastrian fire-temple keeps his presence: the flame tended for centuries is, in the faith, Ašavahišta made visible — the light that does not lie.

lore.culturalLegacy: He is the reason "truth" has a temple: the Zoroastrian moral tradition — good thought, good word, good deed — is his liturgy, and the fire-temples of Yazd and the diaspora are his addresses. The word "Asha" lives in modern Persian and as a common name across South Asia. Scholars read him as the hinge on which the Abrahamic heaven-and-judgment traditions later turned: the first theology of a universe audited for truth.
lore.archaeology: The fire-temples are his monuments: Adur Gušnasp at Takht-e Soleyman (Sasanian, UNESCO) — the shrine of kings; Adur Farnbag in Fars; and the working Atash Behram of Yazd, whose flame has burned since 470 CE. The Achaemenid reliefs of Persepolis show the fire-altar in royal worship, and the Gathas themselves — the oldest hymns of any living scripture — are his charter, preserved in the oldest Avestan manuscripts (K7, 14th c. copies of much older work).
lore.syncretism: His cognate is the Vedic ṛta and its guardian: scholars pair Aša with the Vedic order-principle and note the shared Indo-Iranian root (*rtá/aša). In the Sasanian era his fire became state cult — the great fire-temples of Adur Gušnasp and Adur Farnbag bore his element as national shrines; and the Yasna's ašem-vohū verse ("aša is the best, it is happiness") remains the most-recited line of the living faith. He survives wherever the fire is kept: Yazd's perpetual flame is, by every account, still his.

entries.meaning: Sea (the sea giant who brews ale for the gods)
Lord who looks down in compassion

etymology.derivation: Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara, from avalokita 'beheld, looked down upon' + īśvara 'lord'; the bodhisattva of compassion, source-form of Guānyīn and Kannon.

steps: Sanskrit Avalokiteśvara is written in Devanagari as अवलोकितेश्वर
IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel and consonant to a Latin equivalent
Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

pronunciation.approximation: 'AVALOKITESHVARA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.
pronunciation.note: Avalokiteśvara is Tier 1 because the Buddhist form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

domains.title: Compassion
domains.subtitle: Compassion, Mercy, Bodhisattva
domains.lead: Avalokiteśvara belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is associated with compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

cards.name: Compassion

mythology.lead: The stories of Avalokiteśvara circulate within the Buddhist corpus, where the figure embodies compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

myths.title: Primary Attestation
myths.text: Avalokiteśvara is attested in the canonical Buddhist sources as a figure associated with compassion, mercy, bodhisattva.

myths.title: Name and Meaning

entries.meaning: Fomorian king whose destructive eye blasts armies when its lid is raised, slain by his grandson Lúg with a sling-stone at Cath Maige Tuired.

pronunciation.approximation: 'BAH-lor' — stress the first syllable hard, keep the l dark and broad, and let the final r stay tapped. Modern Irish 'Balor' keeps essentially the same shape.

The capital alone distinguishes the temple form from the input; the Fomorian king's standing in the tradition is beside the point.

domains.title: The King of the Evil Eye
domains.subtitle: The Venomed Gaze, the Fomorian Tribute, the Fortress of Tory, the Grandson's Stone
domains.lead: Balor — Balor Béimnech, 'Balor of the Mighty Blows' — is king of the Fomorians, the sea-borne oppressors of medieval Irish tradition, and owner of the most feared weapon in the whole corpus: a single eye so venomed by the fumes of a druids' brew that no army could stand before its gaze. Grandfather of Lugh and doomed by that very grandson's sling-stone at Mag Tuired, he is the Irish tradition's great figure of destructive sovereignty — power that poisons its possessor and is answered, in the end, by his own blood.

cards.name: The Venomed Eye
cards.desc: One eye, poisoned in boyhood by the fumes of a druids' charm-brew; any army it looked upon was worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

cards.name: The Fomorian Tribute
cards.desc: Under Balor and Indech the Fomorians taxed Ireland from the sea, and set the very gods to serf-work until Mag Tuired broke the yoke.

cards.name: The Tower of Tory
cards.desc: In the Donegal oral tradition, the sea-girt tower where Balor prisoned his daughter Eithne against the prophecy of a grandson's hand.

cards.name: The Grandson's Stone
cards.desc: Lugh's sling-stone at Mag Tuired drove the eye backward through Balor's head, so that its own gaze blasted the Fomorian host.

mythology.lead: Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's revenge, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that medieval manuscripts only glance at.

myths.title: Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét
myths.text:
The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, and it was her spear, or the wound she dealt at Mag Tuired, that killed the Dagda at the Brug years later — the Lebor Gabála records the All-Father's death from Cethlenn's blow as the long-settled price of Balor's war.

His daughter was Ethniu, and she was given to Cian, son of Dian Cécht the healer; their son was Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer — the genealogy that the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns on.

myths.title: How the Eye Was Poisoned
myths.text:
Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it. Any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong.

The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime.

lore.culturalLegacy: Balor entered the modern world through two doors. The first was scholarship: Lady Gregory's Gods and Fighting Men (1904) carried the sling-stone and the tower into English reading, and O'Rahilly's Early Irish History and Mythology (1946) made him the type-case of the Irish death-king, a scholarly afterlife as large as his medieval dossier is short. The second was the folklore itself: the Donegal oral versions — the tower, the stolen cow, the child cast into the sea — were collected in the nineteenth century and never stopped being retold, and 'Balor of the Evil Eye' remains the standing name of the figure in Irish and in English. In the modern imagination he has become the Celtic dark lord par excellence: the remote tyrant in his island fortress whose one weapon poisons everything it touches, answered not by a greater weapon but by the prophesied grandchild the fortress was built to prevent. Tory Island keeps his address; the Irish language never lost his name.
lore.archaeology: Balor is a textual and oral figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. His manuscript witnesses are exact — Cath Maige Tuired survives uniquely in the sixteenth-century British Library MS Harley 5280, the basis of Gray's edition, while Lebor Gabála Érenn is preserved in the twelfth-century Book of Leinster and its sister codices. His geographical anchor is one of the most dramatic pieces of coastline in Europe: Tory Island (Toraigh), nine miles off the Bloody Foreland of Donegal, whose cliffs and sea-stacks — above all the great rock called Tór Mór — the oral tradition names as Balor's fortress and the site of Eithne's tower. The nineteenth-century collectors who wrote the tower story down were recording a living Donegal tradition anchored to those rocks, and the island's medieval monastic remains and round tower have kept the name in continuous local memory.
lore.syncretism: Balor's clearest cross-border witnesses are comparative, not cognate. The Welsh corpus preserves no figure derived from the same name — the Brythonic silence is total, as it is for so many of the Fomorian cycle. The parallels the scholarship actually leans on are typological. First, the Greek Acrisius: the king who prisoned his daughter Danae in a bronze chamber because a prophecy named her son his slayer, and died by that grandson Perseus all the same — the Eithne tower is the same tale-shape, and comparatists have set the two side by side since the nineteenth century. Second, the one-eyed monster answered by aimed cunning — the Polyphemus pattern — where the single enormous eye is both the ogre's strength and the one place he can be struck. Third, and nearest home, the Irish and Mediterranean complex of the evil eye itself: the belief that a look can wither cattle, milk, and men, which Sjoestedt and Mac Cana both treat as the living folk-ground of Balor's venomed gaze. O'Rahilly read him further, as a figure of death and the western sea; the handbooks register the reading without making it doctrine.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is Balor — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Old Irish was written in the Insular Latin script; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, survives on some four hundred stones bearing personal names, but no attestation of this theonym has ever been read on any of them. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: balor.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

entries.meaning: Trembling pathway (from bifa, to shake, + rǫst, league)

pronunciation.approximation: 'BIV-rost' — stress the first syllable; let the f pass as a soft breath between the lips, almost a 'v'; say the ǫ as a short, open 'aw' cut in half, not the long 'oh' of the English Bifrost.
pronunciation.note: Cleasby–Vigfusson (s.v. bifrǫst) glosses the name 'the trembling way,' from bifa 'to shake, tremble' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed'; Zoëga (s.v.) gives the same etymology and records the alternate name Ásbrú 'the Æsir-bridge.' The Eddic codex reads Bilrǫst, with bil 'moment, lapse of time,' and editors still debate which compound is original; Snorri's Bifrǫst is the form that prevailed. The o-ogonek ǫ is a distinctive atomic letter that the ASCII form loses, so the restoration is Tier 1 under the mechanical rule.

domains.title: Rainbow, Fire, Threshold
domains.subtitle: The domain of Bifrǫst
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Bifrǫst is the burning rainbow that joins Miðgarðr to Ásgarðr — the trembling path, from bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'a league, a distance to be traversed.' The gods themselves call it Ásbrú, the Æsir-bridge, and ride it daily to hold court beneath Yggdrasill.

The name encodes a structure built to fail: strong beyond any other work, as Snorri insists, yet fated to shake, to burn, and at last to break beneath the sons of Muspell. Between its watchman's horn and its final shattering, the bridge is the measure of the distance between gods and everything else.

cards.name: The Trembling Way
cards.desc: From bifa 'to shake' and rǫst 'league, path': the bridge is a trembling span of three colors, made with more skill and cunning than any other structure.

cards.name: The Red Band of Fire
cards.desc: Snorri explains the red stripe as burning fire: the bridge is warded in flame so that frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot climb it into heaven.

cards.name: Heimdallr's Watch
cards.desc: At Himinbjǫrg, where the bridge reaches heaven's edge, Heimdallr keeps guard — hearing the grass grow, seeing a hundred leagues by night, holding the Gjallarhorn.

cards.name: The Breaking at Ragnarǫk
cards.desc: When the sons of Muspell ride over it toward the field of Vígríðr, the bridge shatters beneath them; the horses of the gods must swim the flood.

symbols.name: The red band
symbols.meaning: The stripe of burning fire within the rainbow that bars the giants from heaven

symbols.name: Gjallarhorn
symbols.meaning: Heimdallr's horn, kept at the bridge and winded to wake the gods at Ragnarǫk

symbols.name: Himinbjǫrg
symbols.meaning: 'Heaven's castle,' Heimdallr's hall at the bridge's head where it touches the sky

symbols.name: Urðr's well
symbols.meaning: The spring beneath Yggdrasill where the gods ride each day to sit in judgment

symbols.name: The horses of the Æsir
symbols.meaning: The steeds named in Grímnismál — Glad, Gyllir, Glær, Skeiðbrimir and the rest — that bear the gods over the burning span

mythology.lead: Bifrǫst is the one road between the worlds of gods and men, and every story told of it is a story about passage: who may cross, what the crossing costs, and what happens when the road itself gives way. Snorri describes it as the strongest of all constructions and yet builds its destruction into the end of the world. The poems of the Codex Regius, which read the name as Bilrǫst, already know that the bridge will break. Around it gather Heimdallr the watchman, the daily assize at Urðr's well, and the solitary figure of Þórr, who is forbidden the span and wades the rivers instead.

myths.title: The Bridge of Three Colors
myths.text:
Gangleri asks how the gods pass from heaven to earth, and Hárr answers that they built Bifrǫst from earth to heaven: a bridge of three colors, very strong, and made with more skill and cunning than any other work. The red in the rainbow, Hárr explains, is burning fire, so that the frost-giants and mountain-giants cannot mount into heaven over the bridge.

At the bridge's head, where it reaches the edge of heaven, stands Himinbjǫrg, the hall of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods. He needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues by night as by day, and hears the grass growing on the earth and the wool on the sheep. Beside him waits the Gjallarhorn, whose blast is heard in all worlds.

myths.title: The Daily Ride to Judgment
myths.text:
Every day the Æsir ride up over Ásbrú — the Æsir-bridge — on their named horses, to sit in judgment at the ash Yggdrasill. But Þórr does not ride. Grímnismál says that he must wade the rivers Kǫrmt and Ǫrmt and the two Kerlaugar each day on his way to the doomstead, for the Æsir-bridge stands all aflame and the holy waters seethe.

Snorri gives the same exception a physical cause: the thunder-god's passage, with the heat and weight of his thunder, would break the span. The strongest of the gods is thus the one who walks — the bridge that carries everyone else cannot carry him.

lore.culturalLegacy: Wagner fixed the bridge in the modern imagination at the close of Das Rheingold: Donner's hammer summons the storm that clears the air, the rainbow appears, Froh names it as the way to the gods' new castle, and the gods process over it into Valhalla while Loge mutters that they are hastening toward their end — a reading of Bifrǫst's built-in doom that Snorri would have recognized. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century book illustration kept the burning arc as the standard emblem of the passage to Ásgarðr. Marvel's comics and films made Bifrost a household word, reimagining it as a wormhole guarded by Heimdall and gate-keeping travel between realms; games from God of War Ragnarök to Assassin's Creed Valhalla render it as the shimmering road between worlds. Modern heathen practice uses the rainbow bridge as a symbol of the live connection between Miðgarðr and the gods, while the unrelated 'Rainbow Bridge' poem of pet bereavement shows how far the idiom of the shining span has travelled from its Old Norse root. Restoring Bifrǫst in Unicode keeps the trembling in the name — the ASCII Bifrost has forgotten that the bridge shakes.
lore.archaeology: Bifrǫst is a textual figure with no known pictorial or runic attestation: no picture stone, amulet, or runestone names or unambiguously depicts the rainbow bridge, and the riders carved on stones such as Ardre VIII cannot be securely tied to it. Its transmission is manuscriptal. The mythological poems that preserve it — Grímnismál, Fáfnismál, Grípisspá, Lokasenna, Vafþrúðnismál — survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), which reads the name as Bilrǫst. Snorri's extended account in Gylfaginning survives in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, early fourteenth century), the Codex Wormianus (AM 242 fol.), the Codex Upsaliensis (DG 11), and the Codex Trajectinus (Traj 1374), whose divergences editors weigh stanza by stanza.
lore.syncretism: The burning rainbow has no attested continental Germanic counterpart — no Old English or Old High German source names the bridge, so Bifrǫst belongs to the Old Norse material alone, and any deeper common-Germanic pedigree is conjecture. Comparanda crowd around it nonetheless. In Greek tradition Iris is the rainbow made person, the messenger who moves between heaven and earth along the arc; in the Rig Veda the rainbow is Indra's bow (Indradhanush), a weapon hung in the sky; and the rainbow covenant of Genesis 9 was familiar to the Christian Icelanders who copied the Eddas, a juxtaposition that colors, though it does not explain, Snorri's red band of fire. In Finnic and Baltic folklore the Milky Way is a road of birds or souls, another shining path overhead. Later European folk belief kept the rainbow as a bridge and a boundary — the treasure at its foot, the impossibility of reaching its end — and modern popular culture, most openly Marvel's Einstein–Rosen 'Bifrost,' has translated the trembling way into a wormhole, which is the same intuition in newer physics: a bridge that burns, shakes, and cannot be trusted to hold.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is Old Norse Bifrǫst, transmitted in Latin-script codices; no runic inscription preserves it. In a normalized Younger Futhark rendering it would be written ᛒᛁᚠᚱᛅᛋᛏ, with ᛅ for the ǫ. The ǫ is the o-ogonek, the u-umlaut of a — a short open-mid vowel, written ö in Modern Icelandic — and it is the one distinctive feature the ASCII form destroys. The restored registrable form is bifrǫst.com (punycode xn--bifrst-zcc.com); the ASCII fallback bifrost.com flattens the trembling vowel into a plain 'o'.

The name is simply the common noun máni, 'moon', raised to a person — the same word that gives mánaðr, 'month'. domains.title: Moon, Night, Time
domains.subtitle: The domain of Máni
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Máni is the moon itself made personal — the shining body that crosses the night sky, imagined as a god who steers it. Where Sól, his sister, drives the sun, Máni governs the gentler light: Snorri says he 'steers the course of the moon and rules the new and the waning moons,' the phases by which men first learned to count their days.

His is a charged quietness. The gods themselves assigned him his course, a wolf runs forever at his heels, and two earth-born children ride with him, their pail still visible on his face. Every month that turns is his signature: mánaðr, 'month', is his own word, and Monday is his day.

cards.name: Mundilfari's Boast
cards.desc: A father's pride named his children Moon and Sun; the gods answered the boast by setting the pair to drive the lights of heaven.

cards.name: Hati's Pursuit
cards.desc: The wolf Hati Hróðvitnisson runs before the moon and will one day take it; at Ragnarǫk the Moon-Hound swallows the light and spatters the sky with blood.

cards.name: Bil and Hjúki
cards.desc: Two children with a pail on a pole, taken up from the well Byrgir; they follow Máni, Snorri says, 'as can be seen from earth' — the man in the moon.

cards.name: Measurer of Months
cards.desc: He rules the new and waning moons, the counting of time itself; mánaðr, 'month', is his word, and the calendar was his first temple.

symbols.name: Sægr and Simul (pail and pole)
symbols.meaning: The burden Bil and Hjúki carried from the well Byrgir, still legible as the markings on the moon's face

symbols.name: The month-mark
symbols.meaning: Mánaðr, the month — the unit of time that bears his name in every Germanic calendar

mythology.lead: Máni's mythology is brief but exact: he has no hammer-duels and no disguises, only a course to keep and a hunter behind him. The Eddas give him three scenes — a father's fatal boast, a wolf's patient pursuit, and two children lifted from a well — and together they explain both why the moon moves and why it keeps its human face. Around those scenes gathers the quieter charge the Vafþrúðnismál records: the gods shaped the new and waning moons so that men could reckon their years.

myths.title: Mundilfari's Boast
myths.text:
In the Vafþrúðnismál, the giant Vafþrúðnir tells Óðinn that Mundilfari is the father of Máni and of Sól alike. Snorri, in Gylfaginning, gives the story its edge: Mundilfari's two children were so fair that he named his son Máni, 'Moon', and his daughter Sól, 'Sun', and married Sól to a man named Glenr. The gods were angered by this ofdramb — this overweening pride — and took the siblings and set them in the heavens.

The punishment is an appointment. Sól is made to drive the horses of the sun, Árvakr and Alsviðr, while Máni is charged with steering the course of the moon and ruling its waxing and waning. What a father claimed in arrogance, the gods confirmed in office: the names became the duties, and the children became the sky.

myths.title: The Wolf at the Moon's Heels
myths.text:
The moon does not drift; it flees. Snorri explains its speed by its hunter: two wolves run with the lights of heaven, and Hati Hróðvitnisson is the one who runs before the moon and means to take it — 'and so it will come to pass.' The Grímnismál knows the same pursuit, naming Hati as the son of Hróðvitnir who waits upon the bright bride of the sky.

The chase has an ending, and the Eddas do not flinch from it. From the Iron-Wood brood, Snorri says, will come the mightiest wolf of all, called Mánagarmr, the Moon-Hound: he fills himself with the lives of all who die, swallows the moon, and spatters heaven and air with blood, so that the sun loses its shining. The Vǫluspá names him the moon's devourer in a troll's skin. At Ragnarǫk the long pursuit is finished, and the calendar itself goes dark.

lore.culturalLegacy: Máni's deepest legacy is calendrical: every month and every Monday in the Germanic-speaking world is his, for Mōnandæg and its Norse kin are simply the moon's day, and the words descend from his name. In literature his clearest heir is Tolkien's Tilion, the Maia who steers the vessel of the moon across the sky — the personified moon-driver of the Eddas translated into a new mythology. Notably, Wagner left him out: the Ring runs on gold, fire, and Wotan's will, and the moon-driver never steps onto that stage, a measure of how thin Máni's high-cultural afterlife is beside Þórr's or Óðinn's. The chase around him fares better: the pursuing wolves Skǫll and Hati stalk recent retellings, including God of War Ragnarök (2022), where the stolen moon and its hunters drive a whole arc of the story. And the oldest survival is still the most democratic — the face and figures people point out to children in the full moon, which Snorri already explained by Bil and Hjúki eight centuries ago. In modern heathenry Máni is honored quietly, at the turning of the months he still measures.
lore.archaeology: Máni has no secure iconography: no picture stone, runestone, or amulet has been convincingly identified as his image, and his attestation is essentially textual. The Poetic Edda poems that name him — Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál, and Vǫluspá — survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), with Vǫluspá also in the Hauksbók; Snorri's account in Gylfaginning is transmitted by the main Snorra Edda manuscripts (GKS 2367 4to, Codex Upsaliensis, Codex Wormianus). The older strata of Scandinavian sky-religion are, however, material: the Bronze Age Trundholm sun chariot (c. 1400 BC) proves a native tradition of a heavenly body drawn by horse across the sky, and wheel- and disc-marked Gotland picture stones show the sun and moon as enduring cultic signs. The runic record knows the common noun máni and the month-names descended from it, but no runic inscription names the god directly.
lore.syncretism: Máni belongs to the common Germanic inheritance in which the moon is grammatically and mythologically masculine — Old English Mōna, Old High German Māno, Gothic mēna — a striking counterweight to the feminine moons of the classical world, Greek Selēnē and Latin Luna. The word itself runs deeper: Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁nōt- / *mḗh₁n̥s meant both 'moon' and 'month', the double sense Máni still carries in mánaðr, so that his personification is the personification of time-reckoning itself. The pairing of a moon-god with a sun-goddess, brother and sister, is the Germanic reversal of the Greek Selene and Helios pattern, though the daily celestial chase — light pursued by devourer — has echoes from the wolves of Ragnarǫk back to the eclipse-monsters of other traditions. The liveliest survival is folkloric: the Norse reading of the moon's markings as two children with a pail stands at the head of the whole northern 'man in the moon' tradition that later fills English ballads and nursery rhymes, and the tempting equation of Hjúki and Bil with Jack and Jill has been argued since the nineteenth century — as speculation, never as proof.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Old Norse form is máni, the ordinary common noun 'moon' borne as a theonym, attested throughout the manuscript tradition of both Eddas. In the earlier epigraphic medium, the Younger Futhark, the name would be rendered approximately ᛘᛅᚾᛁ — the long á written with the ᛅ (óss) rune, the Younger Futhark's sign for the a-family vowels, nasalized and long alike; no runic inscription preserves the theonym itself. In the normalized Old Norse spelling the acute on á marks vowel length, [ɑː], the same long vowel heard in 'father'. The PUNICODEX registrable form Máni preserves that acute as a Tier-1 restoration — the single distinctive feature the ASCII form Mani loses — carrying the long vowel that links the god directly to mánaðr, the month he measures.

entries.meaning: The Roman god of war and guardian of agriculture, father of Rōmulus and Rēmus; namesake of the planet Mars and the month of March (epigraphic MARS)
'The intoxicating one' (Old Irish medb, cognate with 'mead'), Queen of Connacht who drives the cattle raid of the Táin Bó Cúailnge.

pronunciation.approximation: 'MYETHV' — one short syllable: slender m, brief e, the d melted into the soft 'th' of 'this', finishing on 'v'. The modern Irish Meadhbh, anglicized Maeve, has collapsed the middle consonant and sounds simply 'mayv'.
pronunciation.note: Medb is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: normalized Old Irish writes the name in plain Latin letters — no diacritic and no distinctive letter for ASCII to lose. The temple form differs from the lowercase entry only by the capital; the queen's standing in the tradition is beside the point. The etymology, by contrast, is one of the most secure in the Celtic corpus: Old Irish medb, 'intoxicating, she who intoxicates', cognate with the noun medb, 'mead', continuing Proto-Indo-European *médhu, 'sweet drink'. The name is the sovereignty drink made personal.

domains.title: The Queen Who Chooses
domains.subtitle: The Pillow-Talk, the Bride-Gift Speech, and the Cattle Raid of Cooley
domains.lead: Medb of Crúachan is the ruling queen of Connacht and the driving will of the Táin Bó Cúailnge: the woman who audited fortunes with her husband in the night and invaded Ulster in the morning, who set the terms of her own marriages — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — and whom scholarship reads as Ireland's clearest survival of the sovereignty goddess, the land's own power to make and unmake kings.

cards.name: The Pillow-Talk
cards.desc: The night audit at Crúachan: Medb and Ailill count their wealth and find themselves equal in everything — save one bull.

cards.name: The Two Bulls
cards.desc: Finnbennach the White-Horned, who scorned a woman's keeping, and the Donn of Cúailnge — the balance of power on four legs.

cards.name: The Bride-Gift Terms
cards.desc: A husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear — the bride-gift no woman before her had asked of a man of Ireland.

cards.name: Crúachan and Oweynagat
cards.desc: Her royal rath at Rathcroghan, and beneath it the Cave of the Cats — the gate of the Otherworld in the medieval tales.

symbols.name: The marriage-bed of Crúachan

symbols.name: The two bulls
symbols.meaning: Finnbennach and the Donn of Cúailnge: wealth, prestige, and the one point on which two rulers cannot be equal

symbols.name: The bride-gift terms
symbols.meaning: No meanness, no jealousy, no fear: the queen's own charter, demanded where a dowry was expected

symbols.name: The march of the four provinces
